# Design: Self-service course reserves for the Thornbury University Library

Author: Wen Hartmann, Library Systems
Status: Draft for review
Last updated: 14 October

## 1. Background
Each term, lecturers send the library lists of readings that students need for a course. Today these arrive by email, and two staff members (Reserves Desk) check the catalogue by hand, scan chapters when copyright allows, and add the items to a shelf at the front desk or to the course page on the learning platform. In the last autumn term the desk handled 412 lists, with a median turnaround of 6.5 working days. Lecturers complain about the delay, and about not knowing what was approved.

## 2. Goals
- Lecturers submit a list through a web form and see the status of each item.
- Staff see a queue sorted by course start date.
- Approved scanned chapters appear on the learning platform automatically.
- Median turnaround falls to 3 working days.

## 3. Non-goals
Buying new books (stays with the acquisitions team), changing the catalogue software, and anything for postgraduate research collections.

## 4. Proposed approach
We build a small web application with its own database. Lecturers sign in through the university single sign-on. Each submitted item is matched against the catalogue by ISBN using the catalogue's search interface. If the match is found and a copy is on the shelf, the item is marked "available". If the item is a book chapter, a copyright check runs against a table of licence rules that staff maintain by hand, and the item goes either to "scan" or to "refuse". The application stores scanned files on the library's file server and publishes a link to the learning platform using its public interface once a day, at 02:00.

## 5. Data
Four tables: lecturers, courses, lists and items. An item has an ISBN, a chapter range, a state (submitted, matched, scan, refused, ready) and a staff note. Files are named by item identifier.

## 6. Risks and open questions
- The catalogue search interface allows 60 requests per minute. A long list has 80 items.
- The licence table has 140 rules and is owned by one person, who retires in March.
- Single sign-on returns a staff number, not an email address, so notifications need a second lookup.
- No decision yet on how long scanned files are kept after term ends.

## 7. Rollout
Pilot with the Faculty of Education (31 courses) in the spring term. Full launch for the following autumn term.

## 8. Effort
We estimate 55 working days for one developer, and 10 days of staff time for testing. Hosting is on the existing virtual machine, so no new costs are expected.

## 9. Success measures
We will compare the spring pilot with the same faculty's autumn figures: median turnaround, share of lists finished before the first week of term, and the number of emails the Reserves Desk receives per list. A short survey goes to every lecturer who submits through the form. We also count how many items are refused by the copyright check, and how many of those staff later overturn by hand, because a high number would mean the licence table is wrong.

# Product spec: Milk Round - delivery tracker for Dunmore Valley Farm Cooperative
Version 0.9, owner: Fenella Archer

## Overview
Dunmore Valley Cooperative has 38 member farms. Every day, one lorry collects milk from a fixed route of farms and brings it to the dairy. Milk Round is a simple app, used on a tablet in the lorry cab, that records each pickup and lets farmers see their own pickups on a web page.

## Users
- Driver: records pickups, one route per day.
- Farmer: views own pickups and monthly total.
- Office staff: edits routes, corrects errors, exports monthly totals.

## Feature 1: Recording a pickup
1.1 The driver chooses today's route from a list. A route has between 4 and 12 farms in a fixed order.
1.2 At each farm the driver enters the litres read from the tank gauge. The value must be a whole number between 50 and 12,000.
1.3 The driver enters the milk temperature in degrees Celsius with one decimal. If it is above 6.0, the app shows a red warning and the driver must choose a reason (warm weather, cooler fault, late pickup, other) before saving.
1.4 The app records the time automatically. The driver cannot edit it.
1.5 A pickup can be saved offline. When the tablet has a connection again, saved pickups are uploaded in the order they were made. If the same farm is picked up twice on the same day, the second one is marked "duplicate" and sent to office staff for review.
1.6 The driver can skip a farm with a reason (gate locked, no milk, farmer absent). A skipped farm records zero litres.

## Feature 2: Farmer web page
2.1 A farmer signs in with the email address and a six digit code sent by text message.
2.2 The page shows the last 30 days of pickups for that farm only: date, time, litres, temperature.
2.3 The monthly total in litres is shown at the top of the page and updated within five minutes of upload.
2.4 A farmer can flag a pickup as wrong. The flag adds a note and notifies office staff by email.

## Feature 3: Office tools
3.1 Staff can add, remove and reorder farms on a route. Changes apply from the next day.
3.2 Staff can correct a pickup. The original value is kept and shown in an audit list with the staff member's name.
3.3 Staff can export a CSV of all pickups for a month. Columns: farm id, date, time, litres, temperature, status.
3.4 Exports are available from the third day of the next month.

## Payments note

This is our quarterly review for the bike-share scheme, which I need to present to the council's transport committee on Thursday. Please write a section-by-section summary I can read out, and then a list of recommendations that follow from it, with the reasons. If any figure in the report looks inconsistent, say so.

# Quarterly Operations Review: Q3, Tamsworth Cycle Share
Prepared by: Operations team. Period: 1 July to 30 September.

## 1. Headline figures
The scheme ran 62 stations and 740 bikes throughout the quarter. Trips totalled 218,400, up 14 percent on Q2 (191,600) and 9 percent on Q3 last year. Average trip length was 17.2 minutes. Registered members rose from 9,850 to 11,020, and 38 percent of trips were by day-pass users. Revenue was 412,000 pounds against a budget of 395,000 pounds. Operating costs were 441,000 pounds, giving a gap of 29,000 pounds.

## 2. Availability
The target is that a rider finds a bike at a station at least 92 percent of the time. We reached 89.4 percent across the scheme. The shortfall was concentrated at nine stations near the university and the railway station, which were empty for more than 20 percent of weekday mornings. Stations on the east side, by contrast, were full (no free dock) 15 percent of weekday evenings. Rebalancing vans made 1,930 moves, but ran on two days each week with only one van because of a driver vacancy.

## 3. Fleet condition
Of 740 bikes, 96 were taken out for repair at some point, with a median repair time of 3.1 days. Brake faults were the most common cause (41 bikes), followed by chain and gear faults (27) and flat tyres (18). The remaining ten had a mix of lights, seats and locks. Seventeen bikes were reported stolen or lost, compared with eleven last quarter. The workshop has two mechanics; a third has been approved but not yet hired.

## 4. Customer feedback
The support line received 3,260 contacts, of which 61 percent were about a bike not unlocking or a charge that looked wrong. The average wait to reach an agent was 4 minutes 40 seconds, against a target of two minutes. The app rating on the store was 3.9 out of 5. The most common complaint in free-text reviews was finding stations empty at peak times.

## 5. Safety
There were 14 reported incidents involving riders, none serious. Nine happened on the Mill Road corridor, where the council's cycle lane works have narrowed the road since mid-August. No incident involved a faulty bike.

## 6. Weather and demand
August was warm and dry and produced 41 percent of the quarter's trips. September had eight rainy days, and trips on those days were about 35 percent lower than on dry weekdays.

## 7. Finance
The cost gap is mostly explained by repairs and replacement parts (62,000 pounds against 48,000 budgeted) and by overtime for the rebalancing team. Income from advertising on the bikes was 18,000 pounds, which was on budget.

## 8. Next quarter
Planned work includes adding six new stations around the hospital, hiring the third mechanic and a second van driver, and trialling a discount for riders who return bikes to emptier stations.

Can you review this schema and the queries below? I'd like a critique of the design, a list of the indexes you would add (and any you would drop) with the reasons, and a rewrite of each query that explains why yours is better. It is PostgreSQL 15 and the readings table grows by about 4 million rows a month.

```sql
CREATE TABLE station (
    station_id    serial PRIMARY KEY,
    name          text NOT NULL,
    latitude      numeric(8,5) NOT NULL,
    longitude     numeric(8,5) NOT NULL,
    elevation_m   integer,
    installed_on  date NOT NULL,
    region        text NOT NULL,
    active        boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT true
);

CREATE TABLE sensor (
    sensor_id     serial PRIMARY KEY,
    station_id    integer NOT NULL REFERENCES station(station_id),
    kind          text NOT NULL,   -- 'temperature', 'wind', 'rain', 'pressure'
    unit          text NOT NULL,
    calibrated_on date
);

CREATE TABLE reading (
    reading_id    bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
    sensor_id     integer NOT NULL REFERENCES sensor(sensor_id),
    taken_at      timestamp NOT NULL,
    value         numeric(10,3),
    quality_flag  text DEFAULT 'ok'
);

CREATE INDEX idx_reading_sensor ON reading (sensor_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_reading_taken ON reading (taken_at);
CREATE INDEX idx_reading_flag ON reading (quality_flag);
CREATE INDEX idx_sensor_station ON sensor (station_id);
```

Query 1: daily maximum temperature for one region last month, used on the public site.

```sql
SELECT st.name, date(r.taken_at) AS day, max(r.value) AS max_temp
FROM reading r
JOIN sensor s ON s.sensor_id = r.sensor_id
JOIN station st ON st.station_id = s.station_id
WHERE s.kind = 'temperature'
  AND st.region = 'Northern Uplands'
  AND to_char(r.taken_at, 'YYYY-MM') = '2026-09'
GROUP BY st.name, date(r.taken_at)
ORDER BY day, st.name;
```

Query 2: stations with no readings in the last 24 hours, used by the on-call engineer.

```sql
SELECT name
FROM station
WHERE active = true
  AND station_id NOT IN (
      SELECT s.station_id
      FROM sensor s
      JOIN reading r ON r.sensor_id = s.sensor_id
      WHERE r.taken_at > now() - interval '24 hours'
  );
```

Query 3: the latest reading for each sensor, which the dashboard runs every minute.

```sql
SELECT s.sensor_id, r.value, r.taken_at
FROM sensor s
JOIN reading r ON r.sensor_id = s.sensor_id
WHERE r.taken_at = (SELECT max(taken_at) FROM reading WHERE sensor_id = s.sensor_id);
```

Query 4: how many readings were flagged as suspect per station in the last week.

```sql
SELECT st.name, count(*)
FROM reading r, sensor s, station st
WHERE r.sensor_id = s.sensor_id
  AND s.station_id = st.station_id
  AND r.quality_flag <> 'ok'
  AND r.taken_at >= current_date - 7
GROUP BY st.name
ORDER BY count(*) DESC;
```

Query 1 takes about 40 seconds, query 3 about 12 seconds, and the other two are fine for now.

Here's the opening of a short story I'm writing. Please continue it at length, at least a thousand words, in the same voice and tense, keeping the dry humour. I want the festival to nearly fall apart on the opening night, and for Odile to end up solving it in a way that suits her character. Don't resolve the thing with her sister yet.

**The Last Reel**

The Marenholt Film Festival had an office, in the sense that a drawer is a room. It was one long space above a bakery, with a window that did not open and a radiator that did nothing else. From the first of September until the closing night in October, five people worked in it, and by the second week they had stopped apologising to one another for the smell of bread.

Odile Varga had been programme coordinator for six years. Her job was to know where every film was, on what format, in whose hands, and whether anyone had paid for the rights. She was good at it in the way some people are good at carrying trays: without looking, and with an expression that suggested the whole thing might still end badly.

On the Tuesday before opening night she arrived at seven and found the director already there, standing in front of the whiteboard with his coat on. Bram Lindqvist was a tall man who dressed as if he expected to be photographed and then forgot about it halfway through the day. Today his scarf was on inside out.

"Tell me the opening film is in the building," he said, without turning.

"It's in the building," Odile said. "It's in a box under my desk. The courier came yesterday at five and I signed for it myself."

"And it works."

"I haven't watched it. Nobody's watched it, Bram. It's a hard drive with a very long number on it."

He turned then, and she saw that he had not slept. Behind him the whiteboard was full of her handwriting: eleven days, forty-two features, nineteen shorts, a retrospective of a Norwegian animator who had specified, in writing, that he did not want to be introduced by anyone who had not seen all of his work. Next to the board hung a rota in four colours that Priya, the volunteer manager, had made and laminated. Odile found the lamination slightly insulting, as though the plan could not be trusted to survive on paper.

"The mayor is coming," Bram said. "The mayor, the minister's deputy, and apparently somebody's cousin who writes for a newspaper in the capital. They will all sit in the Grand Hall at seven tomorrow and watch a film that nobody has watched."

"It was selected by a jury."

"Juries lie," said Bram, with great tenderness. "That's why we have them."

Odile took her coat off and hung it on the back of the door, where it joined four other coats. The radiator ticked. Downstairs the baker was starting the first batch, and the smell came up through the floor like a rumour.

Her phone buzzed on the desk. It was a message from her sister Mira, the first in nine weeks. It said only: "I'm in town. Can we talk after the festival?" Odile turned the phone face down and said, to nobody, that she needed a projector.

"We have a projector," said Bram.

"We have three," Odile said. "And one of them is the right one."

I have been asked to referee this write-up for a transport research workshop. Please draft a detailed peer review: summary of the claims, strengths, major concerns about the method and the statistics, minor points, and a recommendation with the changes you would require.

**Does a fixed departure interval cut delays on short ferry routes? Evidence from the Skerrin Sound crossing**

**Abstract.** We study whether replacing a variable departure schedule with a fixed 30 minute interval reduced late arrivals on a 12 km crossing operated by one company with two vessels. Using 14 months of operating data, we find that the share of arrivals more than five minutes late fell from 18.6 percent to 11.2 percent, and conclude that fixed intervals reduce delay.

**Method.** Until 31 March the company ran a timetable of 22 daily sailings at uneven times, tuned to the school day and the lorry bookings. On 1 April it switched to a fixed departure every 30 minutes from 06:00 to 21:30, which gives 32 sailings. We compare the seven months before the change (1 September to 31 March, n = 4,380 sailings) with the seven months after (1 April to 31 October, n = 6,720 sailings). A sailing is late if it arrives more than five minutes after the published time. Data were taken from the vessels' logs. Sailings cancelled for weather were removed, which affected 61 sailings in the first period and 12 in the second. We tested the difference in the share of late arrivals with a two-proportion z-test and report a 95 percent confidence interval.

**Results.** In the first period 814 of 4,380 sailings were late (18.6 percent). In the second period 753 of 6,720 were late (11.2 percent). The difference is 7.4 percentage points (95 percent CI 6.1 to 8.7, p < 0.001). Mean delay among late sailings fell from 13.4 to 9.8 minutes. Table 1 shows the pattern by hour of day: the largest improvements are in the morning peak (07:00 to 09:00), where late arrivals fell from 27 percent to 12 percent. In the evening the shares were 15 percent before and 13 percent after.

**Table 1. Late arrivals (more than 5 minutes) by period of day**

| Period | Before (%) | After (%) |
|---|---|---|
| 06:00-09:00 | 27 | 12 |
| 09:00-15:00 | 14 | 10 |
| 15:00-19:00 | 17 | 11 |
| 19:00-22:00 | 15 | 13 |

**Discussion.** The results support the view that predictable intervals let crews load, refuel and turn the vessels around in a steady rhythm, and reduce the need to hold sailings for late lorries. The company also reports that its mean number of passengers per sailing fell from 61 to 44 after the change, which we take as a sign of spreading demand. We did not model weather, but we note that the winters in the first period were rougher than the summer in the second. We recommend that other operators of short crossings consider a fixed interval.

**Limitations.** This is a single route. The change was not randomised. The second period includes the summer, with longer daylight and lighter wind, while the first covers autumn and winter. A new harbour pilot joined the crew in May.

**Marlow Valley Water - Instalment and Leak Allowance Policy (version 3)**

**1. Who this applies to.** This policy applies to household customers with a metered supply. It does not apply to businesses, landlords with more than three properties, or customers whose account is in arrears for more than 90 days.

**2. Instalment plan.** A customer whose bill is more than 150 pounds may ask to pay it in up to twelve equal monthly instalments by direct debit. The company will add a plan fee of 1.5 percent of the outstanding balance, charged once at the start. The first instalment is taken within 14 days of the plan being agreed.

**3. Missed payments.** If a direct debit fails, the company will try again once, five days later. If the second attempt fails, the plan ends, the remaining balance becomes due in full within 14 days, and a late fee of 25 pounds is added. The company may then pass the account to a collection agency.

**4. Leak allowance.** If a customer finds and repairs a hidden leak on the supply pipe between the meter and the house, the company will, on request, charge for the extra water used at the normal sewerage-free rate, instead of the full rate, for up to 90 days before the repair. The customer must send a plumber's invoice within 60 days of the repair. The allowance can be granted only once in any five year period and does not cover leaks from taps, toilets, appliances or garden hoses.

**5. Estimated bills.** Where the company cannot read the meter, it may issue an estimated bill based on the average of the previous twelve months. Customers may submit their own reading at any time. When a true reading is later taken, any difference is added to or taken from the next bill.

**6. Changes to the policy.** The company may change this policy at any time by publishing the new version on its website. The new version applies to existing plans from 30 days after publication unless the customer cancels the plan in writing within that period.

**7. Disputes.** A customer who disagrees with a bill must tell the company within 12 months of the bill date. The company will reply within 20 working days. If the customer is not satisfied, they may contact the independent consumer ombudsman, whose decision binds the company but not the customer.

**8. Vulnerable customers.** A customer who tells the company that they, or someone in their home, depend on a reliable water supply for medical reasons, or who are over 75, may join the priority register. Registered customers receive a text message before planned interruptions and a bottled water delivery if the supply is off for more than six hours. The company reviews the register every two years and removes any entry if the customer does not reply to a letter within 28 days. The company is not liable for losses caused by an interruption that it has warned about at least 24 hours in advance, nor for any interruption caused by a burst main that is outside its reasonable control.

**9. Switching and moving house.** A customer who moves house must give the company at least five working days' notice and a final meter reading. Instalment plans do not transfer to the new address. Any remaining balance is due on the date of the final bill, and the plan fee is not refunded.

**10. Data.** The company stores meter readings, payment history and contact details for seven years after the account is closed and may share them with credit reference agencies and collection agencies.

These are my lecture notes from the rail operations module that I'm teaching to new control-room staff at a regional rail operator. Please turn them into a study guide with worked examples for each section, and then add a quiz of ten questions with full answers.

**Module 4: Timetable resilience and recovery from delay**

**4.1 Why timetables carry slack**
A timetable is a promise made under uncertainty. Three kinds of slack protect it. Running-time margin is extra time added to the minimum journey time between two stations, usually 3 to 7 percent. Dwell margin is extra time at a stop beyond what boarding needs. Buffer time is the gap between two trains that share a track section or a platform. Margin absorbs small random delays, and buffer stops one delay from spreading to the next train.

Example used in class: the minimum run from Aldport to Hexley is 38 minutes. With a 5 percent margin the timetable allows 40 minutes (38 x 1.05 = 39.9, rounded up).

**4.2 Primary and secondary delay**
A primary delay is caused by an event on a train itself, such as a door fault, a late crew or a trespasser. A secondary delay is caused by another train's delay: waiting for a platform, waiting for a connection, or being held behind a slow service. In our network about 60 percent of delay minutes are secondary, which is why buffer time matters more than most people expect.

**4.3 Headway and capacity**
Headway is the time between two trains passing the same point. On a line with three-minute signal blocks and a safety distance of two blocks, the minimum headway is about 6 minutes, giving a theoretical maximum of 10 trains per hour. In practice, planners keep to around 70 to 80 percent of that, so 7 or 8 trains per hour, to leave room for recovery. Worked example: 8 trains per hour means a train every 7.5 minutes on average, so a 4 minute delay to one train leaves 3.5 minutes of buffer before the next train is affected.

**4.4 Recovery tools available in the control room**
- Hold: keep a train at a station so a connection can be made. It helps passengers on that train and harms those behind.
- Short-turn: end a late train before its final stop and send the empty unit back early. It restores the following service but strands passengers at the end of the line.
- Skip-stop: leave out one or two stops. It saves about a minute per stop and is used rarely because of complaints.
- Swap: exchange the order of two trains when the slower one is ahead of a faster one.
- Cancel: the last resort. We must record a reason code within 15 minutes.

**4.5 Performance measures**
Punctuality on our network is the share of trains arriving within 3 minutes of the timetable at the final stop. Our target is 90 percent. A related measure counts cancellations: no more than 1.5 percent of planned trains. A line can pass one and fail the other, for instance by cancelling difficult trains to protect punctuality, so the regulator publishes both.

**4.6 Case from last winter**
On 14 January a points failure at Corrow closed one of two tracks for 70 minutes. Trains ran every 15 minutes before it. The controller chose to hold the 07:45 for a connection, which delayed 3 later services by 5 to 9 minutes in total.

# Design: Automated Dome Control and Observing Queue, Harrowfield Observatory

Author: M. Teasdale. Status: draft 3, for review. Last edited: 4 March.

## 1. Background

Harrowfield Observatory runs one 0.8 m reflector under a rotating dome, used by volunteers on about 90 nights a year and by two university groups on a booked basis. Today an observer drives everything by hand: opens the dome slit, points the telescope, starts the camera, and watches the sky for cloud. About 30 percent of booked nights are lost or shortened for lack of someone to close the dome. The board has approved a budget of 41,000 for automation.

## 2. Goals

1. Run a night's observing list without a person present, with the dome closing itself safely on bad weather or lost communication.
2. Let remote observers submit targets through a simple web form, with a queue that respects booked time.
3. Keep the telescope usable by hand at any moment, with a physical key switch that disables all automation.

## 3. Architecture

A small industrial controller (the "dome PLC") sits on the dome ring and owns the slit motor, the rotation motor, the azimuth encoder and the rain sensor. It enforces the safety rules in hardware logic and does not trust the computer. A rack PC in the control room (the "observatory host") runs the software described here and talks to the PLC over a serial line at 9600 baud using a simple text protocol.

The host runs four processes:

- **Scheduler**: reads the queue from a local database, picks the next target by priority and altitude, and issues commands.
- **Telescope driver**: slews the mount and reports pointing.
- **Dome service**: keeps the dome slit aligned with the telescope, polling position once per second and sending rotate commands to the PLC.
- **Weather guard**: reads the cloud sensor, rain sensor, wind meter and a humidity probe every 10 seconds and publishes a single status: SAFE, WARN or UNSAFE.

All four processes communicate through a message broker on the same machine. The queue database is SQLite on the host's local disk. The web form is served from the same host and is reachable from the internet.

## 4. Safety behaviour

When Weather guard publishes UNSAFE, the scheduler stops the current exposure, parks the telescope, and asks the dome service to close the slit. If the PLC does not confirm closure within four minutes, the host sends an email and a text message to the duty list.

The PLC also closes the slit by itself if the rain sensor is wet, or if it has received no heartbeat from the host for 90 seconds. This rule protects against a crashed host.

Opening the dome requires SAFE for ten continuous minutes, a sun altitude below minus 12 degrees, and the key switch in the AUTO position.

## 5. Queue and booking rules

Booked groups own fixed time windows. Inside a window, only that group's targets run. Outside all windows, volunteer targets run by priority, then submission time. A target is skipped if it is below 30 degrees altitude or within 20 degrees of the moon. Each target has an exposure plan of up to 40 frames.

## 6. Cost estimate

| Item | Cost |
|---|---|
| Dome PLC, wiring, enclosure | 6,800 |
| Slit motor and limit switches | 4,900 |
| Cloud, rain and wind sensors | 3,700 |
| Rack PC and uninterruptible power supply | 3,100 |
| Installation by electrician | 5,500 |
| Contingency (15 percent) | 3,500 |
| Total | 27,500 |

The remaining 13,500 is reserved for a second year.

## 7. Timeline

Procurement April to May, installation June, supervised trial nights July to August, first unattended nights in September.

## 8. Open questions

- Who is on the duty list overnight, and who answers if nobody replies?

Título: Programación participativa y fidelización de la audiencia en una radio comunitaria rural: un estudio cuasi-experimental

3. Método

3.1 Contexto. Radio Valle Claro es una emisora comunitaria sin ánimo de lucro que emite en frecuencia modulada desde un municipio de unos 6.400 habitantes y cubre otros once pueblos pequeños. Funciona con 38 voluntarios. Hasta 2022 la programación la decidía un comité de cuatro personas. En enero de 2023 se introdujo un sistema de programación participativa: cualquier vecino podía proponer un programa, y las propuestas se votaban en una asamblea trimestral abierta.

3.2 Diseño. Comparamos la audiencia y la participación antes y después del cambio. El periodo previo abarcó de enero a diciembre de 2022 y el periodo posterior de enero a diciembre de 2023. Como comparación utilizamos otra emisora comunitaria de una zona cercana, Radio Peña Alta, que no cambió su sistema de programación. Reconocemos que las emisoras no fueron asignadas al azar.

3.3 Medidas. La audiencia se midió con una encuesta telefónica realizada en febrero de cada año a una muestra de hogares seleccionados de la guía telefónica pública. Se preguntó si el encuestado había escuchado la emisora la semana anterior (variable de audiencia semanal) y cuántas horas aproximadas (variable de horas). La participación se midió con el número de llamadas y mensajes recibidos en antena, contados por los técnicos de la emisora.

3.4 Muestra. En 2022 respondieron 412 hogares de 1.050 contactados para Valle Claro (39 por ciento) y 190 de 520 para Peña Alta (37 por ciento). En 2023 respondieron 388 de 1.020 (38 por ciento) para Valle Claro y 171 de 500 (34 por ciento) para Peña Alta.

3.5 Análisis. Comparamos proporciones mediante pruebas de chi cuadrado y medias con pruebas t. Consideramos significativo un valor p inferior a 0,05.

4. Resultados

4.1 Audiencia semanal. En Valle Claro la proporción de hogares que escuchó la emisora pasó del 31,8 por ciento (131 de 412) en 2022 al 40,5 por ciento (157 de 388) en 2023 (chi cuadrado = 6,9; p = 0,009). En Peña Alta pasó del 28,4 por ciento (54 de 190) al 29,2 por ciento (50 de 171), una diferencia no significativa (p = 0,87). La diferencia de diferencias fue de 7,9 puntos porcentuales a favor de Valle Claro.

4.2 Horas de escucha. Entre los oyentes de Valle Claro, la media semanal subió de 5,1 horas (DE = 3,8) a 6,3 horas (DE = 4,2); t = 2,5, p = 0,013.

4.3 Participación en antena. Las llamadas y mensajes en Valle Claro aumentaron de 1.130 en 2022 a 2.460 en 2023, un incremento del 118 por ciento. En Peña Alta se registraron 640 y 610 respectivamente.

5. Discusión

Los resultados muestran que la programación participativa aumentó la audiencia, la escucha y la participación en Valle Claro. La ausencia de cambios en Peña Alta indica que el efecto se debe al nuevo sistema. Concluimos que las emisoras comunitarias deberían adoptar de forma generalizada este modelo para recuperar a su público. Entre las limitaciones señalamos el uso de una sola emisora de comparación y de una encuesta telefónica que puede no llegar a hogares sin teléfono fijo.

THE LAST DRAWER

1.

The workshop on Fennel Lane smelled of beeswax and cold iron, and had done so for sixty-one years. Ottoline Marsh unlocked it at ten to seven, as she had every working morning since she was seventeen, and stood a moment inside the door while her eyes got used to the grey. The long benches were where they always were. The band saw squatted under its dust sheet.

She put the kettle on the ring and counted the hours of work left in the book. It did not take long. A pair of oak benches for a village hall, due in March. A child's chair, with a carved fox on the back, paid for by a grandmother who kept telephoning to ask after the fox. And the walnut dresser for the Aldous house, which was the only large job and the one that kept her awake.

2.

Pell came in at half past seven, shaking rain from his coat like a dog. He was twenty-three and had been with the workshop for two years, and she had stopped expecting him to leave. He hung his coat on the nail by the glue pot and said, without being asked, that the dresser panels had finished drying overnight and looked all right.

"Looked all right," Ottoline said. "Or are all right?"

"Are, I think." He rubbed his nose. "There's a little bow in the left door. About the width of a coin. I wasn't going to say until you'd seen it."

She went to look. The panel lay on the bench where he had clamped it, its figure dark and rich, as handsome a piece of walnut as she had ever planed. And across it, if she held her eye low, ran a long shallow curve that no customer would forgive. She laid her palm against the wood as if it were a horse that had gone lame.

"Wet board," she said. "My fault. I should have sticked it longer."

"It was Mr. Dunmore's timber."

"It was my signature on the cheque." She straightened. "We will cut it again. Same figure, if there is any left."

There was not enough left. They both knew it, and neither said so.

3.

The post came at eleven. Between a seed catalogue and a flyer lay a thick cream envelope with the Aldous crest on the flap, and Ottoline carried it to the finishing room and opened it with a chisel. The letter was brief. Mrs. Aldous regretted that the family's plans had changed, that the new kitchen would be fitted by a firm in the city, and that she wished to know the sum owed for work already done so the matter could be closed. She hoped Ottoline would understand. She signed it with her first name, which she had never done before.

Ottoline read it twice and then put it in the drawer of the finishing bench, the last drawer, the one that stuck. It was where the firm's bad news had always gone.

She opened the drawer wider than it wanted and looked at what it already held. The tax notice. Two unanswered letters from the bank. A photograph of the workshop in 1964, the men in it long dead. She put the Aldous letter on top of the pile and shut the drawer with her hip.

Pell was in the doorway. He had the careful face of someone who has heard a page turn in another room.

"Tea's brewed," he said.

"Thank you."

"If it was bad, you needn't tell me." He looked at his boots. "But I'd rather know before the others do. Somebody ought to tell Dev and Marguerite before they hear it in the pub."

Ottoline looked at him for a long while. Out in the yard, the rain had slackened to a drip from the gutter, steady as a clock, and for the first time that year she thought she might not be able to keep the doors open past Easter.

"Come and sit down, Pell," she said. "I'll tell you now. Then we'll go and tell them together."

SPEC: Lane and Session Booking, Aldermoor Leisure Pools. Version 0.4

1. Purpose
Members and guests of Aldermoor Leisure Pools book swimming sessions online instead of queueing at the desk. Capacity limits keep lanes safe and let families plan.

2. Facilities
- Main pool: 6 lanes, 25 m. Each lane holds up to 8 swimmers per session.
- Learner pool: open water, holds up to 24 people per session, no lanes.
- Sessions run on the hour, 06:00 to 21:00, each 55 minutes long, with five minutes for turnover.

3. Users
- Member: has an account and a monthly pass. Can book up to 4 sessions in advance at any time and 1 per day on the same lane type.
- Guest: no account, pays per session by card. Can book up to 2 sessions, only within 3 days of today.
- Staff: can book on behalf of anyone and can cancel any booking.

4. Booking rules
4.1 Members can book from 14 days ahead. Guests from 3 days ahead.
4.2 A booking is for one person. A family needs one booking per person; the system offers "add another swimmer" which repeats the booking for up to 5 people in one purchase if capacity remains for all of them.
4.3 Under-8s must be accompanied. A booking for a child under 8 requires an adult booking in the same session; the system warns but does not block.
4.4 Lane types: Fast, Medium, Slow, Lessons. Lessons lanes are only bookable by members enrolled in a course.
4.5 Capacity is checked at the moment of payment confirmation. If capacity has run out, the user sees a message and nothing is charged.

5. Payment
5.1 Members: session is deducted from the monthly pass, which gives 12 sessions per calendar month. Unused sessions do not carry over.
5.2 Guests: price is 6.50 for adults, 4.00 for children (ages 3 to 15) and free for under-3s. Payment by card only.
5.3 If payment fails, held places are released after 10 minutes.

6. Cancellation and changes
6.1 Members may cancel up to 2 hours before the session; the session is returned to their pass.
6.2 Guests may cancel up to 24 hours before for a full refund. Later cancellations are not refunded.
6.3 If the pool closes (maintenance or an incident), all bookings are cancelled automatically and the user receives a refund or a returned session within 5 working days, plus an email and a text message.
6.4 A swimmer may be moved to another session at the same price if the new session has space. Moves to a different day are limited to 7 days ahead.

7. Check-in
7.1 Users show a QR code at the desk. Staff scan it with the handheld app.
7.2 Check-in opens 15 minutes before the session and closes 10 minutes after it starts. No-shows are logged. A member with 3 no-shows in a month cannot book same-day sessions for the next 30 days.

8. Notifications
Email confirmation immediately after booking. A reminder 24 hours before. A text message 2 hours before for members who opted in.

9. Accessibility
The booking pages must work with screen readers and support text up to 200 percent zoom. A "needs hoist access" checkbox reserves the hoist for the booked session. There is one hoist and it can serve one swimmer per session.

10. Performance
The availability page loads in under 2 seconds with 200 simultaneous users. The system must not allow two people to take the last place at the same time.

11. Out of scope
Party bookings, swimming club block bookings, and changing pass prices.

Please turn my lecture notes below into a study guide for the new trainees: a clear summary of each topic, at least four worked examples with the arithmetic shown, and a ten-question quiz with full answers. The trainees are school leavers with no baking experience, so explain anything that is not obvious.

LECTURE 3: DOUGH FORMULAS, BAKER'S PERCENTAGES AND SCALING (Hartwell & Daughters Bakeries, trainee programme)

1. Why we use baker's percentages
Every ingredient is written as a percentage of the flour weight. Flour is always 100 percent. This lets us compare recipes at a glance and scale any batch without recalculating by hand. Example formula for the standard white loaf: flour 100, water 65, salt 2, yeast 1, which totals 168 percent.

2. Calculating weights from a total
To find how much of each ingredient is needed for a total dough weight:
- total percentage = sum of all percentages
- flour weight = total dough weight x 100 / total percentage
- every other weight = flour weight x its percentage / 100
For the white loaf formula, 16.8 kg of dough needs 10 kg flour, 6.5 kg water, 200 g salt and 100 g yeast.

3. Hydration
Hydration is the water percentage. 65 percent is a firm sandwich-loaf dough. Our sourdough runs at 78 percent and is stickier, so it needs a longer rest and gentle handling. Higher hydration gives a more open crumb but a flatter loaf if shaped poorly.

4. Pre-ferments
We use a poolish (equal weights of flour and water, plus a pinch of yeast) for baguettes. The flour and water in the poolish count toward the final formula. If the final dough uses 10 kg of total flour and 30 percent of it is pre-fermented as poolish, the poolish contains 3 kg flour and 3 kg water. The remaining flour is 7 kg. Water to be added at mixing is the total water minus 3 kg.

5. Dough temperature
Target dough temperature after mixing is 24 C. We calculate the water temperature using the formula: water temperature = (desired dough temperature x 3) minus (flour temperature + room temperature + friction factor). The friction factor for our spiral mixers is 12 C. Example: flour 20 C, room 26 C, desired dough 24 C. Water = 72 minus (20 + 26 + 12) = 14 C. In summer we use ice for part of the water. Weigh the ice as water.

6. Scaling and yield
After mixing, dough loses about 1.5 percent of its weight during fermentation and 12 percent as moisture during baking. To get 600 g loaves, scale the raw dough at 600 divided by 0.88, which is about 682 g. Forgetting baking loss is the most common reason new trainees produce underweight bread, which breaks the labelling rules.

7. Costing
Flour costs 0.72 per kg, yeast 4.80 per kg, salt 0.40 per kg. Water is ignored. The ingredient cost of one 16.8 kg batch of white dough is flour 7.20, yeast 0.48, salt 0.08, total 7.76. Divided by 24 loaves, that is about 0.32 per loaf.

8. Common mistakes
- Using volume (cups) rather than weight.
- Forgetting to subtract pre-ferment flour and water from the final mix.
- Adding salt directly onto yeast. Salt slows the yeast, so keep them apart in the bowl until mixing begins.
- Not checking dough temperature with a probe.

Homework for next week: Scale the sourdough formula (flour 100, water 78, salt 2, starter 20 percent of flour, with the starter at 100 percent hydration) to make 40 kg of dough. Remember to include the starter's flour and water in the totals. Bring your working to the practical session on Thursday.

Here is our incident report from the January network outage. Could you summarise it section by section for the executive committee, then list your recommendations, and flag anything in the report you think is weak, missing or inconsistent? Keep the summary clear enough for people who are not engineers.

INCIDENT REPORT IR-2025-003: Loss of heat supply to the Northgate network, 14 to 15 January
Prepared by: Operations Engineering, Calderbrook District Heat Ltd. Reviewed by: Head of Operations. Status: final.

1. Executive summary
Between 03:40 on 14 January and 11:15 on 15 January, about 2,300 homes and 14 commercial buildings on the Northgate network received reduced or no heat. Outside temperatures fell to minus 9 C. The cause was a failure of the primary circulation pump P2 at the Northgate energy centre, followed by a failure of the automatic switch to standby pump P3. Total customer-hours without adequate heat were roughly 41,000.

2. Timeline
- 03:40: Alarm for low differential pressure. The on-call operator acknowledged it at 03:52.
- 04:05: Operator found P2 had tripped on motor overheating and tried to start P3 manually; P3 would not start because its breaker was open following maintenance on 9 January.
- 04:30: Duty engineer called in. Breaker closed at 05:10 after it was confirmed safe.
- 05:25: P3 running, but at reduced speed because of a faulty frequency drive setting. Supply temperature recovered only to 61 C against a target of 85 C.
- 08:00: Customer calls reached 340 per hour. The call centre had no scripted message.
- 09:30: Contractor attended to correct the drive settings. Full flow was restored for most streets by 14:30.
- 15 January, 06:00: A second, smaller dip in pressure followed when valves in the Eastfield branch were opened too quickly during refilling. Eastfield streets (about 600 homes) were not fully warm until 11:15.

3. Root causes
(a) The standby pump breaker was left open after maintenance and no checklist step required it to be closed and signed off. (b) The automatic changeover had been disabled for testing in November and was not re-enabled. (c) The frequency drive settings on P3 had never been tested under winter load. (d) Alarms went to a single on-call phone with no escalation.

4. Impact
The company received 1,420 complaints and 96 requests for compensation. Under our customer charter, households that lose heat for more than 24 hours receive 60; a further 38 vulnerable households (elderly, ill or with infants) were offered portable electric heaters. Direct costs are estimated at 118,000, made up of compensation 61,000, extra staff and contractors 32,000, heaters 9,000 and repair 16,000. Reputational effects have not been quantified.

5. Actions already taken
The breaker was locked closed and a new sign-off step added to the maintenance checklist. The changeover logic was restored and tested on 17 January. The frequency drive on P3 was reprogrammed. A second on-call phone was added.

6. Open items
- The cause of P2's overheating is not yet known; the motor has been sent to the manufacturer.
- A review of the call centre scripts is pending.
- The regulator was told of the incident on 16 January, 36 hours after the 24-hour deadline.
- Winter readiness testing for all three energy centres has not been scheduled.

7. Lessons learned
Maintenance and operations did not share a view of equipment status. Customers were not informed in time. Staff worked well under pressure but a number of procedures were found to be out of date.

Appendix: Pump data. P2: installed 2011, last overhaul 2019. P3: installed 2016, never overhauled. P1: removed 2022, not replaced.

I'd like a proper critique of this design from someone who has built this kind of thing. Please tell me what is weak or risky, give two or three alternative approaches with their trade-offs, and then lay out an implementation plan with milestones for a team of two part-time volunteers. We have about 400 members and almost no budget.

Design: Hive Records and Disease Alert System, Wessex Vale Beekeepers' Association
Author: Gareth Pomeroy (volunteer). Version 2.

1. Problem

Our 400 members keep around 1,900 colonies in apiaries spread across three counties. Each member inspects hives through the season and keeps notes on paper or in their own spreadsheets. When foulbrood or a Varroa surge appears, the regional bee inspector contacts us and we phone round by hand. In last year's American foulbrood case it took four days to warn members within five kilometres, and two of them had moved equipment in the meantime. We want a shared system that records inspections and warns nearby members quickly.

2. Requirements

- Members can record an inspection in under a minute, from a phone, in a field with poor signal.
- The association can see aggregate data: Varroa counts by month, winter losses, swarm reports.
- When a notifiable disease is confirmed, the system alerts every member with an apiary within a chosen radius, by text and email, within an hour.
- Members control what others see. Exact apiary locations are private by default; only distance-based alerts are shared.
- Cost under 30 a month, run by volunteers.

3. Proposed solution

A single web application written in a popular framework, with a PostgreSQL database hosted on a small rented virtual server. The server also sends the alerts through a commercial text message provider, charged per message. Members log in with an email address and a password.

The mobile experience is a responsive web page. To handle poor signal, the page keeps inspection forms in the browser's local storage and sends them when a connection returns.

Data model: a member has apiaries (with latitude and longitude, rounded to 100 m); an apiary has colonies; a colony has inspections (date, queen seen, brood pattern, Varroa count per 24 hours, temperament, notes, treatment given). Disease reports carry a type, a date, and the location of the confirmed case supplied by the inspector.

4. Alert logic

When the secretary confirms a case, she enters a location and a radius (default 5 km). The server selects all apiaries within the radius using straight-line distance computed in application code and sends a text message to each affected member. A message is retried once after ten minutes if the provider reports a failure. Alert history is stored so members can see when they were warned.

5. Privacy

Exact locations are visible only to the member and to the two administrators. Other members see only aggregates by area of at least 20 apiaries. Data is deleted on request. Backups are taken nightly onto the same server and kept for seven days.

6. Operations

The two volunteers will deploy by hand over SSH. Updates will be applied when needed. Monitoring consists of the hosting provider's uptime email. There is no test server; we will test on the live system in winter, when members are not inspecting.

7. Risks identified so far

- Members who are not comfortable with phones.
- Volunteer turnover: the author may move away next year.
- Text message cost if there are many alerts.

8. Rough plan

Build the data model in March, forms in April, alerts in May, invite 30 pilot members in June, full launch before the next season.

Peux-tu rédiger une évaluation détaillée de ce passage, comme le ferait un relecteur d'une revue d'urbanisme ? Je voudrais les forces, les faiblesses de la méthode, les problèmes d'interprétation des résultats, les analyses manquantes et une recommandation finale argumentée.

Titre : L'effet des tontes différées sur la biodiversité florale et la perception des habitants dans les parcs urbains

2. Méthode

2.1 Sites. L'étude a été menée en 2023 dans douze parcs de la ville de Saint-Orval (190 000 habitants), d'une surface comprise entre 0,8 et 6 hectares. Dans chaque parc, nous avons choisi une pelouse de 1 000 m² environ. Six pelouses ont été tondues toutes les deux semaines (régime « classique ») et six ont été tondues une seule fois, à la mi-juillet (régime « différé »). L'attribution a été décidée par le service des espaces verts, qui a réservé le régime différé aux parcs où les jardiniers étaient volontaires.

2.2 Relevés floraux. Entre mai et septembre, un botaniste a réalisé quatre relevés par pelouse, dans cinq quadrats de 1 m² placés au hasard. Pour chaque quadrat, il a compté le nombre d'espèces de plantes à fleurs en fleur. Nous avons ensuite calculé la richesse moyenne par pelouse et par date.

2.3 Enquête auprès des habitants. En juillet, un questionnaire a été distribué à l'entrée de chaque parc, un samedi matin. Les visiteurs ont évalué sur une échelle de 1 à 5 l'aspect du parc (« Ce parc vous paraît-il bien entretenu ? »). Au total, 482 personnes ont répondu : 231 dans les parcs classiques et 251 dans les parcs différés. Nous n'avons pas relevé l'âge ni le quartier des répondants.

2.4 Analyses. Nous avons comparé la richesse florale entre les deux régimes avec un test t de Student sur les moyennes par pelouse (n = 6 par groupe). Les notes d'aspect ont été comparées par un test de Mann-Whitney sur l'ensemble des réponses individuelles. Le seuil de signification est fixé à 0,05.

3. Résultats

3.1 Richesse florale. La richesse moyenne en juillet était de 14,2 espèces par quadrat (écart-type 2,9) dans les pelouses différées contre 5,8 (écart-type 1,7) dans les pelouses classiques, soit une différence de 8,4 espèces (t = 6,0 ; p < 0,001). En septembre, après la tonte des pelouses différées, les moyennes étaient de 7,1 et de 5,2 espèces (p = 0,09).

3.2 Perception. La note moyenne d'aspect était de 3,2 dans les parcs différés (n = 251) et de 3,9 dans les parcs classiques (n = 231), ce qui est significatif (p < 0,001). Dans les commentaires libres, 38 personnes ont jugé les pelouses différées « abandonnées » ; 22 ont écrit qu'elles aimaient voir « de vraies fleurs ».

3.3 Coûts. Les équipes ont consacré en moyenne 41 heures de travail par pelouse classique pendant la saison et 9 heures par pelouse différée. Nous n'avons pas mesuré les coûts de ramassage du foin.

4. Discussion

Nos résultats démontrent que la tonte différée multiplie par deux et demi la richesse florale des pelouses urbaines et qu'elle réduit sensiblement les coûts d'entretien. Toutefois, la perception négative des habitants constitue un obstacle ; nous recommandons donc de généraliser la tonte différée à l'ensemble des parcs de la ville, accompagnée d'une campagne d'information. Les limites de l'étude tiennent à la durée d'une seule saison.

I'd like you to carry on this story for me, at length, in the same dry and affectionate voice. Write the next two or three scenes. In them the night shift should discover what is wrong with the big press, and Wilhelmina should have to decide whether to tell her brother. Keep the tone and the details consistent with what I've written.

THE NIGHT SHIFT AT MERRIWETHER AND SONS

I.

Merriwether and Sons, Printers, had been printing the Tarnbury Gazette since before the railway came, and the men who ran the big press believed that the paper would not appear if they stopped believing in it. This was a harmless superstition, and like most harmless superstitions it cost the firm a fortune in candles, lucky bolts and tea.

Wilhelmina Merriwether had inherited the business at thirty-four, together with her brother Augustin, who had inherited the debts. They shared the office on the first floor above the composing room. She kept the books and he kept an optimistic mood, and between them they had maintained the arrangement for eleven years without either of them mentioning which of the two jobs was harder.

On the night this story begins, a Thursday in late November, the Gazette was due to carry the full report of the county agricultural show, the results of the council by-election and a notice of sale for the Fox and Compass, which the brewery had finally given up trying to run. It was a thick issue. It needed the big press, which was called Hortensia, for reasons nobody remembered.

II.

At ten past eleven Hortensia coughed, shuddered, and produced a sheet in which every letter e had been replaced by a smudge.

Old Barnaby Tuck, the head pressman, was the first to reach it. He had spent forty-one years with the machine and spoke to it in a low, reasonable voice, the way a man speaks to a horse that has stopped at a gate. He stopped the rollers, wiped his hands on a rag, and took off his cap, which was how the other men knew it was serious.

"Not the ink," he said.

"Not the paper," said Dorrit, the apprentice, who was seventeen and had learned from Barnaby that you could eliminate a fault by naming everything else.

"Not the plates. I set them myself, Thursday afternoon, with the whole shop watching." Barnaby bent to look under the cylinder with a lantern. He stayed there a long time. When he straightened his face had gone the colour of putty.

"It is the e," he said, quietly. "The letter itself. Somebody has been at the type."

They carried the forme to the stone and looked at it under the lamp. Every lower-case e in the whole issue, two thousand and some, had been filed down by a hair, so slightly that no eye would find it until the ink went on. It was done carefully, by someone who knew the trade, and who had known exactly which case to open.

Dorrit whistled. Barnaby told him not to.

III.

Wilhelmina was asleep in the office armchair, in her coat, when Dorrit woke her. She listened to the whole account without a word, then asked what time the first newsagent's van left.

"Five," said Barnaby.

"Then we have six hours, a spare font in the cupboard, and an apprentice who whistles." She rubbed her eyes. "Barnaby, who has the key to the type cupboard?"

He did not answer at once, and she understood from the silence that the answer was a short list, and that her brother's name was on it.

PRODUCT SPEC: Berth Booking and Landing Declarations (v1.2), Port of Selmouth Harbour Authority

1. Overview
Fishing skippers use a web page and a mobile app to reserve a berth, declare landings and pay harbour dues. Harbour staff use a back-office screen to approve and audit declarations.

2. Berths
2.1 The harbour has 46 berths in three zones: A (large trawlers, 14 berths, up to 24 m), B (medium boats, 20 berths, up to 15 m) and C (small boats, 12 berths, up to 9 m).
2.2 A vessel may use a berth in its own zone or in a larger zone, never a smaller one.
2.3 Reservations run for a minimum of 12 hours and a maximum of 14 days. Reservations may not overlap on the same berth.
2.4 Visiting vessels (registered in another harbour) may stay at most 7 nights in any 30 days.

3. Accounts
3.1 A skipper registers with a vessel registration number, a vessel length and an email address. The registration number must match the national register through a lookup service. If the lookup service is down, the registration is held as "pending" and the skipper can look but not book.
3.2 One account can hold up to 3 vessels.

4. Landing declarations
4.1 A declaration must be submitted within 2 hours of landing and always before the catch leaves the harbour area.
4.2 It lists species, weight in kilograms (to one decimal place) and the fishing area code. Species come from a fixed list of 60 codes.
4.3 The weight total per declaration must not exceed the vessel's quota for the species. Quotas are loaded each Monday from a spreadsheet by an administrator. If a declaration would exceed a quota, it is accepted but flagged for inspection, and the skipper sees a warning.
4.4 Declarations cannot be edited after submission. A correction is made by a new declaration marked "amendment" that links to the original and needs staff approval.

5. Dues and payment
5.1 Berth dues are 1.20 per metre of vessel length per night, plus 8 percent of the first sale value for catches of shellfish landed on site. Dues are calculated at the end of the stay.
5.2 Payment is by card within 14 days. Overdue accounts cannot make new reservations.
5.3 A vessel that departs earlier than reserved is charged for the reserved nights unless it cancels at least 24 hours before.

6. Notifications
Skippers receive an email when a reservation is confirmed, 24 hours before arrival, and when a declaration is flagged. Weather warnings for gale force 8 or above are sent to all vessels with a current reservation.

7. Roles
Skipper, Harbour clerk (can approve amendments and see all declarations), Inspector (read-only, can export declarations as CSV) and Administrator (quota upload, berth management).

8. Non-functional
Pages load in under 3 seconds on a mobile connection. The mobile app must work offline for declarations and send them when a signal returns. All times are shown in local time with daylight saving handled correctly.

Here are my lecture notes from the week on bicycle frame design in our apprenticeship course at the factory. Please turn them into a study guide for the new apprentices, with worked examples that show the calculations step by step, and finish with a quiz of about ten questions and a full answer key.

# Week 6: Frame geometry and tube selection

Lecturer: Mr. Tomasz Weller, Ostfeld Cycle Works, apprentice programme, group B

## 1. Why geometry matters

A frame is a set of tubes joined at fixed angles. The angles and lengths decide how the bicycle handles, how comfortable it is, and how the rider's weight is carried. Three numbers are measured first on every new design: the seat tube angle, the head tube angle, and the wheelbase.

- Seat tube angle: usually between 72 and 74 degrees for a touring frame. A steeper angle moves the rider forward over the pedals.
- Head tube angle: usually 70 to 72 degrees. A slacker angle (smaller number) makes steering calmer but slower.
- Wheelbase: the distance between the two wheel axles. Longer is more stable, shorter is more nimble.

## 2. Trail

Trail is the distance on the ground between the point where the steering axis meets the road and the point where the front tyre touches the road. It is calculated as:

trail = (R * cos(h) - offset) / sin(h)

where R is the wheel radius including the tyre, h is the head tube angle measured from horizontal, and offset is the fork rake. Typical trail for our city bike is 55 to 65 mm.

Example from class: R = 340 mm, h = 71 degrees, offset = 45 mm. Then cos(71) is about 0.326 and sin(71) is about 0.946. R * cos(h) = 110.8 mm. Subtract the offset: 65.8 mm. Divide by 0.946: trail is about 69.6 mm. Mr. Weller said this is a little high and would feel stable but heavy at low speed. Using a 50 mm fork rake instead gives about 64 mm.

## 3. Tube selection

We use three tube materials at Ostfeld: plain carbon steel for the budget line, chromium-molybdenum steel for the touring line, and 6061 aluminium for the sport line.

| Material | Density (g/cm3) | Yield strength (MPa) | Typical wall (mm) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Plain carbon steel | 7.85 | 350 | 1.2 |
| Chromium-molybdenum | 7.85 | 650 | 0.9 |
| Aluminium 6061-T6 | 2.70 | 270 | 1.6 |

The point made in class: chromium-molybdenum can use a thinner wall for the same strength, so the frame is lighter even though the metal is just as dense. Aluminium is the lightest by volume but needs thicker walls and larger diameters, which makes the frame stiffer and less forgiving.

Worked example: a down tube 600 mm long, outside diameter 31.8 mm. With a 1.2 mm wall the cross-section area is pi * (15.9^2 - 14.7^2) = about 115 mm2, so the tube volume is about 69,200 mm3, or 69.2 cm3, and the mass of plain steel is 69.2 * 7.85 = 543 g. With a 0.9 mm wall in the chromium-molybdenum steel, the area is pi * (15.9^2 - 15.0^2) = about 87.5 mm2, volume 52.4 cm3 and mass 411 g. The saving is 132 g on one tube.

## 4. Homework

Calculate trail for the new commuter prototype (R = 350 mm, head angle 70.5 degrees, offset 48 mm) and the mass of its top tube in aluminium (length 540 mm, outside diameter 34.9 mm, wall 1.6 mm).

Please summarise this quarterly operations report for the plant board, section by section, and finish with your recommendations. I would like the summary to flag anything the board has to decide and anything that looks like a risk to our discharge permit.

**Hollowbrook Wastewater Treatment Plant: Operations Report, Third Quarter**
Prepared by: Marit Sandvik, Plant Manager
Distribution: Board of the Hollowbrook Water Authority

**1. Overview**

The plant treated an average of 18,400 cubic metres per day during the quarter, against a design capacity of 24,000. The wettest month was August, with a peak day of 31,200 cubic metres on 14 August after a storm that delivered 52 mm of rain in nine hours. On that day, the storm tank filled to 94% and released 1,900 cubic metres of screened overflow to the Hollow River for roughly two hours. The release was reported to the regulator within the required 24 hours.

**2. Effluent quality**

All monthly averages met the permit limits. The table shows the quarter's results.

| Parameter | Permit limit | July | August | September |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| BOD (mg/l) | 15 | 6.1 | 8.4 | 5.7 |
| Total suspended solids (mg/l) | 25 | 11 | 17 | 10 |
| Ammonia (mg/l) | 4 | 1.2 | 2.9 | 1.0 |
| Total phosphorus (mg/l) | 1.0 | 0.62 | 0.71 | 0.58 |

Ammonia in August reached 2.9 mg/l, the highest value in three years. Mr. Okonkwo, the process engineer, attributes this to cold, diluted inflow after the storm and to the loss of one of the four aeration blowers for eleven days.

**3. Equipment and maintenance**

Blower 3 failed on 6 August when a bearing seized. The replacement part took nine days to arrive because the supplier had no stock, and the repair cost 14,700 euros. Blower 1 has now run 41,000 hours and its vibration readings are rising. The inlet screen was cleared of rags 23 times in the quarter, compared with 14 in the second quarter, and operators believe the increase comes from wet wipes in the network. The sludge dewatering press ran for 61% of planned hours; the rest was lost to two belt replacements.

**4. Sludge and energy**

The plant produced 1,260 tonnes of dewatered sludge, all of which went to the agricultural contractor under the existing agreement. The contractor warned that from next spring it can only accept sludge below a certain heavy metal threshold and asked us to supply new test results by December. Energy use was 0.41 kWh per cubic metre, a 4% rise on last quarter, mostly because the blowers ran longer in August. The new solar array on the sludge building supplied 11% of the plant's electricity.

**5. Safety and staffing**

There were no lost-time injuries. Two near misses were recorded: a hose burst in the chemical store, and a lone worker who entered the inlet chamber without the gas monitor. Both led to retraining. Two of the fourteen operators will retire by March, and one position has been open since June without a suitable applicant.

**6. Budget**

Spending was 2.31 million euros against a plan of 2.18 million. The overspend of 130,000 euros is explained by the blower repair, storm-related overtime of 21,000 euros and higher electricity prices. Income from the authority's tariff matched the plan.

**7. Proposed decisions**

The board is asked to approve a new spare blower at 38,000 euros, a two-year study of the inlet network at 55,000 euros, and an extra operator trainee post.

**Staybright kickoff: "Instant Confirm" project**
Date: Tuesday 6 October, 14:00 to 15:30

**Background**

Today, when a guest books a room through Staybright, the booking is only "requested" until the hotel confirms it by email or by phone. The median confirmation time is 3 hours 40 minutes, and 17% of requests are never confirmed, which is our biggest complaint category. Lena wants "Instant Confirm" live for at least 40 partner hotels before the winter ski season starts on 5 December. Currently 212 hotels are on the platform, but only 31 have a live connection to a property management system.

**Discussion**

Omar said the technical idea is to read availability and rates directly from each hotel's property management system every five minutes, and to write the booking back as soon as the guest pays. Three of the systems used by our hotels have a usable interface, and two of them are used by about 70% of the connected hotels. Jonas thinks the first connector can be ready in four weeks if nobody else uses his time, but he is also the only person who knows the payment module, and the payment provider's new rules come into force on 1 November. Omar said he would borrow a contractor for six weeks, budget up to 18,000 euros, but has not found anyone yet.

Priya said the biggest risk is not technical. Many hotel owners do not want to give us write access. She suggested a pilot with 8 friendly hotels in the mountains, using a simple contract addendum that her team can write by the end of next week. This is the database for our taxi dispatch centre (PostgreSQL 15). The dashboard has become slow since we passed about 4 million trips. Please review the design, suggest indexes, and rewrite the three queries with an explanation of why each rewrite is better. Also point out any design problems that will hurt us later.

```sql
CREATE TABLE drivers (
    id            serial PRIMARY KEY,
    full_name     text NOT NULL,
    phone         text,
    licence_no    text,
    active        boolean DEFAULT true,
    hired_on      date
);

CREATE TABLE vehicles (
    id            serial PRIMARY KEY,
    plate         text NOT NULL,
    seats         int,
    fuel_type     text,
    in_service    boolean DEFAULT true
);

CREATE TABLE trips (
    id            bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
    driver_id     int REFERENCES drivers(id),
    vehicle_id    int REFERENCES vehicles(id),
    pickup_time   timestamp,
    dropoff_time  timestamp,
    pickup_zone   text,
    dropoff_zone  text,
    fare_cents    int,
    status        text,
    payment_type  text,
    customer_phone text
);

CREATE TABLE complaints (
    id            serial PRIMARY KEY,
    trip_id       bigint,
    created_at    timestamp DEFAULT now(),
    category      text,
    resolved      boolean DEFAULT false
);
```

Query 1: revenue per driver for last month, shown on the manager's page.

```sql
SELECT d.full_name, SUM(t.fare_cents) / 100.0 AS revenue
FROM drivers d, trips t
WHERE d.id = t.driver_id
  AND to_char(t.pickup_time, 'YYYY-MM') = to_char(now() - interval '1 month', 'YYYY-MM')
  AND t.status = 'completed'
GROUP BY d.full_name
ORDER BY revenue DESC;
```

Query 2: the dispatcher's list of drivers who have not had a trip in the last two hours, so they can be called.

```sql
SELECT d.id, d.full_name, d.phone
FROM drivers d
WHERE d.active = true
  AND d.id NOT IN (
      SELECT driver_id FROM trips WHERE pickup_time > now() - interval '2 hours'
  );
```

Query 3: busiest pickup zones by hour of the day, plus the number of complaints on those trips.

```sql
SELECT t.pickup_zone,
       extract(hour from t.pickup_time) AS hr,
       count(*) AS trips,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM complaints c WHERE c.trip_id IN
           (SELECT id FROM trips t2 WHERE t2.pickup_zone = t.pickup_zone
              AND extract(hour from t2.pickup_time) = extract(hour from t.pickup_time))) AS complaints
FROM trips t
GROUP BY t.pickup_zone, extract(hour from t.pickup_time)
ORDER BY trips DESC
LIMIT 20;
```

More facts: we add about 9,000 trips per day, and the only indexes are the primary keys. Trips are never updated after they are finished, apart from adding a complaint. Dispatchers usually look at the last 24 hours; managers look at whole months. Some drivers share names, and a few trips have a null driver_id because they were dispatched by phone and entered afterwards. The data protection officer has asked us to delete customer phone numbers after 90 days.

Please critique it honestly, suggest at least two alternative approaches with their trade-offs, and give me an implementation plan with phases and milestones. I am the only developer, plus a few volunteers who help part-time, so be realistic.

# Design: Pickup Slot Booking for Partner Charities

Author: Gwen Takahashi
Status: Draft v2
Last updated: 12 October

## 1. Problem

Riverside Food Bank collects surplus food from supermarkets and distributes it to about 85 partner charities (soup kitchens, shelters, community fridges). Charities collect on Tuesdays and Fridays from 9:00 to 14:00. At present, they phone or text the warehouse manager to say when they are coming. In busy weeks there are 40 or more pickups in one morning, but the loading dock fits only two vans at once. Queues of up to 50 minutes form, volunteers get frustrated, and chilled goods wait outside. Twice in September, a charity arrived and found that its allocation had been given to someone else because two people had promised the same slot.

## 2. Goals

- Let each charity book a 20-minute pickup slot online or by text message.
- Keep at most two vans at the dock at any time.
- Show the warehouse team a clear list of who comes when and what they are collecting.
- Work on cheap phones with poor connections.

## 3. Non-goals

- Routing or delivery to charities.
- Stock management. The warehouse already uses a separate spreadsheet.

## 4. Proposed solution

A small web application with a PostgreSQL database, hosted on a single virtual server that costs 14 euros per month. Each charity gets a login link sent by email. A booking page shows the open slots for the next two Tuesdays and Fridays. A charity picks a slot and enters how many pallets it expects to collect (maximum six). The system refuses a booking if two slots already overlap in that time window.

Text messages are handled by an SMS provider: a charity can send "BOOK TUE 10:20" to a short number and gets a confirmation. A reminder goes out the evening before.

## 5. Data model

- charity (id, name, contact_phone, contact_email, status)
- slot (id, date, start_time, capacity)
- booking (id, charity_id, slot_id, pallets, created_at, cancelled_at)

Capacity is set to 2 for every slot. Booking creation does a count query and inserts if the count is below capacity.

## 6. Risks and open questions

- Charities with no phone data, or no internet, may be excluded. About 10 of the 85 only use a landline.
- Priority for charities serving children has not been decided.
- We have not decided what happens when a van is late. The current idea is that the slot is lost after 15 minutes.
- No plan for backups yet.

## 7. Security and privacy

Charities log in with an emailed link that expires after 24 hours. The system stores contact names, phone numbers and emails of volunteers at the charities, but nothing about the people they feed. Warehouse staff use one shared account on the dock tablet to see the daily list. Logs are kept for 30 days.

## 8. Timeline

Four weeks of development, two weeks of testing with five charities, then launch for all.
