Our cement plant has just put this contractor safety policy in front of the small companies who work on site, and several of them asked me what it really means. Please explain it clause by clause in plain language, and then list the risks and obligations a small contractor should watch out for.

**Stonebridge Cement Works: Contractor Safety and Site Access Policy (version 3.1)**

**1. Scope.** This policy applies to every contractor, subcontractor and visitor who enters the Stonebridge Cement Works ("the Site") to perform work, including their employees, agents and any person acting under their direction.

**2. Induction.** No person may enter any operational area of the Site until that person has completed the Company's safety induction, which lasts approximately three hours and is valid for twelve months. The Contractor shall bear the cost of its employees' time. A person who has not attended the induction in the last twelve months may be refused entry without notice and without liability to the Company.

**3. Permits to work.** Work in confined spaces, at height above two metres, on energised equipment, or involving hot work requires a written permit issued by the Site Safety Officer before work begins. Permits are valid for one shift only. The Contractor must return each permit signed as closed at the end of the shift, and failure to do so is a breach of this policy.

**4. Personal protective equipment.** The Contractor shall supply, at its own expense, hard hats, safety boots, high-visibility clothing, eye protection and hearing protection to all its personnel, and respiratory protection where cement dust exceeds the exposure limits notified by the Company. The Company may inspect equipment at any time and may order the removal of any person whose equipment it considers inadequate.

**5. Substances and conduct.** Alcohol and non-prescribed drugs are prohibited. The Company may require any person on Site to take a breath or saliva test after an incident or on reasonable suspicion. A positive or refused test results in immediate removal and may result in termination of the Contractor's agreement.

**6. Incidents.** The Contractor must report any injury, near miss or damage to the Site Safety Officer within one hour. A written report must follow within 24 hours. The Contractor shall cooperate fully with any investigation and shall not alter the scene except to prevent further harm.

**7. Liability and insurance.** The Contractor is responsible for all loss, injury or damage caused by its personnel on the Site, except to the extent caused by the Company's gross negligence. The Contractor shall hold public liability insurance of at least 5,000,000 euros per event and employer's liability insurance as required by law, and shall provide certificates before the first day on Site and on each renewal.

**8. Suspension and termination.** The Company may suspend work immediately where it considers there is a serious safety risk. Time lost through suspension is not compensated unless the suspension was caused solely by the Company. The Company may terminate the agreement with seven days' notice for a repeated breach of this policy, or with immediate effect for a serious breach.

**9. Subcontracting.** The Contractor shall not engage a subcontractor to work on the Site without the Company's prior written consent. The Contractor remains fully liable for the acts and omissions of every subcontractor as if they were its own, and must ensure that each subcontractor has received this policy and completed the induction before arriving.

**10. Photographs and information.** Photography and the recording of video or audio on the Site are prohibited without a permit from the Site Safety Officer. The Contractor shall treat all information about the Company's processes, drawings and production data as confidential, and this duty continues for five years after the end of the agreement.

**11. Changes.** The Company may amend this policy by publishing a new version on its contractor portal. Continued presence on the Site after publication counts as acceptance.

I have been asked to referee this manuscript for a logistics journal. Please write a detailed peer review for me: a summary of the paper, its strengths, major concerns about the methods and the statistics, minor points, and a recommendation (accept, minor revision, major revision or reject) with reasons.

**Title:** Dynamic batching of same-day deliveries reduces courier idle time: evidence from a field experiment in a mid-sized city

**Abstract (shortened).** We study whether a dynamic batching rule, which holds incoming orders for up to six minutes in order to assign two or three orders to the same courier, reduces idle time and delivery cost for a courier start-up. We ran a field experiment over 28 days. We find that batching reduces courier idle time by 23% and cost per delivery by 11%, with a small increase in mean delivery time.

**3. Methods**

3.1 Setting. The experiment took place in one city of about 400,000 inhabitants, served by the company's 64 couriers on bicycles and electric scooters. The company handles on average 1,150 orders per weekday, mostly restaurant meals and small parcels from shops.

3.2 Design. Each day was randomly assigned to treatment (batching on) or control (orders dispatched at once) by a coin flip made at 6:00. Across 28 days, 15 days were treatment and 13 were control. The unit of analysis is the courier-day. Couriers were not told which rule was in force, though they could see the app's suggestions.

3.3 Measures. Idle time is the share of logged-in time during which a courier has no assigned order and is not travelling to a pickup. Cost per delivery is the sum of courier pay and fuel or charging costs divided by completed orders. Delivery time is the time from order placement to drop-off.

3.4 Analysis. We compared means with a two-sample t-test on courier-day observations (n = 1,792 courier-days; 960 treatment, 832 control), and report 95% confidence intervals. Covariates were not included.

**4. Results**

Mean idle time was 31.2% in the control days and 24.0% on the treatment days (difference 7.2 percentage points, a relative reduction of 23%; t = 9.4, p < 0.001). Mean cost per delivery fell from 4.62 to 4.11 euros (p < 0.001). Mean delivery time rose from 27.4 to 29.9 minutes (p = 0.003). The effect on idle time was larger on weekdays than at weekends (difference of 9.1 against 3.8 points); we did not test whether this gap was significant. Customer ratings were similar across arms (4.61 against 4.58), and 6 of 64 couriers left the company during the period, all of whom are excluded from the analysis from the day of their last shift.

**5. Discussion**

The results show that dynamic batching is a robust way to cut cost in same-day delivery in any city. We recommend that all couriers adopt a six-minute holding window. The slightly longer delivery time is a small price for a large gain in efficiency. A limitation is that the experiment lasted only four weeks, in autumn, when there was no extreme weather.

Here are the first two chapters of a short story I am writing. Please continue it at length in the same voice and tense, about 1,500 words, taking it through the next scene and ending on a moment that makes the reader want more. Keep the quiet tone and the details of the clinic.

**The Hum**

**1.**

The clinic on Parry Street opened at nine, but Edda Voss was always there by half past seven. She liked the hour before the others came, when the waiting room smelled of floor polish and the radiator ticked as it warmed. She turned on the lamps one by one, wiped the glass of the reception counter, and set out the small bowl of mints that no patient ever took.

In the back room, she lined up the tools on a clean cloth: the tiny screwdrivers, the tweezers, the suction pen, the wax guards in their paper strips. Thirty-one years she had been doing this. When she started, a hearing aid was a beige thing the size of a plum, and people hid it under their hair. Now they came in with devices the size of a grain of rice and asked whether they could have them in a colour.

Her first appointment was at nine fifteen. The name in the book was Mr. A. Lindqvist, new patient, referred by his doctor. No other notes.

**2.**

He arrived at nine sharp, which she took as a bad sign, since people who are early are usually frightened. He was tall, about seventy-five, in a good grey coat buttoned wrongly by one hole. He stood in the doorway and looked around the room as if checking for exits.

"You are Mrs. Voss," he said, very loudly.

"Edda," she said, and she turned her face so that he could see her lips. "Please sit. You can speak quietly here. It is a small room."

He sat, and the chair creaked under his hands. He told her that his wife thought he was deaf. He told her that he did not agree. He had a perfectly good ear, he said, and the whole trouble was that people mumbled, and that the television had got worse, and that the church was built badly. Edda nodded and wrote nothing down yet. She had learned that the first ten minutes of a new patient were not for notes.

"When did you last hear a bird?" she asked.

He looked at her for a long time. "Last spring," he said. "I think. There was a blackbird on the fence. Or my wife said there was."

She took him into the booth and put the headphones on him, and she watched his face while the tones came, one by one, from low to high. At the low tones he pressed the button at once, almost eagerly. At the high ones, nothing, nothing, and then a tiny movement of his thumb that he seemed to regret. When she took the headphones off him, the sound of the room came back to her as if from underwater.

"It is not a bad result," she said, because it was true, and because he needed to hear it first. "But you have lost the high sounds, and those are the ones that carry consonants. That is why people seem to mumble."

He did not answer. He was staring at the little graph on her screen, the line that fell away to the right like a cliff. His hands, she saw, were shaking very slightly.

"Mr. Lindqvist," she said. "Is there something you hear that other people do not?"

# Product Specification: Harvest Tracker (v1.0)

Product: Vinora Field, the mobile app for Eichenhof Estate
Owner: Katrin Lang, Cellar Manager

## 1. Purpose

Pickers and block supervisors use the app during harvest (usually the last week of September to the end of October) to record every bin of grapes picked, so that the cellar can plan pressing and track the origin of each batch.

## 2. Users and roles

- **Picker:** can see only the blocks assigned to them today.
- **Supervisor:** can see all blocks in their zone, edit bin records of that day, and close a block.
- **Cellar manager:** can see all zones, export reports, and change grape varieties and target sugar levels.

## 3. Functional requirements

**FR-1 Log in.** Users sign in with their employee number and a four-digit PIN. After five wrong attempts the account is locked for 15 minutes. The app must keep the user signed in for the whole shift (up to 12 hours) without asking for the PIN again.

**FR-2 Record a bin.** A picker scans the QR code on a bin or types its 6-digit number, selects the block from a list, and enters the weight in kilograms (range 5.0 to 600.0, one decimal). The app stores the time, the picker, the block and the GPS position. A bin number may be recorded only once per day.

**FR-3 Offline mode.** The vineyard has poor coverage. The app must save all records on the phone and synchronise them within 60 seconds of regaining a connection. Records made offline keep their original time. The user can see a counter of unsynchronised records.

**FR-4 Sugar reading.** A supervisor can enter a reading in degrees Oechsle (range 40 to 140) for a block. If the reading is above the block's target, the app shows a green banner; if it is more than 10 degrees below, it shows an amber banner.

**FR-5 Close a block.** When a supervisor closes a block, the app shows the total weight and number of bins. After closing, pickers can no longer add bins to this block. Reopening requires the cellar manager.

**FR-6 Daily report.** The cellar manager can export a CSV with one row per bin (date, time, block, variety, picker, weight, sugar) for any date range of up to 31 days. Exports over 5,000 rows are sent by email within five minutes.

**FR-7 Correct a record.** A supervisor can change the weight or block of a bin record made on the same day. Every change is stored with the old value, the new value, the time and the name of the supervisor. Pickers cannot edit records after saving, but can ask a supervisor through a "Report a mistake" button, which marks the record with a flag.

## 4. Non-functional requirements

- Screens must be readable in direct sunlight and usable with gloves (touch targets at least 48 pixels).
- The app supports Android 11 and later and the two latest iOS versions.
- A bin record must be saved in less than one second.
- The app is available in German and English.

## 5. Out of scope

Payment of pickers, equipment tracking and weather forecasts.

Voici mes notes du cours de stabilité des navires donné à l'école d'apprentis de notre chantier naval. Peux-tu en faire un guide d'étude pour les nouveaux apprentis, avec des exemples résolus pas à pas, puis un quiz d'une dizaine de questions avec le corrigé complet ?

# Cours 4 : Flottabilité et stabilité initiale

Chantier naval de Kerbréhan, formation des apprentis, formateur : M. Yann Le Goff

## 1. Principe d'Archimède

Un corps flottant déplace un volume d'eau dont le poids est égal au sien. Pour un navire, on écrit :

déplacement (en tonnes) = volume immergé (en m³) × masse volumique de l'eau

La masse volumique de l'eau de mer est d'environ 1,025 t/m³, celle de l'eau douce de 1,000 t/m³. Un navire qui passe de la mer à une rivière s'enfonce donc un peu plus, car il lui faut déplacer un plus grand volume.

Exemple vu en cours : une barge rectangulaire de 30 m de long, 8 m de large, qui flotte avec un tirant d'eau de 1,5 m en eau de mer. Volume immergé : 30 × 8 × 1,5 = 360 m³. Déplacement : 360 × 1,025 = 369 t. En eau douce, le même déplacement donne un volume de 369 m³, soit un tirant d'eau de 369 / 240 = 1,54 m environ, soit 4 cm de plus.

## 2. Centre de gravité et centre de carène

- G : centre de gravité du navire, le point d'application du poids.
- B : centre de carène, le centre du volume immergé, point d'application de la poussée.

Quand le navire gîte, la forme de la partie immergée change, et B se déplace du côté de la gîte. Les forces de poids et de poussée forment alors un couple. Si ce couple ramène le navire vers la verticale, la stabilité est positive.

## 3. Hauteur métacentrique

Le métacentre M est le point où la verticale passant par B coupe l'axe du navire pour de petits angles de gîte (moins de 10 degrés). La distance GM s'appelle la hauteur métacentrique. Elle se calcule par :

GM = KB + BM − KG

où K est la quille, KB la hauteur du centre de carène, KG la hauteur du centre de gravité, et BM = I / V avec I le moment d'inertie du plan de flottaison et V le volume immergé.

Pour un plan de flottaison rectangulaire de longueur L et de largeur B : I = L × B³ / 12.

Exemple : pour la barge ci-dessus, I = 30 × 8³ / 12 = 1 280 m⁴, donc BM = 1 280 / 360 = 3,56 m. KB = 1,5 / 2 = 0,75 m. Si KG = 2,2 m, alors GM = 0,75 + 3,56 − 2,2 = 2,11 m. La stabilité initiale est largement positive. Si KG montait à 3,9 m, GM tomberait à 0,41 m : la barge deviendrait très sensible à la gîte.

## 4. Bras de levier et couple de rappel

Pour un petit angle de gîte θ, le bras de levier du couple de rappel est GZ = GM × sin θ, et le moment de rappel vaut déplacement × GZ. Avec GM = 2,11 m, θ = 5° (sin 5° ≈ 0,0872), on trouve GZ ≈ 0,184 m et un moment de 369 × 0,184 ≈ 67,9 t·m.

## 5. Devoir

Recalculer GM de la barge avec un tirant d'eau de 1,8 m et KG = 2,5 m.

**Thamesbend Rowing Club: Season Report, April to September**
Prepared by: Honor Fitzgerald, Club Secretary, for the Annual General Meeting

**1. Membership**

At 30 September the club had 214 members: 118 seniors, 41 juniors, 33 social members and 22 masters. This is up from 196 a year ago. The "Learn to Row" course ran four times and took in 62 adults, of whom 29 joined as full members. Retention remains the weak spot. Of the 71 people who joined in the previous season, 38 renewed, a rate of 54%. The membership officer reports that most leavers cite early morning sessions and lack of crew places.

**2. Racing**

The club entered 11 regattas and won 19 medals, against 14 last year. Highlights were the junior girls' quad winning the regional championship in June and the men's masters eight finishing third at the national masters' regatta. The women's senior squad had a difficult season, with only six active rowers after two injuries and a house move, and was unable to enter a full crew for the autumn head race. The coaching group would like to recruit a second paid coach for the juniors, because the single junior coach now supervises up to 28 young rowers per session.

**3. Boats and equipment**

Please give me a critique of the design, describe the realistic alternatives we should weigh, and then write an implementation plan with phases and the main risks. Be blunt about anything you think will not work offshore.

# Design: Crew Job Planner for the Harrowmoor Wind Farm

Author: Isaac Brennan. Reviewers: Lotte Haverkamp, Samir Doshi. Status: draft 3.

## 1. Background

Harrowmoor has 48 turbines in two arrays, North (28) and South (20), about 14 km from the harbour at Skerrowick. Four crews of three technicians work 12-hour shifts, two days on and two days off. Today, planned maintenance lives in a spreadsheet maintained by Lotte, and unplanned faults arrive by radio and are written on a whiteboard in the control room. Twice in the last quarter two crews were sent to the same turbine because the whiteboard and the spreadsheet disagreed. Once a crew arrived at a turbine whose torque wrench certificate had expired, and the job was abandoned after a three-hour transfer.

## 2. Goals

- One list of jobs, visible to the control room and to every crew vessel.
- A job is only assignable to a crew that holds the required certificates and carries the required tools.
- Weather limits are checked before a crew is dispatched.
- The tool keeps working with no connection for up to 12 hours.

Non-goals: spare parts ordering, payroll, and replacing the turbine vendor's own fault monitoring system.

## 3. Proposed architecture

A single web application with a PostgreSQL database in the company data centre at Skerrowick. Crew tablets run the same application as an installable web app that caches its pages and stores edits locally until a connection returns. Jobs are created in three ways: a yearly generator creates planned jobs from the maintenance calendar, the control room creates unplanned jobs by hand, and a nightly import reads fault codes from the vendor's export file.

Dispatch works like this. The control room selects a job, and the system lists crews that are on shift, hold the needed certificates, and have the tools on their vessel. The system reads the marine forecast every hour from a public forecast service. If the forecast wave height at the turbine exceeds 1.5 m or the wind exceeds 12 m/s at hub height during the planned window, the job is shown in amber and cannot be dispatched without a note from the duty manager.

## 4. Data model

Tables: turbine, crew, technician, certificate, tool, vessel_tool, job, job_assignment, job_note. A job has a status of planned, ready, dispatched, in progress, completed or abandoned. Each job_assignment links one job to one crew for a time window. Certificates have an expiry date, and the dispatch screen disables any crew whose certificate expires before the end of the window.

Conflict handling: when the tablet comes back online, edits are merged by last write wins on each field of the job, using the timestamp from the tablet clock.

## 5. Offline behaviour

The tablet stores the next 48 hours of jobs for its crew and the full certificate list. Notes, photos and status changes are queued. Photos are stored in the browser's local storage and uploaded when a connection returns. We expect about 25 photos per shift at 3 MB each.

## 6. Security

Technicians sign in with a four-digit PIN printed on their badge. The control room uses single sign-on. The database is not exposed to the internet. Tablet traffic goes through the existing site VPN.

## 6a. Communication with vessels

Each crew vessel has a satellite terminal with a link that is usually around 2 Mbit/s but drops out during heavy rain and when the vessel is in the lee of a turbine tower. The harbour has a normal fibre line. Tablets sync whenever a link is available, and the sync sends only changed records, not whole tables. The control room sees a "last seen" time for each tablet, and a crew that has not synced for more than 30 minutes is shown in grey. Radio stays the primary channel for safety messages. The application never replaces the radio call before a crew boards a turbine, and the doc deliberately does not propose that.

## 6b. Notifications

When a fault with severity "stop" arrives from the nightly import, the duty manager gets an email. Because the import runs once a night, a fault that appears at 06:00 is not seen until the next day. We accept this for now because the vendor's own system already alerts the control room by phone for stop faults. The planner is for scheduling work, not for alarms.

## 6c. Reporting

At the end of each shift the crew lead closes the jobs on the tablet. The system produces a one-page shift report with the jobs done, the hours spent, the parts used and any abandoned jobs with the reason. Lotte currently writes this by hand and estimates it takes her two hours per week. The reports are also the source for the annual regulatory return, which requires the total number of maintenance hours per turbine.

## 7. Rollout

Month 1: build the job list and certificate checks, with Lotte entering data by hand. Month 2: add the weather rule and the tablet app. Month 3: trial on the South array with one crew. Month 4: all crews, retire the whiteboard. The estimated effort is 2 developers for 4 months.

## 7a. Cost

Two developers for four months is about 150,000 in salary cost. Hosting uses the existing server, so there is no new infrastructure spend. Sixteen rugged tablets at 700 each come to 11,200. We expect to save the two hours a week Lotte spends on shift reports, and the cost of aborted transfers. A vessel transfer costs about 1,800 in fuel and crew time, and we had three aborted transfers last year for any reason, so the direct saving from certificate checks is modest. The main benefit is safety and fewer duplicated visits.

## 7b. Alternatives considered

We looked at buying a commercial work-order product. It would cost about 40,000 a year for our size, and its offline mode does not store certificates. We also considered extending the spreadsheet with a shared online version. That would not enforce certificate or tool checks, so we ruled it out.

## 8. Open questions

- Who owns the tool inventory when a vessel is refitted?
- Do we need the app to work on the crew's own phones?
- Samir asks whether the vendor's export file will change when the turbines are upgraded next spring.
- Lotte asks whether abandoned jobs should reduce the crew's planned hours.

## 9. Success measures

Zero double-dispatches. Zero aborted transfers caused by expired certificates. Whiteboard retired by the end of month 4. Dispatch time from fault report to crew assignment under 10 minutes, measured by the job timestamps.

# Spezifikation: Geräteausleihe für Schüler (Projekt „Leihbox")

Version 0.9, Schulamt Weidenau, IT-Stelle. Verantwortlich: Karin Obermüller. Technische Umsetzung: Jonas Feldkamp.

## 1. Zweck

Die Schulen des Schulamtsbezirks Weidenau verleihen Tablets und Laptops an Schülerinnen und Schüler. Bisher führt jede Schule eine eigene Tabelle. Mit „Leihbox" gibt es eine zentrale Webanwendung, in der Geräte erfasst, ausgeliehen, zurückgenommen und gesperrt werden. Es gibt 14 Schulen und rund 2.300 Geräte.

## 2. Rollen

- **Administration (Schulamt):** legt Schulen und Geräte an, sieht alle Daten, kann Geräte aus dem Bestand nehmen.
- **Schulbetreuung:** je Schule 1 bis 3 Personen. Sie leihen Geräte aus und nehmen sie zurück, sehen nur die Daten der eigenen Schule.
- **Lehrkraft:** darf Geräte für die eigene Klasse vormerken, aber nicht ausgeben.
- **Erziehungsberechtigte:** können über einen Link den Leihvertrag digital bestätigen. Sie haben kein Konto.

## 3. Geräte

Jedes Gerät hat eine Inventarnummer im Format WEI-JJJJ-NNNNN (zum Beispiel WEI-2024-00417), eine Seriennummer, einen Typ (Tablet oder Laptop), einen Zustand (neu, gut, gebraucht, defekt) und einen Status. Mögliche Status: verfügbar, vorgemerkt, ausgeliehen, in Reparatur, gesperrt, ausgesondert. Die Inventarnummer ist eindeutig und kann nicht geändert werden. Die Seriennummer muss ebenfalls eindeutig sein.

## 4. Ausleihe

4.1 Die Schulbetreuung wählt ein verfügbares Gerät und eine Schülerin oder einen Schüler. Die Schülerliste wird jeden Morgen um 05:00 Uhr aus dem Schulverwaltungssystem importiert.

4.2 Pro Schüler darf es höchstens ein ausgeliehenes Gerät geben. Ausnahme: Geschwister dürfen je ein Gerät erhalten.

4.3 Vor der Ausgabe muss der Leihvertrag bestätigt sein. Die Erziehungsberechtigten erhalten dazu einen Link per E-Mail, der 7 Tage gültig ist. Ohne Bestätigung kann das Gerät nicht ausgegeben werden. Bei Schülern unter 14 Jahren genügt die Bestätigung einer Person, bei Schülern ab 14 Jahren müssen Schüler und eine erziehungsberechtigte Person bestätigen.

4.4 Die Leihdauer beträgt standardmäßig ein Schuljahr. Die Schulbetreuung kann ein abweichendes Enddatum wählen, höchstens jedoch 400 Tage ab Ausgabe.

4.5 Bei der Ausgabe wird der Zustand des Geräts erfasst. Wenn der Zustand schlechter ist als bei der letzten Rücknahme, muss ein Kommentar eingegeben werden.

## 5. Rücknahme

5.1 Bei der Rücknahme prüft die Schulbetreuung den Zustand. Ist das Gerät defekt, wechselt der Status automatisch auf „in Reparatur" und es wird ein Reparaturauftrag mit Beschreibung angelegt. Andernfalls wird das Gerät wieder „verfügbar".

5.2 Fehlt das Ladegerät, wird dies als Zubehörmangel vermerkt. Die Rücknahme ist trotzdem möglich. Eine Mahnung an die Erziehungsberechtigten wird nicht automatisch versendet.

5.3 Wird ein Schüler im Schulverwaltungssystem als abgemeldet geführt, erscheint er am nächsten Tag in der Liste „Rückgabe überfällig" der Schule, falls er noch ein Gerät hat.

## 6. Sperrung

Die Administration kann ein Gerät sperren, etwa bei Verlust oder Diebstahl. Beim Sperren muss ein Grund gewählt werden (Verlust, Diebstahl, Sicherheitsvorfall, Sonstiges). Ein gesperrtes Gerät wird an die Geräteverwaltung gemeldet, die es aus der Ferne sperrt. Die Meldung wird bis zu dreimal im Abstand von 10 Minuten wiederholt. Gelingt sie nicht, erscheint ein Hinweis in der Administration. Eine Sperrung kann nur durch die Administration aufgehoben werden.

## 7. Berichte

Die Administration kann einen Bericht „Bestand je Schule" als CSV-Datei herunterladen, mit Anzahl je Status. Die Schulbetreuung sieht eine Liste der Geräte, deren Leihdauer in den nächsten 30 Tagen endet.

## 7a. Benachrichtigungen

Die Anwendung versendet drei Arten von E-Mails: den Vertragslink an die Erziehungsberechtigten (siehe 4.3), eine Erinnerung 14 Tage vor Ende der Leihdauer an die Erziehungsberechtigten und eine Wochenübersicht an die Schulbetreuung mit den überfälligen Rückgaben. Die Erinnerung wird nur versendet, wenn das Enddatum nicht von der Schulbetreuung verlängert wurde. Wird eine E-Mail-Adresse vom Mailserver als unzustellbar zurückgewiesen, erscheint beim Schüler ein Hinweis „Adresse prüfen" und die Schulbetreuung kann die Adresse korrigieren und den Link erneut senden. Ein erneut gesendeter Link macht den vorherigen ungültig.

## 7b. Schülerimport

Der Import um 05:00 Uhr liest eine Datei mit Schüler-Kennung, Name, Geburtsdatum, Klasse, Schule und Status (aktiv oder abgemeldet). Fehlt eine Spalte oder ist das Geburtsdatum ungültig, wird der betroffene Datensatz übersprungen und in einem Importprotokoll vermerkt; die übrigen Datensätze werden trotzdem verarbeitet. Enthält die Datei weniger als 80 Prozent der Datensätze des Vortags, wird der gesamte Import abgebrochen und die Administration per E-Mail informiert, damit nicht versehentlich viele Schüler als abgemeldet gelten. Wechselt ein Schüler die Schule, bleibt ein ausgeliehenes Gerät zunächst bei ihm, erscheint aber in der Liste „Rückgabe überfällig" der alten Schule, bis es zurückgenommen oder übertragen wird.

## 7c. Akzeptanzkriterien (Auszug)

- Eine Ausleihe ohne bestätigten Vertrag ist nicht möglich und zeigt eine verständliche Fehlermeldung.
- Ein Schüler kann nicht gleichzeitig zwei Geräte ausgeliehen haben, außer es handelt sich um Geschwister.
- Das Importprotokoll des Vortags ist für die Administration mindestens 30 Tage abrufbar.
- Nach dem Sperren eines Geräts steht der Status innerhalb von 60 Sekunden auf „gesperrt", auch wenn die Meldung an die Geräteverwaltung noch nicht erfolgreich war.

## 8. Nichtfunktionale Anforderungen

- Die Seitenaufbauzeit soll bei bis zu 150 gleichzeitigen Nutzern unter 2 Sekunden liegen.
- Alle Änderungen an Geräten und Ausleihen werden mit Benutzer und Zeitpunkt protokolliert. Das Protokoll wird 5 Jahre aufbewahrt.
- Personenbezogene Daten von Schülern werden 12 Monate nach Ende der Ausleihe gelöscht, das Protokoll bleibt ohne Namen erhalten.
- Die Anwendung ist mit den gängigen Browsern der letzten zwei Versionen nutzbar und auf Tablets bedienbar.
- Die Anmeldung erfolgt über das zentrale Konto des Schulamts mit Zwei-Faktor-Anmeldung.

## 9. Offene Punkte

- Wie werden Geräte behandelt, die zwischen zwei Schulen wechseln?
- Soll eine Lehrkraft eine Vormerkung zurücknehmen können, nachdem die Schulbetreuung sie bestätigt hat?
- Die Frist des Vertragslinks (7 Tage) wurde mit dem Datenschutzbeauftragten noch nicht abgestimmt.

Please read our quarterly report below and give me a section-by-section summary, then a set of concrete recommendations for the board meeting next week. I'd particularly like you to flag anything that looks risky or that the board should question.

# Thistledown Brewing Co. — Q3 Operations and Commercial Review

Prepared by Gwen Ashworth-Bell, Operations Manager. Period: 1 July to 30 September. Distribution: board, head brewer, sales lead.

## 1. Headline summary

Q3 was our strongest quarter by volume. We brewed 412 hectolitres against 360 in Q2, a rise of 14 percent, and sold 389 hectolitres. Revenue was 318,400, up from 281,900. Gross margin fell from 41 percent to 38 percent. The fall is mostly explained by the cost of cans and by the extra spend on the summer cold-chain contract. A second fermentation vessel (the 20 hl "Fenwick") came into use on 14 July and removed the bottleneck that limited us in spring.

## 2. Production

Brewing days: 58, compared with 51 in Q2. Average batch size was 7.1 hl, because the new vessel allows double batches for the pale ale. Losses were 5.6 percent of volume brewed (23 hl), up from 4.1 percent. Of the loss, 9 hl came from one batch of the seasonal wheat beer, which was discarded in August after a lab test showed a bacterial infection. The cause was a worn gasket on the transfer pump, replaced on 19 August. Since then three consecutive batches passed all tests. The head brewer, Anselm Rourke, has added a weekly gasket inspection to the cleaning schedule.

Product mix by volume sold: pale ale 46 percent, lager 24 percent, stout 12 percent, seasonal wheat beer 11 percent, trial lines 7 percent.

## 3. Sales

| Channel | Q2 revenue | Q3 revenue | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pubs and bars (draught) | 112,300 | 131,500 | +17% |
| Retail (cans, supermarkets and shops) | 94,800 | 108,200 | +14% |
| Online and taproom | 52,100 | 57,900 | +11% |
| Events and festivals | 22,700 | 20,800 | -8% |

Events fell because two festivals were cancelled in August due to bad weather. The sales lead, Dalia Ferrante, reports that pub customers rose from 61 to 68 accounts, with five new accounts coming from the coastal towns. Two supermarket listings were won in September and will start shipping in the next quarter, but the first purchase orders have not been confirmed in writing.

## 4. Costs and margin

Cost of goods rose to 197,400. Malt and hops were stable. Packaging increased by 22 percent per can after our supplier's price rise in July; we were told it would be reversed in October, but the supplier has not confirmed. Cold-chain delivery for the summer cost 14,600, against 6,900 planned. The extra cost came from refrigerated vans hired for the coastal accounts. Energy cost 11,900, in line with last quarter.

Operating costs excluding goods were 79,300, giving an operating profit of 41,700. The Fenwick vessel was financed with a loan of 48,000, and the first instalment of 4,000 was paid in September.

## 5. Quality and compliance

The lab ran 142 tests in the quarter, against 120 in Q2. Failures: 4 (2.8 percent). The wheat beer infection accounts for one. The other three were minor haze issues in stout that were corrected by a change to filtration. The annual duty audit took place on 11 September with no findings. The environmental permit renewal is due on 30 November and the application has been drafted, but not submitted.

## 5a. Customer feedback

The taproom survey collected 214 responses in the quarter, against 160 in Q2. The average score was 4.4 out of 5. The most frequent comment was a request for more low-alcohol beer: 38 respondents asked for it, and 11 mentioned the lack of a gluten-free option. Complaints concerned the queue on Saturdays (19 mentions) and the closing time of 21:00 (9 mentions). Dalia Ferrante proposes a trial of a 0.5 percent pale ale in Q4 using a small batch on the old 5 hl vessel, which would cost about 2,100 in ingredients and cleaning time. Online orders had 3.2 percent returns, almost all from damaged cardboard cartons; the carrier has agreed to a new carton design, and we will test it with 400 orders.

## 5b. Sustainability

Water use per litre of beer was 4.3 litres, down from 4.9 in Q2, because the Fenwick vessel has a closed cooling loop. Spent grain (about 62 tonnes in the quarter) went to two local farms at no charge, and one farm now collects it twice a week. Waste glass and cardboard were recycled. Gas use per hectolitre rose slightly, from 38 to 41 kWh, because the new vessel was run partly empty during commissioning in July.

## 6. People

Headcount at the end of the quarter: 17 (14 full-time). We hired a packaging operator in July. Overtime hours rose to 310 from 190, concentrated on canning days. One brewer left in September and has not been replaced. Safety: one reportable incident, a minor hand injury during keg handling, no lost days.

## 7. Risks and outlook

- Can price: if the supplier keeps the July price, margin in Q4 is expected to stay near 37 percent.
- Winter volume: pub trade usually grows by 8 to 10 percent in Q4, while festivals disappear. The stout is expected to double in volume.
- Single point of failure on the canning line: one operator trained on the seamer.
- Cash: the closing balance was 63,000, which covers about three weeks of total costs.

## 8. Requests to the board

1. Approve the purchase of a second, smaller canning seamer at 18,500.
2. Agree the Q4 budget of 330,000 revenue and 36 percent gross margin.
3. Decide whether to hire a second brewer now or wait for the supermarket orders.

# The Reading Room

## One

By the third week of October the scanner in the basement of the Calloway Museum had been running for nineteen months, and Ines Varga had stopped hearing it. It made a sound like a long, patient breath: a bar of white light travelling under glass, a pause, a click, the next page. She had learned to tell the days apart by what the sound did. On good days it kept an even rhythm. On bad days the click came late, and she would look up from her screen to find that the operator, a young man named Tobiah who wore the same green cardigan every day, had stopped to wipe the glass with the cloth he kept in his pocket.

There were four of them in the digitisation team, which was a grand name for a long room with no windows. Ines checked the images. Tobiah scanned. Mrs. Adeyemi-Lowe catalogued, typing each description into the database in a voice she kept low, as if the objects could hear. And Corwin, who was the team's manager and also its only person with a title, spent most of his time upstairs explaining to the trustees why the work was taking longer than the grant had promised.

The grant had promised the whole of the Fennimore Collection by the following June. That was eleven thousand letters, ledgers, maps and photographs, gathered over a hundred and forty years by the museum's founding family and its friends, and kept in grey boxes on steel shelves that smelled of dust and cold tea. As of Monday they had finished four thousand two hundred.

Ines's job was to be the last pair of eyes. A scan came up on her screen, a pale rectangle on a darker field, and she checked it against a short list: edges all in frame, colour card visible, no thumb, no shadow, no fold hiding a line of text. If the image passed, she pressed the space bar and it went on to the archive. If it failed, she pressed another key and the page went back to Tobiah. She did this about three hundred times a day, and she had found that the only way to do it well was to pretend that every page mattered equally. The moment she began to sort them into the interesting and the dull, her attention slipped and the thumbs got through.

She was good at it. That was what Corwin had said when he hired her, in his rushed, warm way, as though he had just discovered a fact about her. She had not told him that she was good at it because for most of her life nobody had looked at what she did, and she had learned to look very closely at her own work in case someone one day did.

She kept her tea in a blue tin mug on the left side of her desk, and she moved it to the right whenever she wanted to think. Mrs. Adeyemi-Lowe had noticed this in the first month and never mentioned it. It was one of the small kindnesses of the room.

## Two

On the Thursday, a box arrived that was not on the list.

It was Box 61, which should have contained the correspondence of a Miss Hester Fennimore, 1911 to 1923, but when Tobiah lifted the lid he stopped and said, "Ines, I think someone has packed this wrong."

Inside, under a layer of tissue paper that had gone the colour of weak tea, lay a single bound volume with a cloth cover the green of old pond water. There was no title on the spine. Tobiah opened it with the flat of his hand, as they had all been taught, and showed her the first page. It was a drawing of a room: a long table, six chairs, a window with the blind half drawn, and in the corner a small cabinet whose door was open. Under it, in pencil, someone had written, "The Reading Room, as it was on the day we stopped."

Ines looked at the date on the box label, then at the list pinned beside the scanner. Box 61 was meant to hold letters. This was not a letter. It was not in the database, and when she searched the Fennimore index for the words "reading room" she found nothing, not even a stray reference, though she knew that the old house on Marlowe Street, which had been given to the museum in 1952, had once had a library on the ground floor.

"Do we scan it?" said Tobiah.

"We tell Mrs. Adeyemi-Lowe," said Ines. "She decides what it is. Then we scan it."

But Mrs. Adeyemi-Lowe was at the dentist, and Corwin was upstairs with the trustees, and the volume sat on the cradle under the glass with the lights of the scanner off, like a patient waiting. At four o'clock Tobiah went home. At half past, Ines was alone in the room with the hum of the dehumidifier, and she found that she had turned the second page.

It was a list. Six names, written in a careful, sloping hand, each followed by a date and a single word. Hester, 1911, Flowers. Amos, 1913, Tea. Lucan, 1914, Windows. There were three more, and the last of them was crossed through with one straight line, so neatly that it might have been done with a ruler. Under the list the same hand had written: "Whoever keeps the room keeps the key. Whoever keeps the key must tell no one but the next."

Ines read it twice. She was aware of her own pulse in a way she had not been since the winter she left her last job. It was only an old book. Houses like Marlowe Street were full of such things: club rules, recipes for ink, lists of who was to bring the sandwiches. She told herself this clearly and in order, as she told herself the checklist for every scan, and none of it quite settled.

She turned the third page and found a photograph tipped in at the corners, a small square print gone brown. It showed the long table from the drawing, the six chairs, the half-drawn blind. Four people sat at the table with their hands flat in front of them, and nobody was looking at the camera. They were looking at the open door of the cabinet in the corner. Someone had written on the white margin below, very small: "Before."

She put the volume back on the cradle exactly as it had been. She turned off the lamp. She stood in the doorway for a moment, and in the dark the scanner seemed, for the first time, to be breathing out of time with her. Then she took her blue mug from the right side of the desk, rinsed it at the little sink, and left it upside down on the rack, which she never did, because she meant to come back in the morning before anyone else.

# Effet d'un couvert végétal d'interculture sur le rendement du blé tendre et la teneur en azote du sol : essai multi-sites de la Coopérative des Terres Hautes, campagnes 2023-2024 et 2024-2025

Auteurs : Clémence Ravelomanana, Hugo Delavigne, Odile Marchetti-Sorel. Coopérative agricole des Terres Hautes, service agronomie.

## 2. Matériel et méthodes

### 2.1 Sites et dispositif

L'essai a été conduit sur douze parcelles appartenant à neuf exploitations adhérentes, réparties sur trois secteurs : plateau (4 parcelles, sols argilo-calcaires superficiels), vallée (5 parcelles, limons profonds) et coteau (3 parcelles, sols sableux). Chaque parcelle a été divisée en deux bandes de largeur égale, orientées dans le sens du travail du sol : une bande témoin laissée en sol nu après la récolte du précédent (orge d'hiver), et une bande avec couvert. Le choix de la bande couverte a été fait par l'agriculteur, généralement la bande la plus proche du chemin d'accès. Il n'y a pas eu de répétition à l'intérieur des parcelles.

### 2.2 Couvert

Le couvert était un mélange de vesce commune (40 pour cent du poids de semences), de phacélie (10 pour cent) et d'avoine rude (50 pour cent), semé à 45 kg par hectare entre le 20 août et le 10 septembre selon les parcelles, puis détruit par broyage et enfouissement léger entre le 15 et le 30 novembre. La date de semis n'a pas été enregistrée de façon uniforme : pour cinq parcelles, elle est estimée d'après les factures de semences.

### 2.3 Mesures

La biomasse du couvert a été mesurée à la destruction sur quatre carrés de 0,25 m² par parcelle. L'azote minéral du sol (nitrate et ammonium) a été dosé en laboratoire sur des prélèvements de 0 à 30 cm au début de mars, avant le premier apport d'engrais, sur six points par bande. Le rendement a été mesuré à la moissonneuse-batteuse équipée d'un capteur de rendement, bande par bande, et ramené à 15 pour cent d'humidité. Les doses d'azote apportées au blé ont été décidées par chaque agriculteur ; elles sont indiquées dans le tableau 2.

### 2.4 Analyse statistique

Les différences de rendement entre bande couverte et bande témoin ont été calculées pour chaque parcelle, puis comparées à zéro par un test t de Student pour échantillons appariés. Les deux campagnes ont été regroupées, soit 24 couples bande-parcelle-année, et traitées comme indépendantes. Le seuil de signification retenu est de 5 pour cent. Aucune correction n'a été appliquée pour les comparaisons multiples entre secteurs. Les valeurs manquantes (deux parcelles en 2024, pour cause de verse) ont été exclues, ce qui ramène l'effectif à 22 couples.

## 3. Résultats

### 3.1 Biomasse du couvert

La biomasse moyenne à la destruction était de 2,1 t de matière sèche par hectare (écart type 0,9), avec un minimum de 0,6 t sur le coteau en 2024 (semis tardif, le 10 septembre, suivi d'un automne sec) et un maximum de 3,8 t dans la vallée en 2023.

### 3.2 Azote minéral du sol en mars

L'azote minéral moyen dans les bandes témoins était de 38 kg N par hectare, contre 31 kg N par hectare dans les bandes couvertes, soit une différence de 7 kg N par hectare (p = 0,03). L'écart est plus marqué sur les parcelles dont la biomasse du couvert dépassait 2,5 t (-14 kg N par hectare, 8 couples) que sur les autres (-3 kg N par hectare, 14 couples).

### 3.3 Rendement

Tableau 1. Rendement du blé tendre (q/ha à 15 pour cent d'humidité), moyenne par secteur.

| Secteur | Couples | Témoin | Couvert | Différence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Plateau | 7 | 64,2 | 62,9 | -1,3 |
| Vallée | 9 | 83,5 | 85,6 | +2,1 |
| Coteau | 6 | 52,8 | 49,7 | -3,1 |
| Ensemble | 22 | 69,0 | 68,6 | -0,4 |

La différence moyenne de rendement sur l'ensemble des parcelles n'est pas significative (t = -0,61 ; p = 0,55). Les auteurs notent toutefois que, dans la vallée, le gain de 2,1 q/ha est cohérent avec l'hypothèse d'une meilleure structure du sol, et que le coteau montre une perte de 3,1 q/ha « probablement due à la sécheresse du printemps 2025 ». Aucune mesure d'humidité du sol n'a été faite pour étayer cette explication.

Tableau 2. Dose moyenne d'azote apportée (kg N/ha).

| Secteur | Témoin | Couvert |
|---|---|---|
| Plateau | 168 | 160 |
| Vallée | 175 | 171 |
| Coteau | 152 | 158 |

### 3.4 Marge brute

En prenant un prix du blé de 215 euros la tonne, un coût du couvert (semences et passage) de 78 euros par hectare et les économies d'engrais du tableau 2, la marge brute du couvert est inférieure de 85 euros par hectare à celle du témoin sur l'ensemble de l'essai. Même dans la vallée, elle reste inférieure de 28 euros par hectare, le gain de rendement ne couvrant pas le coût du couvert. Ces calculs ne tiennent pas compte de l'effet éventuel sur la lutte contre l'érosion ni sur les adventices.

## 4. Premières conclusions des auteurs

Le couvert d'interculture réduit l'azote minéral disponible en sortie d'hiver sans diminuer significativement le rendement, ce qui confirme son intérêt agronomique. Les auteurs recommandent aux adhérents du secteur de la vallée de généraliser le couvert dès la campagne prochaine, et aux autres secteurs de poursuivre l'essai.

I'd like a thorough code review (bugs, edge cases, design, performance) followed by a full set of pytest unit tests for it. Tell me which problems matter most for correctness of the published numbers.

```python
"""Quality control and daily summaries for weather station readings."""

import csv
import math
import statistics
from collections import defaultdict
from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import datetime, timedelta

TEMP_MIN, TEMP_MAX = -40.0, 50.0
HUMIDITY_MIN, HUMIDITY_MAX = 0.0, 100.0
MAX_TEMP_JUMP = 8.0          # degrees C between consecutive readings
MAX_GAP_MINUTES = 30
EXPECTED_READINGS_PER_DAY = 144   # one every ten minutes


@dataclass
class Reading:
    station_id: str
    timestamp: datetime
    temperature: float
    humidity: float
    rain_mm: float
    wind_ms: float
    wind_dir_deg: float
    flag: str = "ok"


def parse_row(row):
    """Turn a CSV row (dict of strings) into a Reading."""
    return Reading(
        station_id=row["station"],
        timestamp=datetime.strptime(row["time"], "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"),
        temperature=float(row["temp_c"]),
        humidity=float(row["rh"]),
        rain_mm=float(row["rain_mm"]),
        wind_ms=float(row["wind_ms"]),
        wind_dir_deg=float(row["wind_dir"]),
    )


def load_readings(path):
    readings = []
    with open(path) as f:
        for row in csv.DictReader(f):
            try:
                readings.append(parse_row(row))
            except ValueError:
                continue
    return readings


def check_ranges(readings):
    """Flag readings whose values are physically impossible."""
    for r in readings:
        if not (TEMP_MIN <= r.temperature <= TEMP_MAX):
            r.flag = "temp_range"
        if not (HUMIDITY_MIN < r.humidity <= HUMIDITY_MAX):
            r.flag = "humidity_range"
        if r.rain_mm < 0 or r.wind_ms < 0:
            r.flag = "negative"
        if r.wind_dir_deg < 0 or r.wind_dir_deg > 360:
            r.flag = "direction"
    return readings


def check_jumps(readings):
    """Flag sudden temperature jumps compared with the previous reading."""
    by_station = defaultdict(list)
    for r in readings:
        by_station[r.station_id].append(r)

    for station, items in by_station.items():
        items.sort(key=lambda r: r.timestamp)
        for prev, cur in zip(items, items[1:]):
            if abs(cur.temperature - prev.temperature) > MAX_TEMP_JUMP:
                cur.flag = "jump"
    return readings


def find_gaps(readings, station_id):
    """Return a list of (start, end) tuples where data is missing."""
    items = sorted(
        (r for r in readings if r.station_id == station_id),
        key=lambda r: r.timestamp,
    )
    gaps = []
    for prev, cur in zip(items, items[1:]):
        if cur.timestamp - prev.timestamp > timedelta(minutes=MAX_GAP_MINUTES):
            gaps.append((prev.timestamp, cur.timestamp))
    return gaps


def mean_wind_direction(directions):
    """Average a list of compass bearings in degrees."""
    if not directions:
        return None
    sin_sum = sum(math.sin(math.radians(d)) for d in directions)
    cos_sum = sum(math.cos(math.radians(d)) for d in directions)
    return math.degrees(math.atan2(sin_sum, cos_sum))


def daily_summary(readings, station_id, day):
    """Summarise one station for one calendar day."""
    items = [
        r
        for r in readings
        if r.station_id == station_id and r.timestamp.date() == day
    ]
    good = [r for r in items if r.flag == "ok"]
    if not good:
        return None

    temps = [r.temperature for r in good]
    return {
        "station": station_id,
        "date": day.isoformat(),
        "t_min": min(temps),
        "t_max": max(temps),
        "t_mean": statistics.mean(temps),
        "t_median": statistics.median(temps),
        "rain_total": sum(r.rain_mm for r in items),
        "wind_max": max(r.wind_ms for r in good),
        "wind_dir_mean": mean_wind_direction([r.wind_dir_deg for r in good]),
        "completeness": len(good) / EXPECTED_READINGS_PER_DAY,
        "flagged": len(items) - len(good),
    }


def write_summaries(summaries, path):
    fields = [
        "station", "date", "t_min", "t_max", "t_mean", "t_median",
        "rain_total", "wind_max", "wind_dir_mean", "completeness", "flagged",
    ]
    with open(path, "w", newline="") as f:
        writer = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=fields)
        writer.writeheader()
        for s in summaries:
            if s:
                writer.writerow(s)


def run(path_in, path_out, day):
    readings = load_readings(path_in)
    check_ranges(readings)
    check_jumps(readings)
    stations = sorted({r.station_id for r in readings})
    summaries = [daily_summary(readings, s, day) for s in stations]
    write_summaries(summaries, path_out)
    return summaries
```

Background: the network has 61 stations and each sends a reading every ten minutes, so a day's file holds about 8,800 rows, though the yearly reprocessing job loads 3.2 million rows at once. Some older stations send timestamps in local time, not UTC, and a few send humidity as a fraction between 0 and 1. Rain readings are the amount since the previous reading, not cumulative totals. The summaries feed a public website, so a wrong number is embarrassing, and we occasionally get duplicate rows when a station resends after a connection drop.

# VOLUNTEER SERVICES AND VENUE LICENCE AGREEMENT

This Agreement is made on 2 September between **Saltmarsh Film Festival CIC** ("the Festival"), whose office is at 14 Quay Lane, and **Harbourlight Cinemas Ltd** ("the Venue Owner"), whose registered office is at 3 Grain Street.

## 1. Definitions

"Festival Period" means the eleven days from 9 October to 19 October inclusive. "Premises" means Screens 1, 2 and 4, the foyer and the upstairs bar area of the Venue Owner's cinema at 3 Grain Street. "Volunteers" means individuals recruited by the Festival who give their time without payment. "Venue Staff" means employees of the Venue Owner.

## 2. Licence

2.1 The Venue Owner grants the Festival a non-exclusive licence to use the Premises during the Festival Period between 09:00 and 23:30 each day for the public screening of films and related talks.

2.2 The Festival may not sub-license the Premises or allow a third party to run any event there without written consent, which the Venue Owner will not unreasonably withhold.

2.3 Screen 3 and the café remain under the Venue Owner's control. The Festival may not place signs or equipment in either.

## 3. Fees

3.1 The Festival shall pay a licence fee of 18,000, in two instalments: 9,000 on signing and 9,000 no later than 5 October.

3.2 If the Festival fails to pay an instalment within seven days of the due date, the Venue Owner may suspend access to the Premises until the sum is paid, and the Festival remains liable for the full fee.

3.3 The Venue Owner keeps all income from food and drink. The Festival keeps all ticket income, less a booking charge of 4 percent which the Venue Owner collects through its ticketing system and pays over within 30 days after the Festival Period.

## 4. Volunteers

4.1 The Festival shall provide up to 60 Volunteers. Each shift lasts no more than six hours without a break of at least 30 minutes.

4.2 The Festival is responsible for recruiting Volunteers, checking that they are at least 16 years old, and giving them a safety briefing before their first shift. Volunteers under 18 shall not work in the upstairs bar area or after 22:00.

4.3 Volunteers are not employees or workers of the Venue Owner, and nothing in this Agreement creates an employment relationship. The Venue Owner may give reasonable instructions to Volunteers about safety, but shall not direct them to do work normally done by Venue Staff, such as handling cash in the café or operating projectors.

4.4 The Festival shall keep a record of each Volunteer's name, contact details, shift times and briefing date, and shall give the record to the Venue Owner on request.

## 5. Insurance and liability

5.1 The Festival shall hold public liability insurance of at least 2,000,000 for the Festival Period and shall give the Venue Owner a copy of the certificate by 25 September.

5.2 The Festival shall indemnify the Venue Owner against all claims, losses and costs arising from the acts or omissions of the Festival or its Volunteers at the Premises, except to the extent that they are caused by the negligence of the Venue Owner or Venue Staff.

5.3 The Venue Owner's total liability to the Festival under this Agreement, whether in contract or otherwise, shall not exceed the licence fee paid. Nothing in this Agreement limits liability for death or personal injury caused by negligence.

5.4 The Venue Owner is not liable for loss of, or damage to, equipment or property belonging to the Festival or Volunteers kept at the Premises.

## 6. Cancellation

6.1 If the Festival cancels all or part of the Festival Period more than 60 days before it begins, it shall pay 25 percent of the licence fee. If it cancels within 60 days, it shall pay the full fee.

6.2 If the Venue Owner cannot make the Premises available for reasons within its control, it shall refund the fee for each day lost and may be required to pay the Festival's reasonable costs of finding a substitute venue, up to 5,000.

6.3 Neither party is liable for failure to perform caused by events outside its reasonable control, including fire, flood, government order or the closure of the Premises on police advice. In that case the Venue Owner shall refund the fee for the days lost, but the Festival shall not be entitled to any other compensation.

## 7. Data and publicity

7.1 Each party shall comply with data protection law in relation to personal data it holds about Volunteers and audiences. The Venue Owner shall not use Volunteer contact details for marketing.

7.2 The Venue Owner may use the Festival's name and photographs taken in public areas for its own promotion until the end of the following year.

## 7A. Safety and access

7A.1 The Venue Owner shall ensure that fire exits, alarms and emergency lighting in the Premises are in working order throughout the Festival Period, and shall give the Festival's safety lead a copy of the current fire risk assessment by 25 September.

7A.2 The Festival shall appoint a named safety lead for each day of the Festival Period. The safety lead shall brief all Volunteers on evacuation routes and shall be present in the Premises whenever the public is admitted.

7A.3 The Venue Owner confirms that Screens 1 and 2 have step-free access and a wheelchair space in each row marked "A". Screen 4 is reached by a staircase only. The Festival shall not schedule events in Screen 4 which it has advertised as step-free.

7A.4 The maximum number of people in each room is the number stated on the Venue Owner's licence from the local council. The Festival shall not sell more tickets than that number for any screening.

## 8. Termination and general

8.1 Either party may end this Agreement immediately by written notice if the other commits a serious breach that cannot be put right, or does not put right another breach within 14 days of written notice.

8.2 This Agreement is governed by the law of England and Wales. Any dispute shall first be discussed by the directors of both parties for 21 days before either may start court proceedings.

8.3 Notices under this Agreement must be in writing and sent by post or by email to the address at the head of this Agreement. A notice sent by email is treated as received on the next working day. Changes to this Agreement are only valid if both parties sign them.

Signed for the Festival: Rosalind Achterberg, Director. Signed for the Venue Owner: Desmond Quillfeather, Managing Director.

The trainees are dental nurses and reception staff, so please keep the language practical.

# Instrument decontamination and cross-infection control — Session 3

Presenter: Wilhelmina Oyelaran, Lead Nurse, Birchfield Dental Group (9 clinics)

## 1. Why this session matters

Every instrument that enters a patient's mouth must be treated as contaminated afterwards, whatever the patient looks like or says. We cannot tell by looking who carries a blood-borne virus. So we follow one standard: "standard precautions" for everyone. Our group inspection last spring found that the weakest point was not the sterilising machine but the steps either side of it: the moment instruments leave the surgery, and the moment they are put away.

## 2. The decontamination cycle

The route is always one way, from dirty to clean, and never back:

1. Collect and transport (dirty zone)
2. Clean (manual wash or washer-disinfector)
3. Rinse
4. Inspect under a magnifier
5. Sterilise (autoclave)
6. Package and date-label
7. Store (clean zone)

Each clinic has a decontamination room divided into a dirty side and a clean side, with a separate sink for hand washing. Staff must never carry a tray from the clean side back to the dirty side.

## 3. Cleaning

Cleaning removes the blood, saliva and debris that protect germs from sterilisation. An instrument that is not clean cannot be made sterile.

- **Washer-disinfector (preferred).** A cycle runs a cold rinse, a wash at 55 degrees C, and a thermal disinfection hold at 90 degrees C for at least one minute. Never overload the racks: instruments must not overlap or touch.
- **Manual cleaning (backup only).** Use a dedicated sink, water at no more than 45 degrees C (hotter water fixes proteins onto the metal), detergent at the dilution on the label, and a long-handled brush. Keep instruments below the water surface while brushing to avoid splashes. Use a second sink or a clean bowl to rinse.

Routine test: a cleaning-efficacy test strip is run through the washer-disinfector once a week, and its result is recorded in the log.

## 4. Inspection

Check every instrument under a lit magnifier. Look for remaining debris, rust or pitting, bent tips and loose joints. Dental handpieces should be flushed and lubricated according to the maker's instructions. Anything damaged is taken out of use and reported to the practice manager.

## 5. Sterilisation

Our clinics use bench-top vacuum autoclaves, type B, which can sterilise wrapped and hollow instruments.

- Standard cycle: 134 degrees C for 3.5 minutes at about 2.1 bar of pressure.
- Each load must have a printout or data record showing that temperature, pressure and time were reached.
- Do not overload: the chamber should be at most two thirds full. Pouches go in with the paper side facing the plastic side of the next pouch so steam can pass.
- A helix test is run every morning before the first load. A vacuum leak test (a "Bowie-Dick type" test) is run weekly. If the test fails, take the autoclave out of use and do not process any instruments until it is checked.
- Pouches are valid for 12 months if stored dry and intact. Unwrapped instruments must be used immediately.

## 6. Storage and dating

After the autoclave finishes, wait until the pouches are dry. A wet pouch is considered unsterile and must be repackaged and put through the autoclave again. Label each pouch with the date of sterilisation, the autoclave number and the initials of the person who packed it. Store pouches in closed drawers on the clean side, at least 20 cm from the floor.

## 7. Worked case for the tutorial

At the Elmbridge clinic, the morning helix test strip shows an incomplete colour change. The nurse, Tavita, has already run a load of 14 pouches at 08:05 for the 08:30 patient.

What should she do? First she stops using the autoclave and puts a sign on it. Then she informs the practice manager. The pouches from the 08:05 load are quarantined and must be reprocessed in a different autoclave once a passing test has been recorded on that machine. The 08:30 patient's treatment must use instruments from a verified source, such as a second autoclave in the same clinic or a sealed set sterilised at another site. The incident is written in the log with the time, the machine number, the test result and the action taken.

## 8. Personal protective equipment

Before touching dirty instruments: gloves (heavy-duty for cleaning, single-use nitrile for chairside work), a plastic apron, eye protection and a fluid-resistant mask. Gloves are never washed and reused. Hands are washed before and after glove use, for at least 20 seconds, using the six-step technique on the poster above each sink.

## 9. Sharps and spillages

Needles and blades go into a sharps box immediately after use, by the person who used them. Never re-sheath a needle with two hands. If you suffer a needlestick injury: let the wound bleed, wash with soap and running water, do not scrub or suck, cover it, and tell the practice manager at once. A medical assessment is needed within two hours if possible. A blood spill is covered with absorbent granules containing chlorine at 10,000 ppm, left for the contact time on the label, and then removed with a scoop into a clinical waste bag.

## 10. Mistakes we found in last spring's inspection

- Instruments left to soak in a bowl on the dirty side for over an hour. Soaking is allowed only to stop blood drying, and for no more than 30 minutes.
- Handpieces put in a pouch without lubrication, which shortened their life and left residue in the autoclave.
- Pouches stored on the windowsill of the decontamination room, where sunlight and condensation damaged the seals.
- Missing initials on pouches, so no one could tell who packed a failed load.
- Reception staff carrying used trays through the waiting room instead of using the sealed transport box.

## 10a. Second worked case

At the Holloway clinic, the washer-disinfector breaks down on a Tuesday and the engineer cannot come until Thursday. The clinic has 38 patients booked on Wednesday and has only two spare sets of instruments per surgery. Nurse Alinta decides to wash manually. Her checklist: fill the dedicated sink with water at 40 degrees C and add detergent; brush each instrument under the surface for at least 30 seconds, paying attention to hinges and serrations; rinse in the second sink; dry on a lint-free cloth; inspect under the magnifier; then autoclave as normal. The manual method takes about 6 minutes per tray and it must be recorded in the log that the washer was out of service. She also asks the practice manager to cancel the weekly efficacy test, which no longer applies, but to restart it as soon as the machine is repaired.

## 11. Records to keep

Daily autoclave log, weekly cleaning-efficacy test, helix and vacuum tests, load printouts for two years, sharps injury register, and training records for every member of staff.

Please critique it honestly, suggest the main alternatives we should compare it with, and then give me an implementation plan with phases, staffing and the risks. I'm especially unsure about the alerting logic and the data volumes, so please check those closely.

# Design: Night-flow Leak Detection Service (NLDS)

Author: Philippa Underhill-Okoye. Reviewers: Gustav Linnemann, Rashida Mbeki. Status: draft 2, for architecture review.

## 1. Problem

Aldermere Water supplies about 94,000 homes through 212 district metered areas (DMAs). Each DMA has an inlet flow meter and a pressure logger that reports every 15 minutes. Leaks are currently found in two ways: customer calls, and a monthly spreadsheet exercise in which an analyst compares the minimum night flow (between 02:00 and 04:00) of each DMA with its value in the previous month. Last year the average time from a leak starting to a repair crew arriving was 19 days. The regulator has set a target of 7 days by the end of next year.

## 2. Goals and non-goals

Goals: detect a significant new leak in a DMA within 48 hours of its start; provide the dispatch team with a ranked list of the DMAs most likely to hold a new leak; reduce false alarms to no more than 5 per week across the network.

Non-goals: locating the leak on the street (a separate acoustic survey does that), customer-side leaks, and billing.

## 3. Inputs

- DMA inlet flow in cubic metres per hour, every 15 minutes, from the telemetry platform's export (a CSV file dropped into a storage bucket every hour).
- Pressure at the average-zone-point logger, every 15 minutes.
- A table of DMA properties: number of connections, length of mains, percentage of non-domestic use, and the last known leakage level.
- A calendar of events that affect flow, such as flushing, planned shutdowns and mains refilling after repairs. This calendar is currently a shared spreadsheet filled in by crews, on a best-effort basis.

Data volume: 212 DMAs x 96 readings x 2 signals per day, about 41,000 rows a day, or 15 million a year.

## 4. Approach

For each DMA, the service computes the night flow each day as the minimum of the 1-hour rolling mean between 02:00 and 04:00. It then calculates a baseline from the previous 28 days, using the median. A DMA is flagged when the night flow exceeds the baseline by more than the larger of 2.5 cubic metres per hour or 3 times the DMA's own standard deviation of night flow over the baseline period. The pressure is used to correct for changes in demand: when the average pressure on the night differs from the baseline by more than 4 metres of head, the night flow is scaled using a fixed exponent of 1.15.

A flag becomes an alert when the same DMA is flagged on two consecutive nights. Alerts go to the dispatch team's work queue as a ticket with the DMA name, the estimated extra flow, the date it began, and a link to a chart.

## 5. Architecture

A scheduled job runs every hour, reads new files from the bucket, loads them into PostgreSQL, and recomputes the night flow for the current day. A second job runs at 06:00 to compute the baseline and the flags. The services run as containers on the utility's existing Kubernetes cluster. A small web page shows each DMA's last 60 days of night flow with the baseline and alert markers. There is no machine learning in the first version.

## 6. Failure handling

If a DMA's data has more than 8 missing readings in the night window, that day is skipped and not counted towards an alert. If the telemetry export is more than 3 hours late, the on-call analyst receives an email. An alert that has been open for more than 5 days with no repair visit is escalated to the network manager.

## 7. Event calendar

A flag is suppressed if the event calendar lists a flush, a shutdown or a refill for the DMA on that day or the day before. Because the calendar is incomplete, we estimate that 1 in 4 such events is missing, and the analysts will mark such alerts as false by hand. A button on the ticket allows them to do this.

## 7a. Data quality

Flow meters drift, and some of the older electromagnetic meters under-read by up to 3 percent. A step change in a DMA's baseline that follows a meter replacement would look like a leak (or a leak repair). The service therefore reads a table of meter work orders and ignores the three nights after any meter service on that DMA. Readings that are exactly zero for more than an hour on a DMA with more than 100 connections are treated as telemetry faults and removed. For 14 of the 212 DMAs, the inlet is fed by two meters, and the service sums them; if one meter fails, the day is skipped.

## 7b. Dispatch integration

The work queue used by the dispatch team has a REST interface that accepts a JSON ticket. The service posts a ticket when an alert is created, and updates the same ticket once a day with the new estimate of extra flow until the ticket is closed. When a crew closes a ticket with the code "no leak found", the service records this as a false alert, and the DMA's threshold is raised by 10 percent for the next 28 days. After two such codes in 60 days, the DMA is excluded from automatic alerts and moved to a manual weekly review. Tickets are never created outside office hours; alerts raised overnight are batched and sent at 07:30.

## 7c. Security and access

The service only reads from the telemetry bucket and writes to its own database and the work queue. Credentials come from the cluster's secret store. The web page is available only on the internal network and uses the staff single sign-on. Analysts can override alerts; the dispatchers can only view them.

## 8. Rollout and measures

Pilot on 20 DMAs for 8 weeks, comparing alerts with the monthly spreadsheet method and with actual crew findings. If at least 70 percent of alerts lead to a confirmed leak, extend to all 212 DMAs. Measures: time from leak start to repair, alerts per week, share of alerts confirmed, number of manual overrides.

## 9. Risks and open points

- Seasonal change in demand, for instance in the school holidays and during the summer, may move the baseline faster than 28 days can follow.
- Large industrial users in some DMAs have night shifts that change from week to week.
- Rashida asks who is accountable when an alert is ignored.
- Gustav asks whether the 15-minute interval is fine enough to detect bursts that last under an hour.

## 10. Staffing

One data engineer for 3 months, one hydraulic analyst at 50 percent for 6 months, and part of a front-end developer for the web page. Philippa estimates the total cost at 95,000.

Please write a complete test plan from the specification below, with numbered test cases (preconditions, steps, expected results), grouped by area, and mark which ones should be automated. Also list any places where the spec is ambiguous or leaves something out, because we need to settle those before testing begins.

# Product Specification: Platform Announcements (PAN) v1.2

Owner: Hildegard Ostrowski-Bell, Passenger Information. Engineering lead: Mikael Dovrenko. Operator: Calderbrook Regional Railways.

## 1. Overview

PAN produces spoken and written announcements at 38 stations from live train data. It replaces the manual announcement desk at the 31 small stations and supplements staff at the 7 major stations. Each platform has a speaker group, a text display and (at major stations) a second display on the footbridge.

## 2. Inputs

PAN receives from the train running system, every 30 seconds, a list for each platform of trains due in the next 60 minutes, with: service number, destination, scheduled time, expected time, platform, number of carriages, and status (on time, delayed, cancelled, platform changed, terminating here).

## 3. Announcement types

3.1 **Approaching.** Played 2 minutes before expected arrival. Text: "The [time] [operator] service to [destination], calling at [stops], is approaching platform [n]." Calling points are read only if there are 6 or fewer; otherwise only the first 3 and the last stop are read.

3.2 **Arrival.** Played when the train is detected in the platform. Text: "The [time] service to [destination] is now arriving at platform [n]. This train has [x] carriages." The carriage number is omitted if it is unknown.

3.3 **Delay.** Played when the expected time is at least 5 minutes after the scheduled time, and again every 10 minutes until the train arrives, at most 3 times. Text: "The [time] service to [destination] is delayed. It is now expected at [expected time]." If the delay exceeds 30 minutes, the sentence "We apologise for the delay" is added.

3.4 **Cancellation.** Played immediately when a train is cancelled, then repeated 5 minutes later. If another train to the same destination departs within 30 minutes, the text adds "The next service to [destination] is the [time]."

3.5 **Platform change.** Played immediately on all platforms involved. Priority over all other announcements. Text: "Platform change. The [time] service to [destination] will now depart from platform [n], not platform [old]." The footbridge display shows the change in red for 10 minutes.

3.6 **Terminating.** For trains that end at the station, "This train terminates here. All change, please." is played after the arrival announcement.

## 4. Queueing and priority

4.1 Only one announcement is played on a speaker group at a time.
4.2 Priority order (highest first): platform change, safety message, cancellation, arrival, delay, approaching.
4.3 A higher-priority announcement waits for the current one to finish; it does not interrupt it, except for safety messages, which interrupt immediately.
4.4 If an announcement has waited more than 45 seconds in the queue, it is discarded, except for platform changes and safety messages, which are never discarded.
4.5 Two announcements of the same type for the same train are never queued at the same time.

## 5. Quiet hours

Between 23:00 and 05:30, spoken announcements are limited to platform changes, cancellations and safety messages. Text displays always show all announcements. Stations with housing within 50 metres of the platform may set their own quiet hours between 22:00 and 06:00.

## 6. Language

Announcements are produced in English. At 6 stations near the border, they are followed by a Welsh version of the same announcement. Place names are pronounced using a pronunciation table that staff can edit. If a place name is not in the table, the default voice pronunciation is used.

## 7. Staff override

A station supervisor can use a tablet to (a) pause all spoken announcements for up to 15 minutes, (b) type and play a custom message, up to 160 characters, and (c) mark a platform as closed, in which case no trains are announced there and the display reads "Platform closed". An override is logged with the supervisor's name and time.

## 8. Fault behaviour

8.1 If no data arrives for 90 seconds, the text display shows "Train information unavailable" and spoken announcements stop. When data resumes, the display clears automatically.
8.2 If a speaker group fails its hourly self-test, the fault is sent to the control room, and announcements for that platform appear only on the displays.
8.3 If the data feed returns a train with an unknown destination code, the announcement uses the text "a service" in place of the destination and an alert is raised.

## 9. Performance

A spoken announcement must start within 3 seconds of the triggering event, measured at the speaker. The system must handle 40 platforms and up to 6 simultaneous events per second.

## 9a. Volume and sound

9a.1 The announcement volume at each speaker group follows the ambient noise measured by a microphone on the platform, between a minimum of 55 dB and a maximum of 85 dB at one metre from the nearest speaker. When a freight train passes without stopping, the volume rises automatically for its duration and the announcement queue is held for up to 20 seconds.

9a.2 At stations with a staffed ticket office, supervisors can lower the maximum to 75 dB between 06:00 and 08:00 if there are complaints. The setting is saved per station and survives a restart.

## 9b. Display text

9b.1 The text display shows the next four trains for its platform, in time order, with destination, scheduled time and expected time. Cancelled trains stay on the display, in red, until their scheduled time has passed plus 10 minutes. Terminating trains show "Terminates here" instead of a destination.

9b.2 Destination names longer than 24 characters are shortened using a table of approved abbreviations. If a name is not in the table, it is cut at 21 characters followed by "...".

9b.3 The display brightness follows a light sensor between 20 and 100 percent. At night it never goes below 20 percent.

## 9c. Logging

Every announcement is written to a log with the time it was queued, the time it started, the platform, the train and the text. Logs are kept for 90 days. A supervisor can view the last 24 hours of logs from the tablet. Discarded announcements are logged with the reason "expired in queue".

## 10. Out of scope

Customer mobile notifications, onboard announcements, and public address calls from the control room.
