# Internal Audit Report: Medicines Management, Inpatient Pharmacy

Hospital: St. Aldric's Hospital (620 beds). Auditor: Cordelia Fairweather-Nkosi, Clinical Governance. Audit period: 1 April to 30 June. Report date: 14 July. Report status: final, for committee.

## 1. Scope and method

The audit covered the main inpatient pharmacy, 14 ward medicine cupboards, the controlled drugs (CD) registers on 9 wards, the fridge temperature records, and the discharge medicines process. The auditor reviewed 120 randomly selected patient drug charts, observed 6 medicines rounds, counted CD stock on 9 wards, and interviewed 11 staff. All wards were given 5 working days' notice of the visit.

## 2. Summary of findings

Of the 31 standards tested, 22 were fully met, 6 were partially met and 3 were not met. Overall compliance was 71 percent for full compliance, up from 64 percent last year. No harm to patients was identified.

## 3. Controlled drugs

Nine ward registers were checked and the physical stock was counted against the register. On 8 wards the stock matched the register. On Ward 7B, the count of morphine sulphate 10 mg ampoules differed by 3: the register showed 18, the cupboard held 15. The ward manager reported a discrepancy to pharmacy two days after the count, not the same day as the policy requires. The three missing ampoules were later found recorded on a patient's chart but not in the register. The CD keys were handed over correctly on all wards, but on two wards, 4A and 7B, the key was in the possession of a nurse who was not on the authorised list. Two entries in the registers on Ward 3C were not countersigned.

## 4. Storage and fridges

Of the 14 cupboards inspected, 12 were locked and tidy. On Ward 5A, the cupboard was left unlocked while the nurse was in a bay, for about 4 minutes during the observed round. Fridge temperature records were reviewed for the 91 days of the audit period across 22 fridges. The expected range is 2 to 8 degrees C. In 19 fridge-days (about 1 percent of the 2,002 fridge-days), the maximum temperature was above 8 degrees, and in 11 of those, the log has no note of action. On 3 April, the fridge on Ward 6B reached 11.2 degrees for an estimated 6 hours after a door was left open; insulin and two vaccines were in it. They were not discarded and no advice was sought from pharmacy.

## 5. Prescribing and administration

In the 120 drug charts, 103 (86 percent) had a recorded allergy status. Of the 17 that did not, 6 belonged to patients admitted via the emergency department overnight. In 9 charts, there was an omitted dose without a reason code. In 4 charts, an antibiotic was prescribed for longer than the 7 days in the policy with no review date. Across 6 observed rounds, 41 administrations were seen; in 3, the nurse did not check the patient's wristband before giving the drug.

## 6. Discharge medicines

Pharmacy reconciled medicines for 74 percent of discharges in the quarter, against a target of 90 percent. The weakest areas were Friday afternoons and the surgical wards, where 58 percent of discharges were reconciled. The median time for a discharge prescription to be dispensed was 118 minutes, against a target of 90. The auditor found that 22 of the 120 charts belonged to patients discharged in the audit period; 7 of them left without a complete medicines list for their GP.

## 7. Staffing

The pharmacy ran at 11 percent vacancy among pharmacy technicians in the quarter, with 4 posts unfilled out of 36. Three of the six ward-based pharmacists were on leave or sick in June. Medicines reconciliation on the surgical wards relies on a single technician.

## 7a. Incidents and reporting culture

In the quarter, 187 medicines incidents were reported on the hospital's incident system, against 214 in the same quarter last year. The auditor notes that a fall in reports is not necessarily a good sign. The most common types were omitted doses (58), wrong time (31) and documentation errors (27). Eleven incidents were graded as causing minor harm, none as moderate or severe. Reports from nurses accounted for 81 percent, from pharmacists 12 percent and from doctors 2 percent. Staff interviews suggested that doctors rarely report because they do not receive feedback on earlier reports. The medication safety officer, Beauregard Tanaka-Weiss, produces a monthly bulletin, but only 4 of the 11 interviewed staff had seen one.

## 7b. Antimicrobial stewardship

Of the 120 charts, 38 included at least one antibiotic. In 31 of the 38 (82 percent), the indication was documented. The policy requires a review at 72 hours; this was recorded in 24 of the 38 (63 percent). The four charts with courses longer than 7 days and no review date are included in this group. The antimicrobial pharmacist visits each ward twice a week but reviewed only the charts flagged by wards.

## 7c. Training

Mandatory medicines management training was up to date for 88 percent of nurses and 69 percent of junior doctors. On Ward 7B, 3 of 22 nurses had not completed the CD training in the last 12 months, and the nurse involved in the discrepancy was one of them. Pharmacy technicians had a completion rate of 97 percent.

## 8. Actions already taken

The Ward 7B discrepancy has been investigated and closed. The authorised key-holder lists have been updated on all wards. Fridge alarm thresholds on the 22 fridges have been set to alert after 15 minutes out of range.

## 9. Recommendations of the auditor

1. Re-audit CDs on wards 4A, 7B and 3C within three months.
2. Introduce a daily fridge check sign-off, with a written action for any excursion.
3. Extend the pharmacist-led reconciliation to Friday afternoons.
4. Add a prompt in the electronic chart for allergy status and for antibiotic review at day 5.
5. Repeat the wristband observation with 30 administrations.

I wrote it for the frame shop at Halden Cycles to plan which frame batches go through the paint booth each week, and I'm not sure the batching and the lead time logic are right. Tell me what is wrong or fragile, what you would change, and show the tests with pytest.

```python
"""paint_plan.py - weekly paint booth planning for the Halden Cycles frame shop.

Frames arrive from welding as orders. Each order has a frame model, a colour,
a quantity and a due date. The booth can only hold one colour per run, and a
colour change needs a flush. We group orders into runs, sort the runs, and
report which orders will be late.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import csv
import datetime as dt
import io
from collections import defaultdict
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

BOOTH_CAPACITY = 24          # frames per run
RUN_MINUTES = 95             # minutes to paint and cure one run
FLUSH_MINUTES = 40           # minutes to flush when the colour changes
SHIFT_MINUTES = 8 * 60       # one working shift
SHIFTS_PER_DAY = 2

COLOUR_FAMILIES = {
    "gloss black": "dark",
    "matt black": "dark",
    "forest green": "dark",
    "signal red": "bright",
    "sunrise orange": "bright",
    "pearl white": "light",
    "sky blue": "light",
}


@dataclass
class Order:
    order_id: str
    model: str
    colour: str
    quantity: int
    due: dt.date
    rush: bool = False

    def family(self) -> str:
        return COLOUR_FAMILIES.get(self.colour.lower(), "other")


@dataclass
class Run:
    colour: str
    orders: list = field(default_factory=list)
    frames: int = 0

    def room(self) -> int:
        return BOOTH_CAPACITY - self.frames

    def add(self, order: Order, count: int) -> None:
        self.orders.append((order, count))
        self.frames += count

    def earliest_due(self) -> dt.date:
        return min(o.due for o, _ in self.orders)


def parse_orders(text: str) -> list:
    """Read orders from CSV text with a header row."""
    orders = []
    reader = csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(text))
    for row in reader:
        due = dt.datetime.strptime(row["due"], "%Y-%m-%d").date()
        qty = int(row["quantity"])
        if qty < 0:
            raise ValueError("negative quantity for " + row["order_id"])
        orders.append(
            Order(
                order_id=row["order_id"],
                model=row["model"],
                colour=row["colour"].strip().lower(),
                quantity=qty,
                due=due,
                rush=row.get("rush", "") == "yes",
            )
        )
    return orders


def build_runs(orders: list) -> list:
    """Group orders into booth runs, one colour per run."""
    by_colour = defaultdict(list)
    for order in orders:
        by_colour[order.colour].append(order)

    runs = []
    for colour, group in by_colour.items():
        group.sort(key=lambda o: o.due)
        current = Run(colour)
        for order in group:
            left = order.quantity
            while left > 0:
                take = min(left, current.room())
                current.add(order, take)
                left -= take
                if current.room() == 0:
                    runs.append(current)
                    current = Run(colour)
        if current.frames > 0:
            runs.append(current)
    return runs


def order_runs(runs: list) -> list:
    """Sort runs: rush first, then earliest due date, then by colour family
    so that similar colours sit next to each other."""
    def key(run: Run):
        has_rush = any(o.rush for o, _ in run.orders)
        family = run.orders[0][0].family()
        return (not has_rush, run.earliest_due(), family)

    return sorted(runs, key=key)


def minutes_for(runs: list) -> int:
    total = 0
    previous = None
    for run in runs:
        if previous is not None and previous.colour != run.colour:
            total += FLUSH_MINUTES
        total += RUN_MINUTES
        previous = run
    return total


def schedule(runs: list, start: dt.date) -> dict:
    """Return a map of order_id to the date its last frame is finished."""
    finish = {}
    day = start
    minutes_used = 0
    capacity_per_day = SHIFT_MINUTES * SHIFTS_PER_DAY
    previous = None
    for run in runs:
        cost = RUN_MINUTES
        if previous is not None and previous.colour != run.colour:
            cost += FLUSH_MINUTES
        if minutes_used + cost > capacity_per_day:
            day += dt.timedelta(days=1)
            minutes_used = 0
        minutes_used += cost
        for order, _ in run.orders:
            finish[order.order_id] = day
        previous = run
    return finish


def late_orders(orders: list, finish: dict) -> list:
    late = []
    for order in orders:
        done = finish.get(order.order_id)
        if done is not None and done > order.due:
            late.append((order.order_id, (done - order.due).days))
    late.sort(key=lambda item: item[1], reverse=True)
    return late


def weekly_report(text: str, start: dt.date) -> str:
    orders = parse_orders(text)
    runs = order_runs(build_runs(orders))
    finish = schedule(runs, start)
    late = late_orders(orders, finish)
    lines = [
        f"runs: {len(runs)}",
        f"booth minutes: {minutes_for(runs)}",
        f"late orders: {len(late)}",
    ]
    for order_id, days in late:
        lines.append(f"  {order_id} is {days} day(s) late")
    return "\n".join(lines)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sample = (
        "order_id,model,colour,quantity,due,rush\n"
        "H-1001,Trail 29,Forest Green,30,2026-03-04,\n"
        "H-1002,City 700,Pearl White,12,2026-03-03,yes\n"
        "H-1003,Trail 29,Forest Green,10,2026-03-06,\n"
        "H-1004,Gravel X,Signal Red,24,2026-03-05,\n"
    )
    print(weekly_report(sample, dt.date(2026, 3, 2)))
```

I run the back office for a coworking operator with five sites, and our reporting database has gotten slow. Can you review the design of this schema, tell me which indexes are missing or useless, and rewrite the six queries at the bottom so they run faster? Please explain each rewrite so I can tell the person who maintains the dashboards what changed and why.

```sql
-- Tablewise Workspaces: members, desks, bookings, invoices
-- PostgreSQL 15

CREATE TABLE site (
    site_id      serial PRIMARY KEY,
    name         text NOT NULL,
    city         text NOT NULL,
    opened_on    date NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE member (
    member_id    serial PRIMARY KEY,
    full_name    text NOT NULL,
    email        text NOT NULL,
    company      text,
    plan         text NOT NULL,           -- 'flex', 'fixed', 'team', 'day-pass'
    joined_on    date NOT NULL,
    left_on      date,
    home_site_id integer REFERENCES site(site_id)
);

CREATE TABLE desk (
    desk_id      serial PRIMARY KEY,
    site_id      integer NOT NULL REFERENCES site(site_id),
    label        text NOT NULL,
    kind         text NOT NULL,           -- 'hot', 'fixed', 'office', 'room'
    seats        integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
    monthly_rate numeric(10,2)
);

CREATE TABLE booking (
    booking_id   serial PRIMARY KEY,
    member_id    integer NOT NULL REFERENCES member(member_id),
    desk_id      integer NOT NULL REFERENCES desk(desk_id),
    starts_at    timestamp NOT NULL,
    ends_at      timestamp NOT NULL,
    status       text NOT NULL,           -- 'confirmed', 'cancelled', 'no-show', 'used'
    created_at   timestamp NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    note         text
);

CREATE TABLE invoice (
    invoice_id   serial PRIMARY KEY,
    member_id    integer NOT NULL REFERENCES member(member_id),
    issued_on    date NOT NULL,
    due_on       date NOT NULL,
    paid_on      date,
    total        numeric(10,2) NOT NULL,
    currency     text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'EUR'
);

CREATE TABLE invoice_line (
    line_id      serial PRIMARY KEY,
    invoice_id   integer NOT NULL REFERENCES invoice(invoice_id),
    description  text NOT NULL,
    quantity     numeric(8,2) NOT NULL,
    unit_price   numeric(10,2) NOT NULL,
    booking_id   integer REFERENCES booking(booking_id)
);

CREATE INDEX idx_member_email ON member (email);
CREATE INDEX idx_member_company ON member (company);
CREATE INDEX idx_member_plan_left ON member (plan, left_on);
CREATE INDEX idx_booking_status ON booking (status);
CREATE INDEX idx_booking_created ON booking (created_at);
CREATE INDEX idx_invoice_member ON invoice (member_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_invoice_paid ON invoice (paid_on);

-- Size today: member ~ 4,100 rows, desk ~ 310, booking ~ 2.3 million,
-- invoice ~ 58,000, invoice_line ~ 410,000.

-- Query 1: occupancy of each site for last month
SELECT s.name,
       count(*) AS bookings,
       sum(extract(epoch FROM (b.ends_at - b.starts_at)) / 3600) AS hours
FROM booking b
JOIN desk d ON d.desk_id = b.desk_id
JOIN site s ON s.site_id = d.site_id
WHERE to_char(b.starts_at, 'YYYY-MM') = to_char(now() - interval '1 month', 'YYYY-MM')
  AND b.status IN ('confirmed', 'used')
GROUP BY s.name
ORDER BY hours DESC;

-- Query 2: members with unpaid invoices more than 30 days overdue
SELECT m.full_name, m.email, m.company,
       (SELECT sum(i.total) FROM invoice i
         WHERE i.member_id = m.member_id AND i.paid_on IS NULL
           AND i.due_on < current_date - 30) AS overdue_total
FROM member m
WHERE m.member_id IN (
    SELECT member_id FROM invoice
    WHERE paid_on IS NULL AND due_on < current_date - 30
)
ORDER BY overdue_total DESC;

-- Query 3: members who joined this year and never made a booking
SELECT m.member_id, m.full_name, m.joined_on
FROM member m
WHERE extract(year FROM m.joined_on) = extract(year FROM now())
  AND m.member_id NOT IN (SELECT member_id FROM booking)
ORDER BY m.joined_on;

-- Query 4: revenue per site per plan, invoiced last quarter
SELECT s.name, m.plan, sum(l.quantity * l.unit_price) AS revenue
FROM invoice_line l
JOIN invoice i ON i.invoice_id = l.invoice_id
JOIN member m ON m.member_id = i.member_id
JOIN site s ON s.site_id = m.home_site_id
WHERE i.issued_on >= date_trunc('quarter', now() - interval '3 months')
  AND i.issued_on < date_trunc('quarter', now())
GROUP BY s.name, m.plan
ORDER BY s.name, revenue DESC;

-- Query 5: the ten busiest meeting rooms by hours booked this year,
-- with how often they were cancelled or not used
SELECT d.label, s.name AS site,
       sum(extract(epoch FROM (b.ends_at - b.starts_at)) / 3600)
           FILTER (WHERE b.status IN ('confirmed', 'used')) AS hours_booked,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE b.status = 'cancelled') AS cancelled,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE b.status = 'no-show') AS no_shows
FROM desk d
JOIN site s ON s.site_id = d.site_id
JOIN booking b ON b.desk_id = d.desk_id
WHERE d.kind = 'room'
  AND date_part('year', b.starts_at) = date_part('year', now())
GROUP BY d.label, s.name
ORDER BY hours_booked DESC
LIMIT 10;

-- Query 6: for each member, the date of their latest booking, used for
-- the "we miss you" email to anyone silent for 60 days
SELECT m.member_id, m.email,
       (SELECT max(b.starts_at) FROM booking b
         WHERE b.member_id = m.member_id) AS last_booking
FROM member m
WHERE m.left_on IS NULL
  AND m.plan <> 'day-pass'
  AND (SELECT max(b.starts_at) FROM booking b
        WHERE b.member_id = m.member_id) < now() - interval '60 days';
```

Here is the design doc for our new aeration control system at the Marsh Lane treatment works. Please critique it honestly, suggest at least two real alternatives to the main approach, and then write an implementation plan I can take to the project board. I am especially worried about the failure behaviour, because the operators do not trust anything that touches the blowers.

# Design: Adaptive Aeration Control for Marsh Lane Works

Author: Pieter Vandenhoek, process engineering
Status: Draft 3, for review
Reviewers: Lena Okafor (operations), Dmitri Salvesen (electrical), Anouk Rademaker (compliance)

## 1. Background

Marsh Lane treats about 38,000 cubic metres of sewage a day for roughly 140,000 people. The biological stage consists of four parallel aeration lanes. Each lane has three zones with fine bubble diffusers, fed by a shared header from three turbo blowers (B1, B2, B3). Today the blowers run on a fixed schedule built from a diurnal curve that the operators adjust by hand, usually twice a day, and again whenever a storm arrives.

Aeration is the biggest single use of electricity on site, about 52 percent of the 6.1 GWh we bought last year. Effluent ammonia is also our tightest consent limit: 3 mg/L as a rolling 24-hour mean, with a hard cap of 8 mg/L on any composite sample. We exceeded the daily mean on 11 days last year, nine of them during the cold weeks of January and February.

## 2. Problem

The fixed schedule over-aerates at night, when the load is low, and under-aerates in the morning peak, when the load rises faster than the operators can react. Dissolved oxygen (DO) in zone 2 of lane 3 swung between 0.4 and 4.1 mg/L on a typical weekday last month. Low DO risks ammonia breakthrough. High DO wastes energy and damages the floc, which then settles badly in the clarifiers.

## 3. Goals

1. Keep zone DO within 1.5 to 2.5 mg/L for 90 percent of the time.
2. Cut aeration energy by at least 12 percent over a full year.
3. Never reduce the number of ammonia consent days met compared with the manual regime.
4. Let an operator take back control of any lane in under 10 seconds.

Non-goals: replacing the PLC, changing the diffuser layout, or controlling the return sludge pumps.

## 4. Proposed design

### 4.1 Overview

We add a supervisory controller that runs on a new industrial PC in the blower hall cabinet. It reads DO, ammonium and nitrate probes from the existing PLC over OPC UA every 10 seconds, computes a DO setpoint for each zone, and writes the setpoints back to the PLC. The PLC keeps its own proportional-integral loops that move the zone air valves and the blower speed. The controller never writes valve positions or blower speeds directly.

### 4.2 Setpoint logic

For each zone the controller uses a cascade. The outer loop looks at the ammonium reading in zone 3 of each lane. If ammonium at the end of the lane is above 1.0 mg/L, it raises the DO setpoint of zones 1 to 3 in steps of 0.2 mg/L. If ammonium is below 0.4 mg/L for 30 minutes, it lowers the setpoints in the same steps. Setpoints are clamped to 1.0 to 3.0 mg/L. The inner loop is the existing PLC DO control.

We also add a feed-forward term from the inflow meter. When inflow rises by more than 15 percent within 20 minutes, setpoints go up by 0.3 mg/L at once, before the ammonium probe can see the change. This addresses the morning peak and the storm response.

### 4.3 Blower sequencing

The controller does not choose which blowers run. The PLC keeps the existing most-open-valve logic: header pressure is held constant, and the blower count follows demand. We only expect the lower DO setpoints at night to reduce the header demand enough that one blower can drop out.

### 4.4 Data and logging

Every cycle the controller writes the inputs, setpoints and a reason code to a local time series store, which is copied to the historian every five minutes. Operators see the current setpoints and the reason code on a new page of the existing SCADA screens. All changes of setpoint are also written to the audit log with the controller version.

### 4.5 Operator override

Each lane gets a new key switch on the local panel, with positions Auto, Manual and Off. In Manual, the PLC ignores the controller and uses the last operator setpoint. A button on the SCADA screen does the same for all lanes, and requires a second operator to confirm.

## 5. Failure behaviour

If the controller stops writing for 60 seconds, the PLC holds the last setpoint for 5 minutes and then reverts to the fixed schedule. If a probe reading is out of range or flat-lined for 20 minutes, the controller marks that lane as degraded and holds the setpoints at 2.0 mg/L. If the OPC UA link drops, the PLC reverts after the same 60 seconds. When the controller returns, it does not take over again until an operator presses acknowledge.

The industrial PC has a single power supply on the plant UPS. We do not plan redundancy for the first release. A watchdog restarts the service if it does not complete a cycle in 30 seconds.

## 6. Safety and compliance

The controller can only move setpoints inside the clamp range, which the PLC enforces again on its own side. Any change to the clamp range requires a PLC program change under our existing management of change procedure. Anouk has confirmed that the consent monitoring does not change, since the composite sampler and the online ammonium analyser at the outfall are independent of the new system.

## 7. Testing

We will build a simple model of one lane in the plant simulator from the last two years of historian data and replay the January weeks. The acceptance test is that the simulated controller meets the DO band and reduces energy against the recorded manual operation. After that, we run it on lane 4 only for eight weeks, with lanes 1 to 3 as the control group. Lane 4 is chosen because it has the newest probes.

## 8. Rollout

Weeks 1 to 4: hardware, network and OPC UA tags. Weeks 5 to 8: simulation and tuning. Weeks 9 to 16: lane 4 trial. Weeks 17 to 24: lanes 1 to 3 one at a time, with a two-week hold between lanes. Go or no-go decision at the end of week 16 by Lena and Anouk jointly.

## 9. Cost

Industrial PC and cabinet work: 14,000. Network switch and firewall: 6,500. Two additional ammonium probes for lane 4: 11,000. Engineering time, internal: about 60 days. Contractor for PLC changes: 18,000. Expected annual saving at 12 percent of aeration energy: about 32 MWh a month, or 380 MWh a year, which is roughly 57,000 a year at our current price of 0.15 per kWh. Simple payback is therefore a little under one year after the trial, and about eighteen months counting the trial period itself.

## 10. Open questions

- Do we have enough probe maintenance capacity? Probes drift, and today they are cleaned every two weeks.
- Should the feed-forward term use the inflow meter or the upstream pump station level?
- Who owns the controller software after the contractor leaves?

I own a small hotel and I have just been sent this partner agreement by a booking startup called Stayloop. I'm not a lawyer and I need to decide by Friday whether to sign. Could you explain it to me clause by clause in plain language, and tell me which clauses carry real risk for a hotel like mine (22 rooms, family owned) and what I should try to negotiate?

PARTNER HOTEL AGREEMENT

between Stayloop Travel Ltd ("Stayloop"), registered in Eastmarch, and the hotel named in the signature block ("the Hotel").

1. Purpose. Stayloop operates an online marketplace on which travellers can search for and book rooms. The Hotel wishes to list its rooms on the marketplace, and Stayloop agrees to display them and to take bookings on the Hotel's behalf under these terms.

2. Listing and content. The Hotel will give Stayloop accurate descriptions, photographs, room types, facilities and house rules. The Hotel grants Stayloop a non-exclusive, worldwide licence to use this content to promote the Hotel on the marketplace and in advertising, including on third-party websites. Stayloop may edit photographs for size and quality. The Hotel confirms that it owns or controls the rights to everything it supplies.

3. Rates and availability. The Hotel sets its own rates and availability through the Stayloop extranet. The Hotel agrees that the rate shown on the marketplace for any room and date will be no higher than the rate the Hotel offers on its own website, by telephone or through any other online agency for the same room, dates and conditions ("rate parity"). If Stayloop finds a lower public rate elsewhere, it may reduce the displayed rate to match it, and the Hotel will honour that rate.

4. Commission. For every confirmed booking, the Hotel will pay Stayloop a commission of 17 percent of the room price excluding taxes. Where a guest books through a promotion labelled "Stayloop Boost", the commission rises to 22 percent for that booking. Commission is due on the room price actually paid by the guest, and also on the price of any breakfast or other service included in the rate. It is not due on services the guest buys separately at the Hotel.

5. Payment. Guests pay the Hotel directly at check-out unless the booking was prepaid. For prepaid bookings, Stayloop collects payment and pays the Hotel the room price less commission within 45 days after the guest's departure. For other bookings, Stayloop will send a monthly commission invoice, and the Hotel will pay it within 14 days. Overdue amounts carry interest of 1.5 percent per month. Stayloop may set off any amount the Hotel owes against any amount Stayloop owes the Hotel.

6. Cancellations and changes. The Hotel will apply the cancellation policy that it entered in the extranet. Where Stayloop's standard "free cancellation" label is used, guests may cancel without charge up to 48 hours before arrival. If the Hotel cancels a confirmed booking, or cannot honour it, the Hotel will find the guest equivalent or better accommodation nearby at the Hotel's cost and will pay Stayloop a handling fee of 150 euros per affected booking. If a guest does not arrive and has not cancelled, the Hotel may charge the first night, and commission is still due on that night.

7. Reviews. Only guests who have completed a stay may post reviews. Stayloop may display, rank and summarise reviews in its own way and is not obliged to remove a review unless it breaks Stayloop's published content rules. The Hotel may post one public reply to each review. Stayloop may use review scores in deciding how prominently to display the Hotel in search results.

8. Visibility and ranking. Stayloop decides how the Hotel appears in search results. Ranking may depend on price, review scores, conversion, cancellation rates, commission level and participation in promotions. Stayloop does not guarantee a minimum number of bookings or any placement.

9. Guest data. Stayloop will pass on the details needed to host the guest. Each party is responsible for its own use of guest data under applicable data protection law. The Hotel will not use guest contact details from Stayloop bookings to market to the guest directly outside the stay, nor to encourage the guest to book directly in the future. Stayloop may keep and use booking data, including prices and occupancy, for analytics and to improve its services, and may share anonymised data with partners.

10. Exclusivity and non-circumvention. For 24 months after a guest's first booking through Stayloop, the Hotel will pay commission on any later booking made by the same guest at the Hotel by any channel, unless the guest has made a separate booking through another independent agency in the meantime. The Hotel will keep a record of the guests concerned and will let Stayloop audit this record once a year.

11. Liability. Stayloop is only a platform and is not responsible for the Hotel's services, safety or accuracy of the Hotel's information. The Hotel is liable to guests and to Stayloop for any loss arising from a failure to honour a booking or from inaccurate content. Stayloop's total liability to the Hotel in any year is limited to the commission it received from the Hotel in the previous three months. The Hotel will indemnify Stayloop against third-party claims arising from the Hotel's content or its premises.

12. Term and termination. The agreement runs for an initial period of 24 months from signature and then renews automatically for successive periods of 12 months unless one party gives written notice at least 90 days before the end of the period. Either party may end the agreement at once for a serious breach not corrected within 14 days of notice. Stayloop may suspend the Hotel's listing immediately if it believes the Hotel has breached rate parity, or if review scores fall below 6.0 out of 10 for two consecutive months. If the Hotel ends the agreement during the initial period without cause, it will pay Stayloop an early termination fee equal to the commission earned in the previous six months.

13. Changes. Stayloop may change the commission rates, promotion rules, or these terms by giving 30 days' notice by email. If the Hotel does not object in writing in that period, it is treated as having accepted the change. If the Hotel objects, Stayloop may end the agreement without liability.

14. Confidentiality. The commission rates and the contents of this agreement are confidential and may not be shared with other hotels, agencies or the press, except to the Hotel's professional advisers.

15. Governing law and disputes. This agreement is governed by the law of Eastmarch. Disputes will be settled by arbitration in the city of Eastmarch Port in English, under the rules of a recognised commercial arbitration centre, by a single arbitrator. The costs of the arbitration are shared equally unless the arbitrator decides otherwise.

16. Insurance. The Hotel will keep public liability insurance of at least 2 million euros per claim for the whole term and will give Stayloop a copy of the certificate on request. If the certificate lapses, Stayloop may suspend the listing until a new one is supplied, and bookings lost during the suspension remain at the Hotel's risk.

17. Force majeure. Neither party is liable for failing to perform because of events outside its reasonable control, such as flood, fire, strikes, government orders or failure of public networks. This does not excuse the Hotel from refunding prepaid amounts for bookings it cannot honour, and it does not excuse either party from paying money already due.

18. Entire agreement. This agreement replaces all earlier discussions and emails between the parties. Any term printed on the Hotel's own forms or confirmation emails does not apply. If a clause is found to be unenforceable, the others remain in force.

Below are the methods and results sections of a manuscript from our process research group, submitted to a paper-industry journal. I've been asked to referee it. Please write a detailed peer review: a summary of the claims, major concerns about the design and statistics, minor points, and a clear recommendation with the changes you would need to see.

Effect of Cationic Starch Dosage and Refiner Intensity on Dry Strength and Drainage in Recycled Testliner: A Pilot-Scale Factorial Study at the Aldermoor Mill

2. Methods

2.1 Furnish and pilot equipment. The furnish was a mixed recovered paper grade (approximately 70 percent old corrugated containers, 30 percent mixed office waste), pulped for 25 minutes at 4.5 percent consistency in a batch pulper and then screened through a 0.20 mm slotted screen. All trials were run on the Aldermoor pilot paper machine (width 0.5 m, speed 40 m/min) over three consecutive weeks. Stock was pumped from a single 12 m3 chest that was topped up with fresh pulp each Monday. Whitewater was recirculated within each week, but the system was drained and cleaned at the end of each week.

2.2 Experimental design. We varied two factors. Cationic starch dosage had three levels (0, 6 and 12 kg per tonne of dry fibre, added at the machine chest). Refiner intensity, set by specific edge load, had two levels (low, 2.0 Ws/m, and high, 3.5 Ws/m), at a fixed specific energy of 90 kWh/t. This gave six treatment combinations. Each combination was run once per week, in the order that suited the operators, giving three runs per treatment. Basis weight was held at 125 g/m2 by adjusting the stock flow, and wet-end pH at 7.1 by adding alum when needed. Retention aid was kept at 400 g/t for all runs.

2.3 Measurements. After each run reached steady state (judged by headbox consistency within 2 percent for ten minutes), we collected five 1 m sheets from the reel, conditioned them at 23 degrees C and 50 percent relative humidity for 24 hours, and tested them. Burst index (ISO 2758), ring crush index (ISO 12192) and tensile index (ISO 1924-2) were measured on ten specimens per sheet, and the values were averaged per run. Drainage was characterised by Schopper-Riegler number on a stock sample taken at the headbox, and by the vacuum level required at the second suction box to hold 18 percent solids after the press. Specific energy of the vacuum system was read from the mill meter.

2.4 Statistics. Run-level means were analysed with a two-way analysis of variance with interaction, at the 5 percent level. Where the interaction was significant, we compared the means pairwise with Student's t-tests without adjustment. The effect of starch was also fitted by linear regression of strength on dosage, using all 18 runs. Normality was checked by eye on residual plots. No runs were excluded.

2.5 Economic estimate. The saving per tonne was calculated from the mill's 2025 average prices: cationic starch at 640 euros per tonne, electricity at 0.14 euros per kWh, and recovered paper furnish at 118 euros per tonne of dry fibre. Fibre saved by lowering basis weight was credited at the furnish price. The extra vacuum energy was taken directly from the mill meter readings during each run. Drying steam was not included because the pilot machine has an electric dryer section that is not representative of the full-scale machine.

3. Results

3.1 Strength. Starch dosage raised all three strength indices. Mean burst index rose from 1.52 kPa m2/g at 0 kg/t to 1.74 at 6 kg/t and 1.83 at 12 kg/t. Ring crush index rose from 6.1 to 6.9 and 7.2 N m/g. Tensile index rose from 31.4 to 35.0 and 36.9 N m/g. The effect of dosage was significant for all three (p < 0.01). The effect of refiner intensity was significant only for tensile index, where the high-intensity setting gave 2.1 N m/g more on average (p = 0.03). The interaction was significant for burst index (p = 0.04): at high intensity, the gain from 6 to 12 kg/t starch was 0.02, whereas at low intensity it was 0.16.

Table 1. Mean burst index (kPa m2/g) by treatment, three runs each.

| Starch kg/t | Low intensity | High intensity |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 1.49 | 1.55 |
| 6 | 1.71 | 1.77 |
| 12 | 1.87 | 1.79 |

3.2 Drainage. Schopper-Riegler number increased with refining intensity from 34 to 38 on average and was not affected by starch (p = 0.41). The vacuum level needed at the second suction box increased with starch dosage, from 31 kPa at 0 kg/t to 34 kPa at 6 and 37 kPa at 12 kg/t. This corresponds to a rise of about 6 percent in vacuum energy per 6 kg/t. We interpret this as starch binding water in the web, though we did not measure water retention value.

3.3 Regression. The linear regression of burst index on starch dosage gave a slope of 0.026 per kg/t (R2 = 0.88, n = 18). We used this slope to estimate that each 1 kg/t of starch would allow a reduction of 1.6 g/m2 in basis weight at constant burst index, and, at the current starch price, a net saving of 2.3 euros per tonne of paper after counting the extra vacuum energy.

3.4 Variation between weeks. Week 3 gave higher strength than week 1 at all treatments, by 0.06 kPa m2/g on average for burst index. We attribute this to a higher proportion of old corrugated containers in the chest after the Monday top-up in week 3, which was not measured. The differences between weeks were not tested.

3.5 Conclusions drawn by the authors. A dosage of 6 kg/t of cationic starch with high refiner intensity gives the best compromise between strength and drainage and is recommended for full-scale trials on the Aldermoor testliner machine. Higher dosage is not justified because of the vacuum penalty and the plateau in burst index at high refining. The results are expected to carry over to other recycled grades.

3.6 Strip test on the full-scale machine. After the pilot trials, the mill ran the recommended setting (6 kg/t, high intensity) on its testliner machine for 36 hours. Mean burst index of the reel samples was 1.69 kPa m2/g against 1.58 during the preceding 36 hours at the usual setting of 3 kg/t and medium intensity. The machine speed was reduced from 820 to 790 m/min during the trial because of web breaks at the first press, which the operators did not attribute to the starch. The authors did not repeat the strip test.

Here are the first two chapters of a short story I'm writing. Please continue it for a long stretch, at least the next two chapters, in the same voice and tense, keeping the details consistent and letting the mystery develop without solving it too early.

THE WELL AT HOLLOWFIELD

1.

The bus left them at the end of the lane, where the tarmac gave up and became chalk, and the driver did not wait to see them off. Marit stood with her rucksack between her feet and watched the tail lights shrink down the valley until the hedges swallowed them. Behind her, eleven other students were making the small noises of people who had been told the place would be rustic and had not believed it.

"Is that it?" said a boy called Jonas, pointing across the field at a long low barn with a corrugated roof and a single chimney. Beside it stood a row of white tents, flapping slightly, and a portable toilet block that had been painted, at some point, with a mural of sunflowers.

"That's the school," said a woman's voice, and they turned. She had come up the lane from the other side, on foot, in boots that had once been yellow. She was perhaps sixty, wiry, with grey hair cut short as if she had done it herself in a car mirror. "I'm Dr Ilse Brandvold. You can call me Ilse, since you'll be seeing me at six in the morning with no coffee in me and I'd rather not be formal. Welcome to the Hollowfield Field School. Six weeks, one trench, no mercy."

She did not smile when she said it, but Marit thought something at the corner of her mouth considered the idea.

They were given tea in tin mugs in the barn, which smelled of woodsmoke and damp canvas, and a long table was cleared of trowels and sieves so that they could sit. On the wall behind Ilse hung a plan of the site drawn in blue and red ink: a large rectangle for the farmhouse that had stood here until the 1890s, a smaller one for the dairy, and in the lower left corner, a circle drawn with a compass and labelled in careful capitals, WELL? The question mark had been gone over so many times that it had torn the paper.

"Before anyone asks," Ilse said, "yes, we think there's a well. No, we have not found it. The tithe map of 1841 shows one in the yard. The 1890s survey shows nothing. A farmer who lived here told my predecessor in 1974 that his grandfather filled it in with the cellar stone from the old chapel, and my predecessor wrote that down and then died, and since then every field school student has dug in a different place and found a different set of nothing."

Somebody laughed. Ilse let them.

"This year we have a new idea," she went on. "Dr Okonkwo-Reyes from the geophysics department has been out with a resistivity meter and says there is something round and soft under the old yard. Round and soft is promising. It might be the well. It might also be a buried tractor tyre. Your job is to find out which, without breaking anything, and to write down everything you do while you do it."

Marit was a second-year, doing the school because her department required it, and because her mother thought fresh air would cure whatever it was that had kept her indoors all of last winter. She had not told anyone that she was a little frightened of soil. Not of dirt, exactly, but of the way it kept things. She had read once that a grave in clay could preserve a body for centuries, and the idea had stayed with her like a coin in her shoe.

2.

On the second morning they were given their trench. It lay thirty metres from the barn, a rectangle of four by three marked out with string and pegs by someone who had clearly been fussy about it. Ilse paired them off. Marit got Jonas, who had talked all through breakfast about a sailing trip he had done, and a supervisor called Wen, a doctoral student with a shaved head and a laminated checklist, who spoke to them in the careful voice of someone who has repeated a speech many times.

"First thing: you don't dig, you scrape," Wen said. "Trowel flat, pull towards you, thin layers. If you can see a colour change, you stop and tell me. If you find anything bigger than your thumbnail, you stop and tell me. If you find something you think you should not touch, you definitely stop and tell me."

"What if it's very shiny?" Jonas asked.

"Then you really stop."

The topsoil came off in a quarter of an hour, dark and crumbly, full of roots and the white threads of fungus. Beneath it, the colour changed to a mottled yellow-brown, and the first thing Marit found was a fragment of blue-and-white pottery no bigger than a postage stamp. She held it up between two fingers like something that might bite.

"Willow pattern," Wen said, without looking. "Victorian. Bag it, label it, put the context number on the tag. Context 104. Write it in your notebook as well, in pencil. Ink runs."

By lunchtime they had filled three finds bags with clay pipe stems, nails, and a button made of bone. By mid-afternoon the sun had come out over the ridge, and Marit had stopped being afraid of the soil, because it was simply hard work and her knees hurt.

It was Jonas who noticed the stones. He had moved to the north corner to clear a patch around one of the pegs, and he sat back on his heels and said, in a voice with no joke in it, "Marit, come and look at this."

A line of flat stones, fitted edge to edge, curved out of the north wall of the trench. They were small, the size of loaves, and set with a precision that did not look like a farmyard. Wen came across, crouched, and ran a finger along the top of the nearest one without touching it.

"That's a curve," she said quietly. "A proper one. Don't clean it. Don't brush it. I'm getting Ilse."

While they waited, Marit noticed that the soil beside the stones had a different smell. It was not the sweetness of rot, nor the dry mineral smell of the chalk. It was cold and metallic, like the inside of a tap that has not been used for years, and it rose from the gap between two stones in a thin breath that she felt on her wrist.

She did not say anything. She told herself that it was only air moving through a loose joint. But when Ilse arrived, jogging across the field with her yellow boots slapping and Dr Okonkwo-Reyes behind her carrying a tablet, Marit saw the older woman stop dead at the edge of the trench, look down at the stones, and then look, very quickly, at the barn, and at the date on the plan pinned inside it, as if she were counting something.

"Everyone out of the trench," Ilse said. "Please. Calmly. And nobody goes near it tonight."

PRODUCT SPECIFICATION: AUTOMATIC JOB ALLOCATION, Northgate Cab Dispatch Console, release 6.2
Owner: Farid Haddad (product). Reviewed by: Joanna Mbeki (dispatch supervisor), Ken Aoyama (engineering)

1. Overview

Northgate Cabs runs a dispatch centre that takes about 2,400 bookings a day by phone, app and the hotel desk portal. Today dispatchers assign each job to a driver by hand. This release adds automatic allocation: when a booking is confirmed, the system proposes the best available vehicle and, if the dispatcher has enabled automatic mode, offers the job to that driver without a dispatcher touching it. Dispatchers keep the ability to override at any time.

2. Definitions

- Job: a booking with a pickup address, optional destination, pickup time (now or later), passenger count and requirements.
- Driver status: Offline, Available, Offered, On job, Break.
- Zone: one of 14 named areas of the city, each with a polygon boundary.
- Requirement: wheelchair ramp, child seat, estate car, or pet friendly. A job may have several.

3. Functional requirements

3.1 Candidate selection
FR-1. For an immediate job, the system considers every driver with status Available whose last known position is no more than 6 km in a straight line from the pickup.
FR-2. A candidate must satisfy every requirement on the job. A vehicle with a ramp counts as having an estate car only if its profile also says so.
FR-3. A candidate must have room for the passenger count. A job with more than four passengers needs a six-seat vehicle.
FR-4. Candidates are ranked by estimated time of arrival (ETA) from the routing service. If the routing service does not answer within 2 seconds, straight-line distance is used instead and the job is marked "approximate ETA".
FR-5. If two candidates differ by less than 60 seconds of ETA, the driver who has waited longest since their last job is preferred.

3.2 Offers
FR-6. The top candidate receives an offer on the driver tablet showing pickup, destination, estimated fare and requirements. The driver has 20 seconds to accept or decline.
FR-7. If the driver accepts, status becomes On job and the job is assigned. If the driver declines or the timer runs out, the offer goes to the next candidate. After three failed offers, the job is returned to the manual queue with a red flag.
FR-8. A driver who declines or ignores three offers in a row is set to Break automatically and the supervisor is notified.
FR-9. A driver can only hold one offer at a time. A driver with status Offered is not a candidate for another job.

3.3 Pre-booked jobs
FR-10. A job with a pickup time more than 30 minutes ahead stays in the pre-book list. The system starts allocation 20 minutes before pickup time.
FR-11. For a pre-booked job, drivers who will finish their current job within 15 minutes and whose destination is within 6 km of the pickup are also candidates, with the finish time added to the ETA.
FR-12. If no driver is found 10 minutes before pickup, the supervisor sees an alert.

3.4 Manual override
FR-13. A dispatcher can reassign any job that has not yet started, with a mandatory reason chosen from a list. An override cancels any open offer on that job.
FR-14. A dispatcher can switch automatic mode on or off per zone. The setting takes effect for jobs confirmed after the switch.
FR-15. When automatic mode is off, the system still shows the ranked candidate list as a suggestion.

3.5 Special cases
FR-16. A job from the hotel desk portal marked "VIP" bypasses ranking and goes first to drivers with a rating of 4.8 or above.
FR-17. A job whose pickup is outside all zones is never allocated automatically and goes straight to the manual queue.
FR-18. During a driver shift change window (05:45 to 06:15 and 17:45 to 18:15), the radius in FR-1 is extended to 9 km.
FR-19. If the passenger cancels while an offer is open, the offer is withdrawn on the tablet within 3 seconds and the driver sees a message "Job cancelled".

3.6 Reporting and supervisor tools
FR-20. The supervisor screen shows, per zone, the number of Available drivers, open offers, jobs in the manual queue and the average time from confirmation to acceptance over the last 30 minutes.
FR-21. A daily report lists for each driver the number of offers received, accepted, declined and timed out, and the average acceptance time. The report is available by 06:00 for the previous day.
FR-22. A supervisor can export the allocation audit log for a chosen job number as a CSV file with one row per offer.
FR-23. A supervisor can set a driver to Break or Offline from the console. If the driver holds an open offer at that moment, the offer is withdrawn and passed to the next candidate without counting as a decline.

4. Non-functional requirements

NFR-1. The time between booking confirmation and the first offer shown on the tablet is under 4 seconds for 95 percent of jobs at a load of 40 bookings per minute.
NFR-2. The system must survive a restart of the allocation service without losing any open offer: open offers are restored from the database within 10 seconds.
NFR-3. If the routing service is down, allocation continues in approximate mode and the supervisor sees a banner.
NFR-4. Every allocation decision is written to an audit log with the candidate list, the reason for the choice and timestamps. Logs are kept for 13 months.
NFR-5. Driver positions older than 90 seconds are considered stale, and the driver is excluded from candidates.
NFR-6. The dispatcher console keeps working with the automatic mode toggle visible in browsers released in the last two years.

5. Out of scope

Fare calculation changes, payment, driver app redesign, and corporate account billing are not part of this release. Jobs shared between several passengers are not supported.

6. Open questions

Q1. Should the 20-second offer timer be longer for drivers who are currently driving and must stop to read the offer? Joanna thinks 25 seconds, Farid wants to measure first.
Q2. What happens to a pre-booked job that is allocated and then the driver goes offline? The draft assumes it returns to the pre-book list, but this needs to be confirmed with Ken.
Q3. How are VIP jobs treated when no driver has a rating of 4.8 or above nearby?

These are my notes from the internal training lecture on pathfinding at our studio, Lanternfish Games, given to the new gameplay programmers. I have a test on Thursday. Could you turn them into a proper study guide with worked examples I can follow by hand, and then a quiz of about ten questions with full answers? Please fix anything in my notes that looks wrong.

LECTURE 4: PATHFINDING AND NAVIGATION FOR NPCs
Speaker: Tomasz Wierzbicki (senior gameplay programmer)

1. Why this matters

Nearly every character in our current game, "Tidewalkers", has to get from A to B on a map with walls, water and moving crowds. Players forgive a lot, but they never forgive an enemy that walks into a wall or a companion that gets lost. Pathfinding runs every frame for dozens of agents, so it has to be correct and cheap. Budget: 0.5 ms per frame in total on the console target.

2. Representing the world

Three options:
- Grid: divide the map into square cells, each walkable or not. Simple, easy to debug, but memory heavy on large maps and paths look jagged (only 4 or 8 directions).
- Waypoint graph: designers place nodes by hand and connect them. Very cheap, but paths look robotic and designers have to maintain it.
- Navigation mesh (navmesh): a set of convex polygons covering the walkable surface. Agents move between polygons through shared edges. Far fewer nodes than a grid, and paths are smooth after a clean-up step. This is what we use for all open areas.

For the examples in this lecture we use a grid, because you can do it on paper.

3. Breadth-first search and Dijkstra

Breadth-first search (BFS) explores outward from the start in rings. It finds the path with the fewest steps when every step costs the same. It does not care about terrain cost. Dijkstra's algorithm fixes that: it keeps a priority queue ordered by the total cost from the start (called g), always expands the cheapest node, and updates neighbours if it finds a cheaper route to them. When the goal comes off the queue, its g is the cheapest cost. Dijkstra explores in all directions equally, which wastes work when the goal is far away in one direction.

4. A* search

A* adds a guess of the remaining distance to the goal, called the heuristic h. The queue is ordered by f = g + h. Nodes that look closer to the goal are expanded first. If h never overestimates the real remaining cost (it is "admissible"), A* still finds the cheapest path. If h is also consistent (h of a node is never more than the step cost to a neighbour plus h of that neighbour), a node never needs to be expanded twice.

Common heuristics on a grid:
- Manhattan distance, |dx| + |dy|: for 4-direction movement.
- Chebyshev distance, max(|dx|, |dy|): for 8-direction movement when diagonals cost the same as straight steps.
- Octile distance: for 8-direction movement when diagonals cost 1.4 (about the square root of 2) and straight steps cost 1. Formula: 1 * (dx + dy) + (1.4 - 2) * min(dx, dy).
- Euclidean distance: always admissible but usually too small on a grid, so A* explores more than needed.

Tomasz stressed: if h is too large (inadmissible, say 2 times Manhattan), A* runs faster but can return paths that are not the cheapest. Sometimes this is fine for background NPCs. For the player's companion we want the true optimum.

5. Worked example from the lecture

4-direction grid, every step costs 1. Start S at (0,0), goal G at (3,1). A wall occupies (1,0) and (1,1). Cells (1,2) and beyond are free.

- Open list: S with g = 0, h = |3-0| + |1-0| = 4, f = 4.
- Expand S. Neighbours: (1,0) is a wall, (0,1) is free, (0,-1) is outside the map. So we add (0,1) with g = 1, h = 3 + 0 = 3, f = 4.
- Expand (0,1). Neighbours: (1,1) is a wall, (0,2) is free, (0,0) is closed. Add (0,2): g = 2, h = 3 + 1 = 4, f = 6.
- Expand (0,2). Neighbours: (1,2) free. Add (1,2): g = 3, h = 2 + 1 = 3, f = 6.
- Expand (1,2). Neighbours: (2,2) free, (1,1) wall. Add (2,2): g = 4, h = 1 + 1 = 2, f = 6.
- Expand (2,2). Neighbours: (3,2) and (2,1). Add (2,1): g = 5, h = 1, f = 6. Add (3,2): g = 5, h = 1, f = 6.
- Expand either one. Take (2,1): neighbour (3,1) is the goal, with g = 6, h = 0, f = 6.
- Expand the goal. Path: S, (0,1), (0,2), (1,2), (2,2), (2,1), G. Cost 6.

Tomasz noted that Dijkstra would have expanded 3 more cells on this map, such as those at the bottom of the grid.

6. Making paths look natural

A* on a grid returns a list of cells. Moving through their centres looks stiff. Three clean-ups:
1. Line-of-sight smoothing: starting from the first node, skip ahead to the furthest node you can reach in a straight line without hitting an obstacle, then repeat from there. Cheap and effective.
2. The funnel algorithm: on a navmesh, once we know the sequence of polygons, we find the shortest path through the shared edges by tightening a "funnel" of left and right corners. Gives the optimal path inside the corridor.
3. Steering: agents follow the path using seek and arrive behaviours, with a small look-ahead so they cut corners softly.

7. Dealing with moving things

- Dynamic obstacles (doors, crates the player can push) are handled by marking navmesh tiles dirty and rebuilding that tile only, which takes about 2 ms on the worker thread. Agents re-plan when their next polygon has changed.
- Other agents: we do not put them in the A* graph. We use local avoidance (reciprocal velocity obstacles) on top of the path. Two agents walking toward each other each step aside by half.
- Crowd congestion: when more than 8 agents want the same corridor, the later ones wait at a queue marker instead of pushing.

8. Performance tips from the lecture

- Never run a path search in the same frame it was requested. Put requests in a queue and give the system a budget of 0.5 ms per frame; unfinished searches continue next frame.
- Cache paths for static destinations, such as "go to your workbench".
- Use hierarchical pathfinding for the big overworld: split the map into 32 by 32 clusters, find a path between cluster entrances first, then refine inside each cluster only as the agent approaches.
- Use a binary heap for the open list. A plain array makes each pop O(n) and killed the old prototype.
- Store g and parent in flat arrays indexed by node number, not in objects.

9. Debugging checklist

If an NPC will not move: is the start on the navmesh (snap it)? Is the goal reachable (flood fill from the start)? Is the agent radius larger than the doorway? Is the heuristic too heavy? Is the path request stuck in the queue?

Homework: implement A* with octile distance on the 64 by 64 test map and compare nodes expanded against Dijkstra.

File 2: collect.sh (called by cron each minute, and also by the nightly archive job)

```bash
#!/bin/bash
# kiln collector - Greywater Cement Works
DEST=/data/kiln
LOG=/var/log/kiln_collect.log
GATEWAY=$GATEWAY_HOST
TODAY=`date +%Y-%m-%d`

mkdir $DEST
cd $DEST

echo "starting $TODAY" >> $LOG

# fetch the latest readings
curl http://$GATEWAY/api/readings?unit=kiln1 -o readings_$TODAY.json

if [ $? = 0 ]; then
  python /app/parse.py readings_$TODAY.json > parsed.csv
else
  echo "fetch failed" >> $LOG
fi

# push to the database
curl -XPOST "http://influx.greywater.example.org:8086/api/v2/write?org=plant&bucket=kiln" \
  -H "Authorization: Token $INFLUX_TOKEN" \
  --data-binary @parsed.csv >> $LOG

# nightly cleanup and archive
HOUR=`date +%H`
if [ $HOUR = 02 ]; then
  tar czf /backup/kiln_$TODAY.tar.gz $DEST/*
  rm -rf $DEST/*
  scp /backup/kiln_$TODAY.tar.gz archive@10.20.4.90:/archive/
  find /backup -mtime +30 -exec rm {} \;
```

Below is our quarterly review for the Clearwater Hearing Clinic. I have to present it to the board on Monday and I haven't had time to read it properly. Could you give me a section-by-section summary, flag the numbers that don't seem to add up or that worry you, and finish with a list of recommendations in order of priority?

CLEARWATER HEARING CLINIC
QUARTERLY OPERATIONS REVIEW, Q3
Prepared by: Marguerite Oyelaran, clinic manager
Distribution: Board of trustees, lead audiologists

1. Executive summary

The clinic saw 1,946 patients in the quarter, up 6 percent from Q2 (1,836). Revenue was 612,400, which is 4 percent above plan, driven by the hearing-aid fitting service. The waiting time for a first assessment fell from 11 weeks to 8 weeks. Patient satisfaction stayed high at 4.6 out of 5. The main concerns are a rise in returns of one hearing-aid model, a staffing gap in the paediatric service, and a supplier price increase effective next quarter.

2. Patient volumes

New patient assessments were 702 (Q2: 655). Follow-up appointments were 1,244 (Q2: 1,181). Of the new patients, 61 percent were aged over 65, 34 percent were between 18 and 65, and 5 percent were children. The did-not-attend rate was 7.8 percent, against a target of 6 percent and 8.9 percent in Q2. The reminder text message pilot, which began in July in the Eastgate branch, reduced non-attendance there to 5.1 percent, while the Millford branch, which did not use reminders, stayed at 10.2 percent.

The clinic offered 2,150 appointment slots in the quarter. Utilisation was therefore 90.5 percent. Evening sessions on Tuesday and Thursday were 98 percent full, while Friday afternoons were 71 percent full.

3. Clinical outcomes

3.1 Hearing-aid fittings. We fitted 538 devices (Q2: 497). Of these, 319 were behind-the-ear models, 164 were receiver-in-canal models and 55 were custom in-the-ear models. The follow-up check at six weeks showed that 87 percent of patients reported improved speech understanding in noise, up from 84 percent.

3.2 Returns. The return rate within 60 days was 9.7 percent overall (52 devices), against 7.0 percent in Q2. Thirty-one of the 52 returns were of the Aria R2 receiver-in-canal model, which has a return rate of 18.9 percent among the 164 receiver-in-canal fittings. The reported reasons for these 31 returns were feedback whistling (14), moisture damage to the receiver (9), discomfort (5) and no reason given (3). The supplier has been notified and has promised a technical visit in October.

3.3 Tinnitus service. Forty-four patients were enrolled in the sound therapy programme. Twenty-nine completed the twelve-week course, and 22 of them reported a clinically meaningful reduction in the tinnitus handicap score. The programme has a waiting list of 17 patients.

4. Paediatric service

The paediatric audiologist, Dr Anselm Karlsson, will be on extended leave from 14 November. The clinic currently has 96 children on its active caseload, and 23 are due for review during his absence. We have asked the regional children's hospital whether it can accept referrals for the period, but it has not yet confirmed. Recruiting a locum has been difficult: we advertised in August and received one application, which did not meet the requirements for paediatric registration.

5. Finance

Revenue by line in thousands: assessments 148.2, hearing-aid sales and fittings 331.5, repairs and servicing 64.1, batteries and accessories 41.3, tinnitus programme 27.3. Total 612.4. The plan for the quarter was 589.0.

Expenditure was 571.9, which is 5 percent above the planned 544.0. Staff costs were 354.0, equipment and supplies 148.7 (of which hearing-aid purchases 119.2), premises 41.6 and other costs 27.6. The operating surplus was therefore 40.5, against a planned surplus of 45.0.

Three items explain most of the overspend, 23.2 of the 27.9. A one-off repair to the sound booth cost 9.8. Overtime in August to clear the assessment backlog cost 7.4. The new patient record software licence started two months earlier than budgeted, at a cost of 6.0.

6. Staffing

The clinic employs 14 full-time equivalent staff. In the quarter, one receptionist left and was replaced after a four-week gap. Sickness absence was 3.1 percent, up from 2.4 percent. The mandatory infection control training was completed by 12 of 15 eligible staff. All audiologists have current registration. The student placement programme took three trainee audiologists from the university for six weeks each.

7. Quality and complaints

We received 17 complaints (Q2: 12). Nine concerned waiting times for fittings, four were about billing, three about the behaviour of staff on the telephone, and one about the Aria R2 device. All were acknowledged within two working days. Fifteen were resolved within the 20-day target. Two remain open: one billing dispute where the patient says that a service plan was cancelled but is still being charged, and one dispute about a warranty claim on a device damaged by moisture. There were no serious incidents. One near miss was reported: a battery was given to a patient in the wrong size. It was caught at the desk.

8. Supplier and costs

Our main hearing-aid supplier has announced a price increase of 5.5 percent on all devices from 1 January, and a new minimum order quantity of 40 units a quarter. At the current volume of about 540 devices a quarter, the cost increase is estimated at 6.6 per quarter in thousands, if the mix does not change. The second supplier we use for the entry-level range offered a 3 percent discount if we commit to 200 units a quarter, which is about 37 percent of our volume.

9. Plans for next quarter

- Extend the text reminder pilot to Millford from 1 October.
- Open two extra Friday evening sessions to relieve the Tuesday and Thursday peak.
- Hold a technical review of the Aria R2 returns with the supplier.
- Confirm cover for the paediatric service before 14 November.
- Complete the infection control training for the remaining three staff.
- Decide on the second supplier offer before 1 December.

10. Risks

The main risks are the paediatric cover gap, a further rise in returns if the Aria R2 issue is not solved, and a cash flow squeeze in the first quarter of next year when the supplier price rise and the new minimum order take effect together with the winter fall in appointments, which has historically been about 8 percent.

Please review the design of this MySQL schema for our tea import business and tell me what you would change: keys, data types, missing constraints, indexes, and anything that will cause wrong numbers in reports. Then rewrite the seven queries at the end so they are correct and efficient, and explain each rewrite in a few sentences. I am not a database specialist, so say it in terms I can pass on to our contractor.

```sql
-- Mistral Leaf Trading: purchasing, stock and wholesale sales
-- MySQL 8.0

CREATE TABLE supplier (
    id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    name VARCHAR(255),
    country VARCHAR(100),
    contact_email VARCHAR(255),
    organic_cert VARCHAR(50)
);

CREATE TABLE tea (
    id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    supplier_id INT,
    name VARCHAR(255),
    type VARCHAR(50),             -- green, black, oolong, white, pu-erh, herbal
    harvest_year VARCHAR(10),
    origin_region VARCHAR(100),
    price_per_kg FLOAT,           -- purchase price in EUR
    sku VARCHAR(30)
);

CREATE TABLE shipment (
    id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    supplier_id INT,
    arrived DATETIME,
    container_ref VARCHAR(40),
    customs_cost FLOAT,
    freight_cost FLOAT
);

CREATE TABLE shipment_line (
    id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    shipment_id INT,
    tea_id INT,
    kg FLOAT,
    price_per_kg FLOAT,
    best_before VARCHAR(10)       -- stored as text like '2027-06'
);

CREATE TABLE customer (
    id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    name VARCHAR(255),
    kind VARCHAR(30),             -- cafe, shop, restaurant, online
    city VARCHAR(100),
    email VARCHAR(255),
    credit_limit FLOAT
);

CREATE TABLE sale (
    id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id INT,
    sold_on DATETIME,
    status VARCHAR(20),           -- open, shipped, paid, cancelled
    discount_percent FLOAT
);

CREATE TABLE sale_line (
    id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    sale_id INT,
    tea_id INT,
    kg FLOAT,
    unit_price FLOAT              -- selling price per kg in EUR
);

CREATE TABLE stock_adjustment (
    id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    tea_id INT,
    kg FLOAT,                     -- negative for losses
    reason VARCHAR(100),
    adjusted_at DATETIME
);

-- Rows today: tea 640, shipment 1,900, shipment_line 9,800, customer 1,350,
-- sale 41,000, sale_line 190,000, stock_adjustment 3,100.

-- Query A: current stock of each tea in kg
SELECT t.name,
       (SELECT SUM(kg) FROM shipment_line WHERE tea_id = t.id)
     - (SELECT SUM(kg) FROM sale_line sl
          JOIN sale s ON s.id = sl.sale_id
         WHERE sl.tea_id = t.id AND s.status <> 'cancelled')
     + (SELECT SUM(kg) FROM stock_adjustment WHERE tea_id = t.id) AS stock_kg
FROM tea t;

-- Query B: gross margin per tea for 2026
SELECT t.name,
       SUM(sl.kg * sl.unit_price) AS revenue,
       SUM(sl.kg * t.price_per_kg) AS cost,
       SUM(sl.kg * sl.unit_price) - SUM(sl.kg * t.price_per_kg) AS margin
FROM sale_line sl
JOIN sale s ON s.id = sl.sale_id
JOIN tea t ON t.id = sl.tea_id
WHERE YEAR(s.sold_on) = 2026
GROUP BY t.name
ORDER BY margin DESC;

-- Query C: customers who bought in 2025 but not yet in 2026
SELECT c.name, c.email
FROM customer c
WHERE c.id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM sale WHERE sold_on LIKE '2025%')
  AND c.id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM sale WHERE sold_on LIKE '2026%');

-- Query D: lots that expire within 90 days and are still in stock
SELECT t.name, l.best_before, l.kg
FROM shipment_line l
JOIN tea t ON t.id = l.tea_id
WHERE l.best_before < DATE_FORMAT(DATE_ADD(NOW(), INTERVAL 90 DAY), '%Y-%m')
ORDER BY l.best_before;

-- Query E: top five customers by revenue per city, excluding cancelled sales
SELECT c.city, c.name, SUM(sl.kg * sl.unit_price * (1 - s.discount_percent / 100)) AS revenue
FROM customer c
JOIN sale s ON s.customer_id = c.id
JOIN sale_line sl ON sl.sale_id = s.id
WHERE s.status != 'cancelled'
GROUP BY c.city, c.name
ORDER BY c.city, revenue DESC;

-- Query F: landed cost per kg of each shipment line,
-- spreading customs and freight by weight
SELECT sh.container_ref, t.name,
       l.price_per_kg + (sh.customs_cost + sh.freight_cost) / SUM(l.kg) AS landed_per_kg
FROM shipment sh
JOIN shipment_line l ON l.shipment_id = sh.id
JOIN tea t ON t.id = l.tea_id
GROUP BY sh.container_ref, t.name, l.price_per_kg, sh.customs_cost, sh.freight_cost;

-- Query G: customers whose unpaid sales exceed their credit limit
SELECT c.name, c.credit_limit,
       SUM(sl.kg * sl.unit_price) AS unpaid
FROM customer c
JOIN sale s ON s.customer_id = c.id
JOIN sale_line sl ON sl.sale_id = s.id
WHERE s.status IN ('open', 'shipped')
GROUP BY c.id
HAVING unpaid > c.credit_limit
ORDER BY unpaid DESC;
```

I'm the volunteer who looks after IT for Tidewater Rowing Club, and I've written up a design for a new boat booking and safety system. Please critique it honestly (what's missing, what's over-engineered, what could go wrong on the water), suggest alternatives to the main choices, and then give me an implementation plan with phases and rough effort that a few volunteers could realistically deliver.

DESIGN DOCUMENT: Boat Booking and Outing Log, version 0.4
Author: Aoife Brennan
Date: 2 October

1. Why we need it

The club has 61 boats (eights, fours, quads, doubles, singles and two coaching launches), about 230 members and a boathouse on a tidal river. Boat use is arranged today on a paper whiteboard in the boathouse and a WhatsApp group. This causes double bookings of the eights on Saturday mornings, no record of who took which boat out and when it returned, and there is no way to find out which boats have damage reports. After the incident in March, when a single sculler was out for four hours after dark without anyone noticing, the committee asked for a system that records every outing and warns when a boat is overdue.

2. Goals

- Members can book a boat and a time slot from their phone, up to 14 days ahead.
- Squad captains can reserve boats for a whole squad's training sessions.
- Every outing is logged on departure and on return, using a tablet at the boathouse door.
- If a boat has not returned by 30 minutes after the end of its booking, or at sunset plus 15 minutes, whichever is earlier, the duty officer's phone gets an alert.
- Damage reports can be filed for a boat, and a boat with serious damage cannot be booked.
- Safety rules are enforced: novices cannot book a single scull without a coach on a launch, and nobody may book a boat during a red flag condition.

Non-goals: payment, race entries, and the club's membership database (we will read from it, but not change it).

3. Users

Members (about 230), squad captains (9), coaches (6), duty officers (a rota of 14 volunteers), the boat captain who handles repairs (1), and the committee, who need reports.

4. Proposed architecture

A small web application written in Python using the Django framework, with a PostgreSQL database, running on a rented virtual server (about 12 per month). Members sign in with the email address in the membership list, receiving a one-time link; no passwords. The mobile experience is a responsive web page, not a native app. Notifications are sent by email and by SMS through a third-party gateway (about 4 pence per message, estimate 150 messages a month). The boathouse tablet runs the same web application in a kiosk mode.

Key tables: Member, Boat, Booking, Outing, DamageReport, Condition (stores the current flag colour and tide state entered by the duty officer), and Alert.

5. Main flows

5.1 Booking. The member picks a date and a slot, sees the available boats which match their grade, and confirms. The system checks the rules (grade, flag, double booking, damage status) before storing the booking. A booking can be cancelled up to one hour before the start.

5.2 Departure. At the boathouse, the member taps their name on the tablet, selects the booking, and confirms the crew list. The outing starts and the boat is marked "on water".

5.3 Return. The member taps "returned" on the tablet and answers a one-question damage check. If they report damage, they enter a short description and a photo may be added from their phone.

5.4 Overdue alerts. A scheduled job runs every five minutes, looks for outings that are on water and past their limit, and sends an SMS to the duty officer on the rota. If the duty officer does not acknowledge within ten minutes, the message goes to the second person on the rota, and then to the club safety officer.

6. Offline behaviour

The boathouse has poor mobile coverage and a flaky Wi-Fi router. The tablet app will keep a local copy of the day's bookings and queue departures and returns until the connection returns. We accept that the overdue alert will not fire while the tablet is disconnected.

7. Data and privacy

We store names, email addresses, mobile numbers (for duty officers only), and outing times. Outing logs are kept for 3 years for insurance reasons. Members can ask to see their data. We do not store location.

8. Security

One-time sign-in links last 15 minutes. Admin rights are given to the committee secretary and the boat captain. The database is backed up daily to a cloud bucket. The tablet is locked into the application and has no access to other apps.

9. Rollout

Pilot with the Tuesday evening squad for four weeks, then the whole club in the spring. The whiteboard stays in place for the first month in parallel. A training evening will be held for the duty officers.

9a. Reports for the committee

Each month the system produces a table of outings per boat, hours per member, and the number of damage reports, so that the committee can decide which boats need replacing and whether the club is using its eights enough to justify the cost of storing them. The reports are generated from the database as CSV files; there is no dashboard in the first release. The boat captain also wants a list of boats ordered by hours since the last service, because oars and riggers are checked every 200 hours of use.

9b. Running costs

Server 12 per month, SMS gateway about 6 per month, domain name 15 per year, backup storage about 2 per month. The club's treasurer has agreed to a budget of 300 for the first year, which the estimate meets with a margin of about 60. The tablet (a second-hand model with a rugged case) costs 140 and has already been bought.

9c. Alternatives considered

We looked at two commercial booking services used by other clubs. Both charge per member per year (3 to 5), which would be 700 to 1,150 a year for us, and neither supports the sunset rule or the red flag rule. We also thought about a shared spreadsheet with a script. It would be cheaper but could not send reliable overdue alerts and would be hard to hand over to a new volunteer.

10. Risks and open questions

- Volunteers may not tap the tablet when they leave in a rush. What then? Some suggested a QR code on each boat, scanned by the phone.
- Who updates the flag colour, and what happens if nobody does? At present it relies on a duty officer who might not be at the club.
- Sunset times change daily. We plan to calculate them from the date and the latitude of the boathouse.
- The system depends on a single volunteer (me). We need a backup person.
- Should coaches be able to override rule blocks? Aoife thinks yes, with a reason, and the safety officer is not sure.
- Is SMS the right channel for an urgent alert, given the poor coverage on the river bank?

11. Estimated effort

Roughly 120 hours of development, 30 hours of testing and 20 hours of training and documentation, over about five months of evenings and weekends.
