I'm a postdoc about to apply for observing time at Kestrel Ridge Observatory, and I've been sent their observing time and data policy. Could you explain it clause by clause in plain language, say what it means for someone in my position in practice, and point out the risks or traps I should watch for (deadlines, ownership of data, authorship, penalties)? Please also list what I should ask the observatory before I submit.

KESTREL RIDGE OBSERVATORY
OBSERVING TIME, DATA AND CONDUCT POLICY
Version 7, effective 1 January

1. Scope

This policy applies to everyone who applies for, receives or uses observing time on the 2.4 metre Harlow Telescope, the 0.8 metre Survey Telescope, or the instruments attached to them ("the facilities"), and to everyone who visits the site at Kestrel Ridge in person or controls the facilities remotely.

2. Eligibility

2.1 Applications for time may be made by researchers who hold a doctoral degree or are enrolled in a doctoral programme, and who are affiliated with a university or research institution that is a member of the Kestrel Consortium or has signed a user agreement with the Observatory.
2.2 The Principal Investigator ("PI") named on the proposal is responsible for the proposal, for the use of the awarded time, and for compliance with this policy by every person acting on their behalf.
2.3 A PI may not lead more than three proposals in any one call. A person may appear as co-investigator on any number of proposals.

3. Calls for proposals and deadlines

3.1 There are two calls each year, with deadlines on 15 March and 15 September at 23:59 Universal Time. Proposals received after the deadline will not be considered, and no exceptions are made for technical problems with the submission system unless the Observatory is at fault.
3.2 Proposals must be submitted through the Observatory portal and may not exceed four pages including figures, plus one page of references. A technical justification, which states the instrument set-up and the exposure times, must be included.
3.3 Applicants will be told the result of their proposal approximately eight weeks after the deadline.

4. Review and allocation

4.1 Proposals are ranked by a Time Allocation Committee ("the TAC") of ten external reviewers. Each proposal is read by at least three reviewers and ranked by scientific merit, feasibility and the suitability of the requested facility. Reviewers declare conflicts of interest, and do not take part in the ranking of any proposal in which they have a conflict.
4.2 The Observatory reserves 20 percent of the time on each facility for its own staff projects and for time-critical events such as supernova follow-up (see section 6). The remaining 80 percent is allocated by the TAC, of which up to 15 percent may be allocated to members of the Kestrel Consortium before ranking.
4.3 Rankings are final. Reviewers' comments are provided to PIs, but the Observatory does not enter into discussion of the ranking. An applicant who believes that the process was not followed correctly may write to the Director within 14 days of receiving the result.

5. Use of awarded time

5.1 Time is awarded in nights or part nights, in a specific semester. Time not used in the semester for which it is awarded lapses, and may not be carried over except where the Observatory decides that the loss was caused by instrument failure.
5.2 Observations are carried out in one of two modes. In visitor mode the PI or a team member travels to the site or connects remotely and operates the instrument with the support of a telescope operator. In service mode the Observatory staff carry out the observations on behalf of the PI, according to the conditions set out in the proposal.
5.3 If the weather or technical faults prevent observation, the Observatory will try to reschedule the time in the same semester. The Observatory does not compensate for lost time, and a refund of any fees is not available.
5.4 A PI who cannot use the time must give at least 14 days' notice. Time cancelled with less notice counts as used for the purpose of the PI's record, and a repeated failure to use time (two nights or more in any 12 months without good reason) may reduce the priority of the PI's later proposals.

6. Time-critical programmes

6.1 The Observatory may interrupt scheduled observations for a transient event of exceptional scientific interest if the event is judged by the Director to need immediate follow-up. The PI whose time is interrupted will be informed as soon as possible and will receive replacement time in the same or next semester, when available.
6.2 The Observatory is not liable for any costs of travel or accommodation incurred by a visiting observer whose time is interrupted under this section.

7. Data ownership and proprietary period

7.1 All data obtained with the facilities remain the property of the Observatory. The PI and the co-investigators named on the awarded proposal have the exclusive right to use the data for 12 months from the date on which the data are made available to them ("the proprietary period"). Data from programmes designated as survey or legacy programmes have no proprietary period.
7.2 After the proprietary period, the data become public through the Observatory archive without further notice. A PI may apply once, in writing, for an extension of up to six months. An extension will be granted only for a good reason, such as the completion of a doctoral thesis.
7.3 Calibration files and engineering data are public from the moment they are taken.
7.4 A PI may share proprietary data with collaborators who are not named on the proposal only if they are first added as co-investigators through the Observatory portal. Sharing data with an unlisted person is a breach of this policy.

8. Publication and acknowledgement

8.1 Every publication, thesis, press release or presentation that uses data from the facilities must carry the following acknowledgement: "Based on observations obtained at Kestrel Ridge Observatory." The PI must send the Observatory a copy of the paper within 30 days of publication.
8.2 The Observatory staff who give substantial scientific or technical support to the observations, such as writing special software or carrying out a non-standard observing procedure, should be offered co-authorship. The decision on co-authorship lies with the PI and the staff member concerned.
8.3 If a PI has not published or submitted a paper within 36 months of the end of the proprietary period, the Observatory may ask them to explain the delay, and may reduce the priority of later proposals.

9. Conduct and safety on site

9.1 Visitors must follow the instructions of the telescope operator and of the site manager at all times. The summit road is closed to visitors without a permit between 18:00 and 08:00 in winter conditions.
9.2 No lights may be used outside the buildings after sunset, except red lights approved by the Observatory. No drones or lasers may be operated on site without written permission.
9.3 Alcohol is not permitted in the control building or the dome.
9.4 Anyone who breaches section 9 may be asked to leave the site at their own cost. The Observatory may also refuse future access.

10. Liability

The Observatory is not liable for any loss or damage to the equipment, data or property of visitors, nor for injuries arising from visits, except where caused by its own gross negligence. Each visitor must have travel and health insurance valid for the site, which is at 2,350 metres above sea level.

11. Changes to the policy

The Director may amend this policy once a year. Changes take effect at the start of the next semester and do not apply to time already awarded.

I'm on the review panel for our internal research series and this write-up landed on my desk today. Could you write me a detailed peer review of it? I'd like you to go through the methods and the results, point out what is convincing and what is not, name any flaws in the design or the statistics, and tell me what the authors should do before we circulate it to the regional managers.

Title: Does a longer first fitting appointment reduce lens remakes? A staggered rollout across 38 Larkfield Opticians branches

Authors: Imogen Tarrant (Clinical Quality), Dev Okonkwo-Pryce (Data and Insight), Marta Lindqvist (Retail Operations)

1. Background

Lens remakes are the single largest avoidable cost in our dispensing operation. A remake happens when a customer returns within 60 days because the glasses do not suit them, for reasons such as the wrong fitting height, an unexpected swim effect, or discomfort with a progressive design. In the 2025 financial year the chain remade 11,420 pairs out of 96,180 dispensed, a remake rate of 11.9 percent, at an average cost of 74 pounds per remake in lenses, labour and postage. Clinical Quality proposed that the first fitting appointment, then scheduled at 15 minutes, was too short for staff to check frame position, explain adaptation and measure properly. The hypothesis was that extending the appointment to 25 minutes would lower the remake rate enough to pay for the extra staff time.

2. Methods

2.1 Design. We used a staggered rollout. Of 38 branches that dispense progressive and varifocal lenses, 12 were assigned to switch to the 25-minute fitting in March 2025, 13 in May 2025 and 13 in July 2025. Assignment was made by Retail Operations, who put the branches with the most available staff rooms into the earliest group so that the longer appointments would not collide with the diary. Branches therefore were not randomised. Each branch contributes the months before and after its own switch, and the main comparison is between the remake rate in switched branches and the remake rate in not yet switched branches in the same calendar month.

2.2 Population. We included every pair of glasses with progressive, varifocal or occupational lenses dispensed between 1 October 2024 and 31 August 2025 and counted a remake if a replacement was ordered for any clinical reason within 60 days of collection. Remakes due to damage, loss or a changed prescription from a new eye test were excluded. In total 41,870 eligible pairs were dispensed over the period, of which 17,310 were dispensed after their branch had switched.

2.3 Outcome. The primary outcome was the 60-day remake rate per branch per month. The secondary outcomes were the customer satisfaction score, a single question on a 1 to 5 scale sent by text message 14 days after collection, and the number of fittings completed per dispenser per day.

2.4 Analysis. We fitted a linear model of the monthly branch remake rate on a treatment indicator, with branch and calendar month fixed effects, weighting each branch month by the number of pairs dispensed. Standard errors were clustered by branch. We also report a simple unadjusted comparison of the average remake rate in the months before and after the switch. No sample size calculation was done in advance, as the rollout schedule was set by operations. Missing satisfaction scores, which were 61 percent of all pairs, were left out of the satisfaction analysis.

3. Results

3.1 Remake rate. In the unadjusted comparison across all groups the average progressive remake rate fell from 14.6 percent before the switch to 10.9 percent after, a drop of 3.7 percentage points. In the fixed effects model the estimated treatment effect was minus 2.4 percentage points (95 percent confidence interval minus 4.1 to minus 0.7). The effect was larger in the first group of branches (minus 3.8 points) than in the third group (minus 0.9 points, interval minus 3.0 to plus 1.2).

Table 1. Remake rate by rollout group (percent of eligible pairs, all months before and after each group's own switch)

| Group | Branches | Before | After | Change |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 (March 2025) | 12 | 15.2 | 11.1 | minus 4.1 |
| 2 (May 2025) | 13 | 14.5 | 10.8 | minus 3.7 |
| 3 (July 2025) | 13 | 14.1 | 10.7 | minus 3.4 |

Note that the group 3 figures rest on only two months after the switch (July and August 2025), because the data end on 31 August 2025, and the group 2 figures on four months. The model estimates in section 3.1 use all available months.

3.2 Satisfaction. The mean satisfaction score rose from 4.21 to 4.34 among customers who answered. The authors note that the response rate was higher after the switch, 42 percent against 36 percent.

3.3 Throughput. Dispensers completed an average of 9.1 fittings per day before the switch and 6.8 after it. Seven branches reported that they lengthened their opening hours on Saturdays to compensate, which is not reflected in the per day figures.

3.4 Cost. Using the 74 pound cost per remake, a 2.4 point reduction applied to 41,870 pairs would avoid about 1,005 remakes, a saving of roughly 74,400 pounds over eleven months. Extra dispenser time was estimated at 6,100 hours at 14.20 pounds an hour, which is 86,600 pounds, so the authors report a net cost of 12,200 pounds. They argue that the figure is acceptable because it ignores the value of customer goodwill and a lower number of complaints, which they did not measure.

4. Discussion

The authors conclude that the longer appointment works and recommend rolling it out to all 104 branches, including those that do not dispense many progressive lenses. They suggest the smaller effect in the third group is a sign that branches learned to use the time well only in the later months, and they attribute the larger early effect to the enthusiasm of the first adopters. They acknowledge that branches were not randomised but state that the fixed effects model removes any difference between them. They add that the weather in the spring of 2025 was unusually bright, which may have affected how many customers came in for sunglasses, but they did not adjust for this.

5. Limitations stated by the authors

The study covers a single financial year, and no data on lens type, frame type or the age of the customer were included in the model. The authors also say that dispensers knew which regime they were working under, so the remake decisions made by the dispensers could have been influenced, although remakes are logged by the laboratory and not by the branch.

6. Appendix: branch characteristics

Group 1 branches had on average 3.2 dispensers, group 2 had 2.8 and group 3 had 2.5. The mean number of progressive pairs dispensed per branch per month was 118 in group 1, 104 in group 2 and 92 in group 3. Four branches in group 3 lost their most senior dispenser during the study period, and one branch in group 2 moved to a new unit in July 2025.

Here are the first three chapters of a story I'm writing. Please carry on from where it stops and write at least the next two chapters, at proper length, in the same voice and with the same tense. Keep the characters consistent, let the tension about the missing container build, and don't wrap it up too early.

THE LAST BERTH

1.

At Harrow Quay the cranes never really stopped, they only changed their minds. Anselm Voss had been listening to them for twenty-six years from the glass box of the gate office, and he could tell from the pitch of the whine whether a driver was new, whether the wind had turned, whether it was going to rain. Tonight the sound was wrong. It was the long, patient drone of a crane holding something up and waiting to be told where to put it.

He put his tea down and looked at the screen. Berth Four, the Calloway Star, a feeder ship out of the northern ports, discharging since six. The yard plan showed every box in its place. The yard plan, as Anselm had learned long ago, showed the world as the planners wished it to be.

"You're doing the face," said Perpetua, without looking up from the stack of seal logs.

"I have no face."

"You have the face you get when a number does not match a number." She was nineteen, three months into the job, and she had a way of speaking to him as if he were a slightly dim relative who ran the family shop. He liked it. Nobody else at the port had talked to him like that since his wife died.

"Berth Four says it has landed three hundred and twelve boxes," he said. "The gate system says three hundred and eleven have been given a yard slot."

"So one is in the air."

"Maybe."

He pulled on his orange jacket and his hat and went out into the wet. The quay smelled of diesel, brine and hot brakes. Rows of containers rose around him, red and blue and a faded green, each stamped with the name of some company in some country he would never visit. The straddle carriers moved between them with their legs apart like patient herons. A driver he knew, Teodoro, lifted two fingers from the wheel in greeting.

Anselm walked the length of the discharge lane and counted aloud, as he always did, under his breath. At the end he found Callum Rae, the night supervisor, standing with a radio against his chest and the sort of expression that made Anselm's stomach go quiet.

"Don't," Callum said.

"I haven't said anything."

"You've said it with your whole body. It's a reefer. One reefer, forty foot, off the Calloway Star, bay twelve. The crane driver swears he set it down on the chassis and the truck driver swears he never got it. The tag in the system is live. It's still talking to us. It says minus eighteen inside and it says it's moving."

"Moving where?"

"That's what I would like to know."

2.

The container was called HMLU 4410862 and it had been loaded in a town Anselm could not pronounce, with a cargo that the manifest described only as frozen goods, chilled, sensitive. Nobody at the terminal paid much attention to a manifest. A manifest was a wish a shipping line made on the customer's behalf.

By midnight they had walked every row in the reefer stack and checked the sockets, the plugs and the alarms. The box was not in any of them. Callum had turned his radio to the open channel, and for an hour the port crackled with voices asking the same question in different accents: has anyone seen a forty-foot reefer, grey, line colours blue and white, number ending eight-six-two.

Perpetua found the first clue, which annoyed Anselm greatly because he had walked past it twice. In the seal log from the afternoon shift, a line had been written in a hand that was neither careful nor hurried, the hand of someone writing with their mind on something else. It recorded a reefer leaving by Gate Two at 17:42 under the name of a haulier called Pellam and Daughters, eight hours before the Calloway Star had even tied up.

"That cannot be right," Anselm said. "The ship wasn't here."

"The number is the same, though." She tapped it with a pencil. "Eight-six-two. Look. And the seal number is one digit different from the one on the ship's papers. Four-four-seven-one-nine against four-four-seven-one-six."

"A typing mistake."

"Or someone sent a truck for a box before the box arrived."

He felt, then, the thing he had spent twenty-six years learning not to feel at work, a quiet cold interest, like a man who has spotted a coin in a drain. He did not say it aloud. He asked instead for the camera footage of Gate Two between five and six, and Callum, with the reluctance of a man whose supervisor will hear about this in the morning, unlocked the room at the back where the old recorders were kept.

The recorders hummed. The picture on the monitor was grey and flickering, and in the corner of every frame the time ran forward in small white digits. At 17:38 a white truck pulled up to the barrier. It had no company name on the door, only a strip of tape where a name had been. The driver wore a cap pulled low. He did not look at the camera, which in itself was unusual, because everyone looked at the camera, if only to curse it.

"I know that truck," said Teodoro, who had come in dripping and stood behind them with his hands in his pockets. "Or I know the way it sits. It leans to the left. Front spring is gone."

"Pellam and Daughters have six trucks," Callum said. "None of them leans."

"Then it's not one of theirs."

Nobody said anything for a moment. Outside, a crane lowered something heavy onto steel, and the whole building trembled very slightly, as if it too were waiting to be told what had happened.

Anselm looked at the clock. It was ten past one. The Calloway Star was due to sail on the morning tide, and in six hours a customs officer named Ilse Brandvold would arrive to sign off the discharge, and she would count, as she always counted, three hundred and twelve boxes.

3.

Harrow Quay at two in the morning belonged to the people who could not sleep and the machines that did not need to. Anselm and Perpetua walked the perimeter fence with a torch, because the camera on the north side had been out since the storm in March and nobody had yet decided whose budget it belonged to.

"Tell me again why we're doing this ourselves," Perpetua said. "There are police. There is a security firm with a van."

"The security firm sends a man called Dennis, who sits in the van and listens to football. And the police will ask for a report, and the report will say a gate clerk wrote the wrong time in a log." He shone the torch along the base of the fence.

They found the gap behind the old cold store, where the fence met the wall of a building that had been abandoned since the fruit trade moved to the southern terminal. The wire had been cut cleanly and then pulled back into place, so that from ten paces it looked whole. Beyond it, in the mud, there were two parallel grooves, deep and curved, the track of something heavy being dragged on a low trailer.

"They didn't take it out through the gate at all," said Perpetua slowly. "The gate log is a decoy. Somebody wanted us to look at Gate Two."

"Or somebody wanted a record that said it left, so that no one would ever look for it inside."

He crouched and put his glove into the groove. The mud was still soft. Not hours old, then. Minutes, or an hour at most. He had the strange conviction, which he would remember later and be embarrassed by, that the container was very close and listening to him breathe.

From the dark behind the cold store came a low, steady hum. It was not a crane. It was the sound a refrigeration unit makes when it has been running for a long time and is beginning to struggle.

Perpetua took out her phone and switched on its light, and Anselm put his hand over it. "Not yet," he said. "Whoever cut that fence is not far away, and a reefer on battery is a reefer with a deadline. If the cold fails, whatever is inside will start to tell its own story."

"What is inside?"

He thought of the manifest, with its three vague words, frozen goods, chilled, sensitive, and of how the word sensitive had no business sitting on a manifest at all.

"Somebody who paid a great deal of money for it not to be asked," he said.

We're about to hand this spec to the volunteers who will test the new scheduling tool at the station. Please write a complete test plan for it, with numbered test cases that give the steps, the data to use and the expected result, and flag any places where the spec is vague or contradicts itself so we can fix those first.

Product specification: AirDesk, the programme and studio scheduler for Wren Valley Community Radio
Version 0.9 (draft for testing), owner: Halima Dufresne, station manager

1. Purpose

Wren Valley Community Radio broadcasts 24 hours a day from one studio and one small production room. Until now the weekly schedule has been kept on a shared spreadsheet and a whiteboard, which has led to double bookings, forgotten live slots and unclear rights for pre-recorded material. AirDesk replaces both. It lets presenters book studio time, lets the station manager publish a weekly programme grid, and produces the log of what was actually played that the station must send to the collecting society each quarter.

2. Users and roles

There are four roles.
- Presenter: a volunteer who hosts a show. A presenter can request bookings, see the grid, and upload a show plan.
- Producer: a volunteer who prepares recorded material. A producer can book the production room and upload audio files.
- Scheduler: the station manager or a deputy. A scheduler can approve or reject bookings, edit the grid and publish it.
- Auditor: the treasurer or a board member. An auditor has read-only access to the grid and the play log and can export the quarterly report.

A person has exactly one role at a time. Only schedulers can change roles.

3. Rooms and time

3.1 There are two bookable rooms: Studio A (live broadcast) and Room B (production). Studio A is the only room from which live output can be sent.
3.2 The day is divided into slots of 30 minutes starting on the hour and half hour. A booking covers one or more consecutive slots and may not cross midnight.
3.3 Studio A is reserved from 06:00 to 09:00 on weekdays for the breakfast show and cannot be booked by anyone except the scheduler.
3.4 A booking can be requested no more than 8 weeks ahead and no less than 24 hours ahead. Schedulers are exempt from the 24 hour limit.
3.5 A presenter may have at most 6 hours of approved bookings in Studio A in any calendar week. Producers may have at most 10 hours in Room B.

4. Booking workflow

4.1 A presenter or producer submits a request with room, date, start slot, number of slots and a show title of up to 60 characters.
4.2 A request that overlaps an approved booking in the same room is refused at once with the message "This time is already taken."
4.3 A request that overlaps another pending request is accepted, and both stay pending until the scheduler decides.
4.4 The scheduler approves or rejects each pending request. Approving a request automatically rejects every other pending request that overlaps it, and each affected requester receives an email.
4.5 A rejection must include a reason of at least 10 characters.
4.6 A requester can cancel their own pending or approved booking up to 2 hours before it starts. Cancelling within 2 hours is not allowed, and the requester is shown a phone number for the station manager.
4.7 If an approved booking is not started within 15 minutes of its start time, the scheduler may release it, and the slot returns to open status.

5. Programme grid

5.1 The grid shows seven days from Monday, with each approved Studio A booking as a block labelled with the show title and presenter name.
5.2 The scheduler can mark a block as Live, Repeat or Automated. A Repeat block must name the original show and the date of first broadcast. An Automated block fills a gap with the music rotation and has no presenter.
5.3 The scheduler publishes the grid for the coming week no later than Thursday 18:00. Publishing locks all blocks for that week except Repeat and Automated blocks, which the scheduler can still change until broadcast.
5.4 A published grid is exported as a PDF and as a public web page at the station's address. Presenters see a banner "Published" on blocks that are locked.

6. Play log

6.1 During a show, a presenter can log each track with artist, title, duration, and whether it is a licensed commercial recording, a station jingle, or a recording owned by a local artist who has given written consent.
6.2 Entries can be added up to 24 hours after the show. After that only the scheduler can edit them, and every edit is recorded with the name of the editor and the time.
6.3 At the end of each calendar quarter the auditor can export the log as a CSV file with one row per track, ordered by date and time. The file must include the column "Rights type" with one of the values Commercial, Jingle or Local consent.
6.4 Tracks of type Local consent must reference a consent record. A consent record has the artist name, the date of signature and an expiry date. A track whose consent has expired cannot be logged, and the presenter is told which consent to renew.

7. Notifications

7.1 Email is sent for: request received, request approved, request rejected, booking cancelled by the scheduler, and a reminder 24 hours before an approved booking.
7.2 A presenter can turn off the reminder but not the other emails.
7.3 The scheduler receives a daily digest at 08:00 listing pending requests older than 48 hours.

8. Accounts and security

8.1 Users sign in with an email address and a password of at least 12 characters. After 5 failed attempts the account is locked for 15 minutes.
8.2 Sessions end after 30 minutes without activity, except during a live show, when the presenter's session stays open for the length of the booking plus 30 minutes.
8.3 All times are shown in the station's local time. The system must handle the clock change in spring and autumn without losing or doubling any slot.

9. Performance and data

9.1 The grid page must load in under 3 seconds on a typical home connection with up to 400 blocks in the visible month.
9.2 The system must support 40 registered users, of whom no more than 10 are signed in at once.
9.3 Booking and grid data are kept for 7 years. Play log data are kept for 7 years after the end of the quarter they belong to. Accounts of people who have left the station are made anonymous 12 months after the scheduler marks them as left, but their bookings and log entries remain.
9.4 A scheduler can export the full list of bookings for any date range as a CSV file with the columns Date, Room, Start, End, Show title, Person and Status.

10. Out of scope for this version

Automatic playout of the music rotation, listener statistics, payment of any kind, and a mobile app. The grid page must still display correctly on a phone browser.

11. Open questions

The board has not decided whether Repeat blocks count towards a presenter's 6 hours. Until it does, they are counted. The wording of the rejection email is also still to be agreed with the volunteers' committee.

These are my notes from the water treatment module of our lifeguard and pool plant operator course, and I have an assessment on Friday. Can you turn them into a proper study guide with worked examples that I can follow step by step, and then a quiz of about fifteen questions with full answers and explanations? Please keep the examples close to the numbers in my notes.

Module 4: Pool water treatment and chemistry (Tideway Leisure Trust, operator training)
Lecturer: Mr. Barnaby Osei, Head of Plant Operations

1. Why we treat the water

A pool is a warm bath shared by hundreds of people a day. Bathers bring sweat, skin cells, hair, sun cream and urine into the water, and these feed micro-organisms. Treatment has three jobs: remove the dirt that can be filtered, kill or inactivate germs, and keep the water chemically balanced so that the disinfectant works and the bathers and the building are not harmed. All three must run at once. A perfect filter with no disinfectant is not safe, and a high chlorine level with poor circulation is not safe either.

2. The treatment loop

Water leaves the pool by two routes, the surface overflow channels and the main drain at the deepest point. It goes to the balance tank, which collects the surge when bathers enter and keeps the pumps from running dry. From the balance tank the pump sends it through the hair and lint strainer, then the filters, then the chemical dosing points, then the heater, and finally back to the pool through inlets placed to spread the flow evenly.

The turnover period is the time needed for the pump to move a volume of water equal to the whole pool. For the 25 metre main pool at Tideway the volume is 625 cubic metres. The design turnover is 4 hours.

Worked example 1. Required flow rate = volume divided by turnover period = 625 divided by 4 = 156.25 cubic metres per hour. The plant at Tideway has two duty pumps, each rated at 90 cubic metres per hour at the working head. Together they give 180 cubic metres per hour, so the actual turnover is 625 divided by 180 = 3.47 hours, or about 3 hours 28 minutes. This is quicker than the design figure, so the plant meets the requirement with a margin. If one pump fails, the flow falls to 90 and the turnover period rises to 625 divided by 90 = 6.94 hours. That is well over the design figure, so we must reduce bather numbers to the limit given in the plant manual.

3. Filtration

Tideway uses high rate sand filters. Water is pushed down through a bed of graded sand, and particles get trapped in the spaces between the grains. As the bed fills with dirt, the pressure difference between the inlet and the outlet of the filter rises. When the difference reaches 0.5 bar above the clean figure, or once a week, whichever comes first, the filter is backwashed. Backwashing reverses the flow, lifts the sand and flushes the dirt to waste, and takes about 5 minutes followed by a rinse of 1 minute to settle the bed.

The filter rate is the flow divided by the surface area of the filter bed. Each of our three filters has a bed area of 3.1 square metres. At 180 cubic metres per hour shared over three filters, each carries 60 cubic metres per hour, so the filter rate is 60 divided by 3.1 = 19.4 metres per hour. The plant manual allows up to 30 metres per hour for sand at this grade. Notes: a coagulant (flocculant) is dosed before the filter at 0.1 to 0.3 milligrams per litre to bind very fine particles together so that the sand can catch them.

4. Disinfection with chlorine

We dose sodium hypochlorite solution, which is liquid chlorine. When it dissolves, it forms hypochlorous acid, which is the active germ killer, and hypochlorite ion, which is much weaker. The balance between them depends on pH. At pH 7.2 about 62 percent of the free chlorine is the active acid, at pH 7.5 about 49 percent and at pH 8.0 only about 22 percent. This is the main reason why pH control matters so much: the same chlorine reading kills germs far more slowly in water with a high pH.

Our targets at Tideway: free chlorine between 1.0 and 3.0 milligrams per litre (we aim for 1.5 in the main pool), pH between 7.2 and 7.6, total alkalinity between 80 and 120 milligrams per litre, and water temperature of 28 degrees in the main pool and 32 degrees in the teaching pool.

Free chlorine is what is still available to kill germs. Combined chlorine, or chloramines, is chlorine that has reacted with sweat and urine. It smells strong, irritates eyes and lungs, and is a poor disinfectant. Combined chlorine equals total chlorine minus free chlorine. We keep it below 0.5 milligrams per litre. If it goes above 1.0, we must take action, which means more fresh water, a higher dose and, in serious cases, a shock dose and closure of the pool.

Worked example 2. A test at 10:00 shows total chlorine 2.2 and free chlorine 1.4. Combined chlorine = 2.2 minus 1.4 = 0.8 milligrams per litre. That is above the 0.5 target but below the 1.0 action level. The operator should check bather load, increase fresh water make-up, and retest in an hour.

Worked example 3. We want to raise free chlorine in the main pool from 1.0 to 1.5 milligrams per litre, so the rise is 0.5 milligrams per litre. Mass of chlorine needed = 0.5 grams per cubic metre times 625 cubic metres = 312.5 grams of chlorine. Our hypochlorite solution is 12 percent available chlorine, which means 120 grams per litre. Volume of solution = 312.5 divided by 120 = 2.6 litres. In practice the dose is added gradually through the dosing pump and not poured in at once.

5. pH and alkalinity

The pH is a measure of how acidic or alkaline the water is, and 7 is neutral. Hypochlorite solution is alkaline, so dosing it raises pH over time. We therefore add acid, normally carbon dioxide gas or dilute hydrochloric acid, to bring it back down. Total alkalinity is the water's ability to resist changes in pH, like a shock absorber. Too low and the pH swings wildly after each dose. Too high and the pH keeps creeping up and is hard to bring down. We raise alkalinity with sodium bicarbonate and lower it by careful acid dosing with aeration.

Calcium hardness should be between 150 and 250 milligrams per litre. Soft water is aggressive and eats away at grout and plaster. Very hard water forms scale on heaters and tiles.

6. Automatic control and testing

Probes in a sample line measure pH and chlorine every few seconds and send the readings to the controller, which adjusts the dosing pumps. The controller is only as good as its probes. Every morning before opening, and every two hours while the pool is open, a member of staff takes a manual sample and tests it with a photometer. If the manual reading differs from the controller by more than 0.3 milligrams per litre for chlorine or 0.2 for pH, the probe is cleaned and recalibrated. All results go in the plant log with the time, the initials of the person testing, and any action taken.

7. Safety of chemicals

Never mix hypochlorite with acid. The reaction releases chlorine gas, which can seriously harm or kill. Store them in separate, bunded areas with separate delivery points. Dosing tanks and pipes are labelled and colour coded. Eyewash stations and the emergency shower must be tested weekly. Anyone handling chemicals must wear gloves, goggles and an apron.

Context: Fernhollow Seed Bank keeps its accession records (about 48,000 rows) in a PostgreSQL database on the host `vault01`, and scanned packet photos in /srv/seedphotos (roughly 90 GB). The backup copies both to the NAS at /mnt/nas/backups and to an offsite bucket.

--- /usr/local/bin/seedbackup.sh ---

#!/bin/bash
# nightly backup for seed bank
# written by Odile, 2023

DB=accessions
USER=seedadmin
PASS=Gr33nhouse2023
DEST=/mnt/nas/backups
DATE=`date +%d-%m-%Y`
LOG=/var/log/seedbackup.log
KEEP=14

echo "backup started $DATE" >> $LOG

cd $DEST

# dump the database
PGPASSWORD=$PASS pg_dump -U $USER $DB > $DEST/db-$DATE.sql
if [ $? -ne 0 ]
then
  echo "dump failed" >> $LOG
fi

# compress it
gzip $DEST/db-$DATE.sql

# photos
rsync -av --delete /srv/seedphotos/ $DEST/photos/ >> $LOG 2>&1

# keep only the last $KEEP days of dumps
find $DEST -name "db-*.sql.gz" -mtime +$KEEP -exec rm {} \;

# offsite copy
export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=AKIAEXAMPLE0000FERN
export AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=example-secret-not-real-0000
aws s3 sync $DEST s3://fernhollow-offsite-2023 --quiet

# check free space
FREE=`df $DEST | tail -1 | awk '{print $4}'`
if [ $FREE -lt 50000000 ]
then
  echo "low space" | mail -s "backup space" admin@example.org
fi

echo "backup finished" >> $LOG

--- /etc/systemd/system/seedbackup.service ---

[Unit]
Description=Seed bank nightly backup

[Service]

Description=Run seed backup every night

[Timer]
OnCalendar=*-*-* 02:00:00
Persistent=false

[Install]

    weekly

}

--- /etc/cron.d/seedphotos-sync (older file, still present on vault01) ---

0 2 * * * root rsync -a --delete /srv/seedphotos/ /mnt/nas/backups/photos/

--- /etc/fstab (relevant line) ---

//nas01.example.org/backups  /mnt/nas/backups  cifs  credentials=/root/.nascreds,file_mode=0777,dir_mode=0777,vers=2.0  0  0

--- /etc/postgresql/16/main/pg_hba.conf (relevant lines) ---

local   all             postgres                                peer
local   accessions      seedadmin                               scram-sha-256

--- /usr/local/bin/seedrestore-check.sh (written by Wilhelmina last week, run by hand) ---

#!/bin/bash
LATEST=$(ls -t /mnt/nas/backups/db-*.sql.gz | head -1)
echo "Checking $LATEST"
createdb -U seedadmin restoretest
gunzip -c $LATEST | psql -U seedadmin restoretest
psql -U seedadmin restoretest -c "select count(*) from accessions;"
dropdb -U seedadmin restoretest

--- /etc/cron.monthly/seedtidy (added by Odile in 2024) ---

#!/bin/sh
# clear old thumbnails and tidy the database
cd /srv/seedphotos
find . -name "*thumb*" -mtime +30 -exec rm -f {} \;

Notes from the restore test (Thursday, done by Wilhelmina):
- The newest dump file db-12-10-2026.sql.gz was only 20 KB. The ones from a few weeks ago are around 310 MB.
- When she unpacked it, it contained a single line: "pg_dump: error: connection to server on socket failed: FATAL: password authentication failed for user seedadmin".
- The log says "backup started 12-10-2026", then "dump failed", then the rsync output, then "backup finished". Nobody read it.
- The NAS had been remounted after a power cut on the 3rd and was mounted read-only for a while. The photos folder on it has not changed since then, and the rsync lines in the log show "Read-only file system" errors for those days.
- The database password was changed by the IT contractor last month, and he told Odile, who has since left.
- The offsite bucket has no lifecycle rules and is now 1.9 TB, though the live data is about 90 GB plus 15 GB of dumps.
- The sync of the whole backup folder goes up every night, including dumps that are removed locally. Because the sync does not use the delete flag, the bucket keeps every dump ever made.
- The server's clock is set to local time. In March 2026 the timer fired twice on the night the clocks changed, according to Wilhelmina.
- We also have a cron file that does the same rsync of the photos at 02:00 as the timer does, so the two jobs run at the same moment.
- Nobody has a record of where the offsite bucket credentials were created, and the same key pair is also used by the website upload form.
- The monthly tidy job is meant to remove thumbnails only. Last month Wilhelmina noticed that a few full size photos with the word "thumb" in the file name, such as 4471-thumbnail-study.tif, went missing.

Our trustees meet next week and I have to present this annual report. Could you go through it section by section, summarising each in a few sentences, and then give me a list of recommendations for the trustees with the reasoning behind each? I'd especially like you to pick out anything where the numbers or the conclusions don't sit comfortably together.

HIGHCRAG MOUNTAIN RESCUE TEAM
Annual Operations Report, 1 October 2025 to 30 September 2026
Prepared by Rosalind Achterberg (Team Leader) and Gethin Mortlock (Treasurer)

1. Summary of the year

Highcrag Mountain Rescue Team was called out 94 times this year, against 81 in the previous year, an increase of 16 percent. The team has 38 active members, down from 41, of whom 24 are fully operational on the hill, 9 are trainees and 5 are support members who work in the base and the control vehicle. Callouts used 2,310 volunteer hours on the hill and in the base. Eleven casualties were airlifted by the coastguard helicopter, and the team assisted the ambulance service on nine occasions with stretcher carries from places where a vehicle could not reach. Three casualties died before or during the rescue, a year in which the team was also asked to recover one body after a search of two days. Income was 148,200 pounds and expenditure 128,400 pounds, leaving a surplus of 19,800 pounds.

2. Callouts

The 94 callouts are broken down below by the activity of the casualty or subject.

| Activity | Callouts | Share |
|---|---|---|
| Walkers and hill walkers | 51 | 54% |
| Climbers and scramblers | 11 | 12% |
| Fell runners | 9 | 10% |
| Medical emergencies (not injury) | 9 | 10% |
| Mountain bikers | 8 | 9% |
| Missing persons (not on a recreational trip) | 6 | 6% |
| Total | 94 | 100% |

Callouts were busiest in July and August with 14 each, and quietest in February with 3. Forty-one callouts, or 44 percent, began between 17:00 and midnight, and 19 callouts needed teams to stay out through the night. The median time from the page to the first team member on the hill was 38 minutes, against 41 last year. The median time from the page to reaching the casualty was 1 hour 52 minutes. In 12 callouts the casualty could not be located for more than three hours because the location they gave was wrong or their phone had no signal.

Causes. Slips, trips and falls accounted for 39 callouts. Navigation errors and being benighted accounted for 23. Equipment failure, such as a broken bike frame or a dead headtorch, was behind 7. The remaining 25 were medical conditions, missing persons and other events.

3. Casualties and outcomes

Of the 94 callouts, 66 casualties were treated and walked or carried to a roadhead, 11 were airlifted, 9 were handed to the ambulance service on the hill, 3 died, 3 were found safe and well and needed no treatment, and 2 callouts were stood down before the team reached the location. Our casualty carers gave oxygen on 14 occasions and used the team's vacuum mattresses 21 times. The average age of casualties was 41, but 17 casualties were under 25 and 12 were over 65.

4. Membership and training

The team lost six members during the year, mostly because of moving away for work, and welcomed three new trainees. Recruitment events in March and September brought 63 applicants, of which 20 attended the assessment weekend and 9 were accepted. Fully operational members are expected to complete at least 20 training evenings and days a year. Average attendance this year was 17, and 8 operational members did not meet the target. The team also ran a three-day casualty care course in May for 14 members, a swiftwater awareness day in June, and a joint search exercise with two neighbouring teams in October. Two members completed the national leadership course and two qualified as search managers.

Concerns. The age profile of the team is rising: 15 of the 24 operational members are over 45. Only five of the 38 members are women. The new trainees all live within 20 minutes of the base, which is good for response, but the team still has no operational members in the western valley, from which 17 of the 94 callouts originated.

5. Vehicles and equipment

A new four-by-four, bought with a grant and a donation, entered service in June at a cost of 36,900 pounds, which includes fitting out. The older ambulance conversion has now been sold for 5,200 pounds. A new set of 24 radios replaced the old handsets at a cost of 11,800 pounds. Spending on personal clothing and technical equipment was 29,500 pounds. A drone with a thermal camera was received as a gift in March and has been used on 7 callouts, finding the casualty on 3. Meeting: Eastfield Network Renewal, project kick-off
Company: Marrowgate District Heat Ltd

Apologies: Sunniva Okafor (Procurement), who sent in a note on the heat exchanger delivery which Kofi read out

1. Purpose and scope

Ingrid reminded everyone why the work is needed. The 1.4 kilometre section of steel mains under Eastfield Road and Mill Lane was laid in 1987 and has had four leaks in the last 18 months. Together the leaks cost about 38,000 pounds in repairs and caused three unplanned outages, of which the longest was 11 hours. The section feeds 612 homes, a primary school and a care home. The scope agreed at the board in September is: replace the 1.4 kilometre section with pre-insulated pipe, replace the plate heat exchanger in the Mill Lane substation, and connect 38 new flats at Harbour Court to the new pipe before they are occupied. The approved budget is 1.86 million pounds, of which 120,000 pounds is held as contingency.

2. Timing

The work must be finished and the network back in full operation before the cold weather starts. Ingrid wants the new pipe live by 20 November, and no later than 4 December. The previous winter's coldest week began on 12 December. Lucan said that the system should not be taken out of service on any day when the forecast low is below 2 degrees. Kofi said it will be tight, because the permits from the city council normally take six weeks, and the roads team has said Eastfield Road cannot be fully closed for more than 14 days in a row.

Bram said his crew can start on 26 October if the permits come through and he has the pipe by 19 October. His crew is eight people, and he has a second crew of six who can join from 9 November. He estimates about 5 weeks for the first crew alone. He wants the trench dug in four sections of about 350 metres each, with each section joined, pressure tested and backfilled before the next one is opened.

3. Heat exchanger

Sunniva's note: the supplier quoted 11 weeks from order for the new plate heat exchanger. If it is ordered by Friday 9 October, delivery is 25 December. That is far too late. A second supplier, whose price is 14 percent higher, quotes 6 weeks, so delivery would be around 20 November. Lucan said he does not want to install the exchanger at the same time as connecting the new pipe, because both need a shutdown, and he would rather combine them in one outage. Priya asked what the extra 14 percent comes to. Kofi said the first quote was 142,000 pounds, so the second is about 161,900. Nobody has decided which supplier to go with. Priya said she can approve up to 160,000 pounds herself and anything above needs the finance director.

4. Customers

Dagmar said that customers will be told by letter 4 weeks before any planned shutdown, and by text message 48 hours before. A planned outage of up to 8 hours is acceptable according to the regulator's guidance, but anything longer needs a temporary heat supply for the school and the care home. She asked who pays for the mobile boiler, which costs 1,900 pounds a day to hire. Ingrid said the cost must come from the project contingency. Dagmar also raised the 38 new flats: the developer, who has not been told about the delay, expects hot water from 1 December. She will talk to the developer this week. She would also like a named person at the company who residents can call during the work, available between 7 and 19 hours.

Osric asked whether any residents on the route are on the priority register for vulnerable customers. Dagmar thinks there are 23, but the list was last updated in March. She will check it.

5. Health and safety

Osric said the old pipe is thought to be wrapped in a material that may contain asbestos, because the original insulation was installed in the late 1980s. A survey must be done before any cutting starts. He has a surveyor who can visit on the week of 12 October but has not yet been booked. If asbestos is found, the removal must be done by a licensed contractor, and that could add two to three weeks. Bram said his crew is not licensed. Osric also wants a traffic management plan approved by the council, a gas and water services drawing check before digging, and a daily check of excavations because the trenches will be 1.8 metres deep. The Eastfield branch can be isolated at two valves, one at Mill Lane substation and one at the junction with Quarry Street, and fed from the standby boiler house at Quarry Street. The standby plant is rated at 2.4 megawatts, but the peak demand of the branch in a cold spell is about 3.1 megawatts, so the standby can cover the branch only when the outside temperature is above about 2 degrees. He also said that the new pipe must be flushed and dosed with treated water before it is connected, which takes two days, and that his team will need the section handed over with the pressure test certificates. His team cannot take on any new work in the week of 23 November because of the annual boiler inspection.

Here is the database behind our translation agency's job tracker, plus the four queries that run the Monday reports. The reports have got slow since we passed 200,000 tasks. Can you review the design, tell me which indexes we should add and why, and rewrite each query with an explanation of what you changed? Please also point out schema problems that will cause us trouble later, even if they aren't causing slowness today.

```sql
-- PostgreSQL

CREATE TABLE clients (
    client_id     SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    name          VARCHAR(200) NOT NULL,
    country       VARCHAR(60),
    vat_number    VARCHAR(30),
    payment_days  INTEGER DEFAULT 30,
    created_at    TIMESTAMP DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE linguists (
    linguist_id   SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    full_name     VARCHAR(120) NOT NULL,
    email         VARCHAR(160),
    is_active     BOOLEAN DEFAULT true,
    rate_per_word VARCHAR(10)
);

CREATE TABLE linguist_languages (
    linguist_id   INTEGER REFERENCES linguists(linguist_id),
    source_lang   CHAR(2) NOT NULL,
    target_lang   CHAR(2) NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (linguist_id, source_lang, target_lang)
);

CREATE TABLE projects (
    project_id    SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    client_id     INTEGER REFERENCES clients(client_id),
    title         VARCHAR(200) NOT NULL,
    status        VARCHAR(20) DEFAULT 'open',
    received_at   TIMESTAMP DEFAULT now(),
    due_at        TIMESTAMP,
    manager       VARCHAR(120)
);

CREATE TABLE tasks (
    task_id       SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    project_id    INTEGER REFERENCES projects(project_id),
    linguist_id   INTEGER REFERENCES linguists(linguist_id),
    task_type     VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,   -- 'translate', 'review', 'proofread'
    source_lang   CHAR(2) NOT NULL,
    target_lang   CHAR(2) NOT NULL,
    word_count    INTEGER NOT NULL,
    status        VARCHAR(20) DEFAULT 'assigned',
    assigned_at   TIMESTAMP,
    delivered_at  TIMESTAMP,
    price_per_word NUMERIC(8,4)
);

CREATE TABLE invoices (
    invoice_id    SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    client_id     INTEGER REFERENCES clients(client_id),
    issued_on     DATE NOT NULL,
    due_on        DATE NOT NULL,
    paid_on       DATE,
    total         VARCHAR(20)
);

CREATE TABLE invoice_lines (
    line_id       SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    invoice_id    INTEGER REFERENCES invoices(invoice_id),
    project_id    INTEGER,
    description   TEXT,
    amount        NUMERIC(10,2)
);
```

Current sizes: clients 1,900 rows; linguists 640; linguist_languages 2,100; projects 41,000; tasks 214,000; invoices 33,500; invoice_lines 96,000. There are no indexes other than the primary keys. About 2,000 tasks are added or updated each working day.

Query 1: Monday report, late deliveries last week, by linguist

```sql
SELECT l.full_name,
       count(*) AS late_tasks
FROM tasks t, linguists l, projects p
WHERE t.linguist_id = l.linguist_id
  AND t.project_id = p.project_id
  AND t.delivered_at > p.due_at
  AND date_trunc('week', t.delivered_at) = date_trunc('week', now() - interval '7 days')
GROUP BY l.full_name
ORDER BY late_tasks DESC;
```

Query 2: words delivered per language pair this month, with the cost to us

```sql
SELECT t.source_lang || '-' || t.target_lang AS pair,
       sum(t.word_count) AS words,
       sum(t.word_count * l.rate_per_word::numeric) AS cost
FROM tasks t
JOIN linguists l ON l.linguist_id = t.linguist_id
WHERE to_char(t.delivered_at, 'YYYY-MM') = to_char(now(), 'YYYY-MM')
  AND t.status = 'delivered'
GROUP BY pair
ORDER BY words DESC;
```

Query 3: overdue invoices with the number of days late and the client's name

```sql
SELECT c.name,
       i.invoice_id,
       i.total,
       current_date - i.due_on AS days_late
FROM invoices i
JOIN clients c ON c.client_id = i.client_id
WHERE i.paid_on IS NULL
  AND i.due_on < current_date
  AND i.client_id IN (SELECT client_id FROM clients WHERE country <> 'UK')
ORDER BY days_late DESC;
```

Query 4: projects that have tasks but have never been invoiced, and clients whose latest project is older than 6 months

```sql
SELECT p.project_id, p.title, c.name
FROM projects p
JOIN clients c ON c.client_id = p.client_id
WHERE p.project_id IN (SELECT project_id FROM tasks)
  AND p.project_id NOT IN (SELECT project_id FROM invoice_lines)
  AND p.status = 'closed'
UNION
SELECT p.project_id, p.title, c.name
FROM projects p
JOIN clients c ON c.client_id = p.client_id
WHERE c.client_id IN (
    SELECT client_id FROM projects
    GROUP BY client_id
    HAVING max(received_at) < now() - interval '6 months'
);
```

Some background that may help: the agency has two offices, one of which works mostly with clients outside the country, and the finance team exports the overdue invoice report to a spreadsheet every Monday. Linguists are paid per word, and the rate in the rate_per_word column is entered by hand by the office staff in the format 0.085, or sometimes with a currency sign. The project managers also want a screen that finds all open tasks for a given language pair that nobody has been assigned to yet, and that screen is the slowest page in the system. Only about 3 percent of the 214,000 tasks are open at any one time, and nearly all queries from the reports look only at the last 12 months of data.

Design document: SiteBook, daily records and snag tracking for the Ashgrove Construction site offices
Author: Ludmila Okonkwo-Reyes, Engineering Lead
Status: Draft 2, for review
Date: 8 October 2026

1. Background

Ashgrove Construction runs between 9 and 14 building sites at a time, from small housing schemes to a 120-unit apartment block. Each site has a site office with a site manager, a clerk of works and one or two assistants. Today the daily record is a paper diary, the snag list (defects found during inspection that must be fixed before handover) is a spreadsheet emailed around weekly, and photographs live on personal phones. Three problems keep recurring. Disputes with subcontractors over who was on site and when cannot be settled without the paper diary, which is often left in the site cabin. Snags get lost or fixed twice because the spreadsheet is out of date within a day of being sent. And the head office cannot see the position on a site without phoning the manager.

2. Goals

- Site staff record the daily diary (weather, labour on site by trade, deliveries, visitors, instructions given, delays) on a tablet or phone in under 10 minutes.
- Snags are created on site with a photo, a location on the building plan, a trade responsible and a due date, and can be tracked to closure.
- Head office sees a live summary of every site.
- The system works in a site cabin with poor or no mobile signal and synchronises when the connection returns.
- Records cannot be altered after the end of the following working day without leaving an audit trail, because they may be used as evidence in a dispute.

3. Non-goals

SiteBook will not replace the programme, cost control or health and safety document systems. It will not handle subcontractor payments. It will not offer a customer-facing portal in this version.

4. Users and scale

About 70 site staff, 25 head office staff and 15 subcontractor foremen who are given limited access to see and close snags assigned to their company. Expected volumes: 14 diaries a day, around 400 snags created a week during busy handover periods, about 60 photographs a day, with a photograph averaging 3.5 MB after compression.

5. Proposed architecture

5.1 Client. A progressive web app built with React, installable on tablets and phones, using a local database in the browser (IndexedDB) for offline storage. All writes go first to the local database and are queued for upload.

5.2 Server. A single Node.js service with a REST interface, backed by one PostgreSQL database, running on two virtual machines behind a load balancer in a single cloud region. Photographs are stored in object storage, with thumbnails created by a background worker.

5.3 Synchronisation. Each client keeps a queue of changes. When online, the client sends the queue to the server in order, and the server applies each change if the record has not been changed by someone else since the version the client last saw. If it has, the server keeps the version with the later timestamp and discards the other. The client then downloads all changes since its last sync.

5.4 Audit. Every change is written to an append-only audit table with user, time, device identifier and the old and new values. Diaries are locked at 23:59 on the next working day. Editing a locked diary needs a site manager's reason and creates a visible amendment note.

5.5 Plans. Building plans are uploaded as PDFs and converted to images at several zoom levels. Snag locations are stored as a plan identifier plus x and y coordinates in the range 0 to 1.

5.6 Authentication. Staff sign in with their company email account through single sign-on. Subcontractor foremen sign in with a one-time code sent to their phone, valid for 12 hours.

6. Data model (outline)

Site, Plan, Diary (one per site per day), DiaryEntry (type: labour, delivery, visitor, instruction, delay, weather), Snag (plan, x, y, description, trade, company, due date, status: open, fixed, verified, rejected), Photo (attached to a diary entry or snag), AuditEvent, User, Company.

7. Reporting

The head office dashboard shows for each site the number of open snags by age, overdue snags, labour on site today, deliveries expected and a flag if no diary has been submitted by 17:00. The queries run directly on the live database. A weekly PDF report is generated on Friday at 16:00 and emailed to project directors.

7a. Non-functional requirements

The app must open and show the current diary within 3 seconds on a tablet that is two years old. A diary must save locally within 1 second, even with no connection. Synchronisation of a typical day's changes, including 10 photographs, must finish within 2 minutes on a 4G connection. The service must be available 99.5 percent of the time between 06:00 and 20:00 on working days. Backups are taken nightly and kept for 35 days, and the database can be restored within 4 hours. All times are stored in UTC and shown in the site's local time.

7b. Cost estimate

Development: three developers for six months at an average loaded cost of 14,500 pounds each a month is 261,000 pounds. A designer for six weeks adds 22,000 pounds, testing and the pilot sites add 17,000 pounds, and 10,000 pounds is held for tablets and accessories for the first four sites. The running cost of 3,200 pounds a month covers the virtual machines (900), the database (700), object storage and bandwidth (600), the single sign-on licence (450) and monitoring, backups and support tools (550).

8. Security and privacy

Data is encrypted in transit and at rest. Access is by site: staff can see only sites they are assigned to, apart from head office staff who see all. Visitor names and company names are personal data and are kept for 7 years, after which they are anonymised. Photographs may show members of the public and should not be shared outside the company.

9. Risks identified by the author

Conflict handling in synchronisation is simple and may lose data. IndexedDB storage can be cleared by the browser if the device runs low on space. Large plan images may be slow on older tablets. The team has no experience with offline-first applications.

10. Delivery proposal

Build the entire system in about 6 months with a team of three developers, release to all sites at the same time in April 2027, and retire the paper diaries one month later. Training is planned as a single half-day session per site. The cost estimate is 310,000 pounds for development and 3,200 pounds a month to run.

11. Open questions

Whether to use an existing off-the-shelf site diary product instead of building. Whether subcontractors should be allowed to add their own comments on snags. How long to keep photographs. Who owns the data if a joint venture partner is involved in a site.

I'm joining the committee of our beekeeping association and I've been told I must sign this apiary hosting agreement along with the landowner policy it refers to. Could you explain it to me clause by clause in plain language, say what each clause actually asks me to do or gives up, and then list the risks to me as a member and to the landowner, including anything that is unclear or one-sided?

MARSHWICK AND DISTRICT BEEKEEPERS' ASSOCIATION
APIARY HOSTING AGREEMENT AND SAFE PRACTICE POLICY
Version 4, adopted at the annual general meeting on 14 March 2026

Parties. This agreement is made between the Marshwick and District Beekeepers' Association, a voluntary association with its secretary's address at 6 Cobbler's Row, Marshwick ("the Association"), the person or organisation who owns or has control of the land described in the Schedule ("the Host"), and the member of the Association who keeps the colonies at the site ("the Keeper").

1. Purpose
1.1 The Host allows the Keeper to place and manage honey bee colonies on the land in the Schedule ("the Apiary") for as long as this agreement lasts.
1.2 The Association supports the arrangement by providing training, a disease inspection service and a swarm collection service, on the terms in this document.

2. Term
2.1 The agreement starts on the date the last party signs it and continues for 3 years. It renews for further periods of 1 year unless a party gives notice under clause 12.
2.2 The Keeper may keep no more than 6 full-size colonies at the Apiary at any one time without the Host's written agreement. Nucleus colonies kept for the purpose of raising queens or for swarm control do not count towards this limit for up to 8 weeks in the season.

3. Membership and training
3.1 The Keeper must be a member of the Association in good standing, which means that all annual subscriptions are paid by 31 March each year.
3.2 A Keeper who has been keeping bees for less than 2 years must complete the Association's beginners' course and be accompanied by an experienced mentor for the first 12 inspections of the season.
3.3 The Keeper must register the Apiary with the national bee health database within 30 days of placing the first colony, and must keep the registration up to date.

4. Siting and layout
4.1 Colonies must be placed at least 10 metres from any public footpath, bridleway, road or boundary shared with a neighbour, unless a hedge or fence at least 2 metres high stands between the colonies and the boundary. The flight path of the bees must be directed away from the boundary.
4.2 A source of clean water must be available within the Apiary at all times from 1 April to 30 September, so that bees do not seek water in neighbouring properties.
4.3 Signs at each access point must say that bees are kept at the site and give the Keeper's telephone number.
4.4 Hives must be on stands at least 30 centimetres above the ground, and strapped down in areas that are exposed to wind or floods.

5. Colony health and inspections
5.1 The Keeper must inspect each colony for signs of disease at least once every 10 days from April to August, and at least once a month at other times when the weather permits. A record of each inspection must be kept for 3 years.
5.2 If the Keeper suspects American foulbrood, European foulbrood or an exotic pest, the Keeper must close the hive, tell the Association's disease officer and the national bee inspector within 24 hours, and not move any bees, honey, comb or equipment from the Apiary until told the position.
5.3 The Association's disease officer may enter the Apiary at any reasonable time, with 48 hours' notice to the Host, to inspect any colony. The Host agrees to allow access.
5.4 Colonies found to have notifiable disease will be treated or destroyed as instructed by the national bee inspector. The Association does not pay compensation for colonies destroyed.

6. Swarms and temperament
6.1 The Keeper must take reasonable steps to prevent swarming, including inspection for queen cells every 7 days during May, June and July.
6.2 If a swarm leaves the Apiary and settles on land that does not belong to the Host, the Keeper must collect it within 24 hours of being told, if it is safe to do so.
6.3 If a colony shows persistent aggression, for example by stinging people or animals at more than 20 metres from the hive, the Keeper must re-queen the colony within 21 days, or move it. The Host may require the Keeper to do so by written notice.
6.4 The Association's swarm collection service is free of charge for members. It does not apply to wasps, hornets or bumblebees.

7. Insurance and liability
7.1 The Keeper must maintain public liability insurance of at least 5 million pounds, which is included in the Association membership fee if the Keeper has not more than 20 colonies.
7.2 The Keeper is responsible for any injury, damage or loss caused by the Keeper's bees or by the Keeper's activities at the Apiary, to the extent that it is caused by the Keeper's negligence or breach of this agreement.
7.3 The Host is not responsible for stings or other harm to the Keeper, to guests of the Keeper, or to people who enter the Apiary without the Host's permission, except where the Host's own act or neglect has caused the harm.
7.4 The Association is not a party to any claim between the Host and the Keeper, and accepts no liability for the conduct of any Keeper, but will, where it can, help to settle disputes between them.

8. Payment
8.1 The Keeper will give the Host 2 kilograms of honey each year, or a hive rent of 40 pounds, as the Host chooses, payable by 1 October.
8.2 The Host may not charge any other fee.

9. Honey and products
9.1 The Keeper owns the bees, the hives, the equipment and everything the bees produce.
9.2 The Keeper must comply with all rules on labelling and the sale of honey and must not sell honey with the name of the Host or the Association on it without permission.

10. Pesticides and other users of the land
10.1 The Host must not spray pesticides, herbicides or fungicides on flowering plants within 100 metres of the Apiary without telling the Keeper at least 5 days before, so that the Keeper can close the hives or move them.
10.2 If land next to the Host's land is being used for crops that are sprayed, the Host will pass on any information that the Host receives.

11. Access
The Keeper and one helper may visit the Apiary at any time of day or night, by the access route in the Schedule, in a vehicle if necessary. The Keeper must close all gates and avoid damage to crops, livestock and tracks.

12. Ending the agreement
12.1 Either the Host or the Keeper may end the agreement by 3 months' written notice, to take effect on 31 January or 30 September. The Association may end it at any time if the Keeper ceases to be a member or seriously breaches clause 5.
12.2 On ending, the Keeper must remove all colonies and equipment within 28 days, and leave the site clean and tidy.

13. Disputes
Any disagreement between the Host and Keeper will first be referred to the Association's welfare officer. If the matter cannot be settled within 28 days, either party may take other action.
