Our crew planning group asked me to referee this internal write-up before it goes to the safety and operations committee. Could you write a detailed peer review of it, covering the methods, the statistics, whether the conclusions follow from the results, and any operational or safety issues the authors have missed? Please finish with a clear recommendation (accept, revise, or reject) and a numbered list of changes you would require.

Title: A rolling-horizon rostering heuristic for reducing reserve call-outs and duty-limit exceedances at Skerry Air

Authors: Tamsin Orchard-Bell (Crew Planning), Yusuf Halvorsen (Operations Research Intern), Gwendolen Faraday (Head of Crew Resources)

Abstract. Skerry Air operates six turboprop aircraft on 14 island and mainland routes with 38 pilots and 52 cabin crew. Rosters are built four weeks ahead by hand by two planners. Last-minute changes cause frequent reserve call-outs and, occasionally, duty periods that exceed our internal limit. We developed a rolling-horizon heuristic that builds the roster week by week and repairs it daily. In an eight-week trial the heuristic reduced reserve call-outs by 41 percent and removed all duty-limit exceedances. We recommend adopting it in the winter schedule.

1. Introduction

Crew costs are the second largest cost of the airline after fuel. Skerry Air's network is small but irregular: three routes fly only on some weekdays, two seasonal routes are suspended between November and March, and the base at Port Merrow has a night-stop requirement for the early morning departures. Pilots are subject to national flight time limits and to a stricter internal limit of 11 hours duty in any 24 hour period. Cabin crew follow national rules and an agreement with their union that guarantees at least 2 consecutive days off in every 7.

When a crew member is sick or a flight is delayed, a reserve crew member is called out. Reserve call-outs are costly, 190 pounds on average in standby pay and overtime, and disruptive. Over the last 12 months there were 312 call-outs at Port Merrow, an average of 6.0 a week, and 9 duty periods that exceeded the internal limit.

2. Methods

2.1 Heuristic. The heuristic works on a rolling horizon of 4 weeks. At the start of each week it fixes the next 7 days, builds the following 3 weeks by a greedy construction that assigns pairings (sequences of flights ending at the base) to crew in order of the hardest to cover first, and then improves the result with a local search that swaps pairings between crew members. The objective penalises, in order, a violation of a legal rule (infinite weight), a violation of the internal limit (weight 1,000), a pairing that gives a crew member fewer than 11 hours of rest (weight 200), and an unequal spread of weekend work (weight 5 per extra weekend over the average). A daily repair step re-runs the local search on the next 72 hours when a disruption is entered, with the aim of changing as few existing assignments as possible.

2.2 Reserve policy. Each day, 4 pilots and 5 cabin crew are placed on standby. The heuristic spreads the standby days so that nobody has more than 2 in any 7 days. The manual rosters used the same numbers but the planners assigned them by experience.

2.3 Trial design. The trial ran for 8 weeks, from 31 August to 25 October 2026. The heuristic's rosters were used for pilots and cabin crew based at Port Merrow, which covers 9 of the 14 routes. For comparison, we used the corresponding 8 weeks in the previous year, which were rostered by hand. The planners did not change the manual method for the trial. The heuristic's recommended roster was reviewed by a planner who could override it, and overrides were logged.

2.4 Measures. The primary measure was the number of reserve call-outs per week. Secondary measures were duty-limit exceedances, the number of days off per 7 days, the number of crew who worked more than 10 days in a row, and the planners' time spent per week. The main comparison used a two-sample t-test on the weekly number of call-outs. No adjustment was made for multiple comparisons.

3. Results

3.1 Call-outs. In the trial weeks there were 29 call-outs in 8 weeks, a mean of 3.6 per week, against 49 in the 8 comparison weeks of the previous year, a mean of 6.1 per week. This is a reduction of 41 percent (t = 4.3, p < 0.001).

Table 1. Weekly reserve call-outs

| Week | Previous year | Trial |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 7 | 4 |
| 2 | 5 | 3 |
| 3 | 6 | 5 |
| 4 | 8 | 3 |
| 5 | 4 | 2 |
| 6 | 7 | 4 |
| 7 | 6 | 5 |
| 8 | 6 | 3 |
| Total | 49 | 29 |

3.2 Duty-limit exceedances. There were no exceedances of the internal limit during the trial, against 3 in the comparison period. The authors note that the period included a spell of unusually good weather with only 4 cancellations for weather, against 17 in the previous year.

3.3 Days off. The average number of days off per 7 days was 2.3 in the trial and 2.2 before. On 5 occasions in the 8 weeks a cabin crew member was given only 1 day off in 7, which breaches the union agreement. The authors explain that these occurred when an override was made by the planner after a crew member went sick.

3.4 Long runs. Four crew members worked more than 10 days in a row during the trial. In the previous year the number was 6 over the same period.

3.5 Planner time. Planners spent an average of 3.5 hours a week on rostering during the trial, compared with 14 hours a week for the manual method. The authors note that the planners spent additional time checking the heuristic's output, which is not included, and that the second planner was on leave for three weeks of the trial.

3.6 Overrides. Planners overrode the roster 23 times, of which 14 were to accommodate shift swaps requested by crew. The authors do not report the effect of the overrides on the call-out numbers.

4. Discussion

We conclude that the heuristic is a better method than manual rostering and recommend that it be used for all crew from the winter schedule. The reduction in call-outs would save about 475 pounds a week at the Port Merrow base, or about 24,700 pounds a year, and the reduction in planner hours would free time for other work. The lower number of duty-limit exceedances improves safety. We believe the heuristic would generalise to other bases.

5. Limitations

The trial lasted 8 weeks at one base. The comparison period was a different year, and the schedule was slightly different, as one route had been added. The heuristic's parameters were tuned using the previous year's data, which was also used in the comparison.

Below is the start of a short story I'm working on, narrated by a junior tax adviser. Please continue it for at least three more chapters in the same first-person voice and dry tone, keeping Mr. Penhallow's habits and the mystery of the receipts consistent. I'd like the story to head towards something surprising, but not a cheap twist, and please keep the office setting central.

THE SHOEBOX

1.

In my first week at Lindqvist and Oyelaran Tax Advisers, Mrs. Oyelaran told me that every client lies, but only the interesting ones lie about the wrong thing. I wrote this on a sticky note and put it on my monitor, where it stayed for eleven months, until a cleaner threw it away along with a half-eaten sandwich I had also been meaning to deal with.

I was twenty-four. I had a degree in accounting, a second-hand suit that had belonged to my uncle, and a desk by the radiator in an office above a shop that sold only umbrellas. The shop was called Rain Check. In all the time I worked there I never saw a customer go in. Mrs. Oyelaran said this meant they were laundering money. Mr. Lindqvist, who was eighty and mostly asleep, said it meant they were very good at umbrellas.

Our busiest season was January, when the self-employed brought us their lives in carrier bags, and our quietest was August, when we alphabetised the filing cabinets and argued about the kettle. It was a Tuesday in late October, which has no season, when Mr. Penhallow came in.

I knew who he was before he sat down, because Mrs. Oyelaran had warned me about him the week before in the tone she used for weather forecasts. Ambrose Penhallow was seventy-one, a retired clockmaker, and a client of the firm for thirty-four years. He had never missed a deadline. He had never claimed a single expense that was not supported by a receipt. And he had never, ever, explained anything.

"Miss Adeyemi," he said, lowering himself into the chair opposite mine as if it might object. "I understand that I'm yours now."

"Mrs. Oyelaran has asked me to look after your return this year," I said.

"Yes. I'm afraid it's a bit larger than usual." He lifted a shoebox onto my desk. It was a man's size eleven, brown, with a lid tied on by what looked like a bootlace. It made a sound as it landed, a soft, dry, papery sound, like a very large bird shifting its feet.

2.

I should explain about the receipts.

In thirty-four years Mr. Penhallow had sent us one folder a year, a grey folder with an elastic strap, and inside it, sorted by month and clipped in bundles, every receipt for every purchase that touched his business. Screws. Brass blanks. Mainsprings, jewelling oil, magnifying lenses, a replacement kettle for the workshop, train fares to a trade fair in Leipzig. The folders were famous in the firm. Mr. Lindqvist used to take them out at the Christmas lunch and read the totals aloud as if they were poetry.

This was not that kind of delivery. I untied the bootlace and lifted the lid, and found some two hundred slips of paper, none of them clipped, none of them sorted, and all of them for the same amount.

Four pounds twenty.

I turned over the first one. It was a till receipt from a café on Quillon Street, dated the fourth of March last year, and it listed one pot of tea for one and a toasted teacake. The second was from the same café, dated the sixth. The third, the ninth. I ran my thumb through the pile and saw the same name printed along the top of every slip, Brannock's Tea Room, in a typeface so cheerful that it felt rude.

"These are all from one place," I said.

"Yes."

"On, I think, every few days for the past year and a half."

"It's two hundred and eleven visits, to be accurate. Tuesdays and Fridays, and the odd Saturday when it rained." He folded his hands. "I should like to claim them."

"As a business expense?"

"As a business expense."

I thought of the sticky note on my monitor. "Mr. Penhallow, I'd need to know what the business was. Tea and a teacake is a personal cost unless there was a client meeting, or a working lunch with a supplier, or a reason connected to the trade. Your workshop closed in March last year, if I'm reading the file correctly."

"The workshop closed. The business did not."

He said it with such calm that I wrote it down. Then I looked at what I had written and felt, for the first time that week, the particular itch of a person who has been handed a question when she was expecting a sum.

I tried once more. I asked whether anyone had met him at the tea room, whether he had taken notes, whether a customer or a supplier or a former apprentice had sat opposite him. He listened to each question with real courtesy and answered none of them. When I ran out, he stood, buttoned his coat from the bottom up, the way men of his generation do, and rested one hand on the shoebox as if it were a sleeping dog.

"Four pounds twenty," he said, "is the price of a pot of tea for one and a toasted teacake. It is also, if you divide it carefully, the price of something else. I would rather you found that out yourself, Miss Adeyemi. Mrs. Oyelaran says you are the sort who does."

Then he went down the stairs, past the umbrellas, and out into the rain without taking one.

3.

I did what any sensible junior would do, which was to take the shoebox to Mrs. Oyelaran and say nothing for forty seconds.

She looked at the receipts. She turned a few of them over. She picked one up by its corner and held it to the window, as if it might have a watermark, and then she put it back and said, "How many?"

"Two hundred and eleven. I counted them twice."

"What's the date range?"

"March last year to last Friday."

"And the amounts?"

"All four pounds twenty."

"Not a penny different?"

"Not one."

She was silent, and the radiator ticked. Through the floor I could hear the faint, gentle, unvisited quiet of Rain Check.

"Tea rooms vary their prices," she said at last. "They put them up in January. They have specials. A person who goes to the same café two hundred times does not spend exactly four pounds twenty each time, unless he orders exactly the same thing, in exactly the same way, and the café does not change its prices for a year and a half, or unless."

"Unless what?"

"Unless the receipts are not from the café." She laid a finger on the printed name. "Ask yourself who prints a receipt that cheerful."

I took the lid, the bootlace and the box back to my desk and sat there until the radiator had finished ticking. On the edge of the lid, in pencil, in the small upright hand of a man who had spent his working life engraving numbers on the backs of watches, was a single line I had not seen. It read: *Ask Brannock, not the bank.*

I rang the number on the slip. It was answered on the first ring by a woman who said, "Brannock's," in the tone of someone who had been waiting for the call for a year and a half.

Produktspezifikation: Baumpflege-Manager (BPM) für das Grünflächenamt der Stadt Lindenau
Version 1.2, Entwurf zur Abnahme
Verantwortlich: Henrike Salzmann-Brandt, Abteilungsleiterin Stadtgrün

1. Zweck

Das Grünflächenamt der Stadt Lindenau pflegt rund 31.000 Straßen- und Parkbäume. Bisher wird das Baumkataster in einer Tabellenkalkulation geführt, Kontrollen werden auf Papier festgehalten, und Pflegeaufträge an die Kolonnen werden per E-Mail verteilt. Der Baumpflege-Manager (BPM) ersetzt diese Werkzeuge. Er verwaltet die Bäume, plant die gesetzlich geforderten Regelkontrollen, erzeugt Pflegeaufträge, dokumentiert Fällungen und Ersatzpflanzungen und liefert dem Amt die Zahlen für den jährlichen Bericht.

2. Rollen

2.1 Baumkontrolleur: erfasst Kontrollergebnisse und legt Pflegeaufträge an. Er darf keine Bäume löschen.
2.2 Kolonnenführer: sieht die ihm zugewiesenen Aufträge, meldet Arbeitsbeginn und Fertigstellung und lädt Fotos hoch.
2.3 Sachbearbeiter: legt Bäume an, ändert Stammdaten, genehmigt Fällungen unter 40 cm Stammdurchmesser und erstellt Berichte.
2.4 Amtsleitung: genehmigt alle Fällungen ab 40 cm Stammdurchmesser und alle Fällungen von Bäumen, die als Naturdenkmal markiert sind. Sie hat Lesezugriff auf alle Daten.
2.5 Jeder Benutzer hat genau eine Rolle. Rollen werden nur von der Systemadministration geändert.

3. Baumdaten

3.1 Pflichtfelder eines Baumes sind: Baumnummer (automatisch vergeben, Format B-000000), Art (aus der Artenliste), Standort (Koordinaten im Landeskoordinatensystem und Straße oder Parkname), Pflanzjahr (oder „unbekannt“), Stammdurchmesser in Zentimetern, Kronenhöhe in Metern und Zustandsklasse.
3.2 Die Zustandsklasse ist eine Zahl von 0 bis 4: 0 gesund, 1 leichte Mängel, 2 deutliche Mängel, 3 stark geschädigt, 4 abgestorben.
3.3 Der Stammdurchmesser muss zwischen 1 und 400 liegen. Die Kronenhöhe muss zwischen 1 und 45 liegen.
3.4 Ein Baum kann als Naturdenkmal gekennzeichnet werden. Dann ist zusätzlich die Nummer der Schutzverordnung anzugeben.
3.5 Bäume werden nie physisch gelöscht. Eine Fällung setzt den Status auf „gefällt“ und speichert das Datum.

4. Regelkontrollen

4.1 Jeder Baum wird in einem festen Intervall kontrolliert, das von der Zustandsklasse abhängt: Klasse 0 und 1 alle 24 Monate, Klasse 2 alle 12 Monate, Klasse 3 alle 6 Monate. Bäume der Klasse 4 werden innerhalb von 14 Tagen gefällt und nicht mehr kontrolliert.
4.2 An Spielplätzen, Schulen und Kindertagesstätten gilt für alle Bäume höchstens ein Intervall von 12 Monaten, unabhängig von der Klasse.
4.3 Das System erzeugt am ersten Werktag jedes Monats eine Kontrollliste für die Bäume, deren Kontrolle im laufenden oder im folgenden Monat fällig ist, sortiert nach Fälligkeitsdatum und danach nach Stadtbezirk.
4.4 Eine Kontrolle gilt als überfällig, wenn das Fälligkeitsdatum überschritten ist. Überfällige Kontrollen werden in der Übersicht rot dargestellt und nach 30 Tagen an die Abteilungsleiterin gemeldet.
4.5 Bei einer Kontrolle erfasst der Kontrolleur: Datum, neue Zustandsklasse, Befund (Freitext, höchstens 500 Zeichen) und, falls nötig, Maßnahmen. Das Datum darf nicht in der Zukunft liegen.
4.6 Ändert sich die Zustandsklasse, wird das nächste Kontrolldatum sofort nach 4.1 neu berechnet.

5. Pflegeaufträge

5.1 Ein Pflegeauftrag hat: Baumnummer, Maßnahme (Kronenpflege, Totholzentfernung, Fällung, Wurzelbehandlung, Nachpflanzung), Dringlichkeit (hoch, normal, niedrig), Frist und zugewiesene Kolonne.
5.2 Aufträge mit Dringlichkeit „hoch“ erhalten automatisch eine Frist von 3 Werktagen, „normal“ von 8 Wochen und „niedrig“ von 6 Monaten. Der Sachbearbeiter kann die Frist verlängern, aber nicht verkürzen.
5.3 Eine Fällung wird erst zur Ausführung freigegeben, wenn sie nach 2.3 oder 2.4 genehmigt wurde. Ausgenommen sind Fällungen bei Gefahr im Verzug (Zustandsklasse 4 mit Dringlichkeit „hoch“), die sofort freigegeben werden, aber nachträglich innerhalb von 5 Werktagen bestätigt werden müssen.
5.4 Ein Auftrag durchläuft die Status offen, zugewiesen, in Arbeit, erledigt und abgenommen. Der Kolonnenführer kann nur von zugewiesen auf in Arbeit und von in Arbeit auf erledigt schalten. Die Abnahme erfolgt durch den Kontrolleur, der den Baum erneut bewertet.
5.5 Für die Fertigstellung sind mindestens ein Foto und der Zeitaufwand in Minuten erforderlich.
5.6 Wird ein Auftrag nicht innerhalb seiner Frist erledigt, erscheint er auf der Liste der verspäteten Aufträge und wird einmal pro Woche per E-Mail an die Abteilungsleiterin gesendet.

6. Fällungen und Ersatzpflanzungen

6.1 Für jeden gefällten Baum mit einem Stammdurchmesser von mindestens 20 cm muss eine Ersatzpflanzung angelegt werden. Der Ersatz erfolgt im Verhältnis 1:1 bei Durchmessern bis 60 cm und im Verhältnis 1:2 bei Durchmessern über 60 cm.
6.2 Die Ersatzpflanzung muss innerhalb der nächsten Pflanzperiode (1. November bis 31. März) erfolgen. Das System legt dafür automatisch einen Auftrag mit niedriger Dringlichkeit an.
6.3 Kann der Ersatz nicht am selben Standort erfolgen, ist ein anderer Standort im selben Stadtbezirk zu wählen und zu begründen.

7. Berichte

7.1 Der Jahresbericht enthält: Anzahl der Bäume nach Art, nach Zustandsklasse und nach Stadtbezirk, die Zahl der Kontrollen, die Zahl der überfälligen Kontrollen am Stichtag 31. Dezember, die Zahl der Fällungen und Ersatzpflanzungen sowie die durchschnittliche Bearbeitungsdauer der Aufträge.
7.2 Berichte können als PDF und als CSV-Datei (Trennzeichen Semikolon, Zeichensatz UTF-8) exportiert werden.

8. Nichtfunktionale Anforderungen

8.1 Eine Karte mit bis zu 5.000 Bäumen im sichtbaren Ausschnitt muss in weniger als 4 Sekunden geladen werden.
8.2 Die Kolonnenführer arbeiten mit Tablets und müssen Aufträge auch ohne Netzverbindung ansehen und abschließen können. Die Daten werden abgeglichen, sobald wieder eine Verbindung besteht.
8.3 Alle Änderungen an Bäumen und Aufträgen werden mit Benutzer und Zeitpunkt protokolliert und mindestens 10 Jahre aufbewahrt.
8.4 Die Anmeldung erfolgt über das zentrale Benutzerverzeichnis der Stadt. Nach 20 Minuten Inaktivität wird die Sitzung beendet.

9. Offene Punkte

Es ist noch nicht entschieden, ob Bäume auf privaten Grundstücken, für die die Stadt eine Verkehrssicherungspflicht übernommen hat, aufgenommen werden. Ebenso ist offen, ob Bürger Schäden über ein Online-Formular melden dürfen.

I'm a new harbour assistant and these are my notes from the induction lecture on landings, fees and quotas. I have a test at the end of the week. Please make me a study guide from them with clear worked examples that go through each calculation step by step, and then a quiz of 12 to 15 questions with full answers. Use the same numbers and rules as in my notes wherever you can.

Induction lecture 3: Landings, dues and quota (Skerrow Haven Harbour Authority)
Speaker: Harbour Master Orla Bannerman-Fisk

1. What the authority does

The Authority owns the quays, the fish market hall, the ice plant and the fuel berth at Skerrow Haven. We do not own the boats and we do not buy the fish. We rent space, supply services and collect fees, and we keep the records that the fisheries office needs. The harbour handles about 140 registered vessels, from 8 metre inshore boats to a few 24 metre trawlers, and lands around 5,200 tonnes of fish and shellfish a year.

2. Berths and tides

The harbour dries out. At low tide the inner basin is mud, so large boats can enter or leave only within about 2 hours either side of high water. The harbour keeps a tide table, and the pilot book gives the height of the tide above chart datum. The sill at the entrance is 3.2 metres above chart datum. A boat needs a clearance of at least 0.5 metres under the keel at the sill. The depth of water over the sill is the tide height minus 3.2 metres, and it must be at least the boat's draught plus 0.5 metres.

Worked example 1. The trawler Marguerite draws 2.6 metres. Required water over the sill = 2.6 + 0.5 = 3.1 metres. Required tide height = 3.2 + 3.1 = 6.3 metres above chart datum. If high water tonight is 7.1 metres, there is 7.1 - 6.3 = 0.8 metres to spare, and the boat can cross the sill for as long as the tide stays above 6.3 metres.

3. Landing procedure

A skipper must give notice of arrival at least 2 hours before landing, giving the species and the estimated weight. When the boat is alongside, the market staff weigh each box on the certified scales, record the species, size grade and the box number on the landing declaration, and the declaration is signed by the skipper. The Authority sends the declaration data to the fisheries office within 24 hours. Boats may not land fish between 22:00 and 05:00 without the permission of the harbour master. Fish landed without a declaration are not allowed to enter the market and the harbour master must report the matter.

Boxes are standard 40 litre boxes. A full box of whitefish holds about 30 kilograms of fish plus 8 kilograms of ice. Weights in the declaration are net weights of fish, so the ice must be deducted. An empty box weighs 1.5 kilograms. The scales are checked every Monday with a 20 kilogram test weight, and the reading must be within 50 grams.

Worked example 2. A boat lands 64 boxes of haddock. The scales show a mean gross weight of 40.2 kilograms per box. Net weight per box = 40.2 - 8 (ice) - 1.5 (box) = 30.7 kilograms. Total net weight = 64 x 30.7 = 1,964.8 kilograms.

4. Dues and charges

The Authority charges landing dues of 2.5 percent of the first sale value of the fish, paid by the seller. A boat that sells through the market hall also pays a market fee of 1.2 percent of the sale value. Boats under 12 metres get a 20 percent discount on landing dues, but not on the market fee. Berthing is charged per metre of vessel length per day at 0.85 pounds, with the first 24 hours free for boats that land at least 500 kilograms of fish. Ice is sold at 118 pounds a tonne.

Worked example 3. The 11 metre boat Kittiwake sells 1,964.8 kilograms of haddock through the market at an average price of 2.40 pounds per kilogram. Sale value = 1,964.8 x 2.40 = 4,715.52 pounds. Landing dues before discount = 2.5 percent x 4,715.52 = 117.89 pounds. The 20 percent discount applies, so the dues are 117.89 x 0.8 = 94.31 pounds. The market fee is 1.2 percent x 4,715.52 = 56.59 pounds. Total payable to the Authority = 94.31 + 56.59 = 150.90 pounds.

5. Ice and cold chain

The ice plant makes flake ice at up to 12 tonnes a day. The rule of thumb is 1 kilogram of ice for every 3.75 kilograms of fish for a landing that will be sold within 12 hours, and 1 kilogram of ice for every 2 kilograms of fish if the fish will be held for more than 24 hours. Fish must be kept at between 0 and 4 degrees. The market hall chiller is checked twice a day and the temperatures are logged. If the temperature rises above 6 degrees for more than 30 minutes, the stock in the chiller must be examined by the market inspector before it is sold.

Worked example 4. A trawler plans to hold 3,000 kilograms of cod for 30 hours before sale. Ice needed = 3,000 / 2 = 1,500 kilograms. At 118 pounds a tonne, the ice costs 1.5 x 118 = 177 pounds.

6. Quota

Each vessel has a monthly quota for each regulated species, set by the fisheries office. The Authority does not set quota but must refuse a landing if the vessel has no quota left for that species and tell the fisheries office. A vessel's quota use is the total of its net landed weights for the month.

Worked example 5. The Marguerite has a monthly cod quota of 18 tonnes. By the 20th she has landed 14.6 tonnes, and she lands another 2.9 tonnes. The total is 14.6 + 2.9 = 17.5 tonnes, which is 17.5 / 18 = 97.2 percent of the quota. She has 0.5 tonnes remaining. If she lands 0.7 tonnes more, she will be 0.2 tonnes over, and the landing must be refused for that amount, or reported.

7. Safety on the quay

Hard hats and high visibility vests are required on the fish market floor. Nobody may stand under a crane load. Fuel berth smoking is banned. A lifebuoy and a throw line must be at every 50 metres of quay edge. A person in the water is to be reported at once on the harbour radio on channel 16, and the harbour master must be called immediately.

We run a small parent portal for our network of kindergartens (daily reports, pick-up authorisations, photos) and the whole setup was put together by a contractor who has left. Please audit these files: list the problems you find from most to least serious, explain in plain language why each matters (we hold data about small children, so privacy matters a lot), and then give me corrected versions of the Dockerfile, the compose file and the deploy workflow.

--- Dockerfile ---

WORKDIR /app
COPY . /app

RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl vim git
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt

ENV FLASK_ENV=development
ENV SECRET_KEY=littlesprouts2024
ENV DATABASE_URL=postgresql://portal:portal@db:5432/portal

EXPOSE 5000
CMD ["python", "app.py"]

--- docker-compose.yml ---

version: "3"
services:
  web:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "80:5000"
    environment:
      - DEBUG=1
      - PHOTO_DIR=/photos
      - SMTP_PASSWORD=Sprout$mail2024
    volumes:
      - ./:/app
      - /srv/photos:/photos
    depends_on:
      - db
    restart: always

  db:
    image: postgres
    ports:

    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: portal
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: portal
      POSTGRES_DB: portal
    volumes:
      - dbdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data

  backup:
    image: postgres
    command: sh -c "while true; do pg_dump -h db -U portal portal > /backup/dump.sql; sleep 86400; done"
    volumes:
      - /srv/backup:/backup

volumes:
  dbdata:

--- .github/workflows/deploy.yml ---

name: deploy
on:
  push:
    branches: [main, develop]
  pull_request:

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@master
      - name: Set up Python
        uses: actions/setup-python@v4
        with:
          python-version: 3.x
      - name: Install
        run: pip install -r requirements.txt
      - name: Test
        run: pytest || true
      - name: Deploy
        run: |
          echo "${{ secrets.DEPLOY_KEY }}" > key.pem
          chmod 600 key.pem
          ssh -o StrictHostKeyChecking=no -i key.pem deploy@portal.example.org "cd /srv/portal && git pull && docker-compose up -d --build"
          echo "Deployed with password ${{ secrets.DB_PASSWORD }}"

--- nginx.conf (on the host, in front of the containers) ---

server {
    listen 80;
    server_name portal.example.org;

    location / {
        proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:80;
    }

    location /photos/ {
        alias /srv/photos/;
        autoindex on;
    }
}

--- requirements.txt ---

flask
flask-sqlalchemy
psycopg2
gunicorn
pillow==8.1.0
requests==2.19.0
pytest

--- config.py ---

class Config:
    SECRET_KEY = os.environ.get("SECRET_KEY", "dev")
    SQLALCHEMY_DATABASE_URI = os.environ["DATABASE_URL"]

    MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH = None
    SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE = False
    SESSION_COOKIE_HTTPONLY = False
