--- /etc/cron.d/portal-cleanup ---

# remove photos older than two years
0 3 * * * root find /srv/photos -mtime +730 -delete

--- scripts/restore.sh (written but never run) ---

#!/bin/bash
# restore the latest dump into the running database
docker exec -i portal_db_1 psql -U portal portal < /srv/backup/dump.sql

--- /etc/cron.d/portal-health ---

*/5 * * * * root curl -s http://localhost > /dev/null || echo "portal down" | mail -s alert ops@example.org

--- /etc/ssh/sshd_config (changed lines) ---

PermitRootLogin yes
PasswordAuthentication yes
AllowUsers deploy root admin

--- Facts about the setup ---

- The portal is used by about 1,100 parents across 7 kindergartens. Staff upload photos of children to the daily reports, and parents see only their own child's photos.
- The server is a single virtual machine at a hosting company. It has a public IP address and the firewall is open on all ports because "it was easier".
- The nginx file above is on the same machine as the containers. TLS has never been set up; staff were told to ask parents to use the "http" link.
- Nobody has ever restored a backup. The backup service writes to the same dump.sql every day, and the host disk has 14 GB free.
- The photo folder /srv/photos is 41 GB and is not included in any backup. There are no photo thumbnails, and the portal sends the full-size images.
- The deploy runs on every push to the main and develop branches and on pull requests, including pull requests from outside contributors, because the repository is public.
- The Python version used in production is whatever the "latest" tag was on the day the image was last built, which was in March.
- The app writes logs to the console only. When the container restarts, the logs are lost.
- A file called .env.production, which contains the real database and mail passwords, was committed to the repository in 2024 and is still in its history.
- The deploy key in the repository secrets belongs to a personal account of the contractor who left, and nobody knows what else it can open.
- Parents are told by the kindergartens that photos are deleted after two years, and the cron job above is how that is supposed to happen.
- Two kindergartens share one staff login each, and the passwords are on a sticker behind the reception desk. There is no second factor and no way to see who uploaded a photo.
- The hosting contract is renewed each year by one person, the network's office manager, who has no technical background and wants to understand the risks in plain language before the next board meeting in November.

Our board meets on Thursday and I need to brief them without reading all of this out loud. Could you go through the Q3 operations review below section by section, give me a short summary of each, and then write a list of recommendations in order of priority, saying what each one costs us if we ignore it?

QUARTERLY OPERATIONS REVIEW, Q3 (July to September)
Ashgrove Valley Water Authority
Prepared by: Operations Directorate, for the Board of Governors
Status: final draft, figures reconciled to the end of September

1. Executive summary

The third quarter was the hottest on our records for the catchment, and demand reflected it. Average daily production was 61.4 megalitres per day (Ml/d), 7.8 percent above the same quarter last year and 4.1 percent above our own forecast. Peak day demand reached 83.9 Ml/d on 17 August, which is 96 percent of the combined rated capacity of our two treatment works. No restrictions were imposed, but we came within eleven days of the trigger in our drought plan for a hosepipe notice, and the Carrow reservoir ended the quarter at 58 percent of useable storage against a seasonal norm of 71 percent.

Compliance with drinking water standards held at 99.96 percent across 4,812 regulatory samples. Two samples failed: one for coliforms at a customer tap in Denby Row, traced to a defective internal fitting, and one for turbidity at the Millbrook service reservoir outlet, described under incidents below. Leakage fell to 18.2 Ml/d from 19.6 Ml/d in Q2, helped by the new pressure management zones, but we remain above the target of 17.0 Ml/d agreed with the regulator for the year end. Customer contacts rose 12 percent, driven by low pressure complaints during the heat. Operating cost was 2.1 percent over budget, almost entirely from electricity and chemicals, and capital delivery reached 71 percent of the year to date plan.

Three matters need a board decision: whether to approve early procurement of the Millbrook filter refurbishment, whether to fund a second summer standby pumping contract, and whether to adopt the revised leakage recovery plan described in section 4.

2. Supply and demand

Production by source for the quarter was as follows.

| Source | Q3 volume (Ml/d avg) | Share | Change vs Q3 last year |
|---|---|---|---|
| Carrow reservoir (Hale treatment works) | 34.9 | 56.8% | +9.2% |
| River Ainsley abstraction (Millbrook works) | 21.3 | 34.7% | +6.1% |
| Boreholes (Thornby and Eastfield) | 5.2 | 8.5% | +4.0% |
| Total | 61.4 | 100% | +7.8% |

The river abstraction licence allows an annual average of 24.0 Ml/d and a daily maximum of 31.0 Ml/d. We touched 29.7 Ml/d on 17 August. The licence has a hands-off flow condition of 6.5 cubic metres per second at the Ainsley gauge, and flow fell to 7.1 on 22 August, so we reduced abstraction by 4 Ml/d for three days to stay clear of the limit. This put extra draw on Carrow, which explains the 9.2 percent rise there.

Demand per head was 148 litres per person per day, up from 141. Household metered consumption rose 6.5 percent, and non-household demand rose 3.0 percent, mostly from horticulture and the two food processing sites on the Hale road. The unmetered household estimate remains a weakness: about 9 percent of connections still have no meter, and we assume they use 14 percent more than metered neighbours, a figure last tested four years ago.

3. Treatment and water quality

Hale works ran at an average of 82 percent of its 42 Ml/d capacity and Millbrook at 78 percent of its 36 Ml/d capacity. Chemical use per megalitre treated rose 5.4 percent because warm raw water increased algal load and coagulant dose. Alum dosing at Hale averaged 31 mg/l against 24 mg/l in Q3 last year. The new dissolved air flotation train at Hale, commissioned in May, handled the algal peak well and kept filter run lengths above 60 hours throughout.

Millbrook was less fortunate. Its rapid gravity filters are original 1994 equipment, and on 3 and 4 September the combined filtered water turbidity crept up to 0.31 NTU at the works outlet, over the internal action level of 0.20 and briefly over the regulatory limit of 0.30 at one reading. The cause was a failed underdrain nozzle set in filter 4, which let media pass into the clearwater tank in small amounts. The filter was isolated within three hours of the alarm, and the sample failure at the service reservoir was recorded as a single exceedance. No boil notice was needed because chlorine contact and subsequent samples showed no risk, and the regulator accepted our report without enforcement action. An inspection of the other five filters found nozzle wear in filters 2 and 6 as well.

Taste and odour contacts, mostly geosmin related, numbered 214, against 96 last year. Granular activated carbon dosing at Hale was started in July and cut complaints by half within three weeks.

4. Network performance and leakage

The network comprises 2,310 kilometres of mains and 71,400 connections. Bursts on mains were 392 in the quarter, against 351 last year, with a sharp cluster in cast iron mains in the Denby and Orchard Hill zones as clay soils dried and shrank. Average time from report to repair was 19.5 hours for mains and 31 hours for communication pipes, both within our service standard of 24 and 48 hours.

Leakage by component, in Ml/d:

| Component | Q2 | Q3 | Target year end |
|---|---|---|---|
| Distribution mains | 9.8 | 9.1 | 8.4 |
| Communication pipes | 5.6 | 5.3 | 4.9 |
| Customer supply pipes | 3.1 | 2.9 | 2.8 |
| Trunk mains and reservoirs | 1.1 | 0.9 | 0.9 |
| Total | 19.6 | 18.2 | 17.0 |

Four new pressure management zones went live in July, covering 11,200 connections, and the average zone pressure fell by 6.3 metres with no rise in low pressure complaints inside those zones. The low pressure complaints that did rise were in zones with older mains and no pressure control, where peak demand simply outran capacity. We also completed 61 percent of planned acoustic loggers, with 480 of 790 installed. Logger deployment slipped because the supplier delivered 140 units late and with a faulty battery batch.

To close the gap of 1.2 Ml/d to target by March, the leakage recovery plan proposes three actions: finishing logger installation by mid-November, a dedicated find-and-fix crew of six on nights through the winter, and replacing 9.5 kilometres of the worst cast iron mains in Denby and Orchard Hill, which together account for 22 percent of bursts on 6 percent of the network. The crew and logger work are covered by existing budget. The main replacement needs 3.4 million in capital that is not currently allocated.

5. Capital programme

The capital programme for the year is 46.8 million. Spend to the end of September was 19.6 million against a plan of 27.6 million, or 71 percent. The shortfall is concentrated in three projects.

| Project | Budget (m) | Spend to date (m) | Plan to date (m) | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hale DAF train and sludge handling | 11.2 | 10.4 | 10.6 | Complete, final account open |
| Eastfield borehole replacement | 4.1 | 1.2 | 2.6 | Late: drilling rig delay, 7 weeks |
| Millbrook filter refurbishment | 8.5 | 0.7 | 3.0 | Not started: awaiting board approval |
| Trunk main renewal, Ainsley crossing | 6.3 | 3.1 | 4.1 | Late: consent for river works |
| Mains renewal, general | 9.4 | 3.3 | 5.0 | Late: contractor labour |
| Meter replacement | 7.3 | 0.9 | 2.3 | Late: smart meter supply |

The meter project illustrates the supply chain problem. We ordered 12,000 smart meters in March; 3,100 arrived by the end of September. The contractor has promised the balance by end of December, but we have no remedy in the contract for further slippage beyond a small delay payment. Mains renewal is delayed because our framework contractor lost two gangs to a competing utility and has told us it can deliver only 70 percent of the planned length this year.

Millbrook is the item the board is asked to decide. The refurbishment replaces all six filter underdrains, media and control valves. Design is complete and the contractor can start in January if we place an early works order of 0.9 million before the end of October. Waiting for the normal budget cycle in December would push the work into next summer, when the works would again run near capacity and have one filter out of service at a time.

6. Customer service

Total contacts were 38,900, up 12 percent. The split was billing 41 percent, supply interruptions and low pressure 29 percent, water quality 12 percent, metering 9 percent and other 9 percent. Calls answered within 30 seconds were 81 percent against a target of 85, and the abandonment rate peaked at 14 percent during the week of 11 August when a burst on the Orchard Hill trunk main interrupted supply to 3,800 properties for between four and nine hours.

Satisfaction with supply interruption handling was 74 percent, compared with 82 percent for the year to date overall. Customers' strongest complaint was a lack of updates: text messages were sent on only 58 percent of unplanned interruptions because the text system required a manual trigger. The system has been changed to trigger automatically from the incident log, effective 20 September, and early results show 91 percent of affected customers now receive a message within thirty minutes.

Complaints that escalated to formal stage numbered 63, down from 71. The ombudsman upheld none. The largest category was property damage after bursts, where three claims totalled 46,000.

7. Finance

Operating expenditure was 24.7 million against a budget of 24.2 million, an overspend of 0.5 million. Electricity cost 0.38 million more than budget because of higher pumping hours and the end of a fixed price contract in July. Chemicals were 0.21 million over, from the dosing increases already described. These were offset in part by vacancies, which saved 0.19 million, although the vacancies also contributed to the delays in repair of communication pipes late in the quarter.

Income from charges was 0.3 percent above plan, thanks to volume. Bad debt was 2.4 percent of billing, flat. The treasury position is unchanged: 62 percent of debt is at fixed rates, and the next refinancing date is June. The board should note that the full-year forecast now shows a 0.9 million operating overspend if hot, dry conditions continue into October and electricity prices stay where they are.

8. Health, safety and people

There were two lost time injuries, both minor: a strained back during a valve exercise and a laceration at the Thornby borehole. The lost time injury rate is 0.9 per 100,000 hours, against 1.4 last year. Contractor near misses rose to 17 from 9, and 11 of them involve vehicles and plant on trench sites. Staff turnover was 11 percent annualised, with the hardest roles to fill being network technicians and treatment process controllers. The authority has 19 open vacancies, eight of them in network operations.

Training completion for confined space entry stands at 88 percent against a target of 100, with 14 staff overdue. Overdue staff have been barred from confined space work until training is complete.

9. Environment and regulation

Energy use rose to 0.61 kilowatt hours per cubic metre delivered, from 0.57, because the heat pushed more water through the high lift pumps at Hale and because the Thornby boreholes ran for 1,940 hours against 1,310 last year. Our carbon target for the year is a 6 percent reduction against the baseline, and the quarter's performance leaves us 2 percent above baseline for the year to date. The authority's roof solar array at Millbrook generated 412 megawatt hours, which covered 9 percent of that site's use. A proposal for a second array over the Hale sludge lagoons has been costed at 1.6 million with a payback of eleven years, and is not in the current capital plan.

Three regulatory items are open. The first is the abstraction licence review for the Ainsley, which the environment regulator opened on 1 September. Its draft position suggests lowering the daily maximum from 31.0 to 28.0 Ml/d from 2028 unless we can show a reduction in demand or a new source. Had the lower limit applied this August, we would have exceeded it on four days. The second is the annual drinking water report, which we filed on time on 15 July. The third is the leakage commitment: if we miss the 17.0 Ml/d year end target, the regulator's published method implies a financial penalty of roughly 0.6 million for each 0.5 Ml/d of shortfall, so a gap of 1.2 Ml/d would cost about 1.4 million.

The pollution incident record is clean. There were no category 1 or 2 events, and one category 3 event, a 400 litre discharge of backwash water to a field drain at Thornby on 29 July, which was contained and reported within two hours. Public complaints about construction noise at the Ainsley crossing numbered 9, all dealt with by agreed working hours.

10. Outlook

The coming quarter carries four risks. First, Carrow will not recover until autumn rain arrives, and a dry October would put the reservoir below 50 percent going into winter, which has implications for next summer. Second, Millbrook has no spare filter capacity, so another failure at the works could cut output by up to 15 percent. Third, the smart meter delay will push back the demand data we need to refine the unmetered household estimate. Fourth, the contractor shortage affects every capital project that needs trench work, and the authority has not yet pursued a second framework supplier.

The directorate asks the board to approve the early works order for Millbrook, to fund a second summer standby pumping contract for a one-off cost of 0.28 million, and to approve the leakage recovery plan including the 3.4 million for cast iron main replacement.

I inherited this timetable and ticketing database at Calder Vale Rail when our previous data engineer left, and the passenger-facing reports have been getting slower every month. Could you review the schema design properly, tell me which indexes are missing or wasted, and rewrite the six queries at the bottom so they run better? Please explain each change so I can defend it to the team.

We use PostgreSQL 15. The tables below hold about 40 stations, 310 daily train services, 1.8 million tickets a year and roughly 9 million service-stop records a year. The schema and queries are exactly as they are in production.

```sql
-- Calder Vale Rail operations database

CREATE TABLE station (
    station_id      integer PRIMARY KEY,
    code            varchar(4) NOT NULL,
    name            varchar(80) NOT NULL,
    zone            integer NOT NULL,
    step_free       boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false,
    opened_on       date
);

CREATE TABLE route (
    route_id        integer PRIMARY KEY,
    name            varchar(60) NOT NULL,
    origin_id       integer NOT NULL REFERENCES station(station_id),
    destination_id  integer NOT NULL REFERENCES station(station_id),
    length_km       numeric(6,2) NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE route_stop (
    route_id        integer NOT NULL REFERENCES route(route_id),
    stop_number     integer NOT NULL,
    station_id      integer NOT NULL REFERENCES station(station_id),
    minutes_from_origin integer NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (route_id, stop_number)
);

CREATE TABLE train_unit (
    unit_id         integer PRIMARY KEY,
    class_code      varchar(10) NOT NULL,
    seats           integer NOT NULL,
    in_service_from date NOT NULL,
    retired_on      date
);

CREATE TABLE service (
    service_id      bigint PRIMARY KEY,
    route_id        integer NOT NULL REFERENCES route(route_id),
    unit_id         integer REFERENCES train_unit(unit_id),
    service_date    date NOT NULL,
    scheduled_departure timestamp NOT NULL,
    status          varchar(20) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'scheduled'
);

CREATE TABLE service_stop (
    service_stop_id bigint PRIMARY KEY,
    service_id      bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES service(service_id),
    station_id      integer NOT NULL REFERENCES station(station_id),
    stop_number     integer NOT NULL,
    scheduled_arrival   timestamp NOT NULL,
    actual_arrival      timestamp,
    scheduled_departure timestamp NOT NULL,
    actual_departure    timestamp,
    platform        varchar(4)
);

CREATE TABLE passenger (
    passenger_id    bigint PRIMARY KEY,
    email           varchar(120) NOT NULL,
    full_name       varchar(100) NOT NULL,
    railcard        varchar(20),
    created_at      timestamp NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE ticket (
    ticket_id       bigint PRIMARY KEY,
    passenger_id    bigint REFERENCES passenger(passenger_id),
    service_id      bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES service(service_id),
    from_station_id integer NOT NULL REFERENCES station(station_id),
    to_station_id   integer NOT NULL REFERENCES station(station_id),
    fare_pence      integer NOT NULL,
    ticket_type     varchar(20) NOT NULL,
    purchased_at    timestamp NOT NULL,
    refunded_at     timestamp,
    seat_number     varchar(6)
);

CREATE TABLE delay_claim (
    claim_id        bigint PRIMARY KEY,
    ticket_id       bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES ticket(ticket_id),
    submitted_at    timestamp NOT NULL,
    delay_minutes   integer NOT NULL,
    status          varchar(20) NOT NULL,
    paid_pence      integer
);

CREATE TABLE crew_member (
    crew_id         integer PRIMARY KEY,
    full_name       varchar(100) NOT NULL,
    role            varchar(20) NOT NULL,
    depot_station_id integer REFERENCES station(station_id),
    hired_on        date NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE crew_assignment (
    assignment_id   bigint PRIMARY KEY,
    service_id      bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES service(service_id),
    crew_id         integer NOT NULL REFERENCES crew_member(crew_id),
    duty            varchar(20) NOT NULL,
    signed_on       timestamp,
    signed_off      timestamp
);

CREATE TABLE incident (
    incident_id     bigint PRIMARY KEY,
    service_id      bigint REFERENCES service(service_id),
    station_id      integer REFERENCES station(station_id),
    category        varchar(30) NOT NULL,
    description     text,
    reported_at     timestamp NOT NULL,
    resolved_at     timestamp,
    delay_minutes_caused integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 0
);

CREATE VIEW v_ticket_detail AS
SELECT t.ticket_id,
       t.purchased_at,
       t.fare_pence,
       t.ticket_type,
       p.full_name,
       p.email,
       fs.name AS from_station,
       ts.name AS to_station,
       r.name  AS route_name,
       s.service_date
FROM ticket t
LEFT JOIN passenger p ON p.passenger_id = t.passenger_id
JOIN station fs ON fs.station_id = t.from_station_id
JOIN station ts ON ts.station_id = t.to_station_id
JOIN service s ON s.service_id = t.service_id
JOIN route r ON r.route_id = s.route_id;

-- Indexes that exist today
CREATE INDEX idx_service_date ON service (service_date);
CREATE INDEX idx_service_route ON service (route_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_service_status ON service (status);
CREATE INDEX idx_stop_service ON service_stop (service_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_stop_station ON service_stop (station_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_stop_station_arrival ON service_stop (station_id, scheduled_arrival);
CREATE INDEX idx_ticket_passenger ON ticket (passenger_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_ticket_service ON ticket (service_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_ticket_type ON ticket (ticket_type);
CREATE INDEX idx_ticket_purchased ON ticket (purchased_at);
CREATE INDEX idx_passenger_email ON passenger (lower(email));
CREATE INDEX idx_claim_ticket ON delay_claim (ticket_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_assign_service ON crew_assignment (service_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_assign_crew ON crew_assignment (crew_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_incident_service ON incident (service_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_incident_category ON incident (category);
```

Some facts about the data that may matter. The `status` column in `service` has five values, and 97 percent of rows are 'completed'. `ticket_type` has six values: 'single', 'return', 'season', 'advance', 'off_peak' and 'group'. About 62 percent of tickets have a null `passenger_id` because they are sold at ticket machines without an account. Tickets are never deleted, and `refunded_at` is set for about 3 percent of them. A delay claim exists for roughly 4 percent of tickets. About 1,100 incidents are logged a year, in twelve categories, and about 40 percent of them have no service attached. Crew assignments run at around four per service. We keep all history since 2019, and the table `service_stop` grows by about 25,000 rows each day.

These are the six queries behind our reports. Each currently takes between 8 seconds and 3 minutes.

```sql
-- Q1: Daily punctuality by route for the last 30 days (dashboard, run every few minutes)
SELECT r.name AS route_name,
       s.service_date,
       COUNT(*) AS stops,
       SUM(CASE WHEN ss.actual_arrival IS NOT NULL
                 AND ss.actual_arrival <= ss.scheduled_arrival + interval '5 minutes'
                THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS on_time_stops,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN ss.actual_arrival IS NOT NULL
                 AND ss.actual_arrival <= ss.scheduled_arrival + interval '5 minutes'
                THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 1) AS on_time_pct
FROM service s
JOIN route r ON r.route_id = s.route_id
JOIN service_stop ss ON ss.service_id = s.service_id
WHERE s.service_date >= current_date - 30
  AND s.status = 'completed'
GROUP BY r.name, s.service_date
ORDER BY s.service_date DESC, r.name;

-- Q2: Revenue per route per month for one year (finance, run monthly)
SELECT to_char(t.purchased_at, 'YYYY-MM') AS month,
       r.name AS route_name,
       SUM(t.fare_pence) / 100.0 AS revenue,
       COUNT(*) AS tickets
FROM ticket t
JOIN service s ON s.service_id = t.service_id
JOIN route r ON r.route_id = s.route_id
WHERE EXTRACT(year FROM t.purchased_at) = 2025
  AND t.refunded_at IS NULL
GROUP BY to_char(t.purchased_at, 'YYYY-MM'), r.name
ORDER BY month, route_name;

-- Q3: Passengers who bought more than 20 tickets this year, with their most recent ticket (marketing)
SELECT p.passenger_id,
       p.full_name,
       p.email,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM ticket t WHERE t.passenger_id = p.passenger_id
          AND t.purchased_at >= date_trunc('year', now())) AS tickets_this_year,
       (SELECT MAX(t2.purchased_at) FROM ticket t2 WHERE t2.passenger_id = p.passenger_id) AS last_purchase
FROM passenger p
WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM ticket t WHERE t.passenger_id = p.passenger_id
          AND t.purchased_at >= date_trunc('year', now())) > 20
ORDER BY tickets_this_year DESC;

-- Q4: Worst ten stations by average arrival delay in the last quarter, where delay is above zero (control room)
SELECT st.name,
       AVG(EXTRACT(epoch FROM (ss.actual_arrival - ss.scheduled_arrival)) / 60.0) AS avg_delay_minutes,
       COUNT(*) AS late_arrivals
FROM service_stop ss
JOIN station st ON st.station_id = ss.station_id
WHERE ss.scheduled_arrival >= date_trunc('quarter', now()) - interval '3 months'
  AND ss.scheduled_arrival < date_trunc('quarter', now())
  AND ss.actual_arrival > ss.scheduled_arrival
GROUP BY st.name
ORDER BY avg_delay_minutes DESC
LIMIT 10;

-- Q5: Delay claims that were rejected but where the train really was more than 30 minutes late at the destination (customer services audit)
SELECT c.claim_id, c.submitted_at, t.ticket_id, p.email
FROM delay_claim c
JOIN ticket t ON t.ticket_id = c.ticket_id
LEFT JOIN passenger p ON p.passenger_id = t.passenger_id
WHERE c.status = 'rejected'
  AND t.ticket_id IN (
        SELECT t2.ticket_id
        FROM ticket t2
        JOIN service_stop ss ON ss.service_id = t2.service_id
                            AND ss.station_id = t2.to_station_id
        WHERE ss.actual_arrival > ss.scheduled_arrival + interval '30 minutes')
ORDER BY c.submitted_at DESC;

-- Q6: Incidents by category and station for the last 12 months, with the crew who were on the affected services (operations review, run weekly)
SELECT i.category,
       st.name AS station_name,
       COUNT(DISTINCT i.incident_id) AS incidents,
       SUM(i.delay_minutes_caused) AS total_delay_minutes,
       STRING_AGG(DISTINCT cm.full_name, ', ') AS crew_involved
FROM incident i
LEFT JOIN station st ON st.station_id = i.station_id
LEFT JOIN service s ON s.service_id = i.service_id
LEFT JOIN crew_assignment ca ON ca.service_id = s.service_id
LEFT JOIN crew_member cm ON cm.crew_id = ca.crew_id
WHERE i.reported_at > now() - interval '1 year'
  AND lower(i.category) LIKE '%signal%'
   OR i.category = 'trespass'
GROUP BY i.category, st.name
ORDER BY total_delay_minutes DESC;
```

Two further constraints. We cannot take the database offline for more than a short maintenance window on Sunday nights, so please tell me which of your suggestions can be done online and which cannot. And our reporting server has far less memory than production, so I would like to know if any of the changes you suggest will make that situation better or worse.

This is the start of a short story I have been working on for a while and I am stuck on what happens next. Could you continue it for me at length, something like the next two chapters, in the same quiet voice and in the same close third person? I want the discrepancy in the controlled drugs register to matter, but I do not want it to turn into a thriller.

THE NIGHT COUNT

1.

The pharmacy at Saint Ambrose Infirmary was in the basement, which the porters called the Cellar and the management called Level B, and which Marguerite Osei had thought of for eleven years simply as the place where her feet stopped hurting. The lift opened onto a corridor painted a green nobody would have chosen. At the end of it was a hatch with a sliding glass panel, and behind the hatch, shelves, and behind the shelves, a second room that few people at the hospital had ever seen, where the controlled drugs lived in a steel cupboard the size of a wardrobe.

She came on at nine in the evening, as she had done on Mondays, Tuesdays and Wednesdays for as long as the rota had allowed her to choose, and the first thing she did was what she always did. She took off her coat, hung it on the third hook, and stood for a moment with her hand on the cold edge of the dispensing bench. The building made a low sound at night, a long machine breath from the ventilation, and the sound told her that things were as they should be. When the sound changed, she noticed, in the way a person with a sleeping child notices a cough.

"You're early," said Tobias.

Tobias Lindqvist was the evening technician, twenty-six, thin, with a habit of reading the labels aloud under his breath while he worked, so that the room always seemed faintly to be conducting a service. He was sitting on the high stool with a tray of returns in front of him, sorting the unopened from the opened. Opened could not go back on the shelf. Opened went into the blue bin, and the blue bin went to be burned, and every month she looked at the cost of what went into it and felt something she had no word for that was neither anger nor sadness.

"Ten minutes," she said. "The buses were kind."

"Wards sent four urgents since six. Two are done. The oncology one is waiting for your check and the other is a discharge for Eleven, which I'd leave until the doctor stops changing his mind." He tapped a printed sheet with a pen. "And the fridge in the aseptic room is at nine point one. Not alarming. But it was seven this morning."

"Did you log it?"

"I logged it."

"Then I'll look at it at midnight, and if it's still climbing I'll call the engineers." She said it lightly. She was already moving toward the oncology prescription, which was waiting in its tray with its small yellow flag, and she felt, as she always did on these first minutes of a shift, the pleasure of an ordinary difficulty. A dose, a weight, a surface area, a sum that must come out the same way twice. There was no one in the world, she thought, who would thank her for getting a sum right. That was what made it a good job.

The prescription was for a woman called Pauline Ardley, aged seventy-one, a standard cycle of a drug Marguerite knew as well as she knew her own telephone number. She worked the figures on paper first, then on the calculator, then she handed the paper to Tobias and said, "Do it yourself without looking at mine," and he did, murmuring, and when the two numbers matched she initialled the sheet, and he initialled it, and the bag went into the clean room. It took eleven minutes. It would have taken three if she had trusted herself alone, and that was exactly why they did it the slow way.

At ten past ten the evening porter brought down the ward requests in a plastic crate, as he did every night, a broad quiet man named Dessie who had worked at the infirmary for thirty years and who had once, at a retirement party, been seen to weep openly at a speech about someone he had not liked. He put the crate on the bench and said, "Seven's got a visitor who fainted. Nothing to do with us. But she was in the corridor all the same, going on about the lift."

"Is she all right?"

"Sitting up, drinking tea. Sister Okafor has her."

"Then she's in the best hands in the building," said Marguerite, and Dessie nodded, because he agreed, and left.

At midnight she looked at the fridge. Eight point four. It had turned back by itself, which was the worst possible outcome, because it meant there was nothing to report and still something not understood. She wrote a line in the log anyway. Tobias had gone to the staff room for his break, and the pharmacy was quiet except for the breath of the ventilation, and for the first time that night she let herself think about the thing she had been avoiding thinking about since Sunday.

2.

On Sunday she had done the weekly reconciliation of the controlled drugs register, a job that fell to her because nobody else wanted it and because, she suspected, her colleagues believed that her kind of patience was a fixed property, like height. It was not hard. You took the book, which was a real book with numbered pages that nobody was allowed to tear, and you compared every entry to the stock in the steel cupboard, ampoule by ampoule and tablet by tablet, and where the book and the cupboard agreed you ticked, and where they did not agree you did not tick, and there was a form.

She had counted the morphine sulphate ten milligram ampoules three times. The book said forty-two. The cupboard held forty. She had put her glasses on, taken them off, checked the batch numbers, counted the empties in the returns tray, and checked the ward registers that Sister Okafor and the other ward managers kept, which had to match, and which did, line for line, down to the last dose given. Two ampoules had left the cupboard and had not been written down. Or two ampoules had been written down as being in the cupboard that had never been there at all. The difference between those two possibilities was the whole of the problem, and she could not find a way to tell them apart.

She filled in the form. She was not frightened, exactly. The form was a good form: it asked what had been checked, and by whom, and she had checked everything, and written it all down in a small upright hand that her mother had taught her, and she had signed it, and she had put it in the tray for the chief pharmacist, Dr. Halloran, whose name was on the door of a room upstairs that she had been inside only four times.

On Monday morning there had been no response, which was normal. On Tuesday, today's Tuesday, she had been on days at the clinic in the annex, and had not gone down to the Cellar at all, and had told herself that she was giving it time. In the afternoon, in the clinic, a patient had asked her whether anyone really checked the pharmacy, and she had said that yes, everything was checked twice, and had heard how bright her own voice sounded, and had felt like a person speaking through the glass hatch.

Now it was ten past midnight on Wednesday and she stood in the second room with the key in her hand. Every controlled drug was in a cupboard that could only be opened by two people, in principle. In practice, on the night shift, with one pharmacist and one technician and no one else, it was understood that the key would sit with the pharmacist and the technician would be called in as witness. She had always obeyed this. She obeyed it now and walked through to the staff room to get Tobias.

He was eating a sandwich in a way that suggested he had been told that he must. He put it down at once.

"Do I need to bring a pen?"

"Always bring a pen," she said, and he did.

She opened the cupboard. The steel door made the faint cough it always made, and the inside smelled of nothing, of cold metal and cardboard. Together they counted the morphine, and the number was forty, as it had been on Sunday, and both of them wrote it down and signed. She did not tell him why. She did not want him to count differently if he knew what he was supposed to find. This, too, was a rule, one she had made for herself years ago and had never had to explain.

"Forty," Tobias said. "Is it supposed to be forty?"

"It's supposed to be what it is."

He looked at her, with the particular expression of the young when they are working out how much of what an older person says is a lesson. "That's a very good answer," he said, "and I'd like to know what it means."

"It means that I would like you to go and sit down for ten minutes with your sandwich, and not ask me anything else tonight."

He went. She heard him pause in the doorway and decide against saying something, and she was grateful, and also faintly ashamed to be grateful, because it was his shift as well and he was entitled to know what was happening in the room he worked in.

3.

The morphine book had two hands in it. This was not strange in itself; the whole department wrote in it, over the years: the technician who left in the spring, the locum with the looping letters, herself, Tobias, and three or four others whose handwriting she knew better than their faces. But she took the book to the bench in the main dispensary and opened it at the page for the previous Thursday, and beside the entries for that day, in the narrow column where the pharmacist on duty entered the receipt of stock from the wholesaler, there was a line she did not recognise.

The delivery had been logged as fifty ampoules, received at 4:40 in the afternoon. She had been told by the wholesaler's paperwork, which was stapled into the back of the book, that the delivery was for fifty. The cupboard had held fifty-two, once those had been added, and so the book said forty-two on Sunday, after ten were used that week. But she had counted forty. So either the delivery was short, and someone had signed for fifty when only forty-eight had arrived, or the stock had been correct and two ampoules had left.

She turned the stapled paper over. The delivery note was signed with a flourish and a surname she could not read, and beside it a time: 4:40. Underneath, in a different pen, someone had written the initials H.B. She frowned. There was no H.B. in the department. There was, on the staff list, a Hamish Brennan, who worked in the stores, and who would, in the ordinary way, take in a delivery from the wholesaler and carry the boxes down to the Cellar and leave them at the hatch. But the controlled drugs did not come to the hatch. They came by hand to the pharmacist on duty, and on Thursday afternoon the pharmacist on duty had been Neil Castellan, who was good, and fast, and almost never without a coffee.

She thought about Neil. She did not think he had done anything. She could have said this to anyone, and it would have been a statement about character, which is not evidence, and which people in Dr. Halloran's position are trained to set aside. She thought about the morning when Neil had brought his daughter in for a school project, and the girl had asked, at the hatch, whether the drugs were kept in a safe, and he had said no, a safe is for money, this is more serious, and the girl had been quiet for a whole minute, taking it in.

At half past one, Tobias came back from his break and found her sitting with the book open and a pencil behind her ear that she had forgotten about.

"Is it something I did?" he asked.

"No."

"Because I'd rather you told me."

"It is nothing you did," she said. "I think it is an arithmetic mistake, and I think I will find it, and I would rather not say more until I have, because if I am wrong I will have said something to you about someone else that I should not have said."

He thought about this. "That's a very high standard," he said.

"Yes. It's inconvenient."

Upstairs, six floors above them, a bell went in the ward corridor and a nurse's shoes crossed the polished floor, and in the Cellar the ventilation changed its note, very slightly, and she heard it. She took the pencil from behind her ear, and she drew a small ruled line under the delivery entry, and wrote the date, and her initials, and the word *query*. Then she put the book in the drawer under the bench, locked it, put the key in her pocket, and went to see whether anyone on Ward Seven needed anything.

4.

Ward Seven was on the fourth floor, and she took the stairs, because the lift was the lift the visitor had gone on about, and because the stairs gave her four flights in which to put away the person she had been in the Cellar. Pharmacists were not expected on wards at that hour. The ward staff tolerated it the way a household tolerates a relative who arrives with a casserole.

Sister Okafor was at the nurses' station with the lights turned down to a shade the hospital called night mode and the nurses called the aquarium. She was a large, unhurried woman in her fifties with reading glasses on a cord, and she looked up at Marguerite and did not ask what she was doing there, which was one of the reasons Marguerite trusted her.

"I haven't ordered anything," said the Sister.

"No. I wanted to ask about your morphine book. Not tonight's. Last Thursday."

"Last Thursday I was on a late. Do you want to sit?" She pushed the second chair out with her foot. Marguerite sat. On the monitor behind the desk a green line moved across the screen in its small, unconcerned way, and from somewhere along the corridor a patient coughed, and another patient, in answer, turned over.

"The ampoules we gave on Thursday," said the Sister. "I'll fetch the book, but I know what it says. Mr. Bellamy in Four had two for his hip, and the woman in Nine, the lady who fell, had one in the afternoon and one at night. That's four. Then the Friday ones. Your count is out."

"How do you know it is my count?"

"Because you came upstairs at one in the morning and you are holding your own elbows." Sister Okafor took her glasses off and let them fall on their cord. "It's no use me pretending I haven't seen you do it before. The last time was the year your mother was ill."

Marguerite let go of her elbows. She laid her hands flat on her knees instead, which was no better. "Two ampoules," she said. "On paper there are two more than in the cupboard. I've checked the wholesaler's note, and the receipt entry, and the ward books, and nothing agrees with anything except itself."

"Which is how you know it is a clerical matter."

"Or how I know it is not."

The Sister considered this, and whatever she thought, she kept to herself for a moment, as one keeps a coin in a closed hand. Then she stood and went into the little office behind the station and came back with the ward's controlled drugs book, a tall volume with a green spine, and she opened it on the desk and turned it to face the pharmacist.

They read it together, with the patience of two women who had both been trained never to assume. The Thursday entries were in the Sister's own round script and in the script of a young staff nurse called Imogen Pryce, with the double signature that the rules required. Mr. Bellamy's two doses were there. The woman in Nine had one in the afternoon and one at night. Nothing was missing from the ward's side. But on the Thursday evening, a little after six, there was a line in a hand that Marguerite did not know, with a pharmacy stock transfer reference, and the words *returned unused, 2 amp*, and two signatures: one a scrawl, and one the careful capitals of someone who wrote slowly in a language not his first.

"Who is this?" she said.

The Sister leaned in. For a long moment her face did nothing at all. "That is Hamish Brennan from the stores. And that is Imogen. They were doing a return, because Mr. Bellamy's dose was changed at the last minute, and two ampoules had been drawn up for the rota and weren't wanted."

"They went back to the pharmacy."

"They'd have gone back to the pharmacy."

"They never arrived," said Marguerite, very softly, and as she said it she felt the thing she had been waiting for since Sunday, which was not relief, and was not alarm, but something nearer to the sensation of a held breath finally leaving the body. The two ampoules had not been stolen from the cupboard. They had been taken out of it, in the ordinary way of business, to a ward, and then they had been taken out of the ward, in the ordinary way of business, and somewhere between the fourth floor and the Cellar they had stopped existing on paper. It was almost worse, she thought, than a thief. A thief at least had a motive.

"Where would he have put them?" the Sister asked.

"He'd have put them on the lift, with a note, and the lift is the one the visitor was talking about," said Marguerite. "The lift that stops between three and two."

I am on the review panel for our regional education technology workshop and have been sent the write-up below. Please write me a detailed peer review: what the study does well, the problems with the method, whether the conclusions follow from the results, and a list of concrete changes that you would ask the authors to make before accepting it. I would like it written so that I can paste most of it into the review form.

Title: Does Replacing Shared Classroom Laptops with Personal Tablets Reduce Help-Desk Load? A Two-Year Study in the Marlow Borough Schools

Authors: R. Penhallow, S. Adeyemi-Cole, and T. Wrenfield, Information Technology Office, Marlow Borough School District

Abstract

Schools in our district have for many years relied on trolleys of shared laptops. In September 2024 the district replaced the trolleys in eight of its sixteen secondary and middle schools with individually assigned tablets, a change expected to cut the volume of IT help-desk tickets. We compared ticket volumes, time to resolution, and teacher-reported lost lesson time between the eight tablet schools and the eight schools that kept trolleys. Over the two school years 2023-24 and 2024-25, tablet schools showed a 31 percent fall in tickets per hundred devices and a 22 percent fall in median resolution time, while trolley schools were nearly unchanged. Teachers in tablet schools reported 39 percent less lost lesson time. We conclude that personal tablets substantially reduce IT support load, and recommend extending them to all remaining schools.

1. Introduction

The IT Office of the district supports 4,950 laptops, 1,420 desktop computers and, since last year, 3,120 tablets across sixteen schools, with a support team of eleven staff. The mix of devices has changed because of a funding decision, not a research design: capital from a state grant allowed the purchase of tablets for roughly half of our schools. Because the grant was to be spent within a single financial year, the district chose the schools that were quickest to complete the required wireless upgrade, and our office was asked to monitor what followed. This paper reports that monitoring.

We expected two effects. First, personal devices should reduce tickets caused by shared use: forgotten passwords, saved work on the wrong machine, and trolley charging failures. Second, a student who is responsible for one device may treat it with more care than a student using a machine shared by five classes in a day. We also acknowledged a possible opposing effect: tablets are a new technology to our teachers, and new technology tends to produce questions.

2. Method

2.1 Schools and assignment. The sixteen schools were divided into a tablet group and a comparison group. The tablet group comprised the eight schools whose wireless upgrade finished by July 2024. Five are middle schools and three are secondary schools. The comparison group comprised the remaining eight, of which four are middle schools and four are secondary schools. Tablet schools had a mean enrolment of 612 students and comparison schools a mean of 748. Assignment was therefore determined by the readiness of the school's network and not by chance. Tablets were issued to all students in years 7 to 9 at tablet schools, with years 10 and 11 continuing to use the shared laptops.

2.2 Data sources. We used three sources. The first was the ticketing system, in which every request to the help desk is recorded with a category, the school, the device identifier, the time of opening and the time of closure. The second was a survey sent each June to all teachers, asking how many lessons in the past term had been disrupted by technology problems and for how many minutes. The third was an inventory extract giving the number of devices at each school on 1 October of each year.

2.3 Outcome measures. The primary outcome was tickets per hundred devices per school per term. The secondary outcomes were median hours to resolution and the teacher-reported lost lesson time. Tickets arising from planned projects, such as the wireless upgrade itself, were excluded from the primary count by the help desk manager, who classified them by hand.

2.4 Analysis. We compared the mean change in tickets per hundred devices between the 2023-24 and 2024-25 years in the two groups, using a t-test on the school-level changes. For resolution time, we compared the group medians with a Mann-Whitney test. The survey responses were summarised as the mean reported minutes of lost time per teacher per term, and groups were compared with a t-test on individual responses. We did not adjust for school size or type. A significance level of 0.05 was used throughout.

2.5 Data handling. Ticket records contain the name of the member of staff who raised the request. Before analysis the help desk manager replaced names with a numeric code and removed free text fields. The teacher survey was anonymous and voluntary, and the responses were kept on a district drive accessible only to the three authors. The study used operational data collected for the ordinary running of the service and was therefore not submitted to an external ethics committee, although the superintendent's office approved the use of the survey results.

3. Results

3.1 Ticket volume. Table 1 shows the mean tickets per hundred devices per term.

| Group | 2023-24 | 2024-25 | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tablet schools (n = 8) | 24.6 | 17.0 | -31% |
| Comparison schools (n = 8) | 22.9 | 22.1 | -3% |

The difference in change between groups was statistically significant (t = 2.41, p = 0.03). Within the tablet group, the fall was largest for password and login tickets (down 54 percent) and trolley or charging tickets (down 89 percent, as there were no trolleys after the change). Tickets for physical damage rose by 19 percent, from 3.1 to 3.7 per hundred devices per term, and tickets for application problems rose by 12 percent.

3.2 Resolution time. The median time to resolution at tablet schools fell from 31 hours to 24 hours (22 percent), and at comparison schools from 29 hours to 28 hours. The Mann-Whitney test gave p = 0.04. The authors note that, because tablets can be re-imaged centrally, many password and login problems were closed within an hour, and that this shifts the median.

3.3 Lost lesson time. The June survey was returned by 212 of 390 teachers at tablet schools (54 percent) and 241 of 462 teachers at comparison schools (52 percent). The reported lost time per teacher per term fell from 46 minutes to 28 minutes in tablet schools (a fall of 39 percent) and from 44 to 43 minutes in comparison schools. The difference was significant (p = 0.01).

3.4 Subgroups. Middle schools in the tablet group showed a larger fall in tickets (38 percent) than secondary schools (21 percent). There was no difference in the comparison group between middle and secondary schools.

3.5 Staff workload and the cost of a ticket. The help desk logged 6,914 tickets across all sixteen schools in 2023-24 and 6,205 in 2024-25. Of the fall of 709 tickets, 664 were at tablet schools. Table 1b gives the breakdown by category for tablet schools only, as tickets per hundred devices per term.

| Category | 2023-24 | 2024-25 | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Password and login | 8.1 | 3.7 | -54% |
| Trolley, charging and cabling | 4.5 | 0.5 | -89% |
| Application problems | 5.2 | 5.8 | +12% |
| Network and wireless | 3.7 | 3.3 | -11% |
| Physical damage | 3.1 | 3.7 | +19% |
| Total | 24.6 | 17.0 | -31% |

The average handling time per ticket was 38 minutes, so the 664 tickets avoided correspond to roughly 420 hours of help desk time per year, or about 0.25 of a full-time post. Our estimate of 41,000 per year in the discussion assumes a fully loaded cost of 97 per hour for a technician, including management overhead and the cost of travel between schools.

3.6 Sensitivity to exclusions. The help desk manager excluded 513 project tickets from the 2024-25 count, 407 of them from the wireless upgrade at the eight comparison schools, which began in January 2025. When we included all excluded tickets, the fall at tablet schools was 29 percent and the change at comparison schools became an increase of 4 percent. The difference between groups was still significant (p = 0.04). We did not test other specifications.

3.7 Timing. The overall figure hides a large difference between terms. The autumn term of 2024 was the first with tablets, and tickets per hundred devices at tablet schools were 25.0, slightly higher than the 24.1 for the autumn of 2023, because staff and students needed support in the first weeks. The fall appeared from the spring term, at 14.9 against 25.2, and continued in the summer, at 11.2 against 24.5. The mean of the three 2024-25 terms is the 17.0 reported in Table 1. The comparison schools showed no pattern across terms.

3.8 Damage and repair costs. Tablet schools sent 212 devices for repair in 2024-25, mostly cracked screens, at an average cost of 84 per repair, or 17,800 in total. The trolley laptops at the same schools in 2023-24 generated 61 repairs at an average cost of 96, or 5,856. The extra repair spend of about 11,900 is not included in the cost comparison in the discussion.

4. Discussion

The results are consistent with our expectations. Personal tablets appear to remove a whole category of problems that arise from sharing, and they allow the IT office to fix many faults remotely. We were surprised by the size of the effect on lost lesson time, because it exceeds the fall in tickets, but we think this is because trolley failures interrupt whole lessons whereas a failed tablet affects one student.

We acknowledge that tablet schools were smaller and that smaller schools might generate fewer tickets per device for reasons not connected to tablets. However, as the comparison is of changes within each school across years, we do not think the difference in size affects the conclusion. We also note that the survey response rate was about half in each group, and we have no reason to think that non-responders differ.

Three alternative explanations deserve more attention than we have given them. The first is the novelty of the programme. Tablet schools received extra visits from our office in the first term, a training day for all teachers and a named contact for each school, and these may have reduced tickets independently of the device. The second is a change in how teachers ask for help: in several tablet schools, the head of department now collects minor requests and sends them as one ticket, which would lower the count without lowering the number of faults. The third is the end of the trolley, which removes a type of ticket by definition; if trolleys had been replaced by better trolleys, the same effect might have appeared.

A cost comparison is given in Table 2. Tablets cost 310 per unit including cases and device management licences, against 540 per laptop. Because one tablet serves one student and a laptop trolley served five classes per day, the district bought more devices: 3,120 tablets against the 1,260 laptops they replaced. The total hardware outlay was therefore about 967,000 for tablets against 680,000 for equivalent laptops. We estimate the reduction in help-desk time to be worth about 41,000 per year, which on its own would not repay the difference. We therefore regard the case for tablets as resting on the educational benefit of the lost lesson time recovered, which we value at about 190,000 per year using the average cost of a teacher hour.

5. Limitations

The study was not randomised. The comparison group was drawn from schools whose wireless networks were not ready, and these schools may differ from the tablet group in ways that affect support load, such as the age of their buildings. Tickets are counted by a system whose categories were adjusted during the study, when the help desk added a new "tablet" category in October 2024. The survey relies on teacher recall. The study covers two years, and we cannot say whether the benefit will persist as the tablets age; the first batch is now fourteen months old and the damage rate has begun to rise.

6. Conclusion and recommendations

Personal tablets reduced help-desk tickets by almost a third and lost lesson time by almost two fifths in the schools where they were introduced. We recommend extending the tablet programme to the remaining eight schools in the next financial year, retaining laptops for years 10 and 11 where examination software requires them, and increasing the repair budget by 15 percent to cover the rise in damage tickets. We further recommend that the district adopt the tablet model as its standard for all new school devices.

Acknowledgements

We thank the school business managers for their help with the inventory, the help desk team for classifying tickets, and the district superintendent's office for access to enrolment figures.
