I have just joined the digitisation team at the Thornfield Museum of Local History as a volunteer coordinator, and I have been told to read and follow the policy below, which I find hard to understand. Could you explain it to me in plain language, clause by clause, and then tell me what the risks are for me and for the museum if the rules are not followed? Please point out anything that looks unclear, contradictory or likely to cause trouble in practice.

THORNFIELD MUSEUM OF LOCAL HISTORY
DIGITISATION, DATA AND IMAGE LICENSING POLICY
Version 3.2, approved by the Board of Trustees. Review date: two years from approval.

1. Purpose and scope

1.1 This policy sets out how the Museum creates, stores, describes, shares and licenses digital copies of objects, documents, photographs and recordings in its collection ("Digital Assets"), and the duties of the staff, volunteers and contractors who handle them ("Team Members").

1.2 It applies to all Digital Assets created by or for the Museum from the date of approval, and to existing Digital Assets when they are next edited, re-published or licensed to a third party.

1.3 It does not apply to the Museum's administrative records, fundraising data or visitor images taken by security cameras, which are covered by separate policies.

2. Definitions

2.1 "Master File" means the highest quality digital copy made from an original item, produced to the standard in Schedule A and never edited.

2.2 "Access Copy" means a lower resolution file derived from a Master File for display, research or publication.

2.3 "Rights Holder" means the person or organisation that owns the copyright or other rights in the original item, which may be the Museum, a donor, a creator or the creator's heirs.

2.4 "Orphan Work" means an item where the Rights Holder cannot be identified or found after a diligent search as described in clause 6.

2.5 "Sensitive Material" means any item that shows or describes living individuals, human remains, sacred or ceremonial objects, or events that may cause distress to a community, whether or not it is subject to copyright.

3. Creating Digital Assets

3.1 Every Master File must be captured by a trained Team Member using the equipment listed in Schedule A. Volunteers may operate equipment only under the supervision of a trained Team Member until they have completed the induction.

3.2 Before an item is digitised, a Team Member must check the item's record in the collections database and confirm that its condition allows handling. Items marked "fragile" or "do not handle" must not be digitised without the written approval of the Conservator.

3.3 Master Files must be saved in the formats given in Schedule A and must not be edited, cropped, colour corrected or compressed. Any improvement must be made on an Access Copy.

3.4 A Team Member who damages an item or equipment in the course of digitisation must report it to the Collections Manager on the same working day. Failure to report a known incident is a breach of this policy.

3.5 Each Master File must be given a unique identifier in the format set out in Schedule B at the time it is created. Identifiers must never be reused, even if a file is deleted.

3.6 Team Members must record in the collections database, for each digitisation session, the date, the items digitised, the equipment used, and the identifiers allocated. The record must be completed on the day of the session.

3.7 Items belonging to another institution and lent to the Museum may be digitised only if the loan agreement allows it. Where the agreement is silent, the Rights Officer must obtain the lender's written consent first.

3.8 A Team Member who finds that an identifier has been given to the wrong file must tell the Digital Collections Officer, who will correct the record and note the correction. The Team Member must not rename the file themselves.

4. Description and metadata

4.1 Every Digital Asset must have, at a minimum, the following metadata before it is published: identifier, title, date or date range if known, creator if known, description, Rights Holder, rights status, and the name of the Team Member who created it.

4.2 Descriptions must be accurate and written in neutral language. Where the Museum is not certain of a fact, the description must say so, using words such as "probably" or "attributed to".

4.3 Where an item is Sensitive Material, the metadata must record the reason and the name of the community or person consulted before publication.

4.4 Team Members must not alter or delete metadata created by others without recording the reason in the history field of the record.

5. Storage and preservation

5.1 Master Files must be stored in three copies on at least two different types of storage, one of which must be held at a different physical site from the Museum building.

5.2 The Digital Collections Officer will check the integrity of all Master Files at least once every six months and record the result. Files that fail the check must be restored from another copy within ten working days.

5.3 Access to Master Files is limited to the Digital Collections Officer and one named deputy. Other Team Members may request an Access Copy, but must not copy a Master File to a personal device, email account or cloud service.

5.4 Storage media must be replaced no later than the age recommended by the manufacturer or five years from first use, whichever is sooner.

5.5 Born-digital material, such as photographs or documents donated on a memory card or by email, must be treated as a Master File from the moment it is received. The donor's original file names and dates must be kept in the metadata, and the files must not be opened in editing software.

5.6 Digital Assets may be deleted only with the written approval of the Collections Manager and the Digital Collections Officer, who must record the reason. A deleted file's identifier remains in the register with a note of the date and reason.

6. Rights and Orphan Works

6.1 Before publishing or licensing a Digital Asset, a Team Member must record the rights status as one of: Museum owned, Licensed to the Museum, Public domain, Third party owned, or Unknown.

6.2 An item is treated as Public domain only where the creator died more than seventy years before the first day of the current calendar year, or where the item is a document produced by a public authority and published without restriction. A Team Member who is unsure must ask the Rights Officer.

6.3 If the Rights Holder is unknown, the Rights Officer must carry out a diligent search, including at least three sources, which must include the donor file, the national archive catalogue and one public notice of the Museum's search that stays open for ninety days. The result must be recorded in the rights record.

6.4 An Orphan Work may be published as an Access Copy for non-commercial purposes after a diligent search is complete, with the statement "Rights holder unknown: contact the Museum". It must not be licensed to a third party for commercial use.

6.5 If a Rights Holder comes forward after publication, the Museum will within fifteen working days either agree terms with the Rights Holder or remove the Digital Asset from public access, and the Rights Officer will record the decision.

7. Access and licensing

7.1 Access Copies of Museum owned items will be published online under a licence that permits reuse with attribution, unless the Director decides otherwise for a stated reason.

7.2 Requests for commercial use of a Digital Asset, including use in books, advertising, products or broadcast, must be sent to the Rights Officer and may be charged a fee set out in the Museum's published fee schedule. Team Members must not agree fees or terms directly with the requester.

7.3 The Museum will not provide a Master File to any third party, except to a conservator, a partner institution under a written agreement, or a court.

7.4 Where a donor has set conditions on the use of an item, those conditions override clauses 7.1 and 7.2. The conditions must be recorded in the item's record at the time of donation and displayed to Team Members when they open it.

7.5 Researchers using Access Copies for study must be told that they cannot republish without permission, even where an Access Copy is shown online.

7.6 The Museum will keep a log of every licence granted for commercial use, showing the requester, the Digital Asset, the purpose, the territory, the length of the licence and the fee. The Rights Officer will report the log to the Board of Trustees each year.

7.7 A licence for commercial use is for the use described in it and no other. A requester who wishes to use a Digital Asset in a different way, or after the licence ends, must apply again.

8. Sensitive Material and communities

8.1 Sensitive Material must not be published online until the consultation recorded in clause 4.3 has taken place and the Director has signed off the release.

8.2 If a living individual shown in an image, or their close family, asks for an image to be taken down, the Museum will remove it from public access within ten working days of a verified request, without needing to give a reason. The Master File will be retained.

8.3 Images of children must not be published with names, and only where the Museum holds a written release from a parent or guardian, or where the image is more than seventy years old.

9. Personal data

9.1 Some Digital Assets, including oral history recordings, letters and registers, contain personal data about living or recently deceased people. The Museum is the controller of this data under the data protection law that applies to it.

9.2 Team Members must not copy, share or transcribe personal data other than as needed for the purposes of this policy. They must not discuss the content of recordings or documents with anyone outside the Museum except in accordance with clause 7.

9.3 A person whose personal data appears in a Digital Asset has the right to see what the Museum holds, to ask for corrections, and, in the circumstances set out in law, to ask for erasure. Requests must be passed to the Data Protection Lead on the same working day and answered within thirty calendar days.

9.4 A loss or suspected loss of personal data must be reported to the Data Protection Lead immediately, and no later than twenty-four hours after discovery.

10. Volunteers and contractors

10.1 Volunteers and contractors must sign the confidentiality statement in Schedule C before they handle any Digital Asset.

10.2 The Museum owns all Digital Assets created by volunteers and contractors in the course of their work, and the creator assigns to the Museum any rights they might have in the files, but not in the original item.

10.3 Contractors must return or delete all Digital Assets at the end of the contract and confirm this in writing. Contractors may not subcontract digitisation work without the Museum's written consent.

11. Partners and online platforms

11.1 The Museum may place Access Copies on the websites of partner institutions or on third party platforms where this has been approved in writing by the Director. Before approval, the Rights Officer must read the terms of the platform and record whether they require the Museum to give the platform a licence over the files.

11.2 A platform may be approved only if it allows the Museum to remove a file at any time, shows the Museum's rights statement beside every file, and does not claim ownership of the file or of any metadata provided with it.

11.3 Team Members must not upload a Digital Asset to any platform, including a personal social media account, unless the upload has been approved under clause 11.1. Sharing a link to an approved page is permitted.

11.4 Where a partner institution receives Access Copies of items that are Sensitive Material, the written agreement must require the partner to follow clause 8, to pass takedown requests to the Museum within two working days, and to delete the files on request.

11.5 The Museum will keep a register of all approved platforms and partners, and the Digital Collections Officer will check it each year to confirm that each approval is still needed.

12. Complaints and corrections

12.1 Any person may complain to the Museum about the way a Digital Asset has been described, published or licensed. Complaints may be made in writing, by email or in person at the front desk, and any Team Member who receives one must pass it to the Collections Manager within one working day.

12.2 The Collections Manager will acknowledge a complaint within five working days and will give a reply within thirty calendar days. If the complaint concerns Sensitive Material, a living person, or the rights status of an item, the Collections Manager must consult the Director before replying.

12.3 Where a complaint shows that a description is wrong or offensive, the Museum will correct it and note the correction in the history field. The earlier wording will be kept in the history field, and not shown to the public.

12.4 While a complaint is being considered, the Collections Manager may restrict access to the Digital Asset to staff only. Restriction in these circumstances is not an admission that the complaint is correct.

12.5 A person who is not satisfied with the Museum's reply may ask the Board of Trustees to review it. The Board's decision will be given within sixty days and is final.

13. Breach and review

13.1 A breach of this policy may lead to withdrawal of access to Digital Assets, to disciplinary action for employees, and to the end of a volunteer placement or contract.

13.2 The Museum may remove a published Digital Asset at any time and without notice if it believes that publication breaches this policy, the law or a donor's conditions.

13.3 This policy will be reviewed after two years, or sooner if the law changes. Questions about its meaning may be put to the Collections Manager, whose interpretation is final.

Schedule A: Capture standards. Master Files of documents and photographs are captured at no less than 600 dots per inch in uncompressed TIFF. Audio is captured at 96 kHz and 24 bits in WAV. Video is captured in an uncompressed or lossless format.

Schedule B: Identifier format. TMLH, a hyphen, the four digit year of capture, a hyphen and a five digit serial number, for example TMLH-2025-00417.

Schedule C: Confidentiality statement. I understand that the Digital Assets and records I handle for the Museum may contain personal and confidential information. I will not copy, keep or share any such information except as the Museum's policy allows. I will report any loss or suspected loss to the Data Protection Lead at once. I understand that my duty of confidentiality continues after my work with the Museum ends. The signed statement is kept by the Collections Manager.

Schedule D: Response times. Takedown request from a living person or family: remove within ten working days (clause 8.2). Rights Holder coming forward: agree terms or remove within fifteen working days (clause 6.5). Personal data request: pass on the same working day, reply within thirty calendar days (clause 9.3). Data loss: report within twenty-four hours (clause 9.4). Complaint: acknowledge within five working days, reply within thirty calendar days (clause 12.2). Failed integrity check: restore within ten working days (clause 5.2). Damage to an item or equipment: report on the same working day (clause 3.4).

Je viens d'intégrer l'équipe de l'application mobile de la banque Lumeris et j'ai pris ces notes pendant la formation interne sur la sécurité des sessions et de l'authentification. Pouvez-vous en faire un guide de révision complet, avec des exemples détaillés et corrigés pour chaque notion, puis un quiz d'une quinzaine de questions avec les réponses expliquées ? Je dois présenter ces points à mon responsable dans deux semaines, donc j'ai besoin que ce soit clair et que les chiffres des exemples soient justes.

NOTES DE COURS : Authentification et sessions dans l'application mobile Lumeris
Intervenante : Hélène Marchetti, responsable sécurité applicative
Public : nouveaux développeurs mobile et équipe de test
Durée : 3 heures, avec une pause

1. Pourquoi ce sujet compte

Hélène a ouvert la séance avec un chiffre : sur les 412 000 clients actifs de l'application, environ 1,9 pour cent utilisent un téléphone dont le système n'a pas été mis à jour depuis plus d'un an. Ces appareils sont les plus exposés, et ils sont aussi ceux qui nous coûtent le plus cher en incidents. L'an dernier, l'équipe a traité 37 cas de prise de contrôle de compte, dont 29 avaient commencé par un code reçu par SMS livré à une personne qui n'était pas le client. Elle a insisté sur un principe : l'application ne doit jamais faire confiance à l'appareil, au réseau ni à l'utilisateur seul, mais à une combinaison de preuves.

Objectifs de la séance :
- comprendre les trois familles de facteurs d'authentification ;
- savoir comment fonctionne le cycle de vie d'une session, de l'ouverture à l'expiration ;
- connaître les règles de stockage des secrets sur le téléphone ;
- savoir calculer la durée de vie des jetons et le nombre de tentatives autorisées ;
- repérer les erreurs de conception les plus fréquentes.

2. Les trois familles de facteurs

Un facteur d'authentification est une preuve qu'on est bien la personne qu'on prétend être. On les classe en trois familles :

- ce que je sais : un code secret à six chiffres, une phrase de passe ;
- ce que je possède : le téléphone enregistré, une clé de sécurité, une carte ;
- ce que je suis : l'empreinte digitale, le visage.

L'authentification forte exige au moins deux facteurs de familles différentes. Hélène a donné un exemple qui revient souvent aux examens internes : un code secret suivi d'une question secrète, comme le nom de jeune fille de la mère, n'est pas une authentification forte, puisque les deux preuves sont de la même famille, « ce que je sais ». À l'inverse, le code secret associé à la reconnaissance de l'empreinte est valide, car on combine deux familles.

À la banque Lumeris, la règle est la suivante. À l'ouverture d'une session, le client saisit son identifiant et son code à six chiffres (premier facteur), puis confirme sur le téléphone enregistré avec l'empreinte ou le visage (second facteur, lié à l'appareil). Pour un virement supérieur à 500 euros, ou vers un bénéficiaire nouveau, une confirmation supplémentaire est demandée : c'est ce qu'on appelle l'authentification renforcée pour opération sensible.

Remarque importante : la biométrie ne quitte jamais le téléphone. L'application reçoit seulement une réponse oui ou non du système, signée par une clé qui reste dans la puce sécurisée. Elle ne voit ni l'image ni le gabarit de l'empreinte.

3. Le cycle de vie d'une session

Hélène a dessiné au tableau les cinq étapes d'une session.

Étape 1, l'ouverture. Après la réussite des deux facteurs, le serveur crée une session et envoie deux jetons : un jeton d'accès, de courte durée, et un jeton de renouvellement, de longue durée.

Étape 2, l'usage. À chaque appel, l'application envoie le jeton d'accès. Le serveur vérifie la signature, la date d'expiration et le périmètre autorisé.

Étape 3, le renouvellement. Quand le jeton d'accès expire, l'application présente le jeton de renouvellement pour en obtenir un nouveau, sans redemander le code.

Étape 4, la rotation. À chaque renouvellement, le serveur émet aussi un nouveau jeton de renouvellement et invalide l'ancien. Si un ancien jeton est présenté une seconde fois, c'est le signe d'un vol : le serveur détruit alors toute la famille de jetons, et le client doit se reconnecter.

Étape 5, la fin. La session se termine par une déconnexion volontaire, par l'expiration du jeton de renouvellement, par un blocage décidé par la banque, ou par un changement d'appareil.

Les durées retenues chez nous :

| Élément | Durée de vie | Remarque |
|---|---|---|
| Jeton d'accès | 5 minutes | Signé, vérifié sans appel à la base |
| Jeton de renouvellement | 30 jours | Stocké côté serveur sous forme de hachage |
| Inactivité maximale | 10 minutes | L'application se verrouille, le jeton reste valide |
| Session absolue | 12 heures | Au-delà, nouvelle authentification complète |

Hélène a précisé la différence entre le verrouillage et la fermeture. Au bout de 10 minutes d'inactivité, l'application affiche un écran de verrouillage, qui demande l'empreinte ou le code, mais la session n'est pas fermée. Au bout de 12 heures, même un utilisateur actif doit se réauthentifier complètement.

4. Exemple corrigé : calculer le nombre de renouvellements

Une cliente, Mme Delorme, ouvre une session à 8 h 00 et utilise l'application sans interruption de plus de 10 minutes. Combien de fois le jeton d'accès est-il renouvelé avant la limite de la session absolue ?

La session absolue dure 12 heures, soit 720 minutes. Le jeton d'accès dure 5 minutes. Le premier jeton est émis à l'ouverture, donc il couvre de 8 h 00 à 8 h 05. Il faut ensuite 720 divisé par 5, soit 144 jetons au total pour couvrir les 12 heures, dont le premier émis à l'ouverture. Il y a donc 143 renouvellements. À chaque renouvellement, le jeton de renouvellement change aussi : 143 jetons de renouvellement ont été invalidés, et le dernier est abandonné à la fin de la session.

Hélène a ajouté un point de vigilance : si la cliente reste inactive plus de 5 minutes mais moins de 10, le jeton d'accès expire sans que l'écran se verrouille. Au prochain geste, l'application renouvelle silencieusement, et la cliente ne voit rien.

5. Stockage des secrets sur le téléphone

Les règles rappelées en cours :

1. Aucun secret en clair dans les préférences de l'application, dans les fichiers ou dans les journaux.
2. Le jeton de renouvellement est stocké dans le coffre sécurisé du système (trousseau sur iOS, magasin de clés matériel sur Android), protégé par le verrouillage de l'appareil.
3. Le jeton d'accès reste en mémoire seulement et n'est jamais écrit sur le disque.
4. Le code secret à six chiffres n'est jamais stocké sur le téléphone : il est envoyé au serveur par un canal chiffré, comparé à une valeur hachée avec un sel et un algorithme lent, puis oublié.
5. Les captures d'écran sont désactivées sur les écrans qui affichent un solde ou un IBAN complet.
6. L'application refuse de démarrer sur un appareil dont le système a été modifié (appareil débridé ou « rooté ») pour les opérations sensibles, et signale l'appareil au serveur pour une analyse du risque.

Hélène a raconté un incident : en 2022, un prototype interne enregistrait le jeton d'accès dans un fichier de préférences « pour gagner du temps au démarrage ». Un testeur l'a retrouvé en copiant la sauvegarde du téléphone sur un ordinateur. Le défaut a été corrigé avant la mise en production, mais elle l'utilise comme exemple pour montrer que « temporaire » ne veut pas dire « sûr ».

6. Limitation des tentatives

Pour résister aux attaques par essais successifs, le serveur compte les échecs de saisie du code secret.

- Après 3 échecs consécutifs : attente de 30 secondes.
- Après 5 échecs : attente de 5 minutes.
- Après 8 échecs : le compte est bloqué, le client doit appeler le centre de relation client ou utiliser la procédure de réinitialisation avec une pièce d'identité.
- Le compteur est remis à zéro après une connexion réussie.

Le blocage est lié au compte, pas à l'appareil, afin d'empêcher un attaquant de changer de téléphone pour contourner la limite.

Exemple corrigé : un code à six chiffres offre 10^6, soit un million de combinaisons. Un attaquant qui connaîtrait l'identifiant et pourrait essayer librement un code par seconde le trouverait en 500 000 secondes en moyenne, soit un peu moins de 6 jours. Avec la limite de 8 échecs, il n'a que 8 chances sur 1 000 000 d'essayer le bon code avant le blocage, soit 0,0008 pour cent. C'est pourquoi la limitation par compte est plus importante que la longueur du code lui-même.

Hélène a reconnu une faiblesse : un attaquant qui veut nuire peut bloquer volontairement le compte d'un client en entrant huit mauvais codes. La banque a choisi d'accepter ce risque, parce que le blocage d'un compte est moins grave que son vol, mais elle étudie un déblocage par l'application d'un second appareil déjà enregistré.

7. Changement d'appareil et récupération

Lorsque le client change de téléphone, il doit enregistrer le nouvel appareil. Le parcours est le suivant : saisie de l'identifiant et du code, puis envoi d'un code à usage unique par courrier postal ou par un appel automatisé sur le numéro enregistré depuis plus de 30 jours, puis, si le client possède encore l'ancien appareil, validation sur celui-ci. Pendant 48 heures après l'enregistrement d'un nouvel appareil, les virements vers de nouveaux bénéficiaires sont limités à 300 euros par jour.

Hélène a expliqué pourquoi la banque a abandonné le SMS comme second facteur pour les opérations sensibles : l'échange de carte SIM frauduleux, ou la redirection du numéro, permet à un tiers de recevoir le code. Les 29 cas mentionnés au début de la séance correspondaient tous à ce scénario. Le SMS reste utilisé uniquement pour avertir le client qu'une alerte a été émise, jamais pour transporter un secret.

8. Erreurs de conception fréquentes

À la fin de la séance, la classe a dressé la liste suivante, que l'intervenante a validée.

- Faire confiance à une vérification faite seulement côté application. Toute règle de sécurité doit être revérifiée côté serveur, car l'application peut être modifiée.
- Mettre une clé secrète dans le code de l'application. Quiconque télécharge l'application peut l'extraire.
- Utiliser un jeton d'accès de longue durée « pour éviter les déconnexions ». Cela transforme un vol en accès durable.
- Afficher des messages d'erreur trop précis, comme « identifiant inconnu » ou « code incorrect », qui permettent de savoir si un identifiant existe. Le message doit rester le même dans tous les cas.
- Oublier d'invalider les jetons quand le client change son code secret ou signale la perte de son téléphone.
- Écrire des données sensibles dans les journaux de débogage, qui sont ensuite envoyés à l'outil de suivi des plantages.

9. Exemple corrigé : détecter le vol d'un jeton de renouvellement

Scénario présenté par Hélène. M. Okonkwo possède un téléphone enregistré. Son jeton de renouvellement, appelons-le R1, est copié par un logiciel malveillant à 10 h 00. À 10 h 02, M. Okonkwo, qui ne se doute de rien, renouvelle sa session : le serveur reçoit R1, émet R2 et invalide R1. À 10 h 07, l'attaquant présente R1.

Que se passe-t-il ? Le serveur constate que R1 a déjà été utilisé. Il ne peut pas savoir lequel des deux porteurs est le client légitime, donc il applique la règle de prudence : toute la famille de jetons (R1, R2 et les jetons d'accès associés) est détruite, une alerte est enregistrée et M. Okonkwo reçoit une notification. Au prochain geste, l'application échoue au renouvellement et lui demande de se reconnecter avec ses deux facteurs. L'attaquant, lui, n'obtient rien, puisque R1 est inutilisable.

Si l'attaquant avait été plus rapide que le client, par exemple en présentant R1 à 10 h 01, le résultat aurait été le même, mais dans l'autre sens : c'est le client qui aurait présenté un jeton déjà consommé à 10 h 02, et la famille aurait été détruite à ce moment-là. Dans les deux cas, la durée pendant laquelle l'attaquant garde un accès utile est au plus de 5 minutes, soit la durée du dernier jeton d'accès valide. C'est la raison pour laquelle on combine un jeton d'accès très court et la rotation.

Calcul de l'exposition maximale : sans rotation, un jeton de renouvellement volé reste valable 30 jours, soit 43 200 minutes. Avec la rotation, la fenêtre utile se réduit à l'intervalle entre le vol et le prochain renouvellement du client légitime, au pire 5 minutes. Le gain est d'un facteur 8 640 (43 200 divisé par 5).

10. Journalisation et alertes

Les évènements suivants sont enregistrés côté serveur, sans jamais inclure de code secret ni de jeton complet : ouverture et fermeture de session, échecs de saisie, changement d'appareil, rotation réutilisée, opération sensible refusée, et appareil débridé détecté. Chaque évènement porte l'identifiant du compte, un identifiant d'appareil pseudonymisé, l'heure et le résultat.

Le centre de supervision reçoit une alerte dans trois cas : plus de 20 comptes bloqués en une heure, ce qui peut indiquer une attaque de masse ; une rotation réutilisée sur un compte déjà alerté dans les 30 derniers jours ; et un virement vers un nouveau bénéficiaire, supérieur à 2 000 euros, dans les 48 heures qui suivent un changement d'appareil. Les journaux sont conservés 13 mois et accessibles seulement à l'équipe sécurité et aux auditeurs.

Hélène a insisté sur la protection de la vie privée : les journaux ne contiennent pas le contenu des opérations, ni les noms des bénéficiaires, mais uniquement ce qui est nécessaire pour comprendre un incident.

11. Consignes pour les tests

L'équipe de test doit vérifier au minimum : l'expiration du jeton d'accès après 5 minutes ; le verrouillage à 10 minutes d'inactivité ; la fermeture à 12 heures ; le refus de l'ancien jeton de renouvellement après rotation ; les paliers de blocage à 3, 5 et 8 échecs ; le comportement sur un appareil débridé ; et l'absence de secret dans les sauvegardes du téléphone.

Prochaine séance : le chiffrement des échanges, l'épinglage des certificats et la détection des fraudes en temps réel. À préparer : relire le document de politique de sécurité de la banque, versions 4.1 et suivantes.

Below are the notes from our last two planning meetings about moving the Harrowgate University Library into the refurbished Aldous Building over the summer. Could you turn them into a full project plan with named owners, dates, dependencies, a risk register and a short list of decisions I still need to get signed off? Please keep the owners and dates exactly as they appear in the notes, and tell me wherever the notes contradict themselves or leave a gap.

---

HARROWGATE UNIVERSITY LIBRARY
Aldous Building Move: Planning Group
Minutes of meeting 4, Tuesday 3 March

Present: Marguerite Osei (University Librarian, chair), Tobias Lindqvist (Head of Collections), Priya Nandakumar (Head of Library Systems), Callum Brightwater (Estates Project Manager), Ines Valdivia (Head of User Services), Dmitri Kowalczyk (Special Collections Curator), Hannah Oyelaran (Finance Business Partner), Wei-Jun Salcedo (Student Union representative), Gareth Pryce (minutes).
Apologies: Fatima Rahimi (Head of Digital Scholarship), who sent comments by email, noted under item 6.

1. Minutes of meeting 3 and matters arising

The minutes of meeting 3 were agreed with one correction: the Aldous Building handover from the contractor is planned for Friday 19 June, not Friday 12 June as written. Callum confirmed that 19 June is the date in the contract and that the earlier date was the contractor's first estimate. Matters arising: the survey of the compact shelving in the old basement stack has been completed (see item 3), and the quotation from the removals firm, Pennant & Crake, has been received (see item 4).

2. Overall timetable and the closure period

Marguerite reminded the group that the Senate has approved a single closure of the main library from Monday 6 July to Friday 14 August, six weeks, and that the new building must be open to readers when the autumn term begins on Monday 14 September. That leaves a margin of four weeks after the closure ends, which she wants to keep as contingency and not plan into the schedule. Ines asked whether a phased reopening, with the ground floor open first, is still being considered. Marguerite said it is not the plan but it is the fallback if the fit-out slips; the decision point is Friday 24 July, when Callum will report on the state of floors 1 and 2.

Wei-Jun said students were worried about the six weeks coinciding with the resit period, which runs from Monday 10 August to Friday 21 August. Ines agreed to arrange a temporary reading room with 60 seats in the Student Union's Fenwick Room, with a click-and-collect service for the 2,000 most requested short-loan items. Hannah said no budget had been set aside for the reading room and asked for a costed proposal. Action: Ines to produce the costed proposal for the temporary reading room by Friday 20 March.

3. Collections: what moves and what does not

Tobias reported on the collection audit. The library holds about 412,000 print volumes. After the weeding exercise approved at meeting 2, he expects to move 351,000 volumes to the Aldous Building and to send about 38,000 to the off-site store at Larkmoor, which leaves roughly 23,000 volumes for withdrawal or donation. He stressed that the withdrawal list has not yet been reviewed by the subject librarians and the figure may move by a few thousand either way. The basement compact shelving survey found that bays 14 to 22 are too deformed to dismantle safely and will have to be scrapped, not reused; the other 31 bays can be relocated to the Larkmoor store. Callum asked that the scrap contractor be told by the end of April, because the basement must be empty before the asbestos clearance team arrives on Monday 6 July.

Dmitri raised the position of Special Collections. About 9,400 items, including the Penhallow Bequest of maps and the Eldritch Press archive, need a climate-controlled move and cannot be loaded onto the general removal lorries. He proposed that the move happen in a separate week, Monday 22 June to Friday 26 June, before the main closure, with the reading room closed to visitors for that week only. Tobias was concerned that this would overlap with the building handover and the first access for the shelving installers. Callum said the shelving installers have access to floors 1 and 2 from Monday 22 June, which means the two activities would be on different floors, since Special Collections is on floor 3. Dmitri also noted that the strongroom door in the new building has not yet been commissioned and that nothing can be moved in until the environmental monitoring has run clean for ten consecutive days. Callum said the monitoring could begin no earlier than Monday 8 June if the plant is commissioned on time. Ten days from 8 June would end on Thursday 18 June, so the date works, but only just. No decision was taken on whether to risk the Special Collections move before the handover date of 19 June. Dmitri was asked to write up the conditions under which he would accept the move.

Action: Tobias to circulate the final withdrawal list to subject librarians by Friday 27 March, with comments due by Friday 17 April.
Action: Dmitri to write up the conditions for the Special Collections move by Friday 13 March.

4. Removals contract

Hannah presented the quotation from Pennant & Crake: 184,000 pounds for moving 351,000 volumes, the 31 compact bays and the furniture, plus 22,500 pounds for the Special Collections move as a separate lot. Together with the Larkmoor transport, which is priced separately at 31,200 pounds, the total comes to 237,700 pounds. The approved project budget for the move is 245,000 pounds, which leaves 7,300 pounds of contingency, less than three per cent. Hannah said she was not comfortable with this and asked that the group either find a saving or ask the Estates Committee for a contingency of at least ten per cent. Priya suggested that the library staff could box and label the lowest-use journal runs themselves, which Pennant & Crake had said would reduce the quotation by about 14,000 pounds. Tobias thought that was realistic only if student helpers were hired, which would cost money too. Marguerite asked Hannah to model both options.

The group also discussed whether to tender the contract. Hannah said the university's procurement rules require a competitive process above 100,000 pounds, which means that the quotation from Pennant & Crake cannot be accepted directly and two further quotations are needed. Callum said he had already approached two other firms, Whitlow Freight and Dunmore Relocations, and expects their quotations by Friday 27 March. Award of the contract needs to happen by Friday 10 April so that the removals firm can plan crews for July.

Action: Hannah to model the two savings options and the ten per cent contingency request by Friday 20 March.
Action: Callum to obtain two further quotations by Friday 27 March and to bring an evaluation to meeting 5.

5. Library systems and the new building

Priya reported that the RFID gates, self-service kiosks and the new wayfinding screens are all part of the fit-out contract, but the library management system configuration is hers. The shelf-location codes in the catalogue must be remapped from the old building's scheme to the new one before the books are moved, and her team has so far mapped about 40 per cent of the locations. She needs the final floor plans with bay numbers from Callum before she can finish; the current drawings are revision C and the final set, revision F, is promised by Friday 10 April. She estimates 15 working days of work once she has them, and she wants to run a full test load into the training copy of the system before the closure starts. That test must be finished by Friday 26 June at the latest, which gives her a comfortable margin only if the drawings arrive on time.

NOTES FROM THE CONTRACTOR'S REPORT

E-bikes made up 17 per cent of the fleet and took part in roughly 24 per cent of trips: about 8.4 trips per e-bike per day, against 5.6 for a standard bike. E-bike trips averaged 17.8 minutes and standard bike trips 15.9 minutes. Most e-bike battery faults occurred at Riverside Quay, Harbour Row and University Gate, which are the three stations with the longest uphill return routes.

Rebalancing is done by two vans working weekdays 06:30 to 14:30 and one van on Saturdays. The contractor estimates that each van visit costs the council about 14 pounds in labour and fuel, and that vans currently move bikes mainly from the "full" stations to the "empty" ones in the morning only. No evening rebalancing is done. The contractor says that adding an evening shift of one van would cost around 38,000 pounds a year.

The contractor also reports that the university's autumn term began on Monday 22 September, and that the university has confirmed it expects 600 more students to join in the next intake than in the year before. Two applications for new stations have been received from residents' associations (Fairview Estate asked for more docks; Kestrel Park asked for a second station at the north gate), and the council has a capital budget of 96,000 pounds for new docks this year. A new dock station of 16 docks costs about 41,000 pounds installed, and an additional 8-dock extension to an existing station costs about 17,500 pounds.

QUESTIONS ALREADY RAISED BY COUNCILLORS

Councillor Abernethy-Wyld has written to ask whether the August price rise "drove people away from the scheme or just moved them into a cheaper product". Councillor Tamsin Odhiambo wants to know whether the stations in the poorer eastern wards, Fairview Estate and Greenfield Road, are used enough to justify keeping them, since they are the quietest in the scheme. The deputy chair of the committee asked for "one figure that tells us whether the scheme is working", and the contractor has suggested trips per bike per day, which was 6.1 over the quarter. Finally, the university's sustainability office has asked whether the council would consider a station inside the new science campus when it opens next year.

DATA CAVEATS

- Rainy day means any day with 2 mm or more of rain recorded at the council depot. It does not distinguish light showers from all-day rain.
- Station "Empty %" and "Full %" are measured only during opening hours, 05:30 to 23:30.
- Student trips were not separated from annual trips before 1 July of last year, so earlier comparisons are not possible.
- The contractor's system does not record the purpose of the trip, and journeys by day pass holders cannot be linked to individuals.
- The September fare-income figure has not yet been reconciled with the bank statements, so I have not included income here.

# Design: Festival Programme, Seating and Ticketing Service (FPST)

Author: Cormac Ellesmere-Boyd (lead developer)
Reviewers: Anneliese Tharp (festival operations), Joss Kimathi (box office), Verity Oduya (programming)
Status: Draft 3, for sign-off
Festival: Saltmere International Film Festival, 10 days in late October, 61 films, 7 venues

## 1. Background and goals

Today the festival runs on a shared spreadsheet for the programme, a third-party ticketing website that charges 8 per cent per ticket, and a paper process for venue allocation. Last year the box office oversold two screenings of "The Lantern Keepers" at the Alderman Cinema because tickets were being sold from a spreadsheet copy that had not been refreshed. About 140 people were turned away or moved, and the festival had to refund and apologise.

This document describes a single service, FPST, that holds the programme, the venues and seating, sells tickets and passes, and checks people in at the door. The goals are:

1. No double selling of any seat or any capacity-limited screening.
2. The programme team can change the schedule up to the day before a screening without the box office having to edit anything by hand.
3. Ticket fees to the festival fall from 8 per cent to under 3 per cent, using a payment provider directly.
4. The system survives the busiest weekend, the middle Saturday and Sunday, when we expect about 9,000 ticket transactions across the two days.
5. Door staff can check in ticket holders even if the venue internet fails.

Non-goals: no mobile app (tickets are PDFs and wallet passes), no dynamic pricing, no integration with the accounting package this year.

## 2. Users and scale

| Group | Count | Needs |
|---|---|---|
| Public customers | about 14,000 accounts, 4,500 active in the busiest week | Browse, buy, download tickets |
| Passholders | about 600 | Reserve seats in advance with a pass |
| Box office staff | 6 | Sell tickets in person, refund, exchange |
| Programming team | 4 | Edit the schedule, assign venues |
| Door staff | about 40 over 7 venues | Scan tickets |
| Press and guests | about 350 | Accreditation, free tickets with quotas |

Venues range from the Alderman Cinema (412 seats) down to the Gallery Room (48 seats, unreserved). Of the seven venues, five have numbered seating and two are general admission. Total capacity per day, if every screening sold out, is about 5,300 seats.

## 3. Architecture

FPST is a single web application written in Python with a relational database (PostgreSQL), deployed as one container on the festival's cloud account, with a managed database and a managed object store for tickets. A second small container runs background jobs (emails, PDF generation, nightly reports). The public site and the staff screens are the same application and differ only by login role. Static assets are served through the cloud provider's CDN.

The decision to keep one application and one database was deliberate. With four developers, only one of them full-time, we cannot run a collection of services, and the traffic is modest apart from two peaks.

### 3.1 Data model

The core tables are:

- venues (id, name, address, capacity, seating_type)
- seats (id, venue_id, row, number, accessible, held_back)
- films (id, title, runtime_minutes, rating, synopsis)
- screenings (id, film_id, venue_id, starts_at, ends_at, price_band, status)
- tickets (id, screening_id, seat_id nullable, order_id, status, barcode)
- orders (id, customer_id, total_pence, payment_status, created_at)
- passes (id, customer_id, type, quota_remaining)
- customers (id, email, name, accessibility_needs)

A ticket row exists only once an order has been paid. Seat availability is computed by checking that no non-cancelled ticket exists for the seat and screening. During checkout the seat is "held" by inserting a row into a table seat_holds (screening_id, seat_id, session_id, expires_at). Holds last 10 minutes.

### 3.2 Selling a seat

The checkout flow for a numbered-seat screening is:

1. The customer picks seats on a seat map. The page reads availability from the database every 5 seconds.
2. When the customer clicks "Reserve", the application starts a transaction, reads the current tickets and holds for those seats, and if none conflict inserts hold rows.
3. The customer pays through the payment provider's hosted page. On the success callback, the application converts holds into tickets.
4. If the callback has not arrived after 10 minutes, a background job deletes the expired holds.

For general-admission screenings, the application counts tickets and holds against the venue capacity, and refuses a hold if the count would exceed capacity.

### 3.3 Scheduling

The programming team edits screenings on a grid, with venues in columns and time in rows. Moving a screening to another venue changes the venue_id; if the new venue has fewer seats, the application tells the editor how many tickets are already sold and refuses the move if the sold number exceeds the new capacity. There is a "clash check" that warns when two screenings in the same venue overlap, or when a guest speaker is booked in two places. The check runs when the editor presses Save.

Cancelling or moving a screening after tickets have been sold sends an email to every ticket holder through the background job, and offers a refund link valid for 14 days.

### 3.4 Passes

A pass has a quota of screenings (the Full Pass is unlimited, the Weekend Pass is 12 screenings, the Day Pass is 4). Passholders reserve seats in the same flow, but with no payment: the hold becomes a ticket straight away and the quota is decremented in the same transaction. Passholders may reserve up to 3 days ahead of the screening. Full Pass holders may reserve up to 7 days ahead, which means Full Pass holders get first choice of the popular screenings.

### 3.5 Check-in and offline mode

Door staff use a web page on a tablet, with a camera scanning the barcode on each ticket. Before the doors open, the tablet downloads the list of valid tickets for the screening and stores it in the browser's local storage. Scans are checked against the local list, and results are sent to the server when the connection returns. If a barcode is scanned twice, the second scan shows "already used" along with the time of the first scan.

### 3.6 Reporting

A nightly job produces a CSV of tickets sold per screening and revenue per film, which is emailed to Anneliese and Verity. Live attendance numbers are shown on a dashboard that reads from the same database.

### 3.7 Refunds and exchanges

Box office staff can refund a ticket from the order screen. The refund is sent to the payment provider through its API, the ticket status is set to cancelled and the seat becomes available again immediately. Exchanges are handled as a refund followed by a new sale, so the customer pays the difference by card at the desk. The rules are: full refund up to 48 hours before the screening, 50 per cent refund from 48 to 6 hours before, no refund after that unless the festival cancels. A ticket bought with a pass cannot be refunded in money, but the quota is returned if the ticket is cancelled more than 6 hours ahead. Refunds above 100 pounds need a second member of staff to approve them in the system.

### 3.8 Staff roles

There are four roles: customer, box office, programming and administrator. Box office staff can sell, refund and see customer details. Programming staff can edit the schedule but not see customer details. Administrators can do everything, including editing the seat maps and creating staff accounts. Every change to a screening, a refund and every login is written to an audit table with the user, the time and the old and new values. The audit table is never edited by the application.

### 3.9 Press and guest allocations

Accredited press and festival guests receive a code by email. The code is entered at checkout and sets the ticket price to zero for up to 6 screenings per person. Press codes are valid for the whole festival; guest codes are tied to one film and allow up to 2 tickets. Each code is stored with a counter of how many tickets have been issued against it. Codes are generated by the programming team in batches from a CSV file, and the application emails them through the background job. Press seats are limited to 15 per cent of the capacity of a screening, and the application checks this at the moment the free ticket is issued. If the screening is already at the limit, the person is told it is full for press and is offered the next showing.

### 3.10 Accessibility

Each venue has a set of accessible seats flagged in the seats table, and these are hidden from the public seat map unless the customer ticks "I need an accessible seat" in their profile. Companions are given a free ticket next to the accessible seat. For general-admission venues, the capacity count reserves 4 places for wheelchair users, which are released two hours before the screening.

## 4. Performance and capacity

We expect the traffic to peak at two moments. When the programme goes on sale, on Friday 25 September at 10:00, we expect about 2,500 people to arrive within the first ten minutes. On the busiest weekend, we expect about 9,000 transactions across two days, with a peak of about 25 orders per minute. A single application container with 4 CPU cores should handle 25 orders per minute without difficulty. For the on-sale moment, we have not load tested yet; we plan to run a test with 3,000 virtual users in mid August. If the single container proves too small, we will add a second and a third behind the load balancer, since the application keeps no session state in memory.

The seat map polling at 5 second intervals from 2,500 users would produce about 500 requests per second against the database. We will add an in-memory cache with a 2 second expiry for the seat map query.

## 5. Security and privacy

Customer data (name, email, accessibility needs) is stored in the database in the clear, with the database encrypted at rest by the cloud provider. Staff log in with email and password; box office accounts require a second factor. We store no card data, since payment is handled by the provider's hosted page. Accessibility needs are visible to box office staff and are used to allocate accessible seats. Customers can request deletion of their account after the festival ends; we will anonymise their orders and keep the financial totals. Backups are taken daily and kept for 30 days.

## 6. Failure modes considered

- Payment provider outage: customers see an error page and holds expire after 10 minutes.
- Database failure: the managed database has a standby in another zone, with automatic failover in about two minutes.
- Venue internet failure: check-in continues from the downloaded list.
- Duplicate payment callbacks: the callback handler ignores a callback if the order is already paid.

## 7. Testing

Developers write unit tests for the pricing rules, pass quotas and the clash check. We will run a full rehearsal at the Alderman Cinema on Saturday 5 September with real tablets and real tickets. Manual testing of the checkout will be done by the box office staff.

## 8. Timeline

| Phase | Dates | Content |
|---|---|---|
| Build | 5 January to 29 May | Data model, scheduling grid, checkout, passes |
| Staff testing | 1 June to 31 July | Box office and programming team use it with dummy data |
| Load testing and fixes | 10 to 28 August | Peak load test, security review |
| Rehearsal | 5 September | Full test at the Alderman Cinema |
| Soft launch | 18 September | Passes go on sale |
| Programme on sale | 25 September | Public sale opens |
| Festival | 23 October to 1 November | Live use |

Note: the build phase is five months for one full-time developer and three part-time contributors, who give about 6 hours each per week.

## 9. Costs

Cloud hosting is estimated at 340 pounds a month in the festival period and 120 pounds a month otherwise. The payment provider charges 1.5 per cent plus 20 pence per transaction. Based on 38,000 tickets sold across about 21,000 orders at an average ticket price of 11.40 pounds, the estimated fee total is about 10,700 pounds (1.5 per cent of 433,200 pounds of ticket sales, plus 20 pence on each order), against about 34,700 pounds under the current third-party arrangement. Development is internal.

## 10. Open questions

1. Should press and guest quotas be tracked as passes or as a separate table?
2. What happens when someone buys a pass after already buying tickets for individual screenings?
3. Who is responsible for the seat map for each venue? Verity says the Alderman plan is out of date.
4. Do we need a waiting list for sold-out screenings?
