ESPECIFICACIÓN DE PRODUCTO
Sistema de citas y recordatorios "Almendral Citas", versión 2.0
Autora: Beatriz Quintanilla Ferrer (producto)
Revisores: Gonzalo Arriaga (operaciones clínicas), Soledad Barrionuevo (atención al paciente), Raimundo Cuesta (tecnología)
Estado: aprobada para desarrollo

1. Contexto y objetivos

Clínicas Dentales Almendral es una cadena de 14 clínicas repartidas en tres provincias, con 62 sillones dentales y unos 38.000 pacientes activos. Hasta ahora las citas se gestionan por teléfono y en una agenda local de cada clínica, lo que provoca citas duplicadas, huecos sin cubrir y un 17 % de ausencias sin aviso. La versión 2.0 de Almendral Citas permite que el paciente pida, cambie y cancele sus citas por internet, que el personal gestione la agenda de forma centralizada y que el sistema envíe recordatorios automáticos. El objetivo es reducir las ausencias sin aviso al 8 % en seis meses y reducir un 30 % las llamadas de recepción dedicadas a gestionar citas.

2. Usuarios y roles

- Paciente: puede reservar, modificar y cancelar sus propias citas y las de sus hijos menores de 16 años registrados como dependientes.
- Recepcionista: gestiona la agenda de su clínica y puede crear, mover y cancelar citas de cualquier paciente de esa clínica.
- Dentista o higienista: consulta su propia agenda y puede bloquear horas.
- Gerente de clínica: además de lo anterior, configura horarios, festivos y tipos de tratamiento de su clínica.
- Administrador central: configura los parámetros comunes de la cadena y consulta informes de todas las clínicas.

3. Requisitos funcionales

3.1 Registro e inicio de sesión

RF-01. El paciente se registra con correo electrónico, teléfono móvil, nombre completo, fecha de nacimiento y número de documento de identidad. El correo debe ser único. La contraseña debe tener al menos 10 caracteres, con al menos una letra y un número.
RF-02. El sistema envía un correo de confirmación con un enlace válido durante 24 horas. Hasta que el paciente lo confirme no puede reservar.
RF-03. Tras 5 intentos fallidos de inicio de sesión consecutivos, la cuenta se bloquea durante 15 minutos.
RF-04. Un paciente puede registrar hasta 4 dependientes menores de 16 años. Al cumplir 16 años, el dependiente deja de aparecer y debe crear su propia cuenta; el sistema avisa al titular con 30 días de antelación.

3.2 Reserva de citas

RF-05. El paciente elige clínica, tipo de tratamiento, profesional (o "cualquiera") y ve los huecos disponibles de los próximos 60 días.
RF-06. Cada tipo de tratamiento tiene una duración fija: revisión (20 minutos), limpieza (40 minutos), empaste (45 minutos), endodoncia (90 minutos), ortodoncia de seguimiento (30 minutos), primera visita (60 minutos).
RF-07. Un paciente nuevo, es decir, sin ninguna cita anterior en la cadena, solo puede reservar "primera visita".
RF-08. El paciente no puede tener más de 3 citas futuras activas al mismo tiempo. Los dependientes cuentan por separado.
RF-09. No se puede reservar con menos de 2 horas de antelación en la web. La recepción puede reservar sin límite de antelación.
RF-10. Si dos usuarios intentan reservar el mismo hueco, solo uno lo consigue; el otro recibe un mensaje y se le ofrecen los tres huecos más cercanos. El hueco elegido queda retenido 5 minutos mientras el paciente completa la reserva.
RF-11. Las endodoncias solo se pueden reservar en las clínicas que tengan un sillón con microscopio (a día de hoy, 6 de las 14).

3.3 Modificación y cancelación

RF-12. El paciente puede mover o cancelar una cita hasta 24 horas antes de su hora de inicio. Con menos de 24 horas, solo puede cancelar llamando a la clínica.
RF-13. Al mover una cita se mantiene el mismo tratamiento y la misma duración. Si el nuevo hueco no está libre, la cita original no se modifica.
RF-14. Una cita cancelada libera el hueco de inmediato y se ofrece a la lista de espera (ver 3.5).
RF-15. Si un paciente falta a una cita sin avisar, la recepción la marca como "no presentado". Tras 2 citas "no presentado" en 12 meses, el paciente deja de poder reservar por internet y debe llamar a la clínica. Un gerente puede levantar esta restricción.
RF-16. Si un profesional se pone enfermo, el gerente puede cancelar todas sus citas de un día. Cada paciente afectado recibe un mensaje con una propuesta de tres huecos alternativos y dispone de 48 horas para elegir uno antes de que la cita se anule definitivamente.

3.4 Recordatorios

RF-17. El sistema envía un recordatorio por correo 72 horas antes de la cita y un mensaje SMS 24 horas antes. Si el paciente tiene desactivadas las notificaciones por SMS, se envía un segundo correo.
RF-18. Los mensajes incluyen la dirección de la clínica, el nombre del profesional, el tipo de tratamiento y enlaces para confirmar, mover o cancelar. Los enlaces caducan cuando se alcanza el límite de 24 horas antes de la cita.
RF-19. Si el paciente pulsa "confirmar", la cita pasa a estado "confirmada". Las citas no confirmadas 24 horas antes se pueden llamar por teléfono; la recepción dispone de una lista diaria de citas sin confirmar.
RF-20. Las citas que se reservan con menos de 72 horas de antelación solo reciben el recordatorio por SMS. Las que se reservan con menos de 24 horas no reciben recordatorio.
RF-21. Las horas de los mensajes se muestran en la zona horaria de la clínica.

3.5 Lista de espera

RF-22. Si no hay huecos en los 60 días siguientes, el paciente puede apuntarse a la lista de espera de una clínica y tratamiento, y elegir los días de la semana y la franja (mañana o tarde).
RF-23. Cuando se libera un hueco compatible, el sistema envía un SMS al primer paciente de la lista y le reserva el hueco durante 15 minutos. Si no responde, pasa al siguiente.
RF-24. Un paciente puede estar en la lista de espera de un máximo de 2 clínicas a la vez. Las citas conseguidas por lista de espera cuentan para el límite de 3 citas de RF-08.

3.6 Gestión de la agenda por el personal

RF-25. La agenda diaria muestra, para cada sillón, las citas con color según su estado: reservada, confirmada, en curso, finalizada, no presentada, cancelada.
RF-26. El gerente define el horario semanal de cada profesional, con descansos, y los días festivos de la clínica. No se pueden dar huecos en festivos.
RF-27. Un profesional o la recepción puede bloquear una franja (reunión, formación). Si ya hay citas en esa franja, el sistema muestra la lista y pide confirmación; al confirmar, esas citas siguen el flujo de RF-16.
RF-28. La recepción puede crear una "sobrecita" (cita que se solapa con otra), pero solo con permiso del gerente. Se registra quién la creó y por qué.

3.7 Informes

RF-31. El gerente de clínica puede ver un informe diario y mensual con el número de citas por estado, la ocupación de cada sillón (minutos con paciente dividido entre minutos de horario) y la tasa de "no presentado".
RF-32. El administrador central puede ver los mismos datos agregados por clínica y por provincia, y exportarlos en formato CSV. La exportación no incluye nombres de pacientes, solo identificadores internos.
RF-33. El informe de ocupación excluye los festivos y los bloqueos de los profesionales del cálculo de minutos de horario.
RF-34. Cada lunes a las 7:00 el sistema envía a cada gerente un resumen por correo de la semana anterior: citas atendidas, ausencias, cancelaciones con menos de 24 horas y huecos que han quedado sin cubrir.

3.8 Notas y preferencias del paciente

RF-35. El paciente puede indicar su preferencia de contacto (correo, SMS o ambos), su idioma y si necesita ayuda de accesibilidad, como acceso para silla de ruedas. Esta información se muestra a la recepción al abrir la cita.
RF-36. La recepción puede añadir una nota interna a una cita, con un máximo de 500 caracteres. Las notas no son visibles para el paciente.
RF-37. Si el paciente marca que es una urgencia (dolor intenso, golpe o inflamación) al reservar, el sistema no muestra los huecos normales sino un mensaje con el teléfono de la clínica y, si hay un hueco de urgencia libre ese mismo día, lo ofrece. Los huecos de urgencia son 2 por clínica y día, de 20 minutos, y no están disponibles para la reserva normal.
RF-38. Un profesional puede marcar a un paciente como "requiere sedación". En ese caso, el sistema solo ofrece huecos en las clínicas y con los profesionales autorizados para sedación, y la duración de cualquier tratamiento aumenta 30 minutos.

3.9 Gestión de datos de las clínicas

RF-39. Cada clínica tiene un nombre, una dirección, un teléfono, un horario general y una lista de sillones con sus características (por ejemplo, microscopio, rayos X, sedación).
RF-40. Si el gerente cambia el horario general de la clínica, las citas ya reservadas fuera del nuevo horario no se cancelan automáticamente: el sistema las lista y el gerente decide si aplicar RF-16.
RF-41. Se puede dar de baja a un profesional con una fecha efectiva. A partir de esa fecha no se ofrecen huecos con él, y sus citas futuras siguen el flujo de RF-16.

4. Pagos y facturación

RF-29. La reserva web no exige pago, salvo la primera visita, que requiere una fianza de 15 euros que se descuenta del importe final. La fianza se devuelve si el paciente cancela con más de 24 horas de antelación y no se devuelve si no se presenta.
RF-30. Las fianzas se cobran con tarjeta mediante un proveedor de pagos externo. El sistema no guarda los datos de la tarjeta.

5. Requisitos no funcionales

RNF-01. Disponibilidad del 99,5 % en horario de clínica (de 8:00 a 21:00, de lunes a sábado).
RNF-02. La búsqueda de huecos debe responder en menos de 2 segundos para el 95 % de las consultas, con hasta 300 usuarios simultáneos.
RNF-03. Todos los datos personales se cifran en tránsito y en reposo y se cumple el reglamento europeo de protección de datos. El paciente puede descargar sus datos y solicitar su eliminación; los datos clínicos se conservan según la ley.
RNF-04. La interfaz debe funcionar en los dos últimos navegadores principales de móvil y escritorio, y cumplir el nivel AA de accesibilidad.
RNF-05. El sistema está disponible en español y en inglés. Los mensajes se envían en el idioma elegido por el paciente.

6. Integraciones

El sistema se integra con el programa clínico existente (historial del paciente) mediante una interfaz de lectura: al crear un paciente, se comprueba si ya existe en el historial por su documento de identidad y, en ese caso, se asocia y se considera "paciente existente" aunque no tenga citas anteriores. Esta integración es de solo lectura. Si el programa clínico no responde en 3 segundos, el registro continúa y se marca al paciente como "pendiente de verificación".

7. Fuera de alcance

Teleconsulta, historial clínico, facturación completa, aplicaciones móviles nativas y pagos de tratamientos.

8. Estados de una cita y transiciones permitidas

| Estado | Transiciones permitidas | Quién puede provocarlas |
|---|---|---|
| Reservada | Confirmada, Cancelada, No presentada | Paciente, recepción, sistema |
| Confirmada | En curso, Cancelada, No presentada | Paciente, recepción |
| En curso | Finalizada | Profesional |
| Finalizada | (ninguna) | |
| No presentada | Reservada (solo por corrección de recepción) | Recepción, gerente |
| Cancelada | (ninguna; se crea una cita nueva) | |

Una cita en estado "En curso" no puede cancelarse ni moverse. El paso a "No presentada" solo puede hacerse a partir de 15 minutos después de la hora de inicio. El sistema pasa automáticamente a "Cancelada" las citas afectadas por RF-16 cuyo plazo de 48 horas ha vencido, y registra el motivo.

9. Cuestiones pendientes de decisión

1. ¿Los dependientes pueden ser "pacientes nuevos" aunque el titular ya tenga historial?
2. ¿Qué ocurre con las citas de pacientes cuyo correo rebota?
3. ¿La restricción por faltas se aplica por clínica o a toda la cadena?

Here is our quarterly report for the Tamsin Valley Open Map project, written by our volunteer coordinator for the steering group meeting on Saturday. Can you give me a section-by-section summary (two or three sentences for each, with the figures that matter), then a list of the things in the report that should worry the steering group, and finally your recommendations, in priority order, with a reason for each? I would also like you to point out anywhere the numbers in the report do not quite agree with each other.

---

TAMSIN VALLEY OPEN MAP PROJECT
Quarterly Report, July to September
Prepared by: Odalys Merriweather-Cho, volunteer coordinator
For: Steering group meeting, Saturday 18 October

1. Summary

The project is a volunteer effort to keep a free, openly licensed map of the Tamsin Valley up to date: roads, paths, buildings, shops, bus stops, flood defences and accessibility details such as step-free entrances. This quarter we had 143 active contributors, up from 118 last quarter, and 61 per cent of the valley's 2,310 square kilometres now has "complete" coverage under our own standard, up from 54 per cent. The headline problem is quality: our spot-check audit found that 9.4 per cent of the features checked had at least one error, against a target of 5 per cent. Our grant from the Tamsin Regional Trust runs out on 31 March and we have used 71 per cent of it. We also had two serious incidents involving contributor conduct and one data-loss event on our own tile server.

2. Contributors

Active contributors are people who made at least one edit in the quarter. Of the 143, 37 were new this quarter, 82 were returning contributors from earlier quarters and 24 were returning after a gap of more than a year. 19 people made more than 100 edits each and together produced 68 per cent of all edits; the top five alone produced 31 per cent. Edits totalled 214,600 in the quarter, a 22 per cent rise on the previous quarter's 175,900.

We ran three mapping evenings (the first Thursday of each month, two in the Wexcombe library and one online in September) and one weekend "mapathon" in Harrowick on 6 and 7 September, which attracted 52 people, of whom 29 were new. Of the 37 new contributors this quarter, 22 came from the mapathon. Retention from the mapathon is, so far, disappointing: only 8 of those 22 made an edit in the three weeks after the event. Volunteer feedback on the mapathon was positive (average 4.4 out of 5 from 31 responses), and the main complaints were the unreliable wifi and a lack of beginner guidance for the tools.

Demographically, our survey of contributors (61 responses) showed that 58 per cent are over 50, 11 per cent are under 25, and 29 per cent describe themselves as having a local connection to a village in the upper valley, the area with the least coverage.

3. Coverage

We measure coverage by dividing the valley into 1 km grid squares (2,310 in total) and rating each square as Empty, Partial or Complete. A square is Complete if it has all roads and paths named and connected, all buildings traced, and the main points of interest recorded. At the end of the quarter the position was:

| Rating | Squares | Share |
|---|---|---|
| Complete | 1,409 | 61% |
| Partial | 647 | 28% |
| Empty | 254 | 11% |
| Total | 2,310 | 100% |

The last quarter's figures were 1,247 Complete (54 per cent), 702 Partial and 361 Empty. The 162 squares that moved to Complete came mainly from the lower valley around Harrowick and Wexcombe, where a school mapping project and the mapathon contributed. Of the 254 Empty squares, 211 are in the upper valley, mostly farmland and moorland with a few scattered hamlets. A further factor is that the aerial imagery we use for tracing in the upper valley is four years old, and the new imagery that the county council has promised for release in November has not yet arrived.

We also added 1,870 accessibility records (step-free entrances, kerb heights and tactile paving) this quarter, bringing the total to 6,420. These were mostly collected by the Wexcombe Access Group, who walked every street in the town centre with a wheelchair user, and make up 83 per cent of the quarter's additions.

4. Data quality

Each quarter a small team of experienced volunteers checks a random sample of 800 features against imagery and, where possible, a site visit. This quarter the sample found errors in 75 features, which is 9.4 per cent. The previous quarter's rate was 7.8 per cent on 800 features. The errors were:

| Type of error | Count | Share of errors |
|---|---|---|
| Wrong or missing name | 21 | 28% |
| Wrong geometry (misplaced or badly traced) | 19 | 25% |
| Wrong category tag (for example a shop tagged as an office) | 16 | 21% |
| Out of date (closed or demolished) | 12 | 16% |
| Duplicate feature | 5 | 7% |
| Other | 2 | 3% |
| Total | 75 | 100% |

The reviewers noted that errors were concentrated in work by contributors with fewer than 20 lifetime edits. Of the 75 erroneous features, 44 (59 per cent) had been last edited by such contributors, even though they produce only 12 per cent of all edits. Errors in the "out of date" category are mostly shops and cafes in the Wexcombe high street, where 6 businesses closed during the summer. Only 31 per cent of the project's contributors have completed the optional online training module.

We agreed last quarter to introduce a "second pair of eyes" review for edits from contributors with fewer than 20 edits. This was not implemented, mainly because the review tool needed work (see section 6) and because we have only 9 reviewers, who are already stretched.

5. Incidents

Incident 1 (conduct, 14 August). A long-standing contributor, anonymised here as Contributor A, posted insulting messages in the project forum about a new contributor's edits, after the new contributor corrected several of A's road names. Three members of the community complained. The coordinator and two members of the steering group spoke to Contributor A, who apologised; a written warning was issued under the code of conduct. The new contributor made no further edits after this incident.

Incident 2 (conduct, 29 September). A contributor made more than 300 edits in one afternoon that changed the names of about 120 villages in the upper valley from their English form to an older local form, without discussion. These edits were challenged by several contributors and reverted within two days. A discussion on the forum was held on naming policy; no agreed position has yet been reached. The contributor has not been banned but has been asked to stop further bulk edits until there is an agreed policy.

Incident 3 (data loss, 3 September). The tile server, which draws the project's web map from a virtual machine rented at a monthly cost, failed when its disk filled up during a rebuild. When the volunteer administrator restored from backup, the most recent backup was found to be 19 days old, because the nightly backup job had been failing silently since 15 August. Edits made to the map's own database were not lost, since these are stored separately, but the web map was out of date and then unavailable for 41 hours. Four local organisations that embed our map on their websites (the Wexcombe Parish Council, the Tamsin Valley Walkers, the Harrowick Bus Users' Group and a community cafe) complained. The backup job has been fixed and an alert added.

6. Tools and infrastructure

The project runs three systems: the map database and editing software (hosted by a free public service, with no cost to us), the tile server for our own web map, and a small review and statistics website built by a volunteer, Casimir Dunleavy. The review website had two outages in the quarter, both caused by Casimir being away on holiday when a software library update broke it. Casimir is the only person who understands the code. He has said he would like to step back from the project in the new year, and he has offered to write documentation and hand over in December.

We also trialled a mobile survey app which volunteers use to collect data in the field, with photos. Forty-one volunteers installed it and 23 used it at least once. It produced 3,100 geotagged photos, of which 2,740 have been matched to features. The app's stability on older phones was criticised by 9 of the 23 users.

The online training module has six lessons (basic tracing, naming, tagging, working with imagery, accessibility records and the code of conduct) and takes about 90 minutes. Of the 44 contributors who completed it, 17 did so this quarter. Casimir's statistics show that contributors who completed the module had an error rate of 4.1 per cent in the audit sample, against 11.2 per cent for those who had not. The module has not been updated since last year and still describes the previous version of the editing software, which two reviewers say is confusing for beginners. Updating the screenshots and the second lesson would take a volunteer about three weekends.

7. Finance

The grant from the Tamsin Regional Trust is 28,000 pounds over 24 months, ending 31 March; we are now 18 months in. At the end of September we had spent 19,900 pounds, which is 71 per cent. The spending to date is shown below.

| Item | Spent | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Part-time coordinator (0.4 FTE) | 12,600 | 18 months at 700 |
| Tile server hosting | 1,540 | 18 months at about 85 |
| Mapathon venue, food and printing | 1,480 | Harrowick, 6 and 7 September |
| Training materials and videos | 1,120 | |
| Field survey app licence | 980 | Annual |
| Volunteer expenses (travel, equipment) | 1,630 | |
| Insurance | 550 | Annual |
| Total | 19,900 | |

The remaining 8,100 pounds is enough to fund the coordinator's post until 31 March at the present rate, which needs another 4,200 pounds for six more months. The expected remaining non-staff costs (hosting, insurance renewal and expenses) are about 2,700 pounds, so only about 1,200 pounds is left unallocated. That is not enough for a second mapathon, which cost 1,480 pounds, nor for more training, and the project has nothing to pay the coordinator after 31 March. A new funding application to the County Heritage Fund (up to 15,000 pounds) has been drafted but not submitted. The deadline is Friday 31 October.

8. Community and partners

Relations with the parish councils are good. The county council has given us access to its planning data on new buildings, which should help in keeping buildings up to date. We have approached the local bus operator about sharing timetable data, but have had no answer after two emails. A teacher at Harrowick School has asked whether pupils can contribute as part of a geography project in the spring term, which would add perhaps 60 new contributors and would need extra moderation.

9. Risks identified by the coordinator

R1. Loss of the only developer. Casimir Dunleavy is the sole maintainer of the review website, and the code has no written documentation. If he leaves before handover, the project loses its sample audit tool and the contributor statistics. Likelihood: medium. Impact: high.

R2. Funding cliff. The grant ends on 31 March and no other funding is yet secured. If the Heritage Fund application fails, the coordinator's post ends, and the project loses most of its organisation of events and training. Likelihood: medium. Impact: high.

R3. Quality drift. The error rate rose from 7.8 to 9.4 per cent while the number of new contributors grew. Without the second-pair-of-eyes review, the rate is likely to rise further when school pupils join in spring. Likelihood: high. Impact: medium.

R4. Community conflict. Two conduct incidents in one quarter, one of them driving a new contributor away, suggest that the code of conduct is not being applied consistently. The unresolved naming policy could provoke further conflict. Likelihood: high. Impact: medium.

R5. Infrastructure. The tile server runs on a single rented machine managed by one volunteer administrator. The next failure could again leave partner websites without a map. Likelihood: medium. Impact: medium.

10. Priorities proposed for next quarter

1. Introduce second-pair-of-eyes review for new contributors.
2. Agree a naming policy for villages in the upper valley.
3. Submit the County Heritage Fund application by 31 October.
4. Arrange the handover of the review website from Casimir.
5. Retain more of the mapathon participants through a follow-up evening in November.
6. Prepare for the new aerial imagery.

Our ferry company's booking database has got slow now that we have three seasons of data, and the operations dashboard queries take up to 40 seconds. Could you review the schema and tell me what is wrong with the design, which indexes we need and why, and then rewrite each of the seven queries so they are correct and fast, explaining every change? It is PostgreSQL 15 and the largest tables are bookings (about 2.1 million rows), booking_passengers (about 4.8 million) and sailing_events (about 9 million).

```sql
-- Schema for Skerryhold Ferries booking system

CREATE TABLE ports (
    port_id        SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    name           VARCHAR(80) NOT NULL,
    country_code   CHAR(2) NOT NULL,
    timezone       VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE vessels (
    vessel_id      SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    name           VARCHAR(80) NOT NULL,
    passenger_cap  INTEGER NOT NULL,
    vehicle_cap    INTEGER NOT NULL,
    cabins         INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    in_service     BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT TRUE
);

CREATE TABLE routes (
    route_id       SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    origin_port    INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES ports(port_id),
    dest_port      INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES ports(port_id),
    distance_nm    NUMERIC(6,1),
    typical_mins   INTEGER
);

CREATE TABLE sailings (
    sailing_id     SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    route_id       INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES routes(route_id),
    vessel_id      INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES vessels(vessel_id),
    departs_at     VARCHAR(25) NOT NULL,   -- stored as text, ISO format, e.g. 2025-07-14T09:30:00
    arrives_at     VARCHAR(25),
    status         VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'scheduled'
);

CREATE TABLE customers (
    customer_id    SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    email          VARCHAR(120),
    full_name      VARCHAR(120) NOT NULL,
    phone          VARCHAR(30),
    loyalty_tier   VARCHAR(10),
    created_at     TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE bookings (
    booking_id     SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id    INTEGER,
    sailing_id     INTEGER NOT NULL,
    booked_at      TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    status         VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,   -- confirmed, cancelled, refunded, standby
    total_pence    INTEGER NOT NULL,
    vehicle_plate  VARCHAR(12),
    vehicle_class  VARCHAR(10),
    cabin_id       INTEGER,
    promo_code     VARCHAR(20),
    notes          TEXT
);

CREATE TABLE booking_passengers (
    id             SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    booking_id     INTEGER NOT NULL,
    passenger_name VARCHAR(120) NOT NULL,
    age_band       VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL,   -- adult, child, infant
    fare_pence     INTEGER NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE payments (
    payment_id     SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    booking_id     INTEGER NOT NULL,
    amount_pence   INTEGER NOT NULL,
    method         VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    paid_at        TIMESTAMP,
    provider_ref   VARCHAR(60)
);

CREATE TABLE cabins (
    cabin_id       SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    vessel_id      INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES vessels(vessel_id),
    deck           INTEGER NOT NULL,
    cabin_number   VARCHAR(8) NOT NULL,
    berths         INTEGER NOT NULL,
    cabin_class    VARCHAR(12) NOT NULL    -- inside, outside, suite
);

CREATE TABLE sailing_events (
    event_id       BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    sailing_id     INTEGER NOT NULL,
    event_type     VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,   -- boarding_open, boarding_closed, departed, arrived, delayed, cancelled
    occurred_at    TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
    detail         JSONB
);

CREATE INDEX idx_bookings_customer ON bookings(customer_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_payments_booking ON payments(booking_id);
```

Notes on the data: `sailings.departs_at` is text for historic reasons (the original import came from a CSV); all values are in UTC and in the same ISO format. `bookings.status` can be confirmed, cancelled, refunded or standby. `sailing_events.detail` for a delayed event looks like `{"minutes_late": 25, "reason": "weather"}`. Ages: the `age_band` column holds adult, child or infant. A booking has one row in `booking_passengers` per traveller, and a driver counts as a passenger. About 4 per cent of bookings have no customer (customer_id is NULL) because they were made at the port desk.

The seven queries below are used by the operations dashboard and by the monthly report. Queries 1, 3 and 4 run on every dashboard refresh, which happens every 60 seconds.

```sql
-- Query 1: Today's sailings with passenger counts and load factor
SELECT s.sailing_id,
       r.origin_port,
       r.dest_port,
       s.departs_at,
       v.name AS vessel,
       (SELECT COUNT(*)
          FROM booking_passengers bp
          JOIN bookings b ON b.booking_id = bp.booking_id
         WHERE b.sailing_id = s.sailing_id
           AND b.status = 'confirmed') AS passengers,
       (SELECT COUNT(*)
          FROM booking_passengers bp
          JOIN bookings b ON b.booking_id = bp.booking_id
         WHERE b.sailing_id = s.sailing_id
           AND b.status = 'confirmed') * 100.0 / v.passenger_cap AS load_pct
FROM sailings s
JOIN routes r ON r.route_id = s.route_id
JOIN vessels v ON v.vessel_id = s.vessel_id
WHERE substring(s.departs_at, 1, 10) = to_char(now() AT TIME ZONE 'UTC', 'YYYY-MM-DD')
ORDER BY s.departs_at;

-- Query 2: Customers who have never made a confirmed booking
SELECT c.customer_id, c.full_name, c.email
FROM customers c
WHERE c.customer_id NOT IN (
    SELECT b.customer_id
    FROM bookings b
    WHERE b.status = 'confirmed'
);

-- Query 3: Delayed sailings in the last 24 hours with minutes late
SELECT s.sailing_id, s.departs_at, e.occurred_at,
       e.detail->>'minutes_late' AS minutes_late,
       e.detail->>'reason' AS reason
FROM sailing_events e
JOIN sailings s ON s.sailing_id = e.sailing_id
WHERE e.event_type = 'delayed'
  AND date_trunc('day', e.occurred_at) >= date_trunc('day', now() - interval '1 day')
ORDER BY (e.detail->>'minutes_late')::int DESC;

-- Query 4: Revenue by route for the current month, with refunds netted off
SELECT r.route_id,
       p1.name || ' to ' || p2.name AS route_name,
       SUM(b.total_pence) / 100.0 AS gross,
       SUM(CASE WHEN b.status = 'refunded' THEN b.total_pence ELSE 0 END) / 100.0 AS refunded,
       (SUM(b.total_pence) - SUM(CASE WHEN b.status = 'refunded' THEN b.total_pence ELSE 0 END)) / 100.0 AS net
FROM bookings b
JOIN sailings s ON s.sailing_id = b.sailing_id
JOIN routes r ON r.route_id = s.route_id
JOIN ports p1 ON p1.port_id = r.origin_port
JOIN ports p2 ON p2.port_id = r.dest_port
WHERE to_char(b.booked_at, 'YYYY-MM') = to_char(now(), 'YYYY-MM')
  AND b.status IN ('confirmed', 'refunded')
GROUP BY r.route_id, p1.name, p2.name
ORDER BY net DESC;

-- Query 5: Top 20 customers by spend in the last 12 months, with their most recent booking date
SELECT *
FROM (
    SELECT c.customer_id,
           c.full_name,
           c.loyalty_tier,
           SUM(b.total_pence) AS spend_pence,
           COUNT(DISTINCT b.booking_id) AS bookings,
           MAX(b.booked_at) AS last_booked
    FROM customers c, bookings b
    WHERE c.customer_id = b.customer_id
      AND b.status = 'confirmed'
      AND b.booked_at > now() - interval '12 months'
    GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.full_name, c.loyalty_tier
) t
ORDER BY spend_pence DESC
LIMIT 20;

-- Query 6: Cabin occupancy for sailings departing in the next 7 days
SELECT s.sailing_id,
       s.departs_at,
       v.name AS vessel,
       v.cabins AS total_cabins,
       (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT b.cabin_id)
          FROM bookings b
         WHERE b.sailing_id = s.sailing_id
           AND b.cabin_id IS NOT NULL
           AND b.status <> 'cancelled') AS cabins_taken,
       (SELECT string_agg(c.cabin_number, ', ')
          FROM cabins c
         WHERE c.vessel_id = s.vessel_id
           AND c.cabin_id NOT IN (SELECT b2.cabin_id
                                    FROM bookings b2
                                   WHERE b2.sailing_id = s.sailing_id
                                     AND b2.cabin_id IS NOT NULL
                                     AND b2.status <> 'cancelled')) AS free_cabin_numbers
FROM sailings s
JOIN vessels v ON v.vessel_id = s.vessel_id
WHERE s.departs_at::timestamp BETWEEN now() AND now() + interval '7 days'
  AND v.cabins > 0
ORDER BY s.departs_at;

-- Query 7: Passenger manifest for one sailing (parameter: sailing 48213)
SELECT bp.passenger_name,
       bp.age_band,
       b.booking_id,
       b.vehicle_plate,
       b.vehicle_class,
       c.full_name AS booked_by,
       c.phone,
       (SELECT SUM(p.amount_pence) FROM payments p WHERE p.booking_id = b.booking_id) AS paid_pence,
       b.total_pence
FROM bookings b
JOIN booking_passengers bp ON bp.booking_id = b.booking_id
LEFT JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = b.customer_id
WHERE b.sailing_id = 48213
  AND b.status IN ('confirmed', 'standby')
  AND UPPER(b.vehicle_plate) LIKE '%'
ORDER BY b.vehicle_plate, bp.age_band, bp.passenger_name;
```

Some more context that may matter. The passenger-count logic in Query 1 should include standby bookings only if they have been promoted to confirmed, and I believe that is how it works today. This is the beginning of a short story I've been writing for a regional writing competition (the limit is 6,000 words and I've used about 2,400). Please continue it at length, in the same voice and tense, taking it through the middle and to an ending, and keep the details I've set up (the keys, the stairwell light, the residents) so they pay off. I'd like it to stay quiet and a bit funny, nothing melodramatic.

THE KEYS TO NUMBER NINE

1.

Marguerite Fenwick-Allsop had worked for Hollin Court Housing Association for twenty-three years, and in all that time she had never once been afraid of a stairwell. She had been afraid of other things: of the regional director, who had a way of saying "just a quick one" before a meeting that was never quick; of the photocopier on the second floor, which jammed whenever she was in a hurry; and, on one memorable occasion, of a goose in the courtyard of the Alder Street block, which had taken against her coat. But stairwells she regarded as honest places. They went up, they went down, they smelled of whatever the people on each landing had cooked for dinner, and there was always someone's pushchair in the way.

So she was a little surprised, on the Tuesday in the third week of November, to find that she was standing at the foot of the north stairwell of Hollin Court with her hand on the banister and no real wish to go up.

It was ten minutes past four and already nearly dark. The light on the first landing was out. It had been out since the end of October, and there was a form about it, filled in by Mr Ignatius Pell from flat six and countersigned by three other residents, which she had sent to Maintenance on the fourth of November and which had come back on the eleventh with a stamp on it saying RECEIVED. This was the sort of thing that happened to forms. They were received, and then they were kept, like pressed flowers.

"It's only a light," she said, aloud, to nobody.

"It's only a light," agreed a voice from above, and a small torch came on and swung down the stairs towards her. Behind it was Mr Pell himself, in a long green anorak, holding the handrail with one hand and a plastic bag of what looked like turnips with the other. He was seventy-nine and had lived in Hollin Court since it was built. He regarded the building as a sort of ship, of which he was the first mate.

"I thought you'd come at four," he said. "It's gone ten past."

"I was held up by the Alder Street goose."

"Is it still there?"

"It's dead, Mr Pell. It was dead in the spring. I was held up by the memory of it."

Mr Pell considered this, and seemed to find it reasonable. He came down the last few steps and stood in front of her, a head shorter, with the torch pointed politely at the floor. "It isn't the light I wanted to show you," he said. "It's number nine."

2.

Number nine was on the second floor, at the end of the corridor, next to the fire door that never closed properly. It had been empty for eleven weeks. Its previous tenant, a retired piano tuner called Lazlo Brandt-Okafor, had gone into a care home in September with two suitcases and a cardboard box of sheet music, and had told everybody on the corridor, one by one, that he would be back by Christmas. Marguerite had not wanted to argue, and neither had anyone else. His daughter had signed the paperwork to end the tenancy, quite properly, on the twenty-eighth of September, and the keys had been handed in at the office. Marguerite knew this because she had put them in the key safe herself, in the grey metal cabinet by her desk, on a hook with a label in her own handwriting: NINE, HOLLIN CT, BRANDT-OKAFOR, RETURNED 28/9.

"I went past on Sunday," Mr Pell said, as they climbed. "And there was a smell of toast."

"Toast."

"Toast. And on Monday the corridor was warm. Not the radiators, they've been off on that side since the boiler man came. The door was warm."

"The door."

"I put my hand on it." He demonstrated, stopping on the landing and laying his palm against the air. "Like that. It was warm like a loaf of bread."

Marguerite had a small private rule, which she had developed over the years and never explained to anyone, which was that when a resident described a phenomenon she did not understand, she should not say what it was until she had looked at it. The alternative was to have two theories, hers and theirs, and to lose a great deal of time deciding which was right. Looking was quicker. So she followed Mr Pell up the second flight, where the light also did not work, and along the corridor, where the carpet gave a faint sigh underfoot, and stopped in front of the door of number nine.

It was a perfectly ordinary door. It was painted the municipal blue that the Association had bought in bulk in 2009, there was a brass numeral nine slightly crooked on it, and under the numeral someone had stuck a small yellow note which said, in capital letters, NO CIRCULARS PLEASE. That had been Lazlo's, of course. It had been there for years. She put her hand against the wood.

It was not warm.

"Well," said Mr Pell, a little deflated. "It was."

"It may have been the sun."

"On the north side?"

"It may have been a very determined sun." But she was already thinking about the other thing, which was that on the door frame, level with the lock, there was a thin bright scratch in the paint, the kind that a key makes when it is not quite aimed.

3.

She did not go in. That was one of the things she was proud of afterwards, when she told the story to her sister over the phone, and to the man at the garage, and eventually to the whole of the Thursday coffee morning. The Association's procedure for a void property (she was very clear about this) was that the housing officer might inspect it in the presence of a second member of staff, and that nobody, absolutely nobody, might enter it alone, because of an unpleasant incident in 2016 involving a wasp nest and a locum.

So she did the sensible thing. She went back downstairs, past the broken light, said goodnight to Mr Pell, who gave her a turnip for the road, and walked across the courtyard to the office, where the key safe was.

The office at Hollin Court was a converted ground-floor flat with a counter in what had been the living room and a kettle in what had been the airing cupboard. It was staffed from nine to four on weekdays by Marguerite, and on Tuesdays and Thursdays by an assistant called Bartholomew Osei-Lindqvist, who was twenty-four, wore a different pair of unusual socks every day, and had been with the Association for fourteen months, a record for the post. He was at his desk when she came in, eating a sandwich over a keyboard, which she had asked him not to do.

"Bartholomew. Number nine."

"Number nine," he said, swallowing, and then, with a look that she would later recognise as the look of a young man who had been hoping not to be asked, "what about it?"

"Where are the keys?"

"In the safe."

"Could you check?"

He went to the grey cabinet. He opened it. She watched his back, in a jumper with a hole in the elbow, and she saw it change; the shoulders went up, very slightly, in the way of a man who is counting hooks.

"Hook fourteen," he said. "It's, um. There's a label. But there's no."

"No keys."

"There's a key ring, but there's nothing on it. It's just the ring."

She came round the counter. It was true. The label said NINE, HOLLIN CT, BRANDT-OKAFOR, RETURNED 28/9 in her own handwriting, and the little steel ring hung beneath it, empty and a little bent, like the ear of a dog that has had a long day.

"When did you last see them?" she asked.

"I haven't ever seen them. I mean, I've seen the label." Bartholomew took a breath. "I did sign out a set on Friday, but that was for the Colne Street flat, and that's hook fifteen, and I might have, I mean it's possible that I took the wrong ring and put the Colne Street one back on fourteen and then, then the one I have here"

He stopped. He put his hand in his trouser pocket, a movement of such conscious innocence that Marguerite almost felt sorry for him, and brought out a ring of three keys on a plastic tag. The tag said COLNE ST 4.

"So those are Colne Street," she said.

"Yes."

"And where are the Colne Street keys?"

"On hook fifteen," said Bartholomew, with sudden, shining hope. They both turned to look. Hook fifteen, according to its label, belonged to FLAT 3, ALDER ST. It was holding a lanyard from a funeral directors' conference.

4.

It took them until a quarter to six to establish the facts, which were as follows. The Hollin Court office had four key safes, of which the grey cabinet was the only one used day to day; the others were in the cellar, under the stairs, in a cupboard that had been locked since before Bartholomew's time. The grey cabinet had sixty hooks and fifty-one labelled sets. Of the fifty-one, forty-eight were present and correct. The missing three were number nine, Hollin Court; the Colne Street flat, which Bartholomew was carrying around like a talisman; and, to Marguerite's mild alarm, the master set, which opened the fire doors, the plant room and the roof.

"The master set," said Bartholomew. "That's, that's the one thing you're not supposed to"

"Yes."

"Who has access to the office?"

She thought about it. "Me. You. The regional director, once a quarter, to say it looks tidy. The cleaner on Wednesdays. The man who checks the extinguishers. Mr Pell has the spare office key, on account of the thing with the boiler last winter." She paused, and the pause was a long one. "And anyone who has ever borrowed a pen from the counter while the kettle was on."

Outside it had begun to rain, softly and persistently, in the way of November rain that has no particular argument with anyone. The courtyard lamp came on. In its yellow circle she could see the bicycle shed, and the bins, and the edge of the north stairwell, and above it, on the second floor, the row of windows that belonged to the corridor of number nine. All dark but one. She counted the windows twice to be sure. The last one, at the end, next to the fire door, had a light on, a low and amber light, like a lamp in a window at the end of a street.

"Bartholomew," she said, "would you mind very much putting your coat on?"

"We're not going in," he said. "Are we? You said nobody goes in alone."

"I said nobody goes in alone." She was already reaching for her own coat, and the torch from the drawer. "We are two people, and Mr Pell makes three. I think it is the sort of evening that calls for a second member of staff, and a turnip."

5.

Mr Pell was waiting at the foot of the stairs when they came back across the courtyard, as though he had never gone home at all. He had taken off the green anorak and put on a cardigan, and he had brought a second torch, larger than the first, and a walking stick that Marguerite had never seen him use.

"Window," he said, pointing upwards.

"We saw."

"It's been on since about half past three. I thought, she'll want to see that."

"You might have said, Mr Pell."

"I did say. I said toast." He looked, for the first time that afternoon, faintly wounded, and she was sorry. Behind him, in the dark of the stairwell, the broken light on the first landing gave a small electric tick, as if it were thinking of recovering, and then thought better of it.

They went up in a line: Mr Pell first, because he knew where the loose tread was; Bartholomew in the middle, holding the Colne Street keys in front of him like a hymn book; Marguerite last, with her phone in her pocket and her thumb, for no reason she could have defended, resting on the number of the regional director. The stairwell smelled of damp coats and somebody's cabbage. On the second floor the corridor lay ahead of them, long and carpeted, with the fire door at the end propped open an inch by a folded leaflet. There was, she noticed, a line of amber at the bottom of the door of number nine.

"Warm," whispered Mr Pell, as they came level with it.

It was not warm. She put the back of her hand against the blue paint to be sure, and it was cool and slightly gritty, like any door. But there was a sound from behind it, very low, which none of them had heard from the stairs. It was one note, held, then another, a little higher, and a third. It took her a moment to place, because it was nothing she had heard in twenty-three years of void inspections, and then Mr Pell said, in the voice of a man naming a bird, "That's a tuning fork."

"It can't be."

"Lazlo had one. He used to strike it on his knee." Mr Pell's face in the torchlight had gone soft and stubborn at once. "He said he could never sleep in a place where the room was out of tune."

Marguerite looked at the scratch on the door frame and the empty ring on hook fourteen, and at the yellow note that said NO CIRCULARS PLEASE. She thought of the care home on the Sallow Road, which she had visited once, and of a man who had told every person on the corridor that he would be home for Christmas. She raised her hand, and found, to her slight annoyance, that it was not quite steady.

"Mr Osei-Lindqvist," she said, "you have the Colne Street keys."

"Yes."

"They won't open this door."

"No."

"Then I think," said Marguerite, "that we had better knock."

Below is our Q3 operations review for the Kelderwick Container Terminal. I have to present it to the board on Thursday and I would like a section-by-section summary I can read out loud, followed by your recommendations for what we should do in Q4 and in what order. Please point out anything in the numbers that does not add up or that the board is likely to ask about.

---

KELDERWICK CONTAINER TERMINAL
Quarterly Operations Review, Q3 (1 July to 30 September)
Prepared by: Operations Planning Office (author: Marit Oosterhuis, Head of Planning)
Distribution: Board of Directors, Terminal Management Team, Harbour Authority liaison
Status: Final

1. Executive summary

Kelderwick handled 412,600 TEU in the third quarter, which is 6.1 percent above the same quarter last year (388,900 TEU) and 2.4 percent above our budget of 402,900 TEU. Vessel calls totalled 311, against 298 a year ago. The average gross crane productivity across the quarter was 27.8 moves per hour per crane, up from 26.1 in Q2 but still below the contractual target of 30 that we committed to in the Meridian Line service agreement.

Three events shaped the quarter. First, the commissioning of the two new ship-to-shore cranes (STS 7 and STS 8) was completed on 19 August, six weeks later than planned. Second, a software fault in the terminal operating system on 2 September caused a gate outage of 5 hours and 40 minutes and a yard planning freeze of about three hours. Third, the strike at the regional rail operator from 22 to 26 September forced us to shift 3,180 TEU of planned rail departures to road, which in turn produced the worst truck queues we have recorded this year.

Revenue for the quarter was 38.4 million euros, 4.9 percent above budget. Operating cost was 29.7 million euros, 7.2 percent above budget, so operating profit came in at 8.7 million euros against a budget of 9.0 million. The shortfall is almost entirely explained by overtime, one-off commissioning costs, and the extra trucking subsidy we paid during the rail strike. Lost-time injuries rose from one in Q2 to three in Q3, which is the item the Management Team regards as most serious.

2. Volumes and vessel calls

Container volumes by trade lane are shown below. All figures are in TEU, import plus export plus transhipment, with empty containers included.

| Trade lane | Q3 this year | Q3 last year | Change | Share of total |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| North Europe feeder | 121,400 | 118,200 | +2.7% | 29.4% |
| Mediterranean | 78,900 | 70,100 | +12.6% | 19.1% |
| West Africa | 54,300 | 49,800 | +9.0% | 13.2% |
| Transatlantic | 92,700 | 91,500 | +1.3% | 22.5% |
| Asia (via hub transhipment) | 65,300 | 59,300 | +10.1% | 15.8% |
| Total | 412,600 | 388,900 | +6.1% | 100.0% |

The growth in the Mediterranean lane comes from the new weekly service operated by Meridian Line that started in late June. The West Africa growth is mostly empty repositioning, and we should not read it as a lasting change in demand. Transhipment accounted for 61,800 TEU, or 15.0 percent of the total, which is slightly lower than the 16.3 percent of last year because two feeder loops were consolidated by their carriers in July.

Of the 311 vessel calls, 87 were of vessels longer than 300 metres, compared with 71 last year. Average call size rose from 1,305 TEU to 1,327 TEU. The number of calls that started more than two hours after their scheduled berthing window was 64, or 20.6 percent. Twenty-three of these delays were caused by late arrival of the vessel itself, 19 by our own berth being occupied by an overrunning call, and 22 by weather, mainly fog in the first half of September and a strong northwesterly wind on 14 and 15 August.

3. Berth and crane performance

The terminal has three berths with a combined quay length of 1,150 metres. Berth occupancy averaged 68 percent, with a peak of 91 percent in the week of 8 September when three large vessels arrived within 30 hours of each other.

Crane productivity by month:

| Month | Gross moves per crane hour | Net moves per crane hour | Crane availability |
|---|---|---|---|
| July | 26.9 | 31.2 | 94.1% |
| August | 27.5 | 32.0 | 91.3% |
| September | 29.0 | 33.4 | 95.6% |
| Quarter | 27.8 | 32.1 | 93.7% |

August availability was reduced by the commissioning work on STS 7 and STS 8, and by a spreader fault on STS 3 that took the crane out of service for four days. September was the best month we have had since the terminal opened its third berth, and the Planning Office attributes this to the new cranes being fully in service and to the revised stowage planning rules introduced on 1 September, which limit the number of consecutive moves in the same bay.

The gap between gross and net productivity is the main reason we remain below the contractual target of 30. Net productivity of 32.1 is above the target, but the contract is written on gross productivity, which counts waiting time for hatch covers, lashing, and vessel-side delays. Roughly 40 percent of the gap is lashing time. We have asked Meridian Line to discuss whether the contract metric can be changed to a berth-window measure, but they have not yet responded.

4. Yard and equipment

The yard holds 31,500 TEU in ground slots. Average yard utilisation was 74 percent, with a peak of 93 percent on 24 September, during the rail strike. When utilisation passes 85 percent, the number of unproductive reshuffles per hundred moves rises sharply. In Q3 reshuffles averaged 11.2 per hundred moves, against 9.8 in Q2. In the week of the rail strike the figure reached 17.4.

Dwell time of import containers averaged 4.6 days (Q2: 4.1 days). Export dwell was 3.2 days. The increase in import dwell is partly explained by customs inspections, which rose by 18 percent following a new risk profile applied by the national customs authority in August, and partly by the rail strike.

Equipment status at the end of the quarter:

- Rubber-tyred gantry cranes: 24 in fleet, 21 available on average. Two units are due for the major overhaul in Q4.
- Terminal tractors: 36 in fleet. Fifteen are more than ten years old and account for 58 percent of unplanned breakdowns.
- Reach stackers: 6 in fleet, all available, used mostly for the empty depot.
- Straddle carriers: none. The terminal uses a tractor and trailer system.

Fuel consumption per move fell by 3.5 percent, which is the first fall in six quarters. The main reason is the electric conversion of eight RTG cranes completed in the spring, and we expect a further fall once the remaining 16 cranes are converted.

5. Gate and landside operations

The gate processed 188,400 truck transactions, an average of 2,048 per day. The average truck turnaround time inside the terminal was 41 minutes, compared with 36 minutes in Q2. The share of trucks that finished within 45 minutes was 71 percent against a target of 85 percent. The pre-booking system for truck slots covered 63 percent of the volume, up from 55 percent.

The gate outage on 2 September began at 06:12 and lasted until 11:52. It was caused by a database lock in the terminal operating system that appeared after a patch was installed on the night of 1 September. The vendor has confirmed that the patch was not tested against our configuration of the gate module. During the outage 410 trucks queued on the access road and, after 45 minutes, the queue reached the public road, which led to a complaint from the municipality. We had no written fallback procedure for manual gate processing; staff improvised with paper lists, which is why the recovery took more than an hour after the system was restored.

During the rail strike, the rail share of landside transport fell from 31 percent to 9 percent for five days. We used 14 additional trucking contractors and paid a subsidy of 38 euros per container to keep export cargo moving. Total subsidy cost was 121,000 euros. Average truck waiting time outside the gate peaked at 118 minutes on 24 September.

6. Safety and environment

Three lost-time injuries occurred, compared with one in Q2 and two in Q3 last year. The total recordable injury frequency rate was 4.1 per million hours worked, against 3.2 in the previous quarter.

- 14 July: a lasher fell from a vessel hatch cover while working on a wet surface. Fractured wrist, 38 days lost.
- 3 September: a tractor driver was struck by a swinging door while handling a damaged container. Back strain, 12 days lost. This happened during the gate outage recovery, when drivers were working extended shifts.
- 20 September: a stevedore twisted his knee after stepping off a twistlock stacking platform. 21 days lost.

Two of the three incidents occurred during or just after periods of high overtime. Average overtime per operational employee rose to 14.6 hours per month, from 9.1 in Q2. Near-miss reports numbered 96, an increase of 31 percent, which the Safety Manager reads as a sign of better reporting rather than greater danger.

Environmental indicators were stable. Shore power connections were used by 17 vessel calls, below the target of 30 for the quarter, because only one berth is equipped and because carriers cite the cost of connection. Noise complaints from the neighbouring Oosterstrand housing area numbered 9, against 14 in Q3 last year, mostly relating to night-time crane alarms.

7. People and staffing

The terminal employs 612 people, of whom 438 are operational. Voluntary turnover over the last twelve months is 11.4 percent. Eleven crane operators left during the quarter, mainly to a competing terminal that offered a retention bonus. We recruited nine operators and have 14 in training, but a newly trained operator takes about eight months to reach full productivity. Sickness absence was 5.8 percent, higher than the 4.9 percent of Q2, with a noticeable rise among night-shift employees.

The labour agreement with the port workers' union expires on 31 March. Opening talks are planned for early December. The union has already signalled that it will ask for a limit on overtime and for a shorter roster cycle.

8. Finance

| Item (million euros) | Actual | Budget | Variance |
|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | 38.4 | 36.6 | +1.8 |
| Personnel cost | 14.9 | 13.8 | -1.1 |
| Equipment and maintenance | 6.2 | 5.9 | -0.3 |
| Energy and fuel | 3.1 | 3.0 | -0.1 |
| Subcontracted trucking and services | 2.9 | 1.9 | -1.0 |
| Commissioning one-offs | 1.2 | 0.0 | -1.2 |
| Other operating cost | 1.4 | 1.3 | -0.1 |
| Total operating cost | 29.7 | 27.7 | -2.0 |
| Operating profit | 8.7 | 9.0 | -0.3 |

Note that the sum of the cost lines above is 29.7 and the budgeted cost lines sum to 27.9 rather than 27.7; the Finance Department has been asked to confirm which figure is correct before the board meeting. Capital expenditure in the quarter was 11.3 million euros, of which 8.4 million related to STS 7 and STS 8 and 1.7 million to the RTG electrification programme. The balance on the port authority's concession fee was paid on schedule.

9. Customer feedback

The customer survey was sent to 41 shipping lines and 120 hauliers. The response rates were 59 percent and 33 percent. Shipping lines gave an average score of 7.4 out of 10 (Q2: 7.1), citing improved crane productivity in September but criticising schedule reliability. Hauliers gave 5.9 (Q2: 6.6), with 71 percent of comments about waiting time at the gate. Two shipping lines, including Meridian Line, have asked for a written recovery plan on berth windows before renewing in the new year.

10. Outlook and proposals for Q4

The Planning Office expects Q4 volume of 405,000 to 420,000 TEU, with the usual increase before the winter holidays in the first half of December. The following items are proposed for management attention:

1. Write and test a manual gate fallback procedure and require the vendor to run patches in a test environment that mirrors our gate configuration. Estimated cost 60,000 euros.
2. Raise the pre-booking share of truck slots from 63 percent to at least 80 percent by introducing a late-arrival charge in January.
3. Begin replacing the oldest 15 terminal tractors, starting with six units in Q4. Estimated cost 1.1 million euros for six units.
4. Introduce a cap on voluntary overtime of 12 hours per month per operator and recruit 20 additional lashers.
5. Negotiate with the rail operator for a guaranteed minimum capacity of 20 percent of volume during strikes, and set up a standing agreement with trucking contractors for surge capacity.
6. Extend shore power to the second berth. The Harbour Authority has offered a grant of 40 percent of the 2.6 million euro cost, subject to a decision by 15 November.
7. Prepare the position for the labour negotiations beginning in December.

Marit Oosterhuis
Head of Planning, Kelderwick Container Terminal

HOLLOWAY & SIMS JOINERY, MEETING NOTES
Date: Tuesday 14 October, 07:30 to 09:10, in the workshop canteen
Present: Gerda Holloway (owner, chairing), Anselm Sims (co-owner, production), Bridie Callaghan (sales and showroom), Dov Rahimi (finishing shop lead), Katya Brzezinski (purchasing and stock), Lowell Nwosu (workshop apprentice, taking notes for the first time, apologies for gaps), Hester Quill (bookkeeper, joined for item 4 only)
Apologies: Tomasz Ferreira (CNC operator, on holiday until 20 October)

ITEM 1. Showroom move

Background for Lowell: the landlord of the town centre showroom on Cutler Street has given notice that the lease ends on 31 January. Gerda found a unit on the Brindle Lane industrial estate, 340 square metres, next to the workshop, which means the showroom would be a two minute walk from the production floor. Rent is lower (2,150 a month against 3,400 on Cutler Street) but there is no passing trade.

Bridie said that passing trade is about 30 percent of showroom sales, from what she has counted over the last year, but she admitted she counts by asking customers how they found us and not everybody answers. The other 70 percent are appointments, repeat customers, and architects. She thinks an appointment-only showroom works if we put money into the website and a proper booking calendar. Anselm worried that people who just walk in at Cutler Street are the ones who buy a 600 euro chair and then come back for a 4,000 euro table.

Gerda said the decision is made, the lease is not renewable and the new unit is the only one that suits us. The question is how to do it without closing for more than ten days. Agreed that the target opening date at Brindle Lane is Saturday 7 February. Agreed that Cutler Street stays open until 24 January and the last week is a clearance sale.

The new unit needs work before we can use it: the landlord will paint and fix the roof lights by 15 December (confirmed by email last Thursday, according to Gerda). We have to install lighting, partition walls for three room sets, a reception desk, and a small meeting area. Dov suggested we build the reception desk and the shelves ourselves in the workshop in November, as they can be a display of our own work. Anselm said he can spare the bench time only if the dining range prototypes (item 2) do not slip.

Quote from the electrician for lighting and sockets: 6,800 euros, valid until 31 October. Gerda wants a second quote. Katya will ask her contact Wilmot Electrics, who did the workshop extraction.

Action: Gerda to get the signed lease for Brindle Lane back from the solicitor. Bridie to draft the layout plan for the three room sets by 31 October. Katya to get second electrical quote by 24 October.

ITEM 2. New dining range, "Orchard" collection

The Orchard range is a dining table (extending, seats six to ten), six dining chairs, a sideboard and a bench. Anselm showed the first drawings. Material is European oak, with an optional ash version for the chairs. The target price for the 180 centimetre table is 2,450 euros, and the chair 340 euros. The competitor we compared to is selling a similar table at 2,900 euros, but it is veneer, not solid.

Production: Tomasz is the only one trained to run the CNC router for the chair legs and the table leaf mechanism. He is back on 20 October. Anselm wants to make two prototypes of each item before committing to a first batch of 12 tables and 72 chairs. Prototype deadline: 28 November. First batch goal: ready for the showroom opening on 7 February, but Anselm said this is "very tight, maybe not realistic" because the oak for the first batch has to be air-dried for at least four weeks after planing, and Katya's supplier has only given a delivery date of 17 November for the first load.

Dov asked about finishing. The range will use a hard wax oil and not lacquer, which means each table takes about 3 days between coats, and a spraying booth is not needed. He estimates 11 working days to finish a batch of 12 tables if he works alone, but he would need Lowell to help with sanding. Anselm agreed that Lowell can be moved to finishing for two weeks in January.

Katya raised that the extending mechanism hardware (a German-made runner, 78 euros a set) has a lead time of nine weeks. If we order now it arrives by mid-December. If we wait for prototype approval it arrives in late January, which would make the first batch impossible. Gerda decided: order hardware for 14 tables now (1,092 euros), and accept the risk of changing it if the prototype fails. Hester later confirmed this is within the monthly purchasing limit.

Action: Katya to order runners for 14 tables this week. Anselm to finalise drawings by 24 October. Tomasz to start chair leg prototypes on 21 October. Dov to test three finish samples on offcuts by 7 November.

ITEM 3. Orders in hand and the autumn backlog

Anselm reported the current backlog: 23 open orders, worth about 71,000 euros, of which 9 are kitchens or built-in wardrobes that need fitting on site. The oldest is the Marlowe wardrobe promised for 10 October, now late. He said the delay was due to a wrong hinge delivery. He believes two more orders will be late by a week or so.

Bridie asked whether we should take on a temporary fitter for November and December. Anselm said yes. Cost about 2,600 euros a month for a freelance fitter. Gerda to decide.

Expected costs for the move and Orchard together: electrician 6,800, partition walls 4,500, showroom fixtures and furniture from our own stock at cost 3,000, signage 1,900, website and booking system 2,400, removal costs 1,800, double rent for January (Cutler Street 3,400 plus Brindle Lane 2,150) of which the Brindle Lane part is already counted as a normal expense, Orchard materials for the prototypes and first batch about 21,000, hardware 1,092, temporary fitter about 5,200 for two months.

Gerda asked Hester to prepare a month by month cash forecast from now to the end of March by Friday 24 October. Hester said she needs the order list with expected payment dates from Anselm and Bridie.

Anselm noticed that the 43,000 figure and the sum of the items were not obviously the same. Hester said she was doing it in her head and will check it. Bridie said the product photos on the website are four years old and half of the products shown are no longer made. A photographer, Imke Danvers, quoted 1,600 euros for a day of photography at the workshop, covering about 25 items, plus 400 euros for the Orchard range once finished. Bridie proposed that the clearance sale run from Saturday 17 January to Saturday 24 January, with floor models and ex-display pieces reduced by 20 to 40 percent depending on age. We run a chain of eleven bakeries (Crumb & Ember) on a PostgreSQL database that I inherited from a contractor. The reports on the head office dashboard are getting slow and the numbers sometimes disagree between reports. Could you review the schema design, say which indexes we are missing or which ones are useless, and rewrite each of the seven queries at the bottom so that they are correct and faster? Please explain every change you make and why.

```sql
-- Crumb & Ember: operational database (PostgreSQL 15)

CREATE TABLE shops (
    shop_id        serial PRIMARY KEY,
    name           text NOT NULL,
    city           text NOT NULL,
    opened_on      date NOT NULL,
    has_cafe       boolean DEFAULT false,
    manager_name   text
);

CREATE TABLE products (
    product_id     serial PRIMARY KEY,
    sku            text NOT NULL,
    name           text NOT NULL,
    category       text NOT NULL,          -- 'bread', 'pastry', 'cake', 'drink', 'sandwich'
    unit_price     numeric(8,2) NOT NULL,
    unit_cost      numeric(8,2),
    is_active      boolean DEFAULT true,
    shelf_life_hours integer
);

CREATE TABLE ingredients (
    ingredient_id  serial PRIMARY KEY,
    name           text NOT NULL,
    unit           text NOT NULL,          -- 'kg', 'l', 'each'
    supplier_id    integer,
    cost_per_unit  numeric(8,3)
);

CREATE TABLE recipes (
    recipe_id      serial PRIMARY KEY,
    product_id     integer NOT NULL REFERENCES products(product_id),
    ingredient_id  integer NOT NULL REFERENCES ingredients(ingredient_id),
    quantity       numeric(8,3) NOT NULL    -- per batch of 12 units
);

CREATE TABLE suppliers (
    supplier_id    serial PRIMARY KEY,
    name           text NOT NULL,
    contact_email  text,
    payment_days   integer DEFAULT 30
);

CREATE TABLE customers (
    customer_id    serial PRIMARY KEY,
    loyalty_number text,
    first_name     text,
    last_name      text,
    email          text,
    joined_on      date,
    home_shop_id   integer REFERENCES shops(shop_id)
);

CREATE TABLE sales (
    sale_id        bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
    shop_id        integer NOT NULL REFERENCES shops(shop_id),
    customer_id    integer REFERENCES customers(customer_id),
    sold_at        timestamp NOT NULL,
    payment_method text NOT NULL,          -- 'card', 'cash', 'app'
    total_amount   numeric(10,2) NOT NULL,
    discount_code  text
);

CREATE TABLE sale_items (
    sale_item_id   bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
    sale_id        bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES sales(sale_id),
    product_id     integer NOT NULL REFERENCES products(product_id),
    quantity       integer NOT NULL,
    unit_price     numeric(8,2) NOT NULL,
    line_discount  numeric(8,2) DEFAULT 0
);

CREATE TABLE production_batches (
    batch_id       bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
    shop_id        integer NOT NULL REFERENCES shops(shop_id),
    product_id     integer NOT NULL REFERENCES products(product_id),
    baked_at       timestamp NOT NULL,
    units_baked    integer NOT NULL,
    baker_name     text
);

CREATE TABLE waste_log (
    waste_id       bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
    shop_id        integer NOT NULL REFERENCES shops(shop_id),
    product_id     integer NOT NULL REFERENCES products(product_id),
    logged_at      timestamp NOT NULL,
    units_wasted   integer NOT NULL,
    reason         text                    -- 'unsold', 'burnt', 'dropped', 'expired', 'other'
);

CREATE TABLE ingredient_deliveries (
    delivery_id    bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
    shop_id        integer NOT NULL REFERENCES shops(shop_id),
    ingredient_id  integer NOT NULL REFERENCES ingredients(ingredient_id),
    delivered_on   date NOT NULL,
    quantity       numeric(10,3) NOT NULL,
    invoice_total  numeric(10,2)
);

CREATE TABLE staff_shifts (
    shift_id       bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
    shop_id        integer NOT NULL REFERENCES shops(shop_id),
    employee_name  text NOT NULL,
    role           text NOT NULL,          -- 'baker', 'counter', 'cafe', 'manager'
    shift_start    timestamp NOT NULL,
    shift_end      timestamp NOT NULL,
    hourly_rate    numeric(6,2) NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE discount_codes (
    code           text PRIMARY KEY,
    description    text,
    percent_off    numeric(5,2),
    valid_from     date,
    valid_to       date
);

CREATE TABLE shop_targets (
    shop_id        integer REFERENCES shops(shop_id),
    month_start    date,
    revenue_target numeric(12,2),
    labour_budget  numeric(12,2)
);

-- Indexes created so far
CREATE INDEX idx_sales_shop ON sales (shop_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_sales_customer ON sales (customer_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_sales_sold_at ON sales (sold_at);
CREATE INDEX idx_sales_total ON sales (total_amount);
CREATE INDEX idx_sale_items_sale ON sale_items (sale_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_waste_shop ON waste_log (shop_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_batches_shop ON production_batches (shop_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_customers_email ON customers (email);
CREATE INDEX idx_products_name ON products (name);
CREATE INDEX idx_products_category ON products (category);

-- Approximate row counts today
--   shops                11
--   products             214
--   ingredients          168
--   recipes              1,340
--   customers            86,000
--   sales                9.4 million (about 14,000 a day, growing)
--   sale_items           27 million
--   production_batches   410,000
--   waste_log            880,000
--   ingredient_deliveries 96,000
--   staff_shifts         190,000
--   discount_codes       64
--   shop_targets         about 130 (one row per shop per month)

-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------
-- QUERY 1: daily revenue per shop for last month (head office dashboard)
-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------
SELECT s.name,
       DATE(sa.sold_at) AS day,
       SUM(sa.total_amount) AS revenue,
       COUNT(*) AS receipts
FROM sales sa
JOIN shops s ON s.shop_id = sa.shop_id
JOIN sale_items si ON si.sale_id = sa.sale_id
WHERE sa.sold_at >= date_trunc('month', now()) - interval '1 month'
  AND sa.sold_at <  date_trunc('month', now())
GROUP BY s.name, DATE(sa.sold_at)
ORDER BY s.name, day;

-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------
-- QUERY 2: top 20 products by gross margin in the last 90 days
-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------
SELECT p.name,
       SUM(si.quantity) AS units,
       SUM(si.quantity * (si.unit_price - p.unit_cost)) AS margin
FROM sale_items si
JOIN products p ON p.product_id = si.product_id
JOIN sales sa ON sa.sale_id = si.sale_id
WHERE sa.sold_at > now() - interval '90 days'
GROUP BY p.name
ORDER BY margin DESC
LIMIT 20;

-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------
-- QUERY 3: waste rate per shop and category for last week
-- Waste rate = units wasted / units baked
-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------
SELECT s.name AS shop,
       p.category,
       SUM(w.units_wasted) AS wasted,
       SUM(b.units_baked) AS baked,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(w.units_wasted) / SUM(b.units_baked), 1) AS waste_pct
FROM shops s
JOIN waste_log w ON w.shop_id = s.shop_id
JOIN products p ON p.product_id = w.product_id
JOIN production_batches b ON b.shop_id = s.shop_id
                         AND b.product_id = p.product_id
WHERE w.logged_at >= current_date - 7
  AND b.baked_at >= current_date - 7
GROUP BY s.name, p.category
ORDER BY waste_pct DESC;

-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------
-- QUERY 4: loyalty customers who have not bought anything for 60 days
-- but spent more than 200 in the 12 months before that
-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------
SELECT c.customer_id, c.first_name, c.last_name, c.email
FROM customers c
WHERE c.loyalty_number IS NOT NULL
  AND c.customer_id NOT IN (
        SELECT customer_id FROM sales
        WHERE sold_at > now() - interval '60 days'
  )
  AND (
        SELECT SUM(total_amount) FROM sales s2
        WHERE s2.customer_id = c.customer_id
          AND s2.sold_at > now() - interval '14 months'
  ) > 200
ORDER BY c.last_name;

-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------
-- QUERY 5: ingredient cost per batch of each product, and the share
-- of the unit price that the ingredients represent
-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------
SELECT p.name,
       SUM(r.quantity * i.cost_per_unit) AS batch_cost,
       SUM(r.quantity * i.cost_per_unit) / 12 AS unit_cost_calc,
       p.unit_price,
       ROUND(100 * (SUM(r.quantity * i.cost_per_unit) / 12) / p.unit_price) AS pct_of_price
FROM products p
LEFT JOIN recipes r ON r.product_id = p.product_id
LEFT JOIN ingredients i ON i.ingredient_id = r.ingredient_id
WHERE p.is_active
GROUP BY p.product_id, p.name, p.unit_price
ORDER BY pct_of_price DESC;

-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------
-- QUERY 6: labour cost against revenue for each shop and week, with the
-- monthly target from shop_targets, for the last 8 weeks
-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------
SELECT s.name,
       date_trunc('week', st.shift_start) AS week,
       SUM(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (st.shift_end - st.shift_start)) / 3600 * st.hourly_rate) AS labour_cost,
       SUM(sa.total_amount) AS revenue,
       t.revenue_target
FROM shops s
JOIN staff_shifts st ON st.shop_id = s.shop_id
JOIN sales sa ON sa.shop_id = s.shop_id
             AND date_trunc('week', sa.sold_at) = date_trunc('week', st.shift_start)
LEFT JOIN shop_targets t ON t.shop_id = s.shop_id
                        AND t.month_start = date_trunc('month', st.shift_start)
WHERE st.shift_start >= now() - interval '8 weeks'
GROUP BY s.name, date_trunc('week', st.shift_start), t.revenue_target
ORDER BY s.name, week;

-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------
-- QUERY 7: use of discount codes last quarter: how many receipts used each
-- code, the revenue on them, and the average basket compared to receipts
-- without a code, only for codes that exist in discount_codes
-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------
SELECT d.code,
       d.description,
       COUNT(sa.sale_id) AS receipts,
       SUM(sa.total_amount) AS revenue,
       AVG(sa.total_amount) AS avg_basket,
       (SELECT AVG(total_amount) FROM sales
         WHERE discount_code IS NULL
           AND sold_at >= date_trunc('quarter', now()) - interval '3 months'
           AND sold_at <  date_trunc('quarter', now())) AS avg_basket_no_code
FROM discount_codes d
LEFT JOIN sales sa ON UPPER(sa.discount_code) = d.code
WHERE sa.sold_at >= date_trunc('quarter', now()) - interval '3 months'
  AND sa.sold_at <  date_trunc('quarter', now())
GROUP BY d.code, d.description
ORDER BY receipts DESC;
```

Some context for the review. The dashboard runs queries 1 and 2 each morning at about 07:00 and they take around a minute and a half now; query 3 is run by the head baker on Mondays and its numbers look much too high for some shops, which I could not explain. Query 4 feeds an email campaign. Query 5 is used when we decide on prices. Queries 6 and 7 are run by the finance manager on the first working day of the month, and she has told me that the labour percentage for some shops looks absurdly high. We are on a single managed PostgreSQL instance with 16 GB of memory, and we do not want to introduce a separate data warehouse unless you think it is really needed. We would like to keep the application's inserts fast, since the tills write a sale every few seconds at busy times. Please also tell us if any of the column types or constraints should change, for instance anything that could let bad data in.

Our volunteer mountain rescue team wants to replace the phone tree and spreadsheets we use for call-outs, and I wrote the design document below. Could you give me an honest critique (what is weak, missing or risky), suggest at least two alternative approaches to the main design choices, and then write an implementation plan with phases, effort estimates and what to do first? I am the only developer and the rest of the team are not technical, so keep that in mind.
