DESIGN DOCUMENT: CALLOUT (Call-out Coordination Tool)
Team: Stonecrest Mountain Rescue (volunteer, 38 active members, covers the Stonecrest massif and the two valleys on either side)
Author: Ingvar Tallis (deputy team leader, volunteer developer)
Status: Draft 2, for review by the team committee
Date: 12 October

1. Background and problem

When the police or the ambulance service request our help, the duty controller (one of five members who rotate weekly) currently starts a phone tree. They call the first six members on a list, each of whom calls two more. Members answer whether they can attend, and the controller writes down who is coming on a printed sheet. Last winter we measured the time from the request to the point where the controller knew that at least eight people were on the way. The median was 27 minutes and the worst case was 51 minutes. On three of the 44 call-outs last year the controller reached the end of the list with fewer than eight confirmed members, and had to ask the neighbouring team for help.

Other problems we have observed:

- Nobody knows during a call-out who is already on the hill, where they are, and when they are expected to return. Team members text the controller, who writes it down.
- Equipment (stretchers, ropes, the two vehicles, the drone) is tracked in a spreadsheet that is out of date after every incident.
- Post-incident reports are written from memory a week later.
- Qualification records (first aid renewals, avalanche course, driving licence for the vehicles) are kept by the training officer in a different spreadsheet. Twice last year a member who had an expired first aid certificate was sent on a call-out.

2. Goals

1. Reduce the time to eight confirmed members to under ten minutes at the median.
2. Give the controller a live view of who is responding, who is on the hill, and who is back.
3. Keep a simple record of each incident that can be turned into the post-incident report.
4. Warn the controller about members whose qualifications are out of date.
5. Keep running costs below 40 euros a month, because we are funded by donations.

3. Non-goals

- Replacing the radio system. We will continue to use handheld radios and the repeater on Eaglesmouth Ridge.
- Casualty medical records. These stay on the paper forms agreed with the ambulance service.
- Public-facing features. The tool is for the team only.

4. Proposed solution

4.1 Overview

Callout has three parts: a web application used by the controller on a laptop, a phone application used by team members (installed as a progressive web app so that we do not have to publish in app stores), and a small server that holds the data and sends messages.

4.2 Alerting

When the controller creates a call-out in the web application, the server sends a push notification to all active members and, at the same time, a text message through an SMS gateway to members who have not opened the notification within 90 seconds. A member responds with one of three buttons: "Coming", "Not available", or "Coming, 30 minutes". The text message contains a link with a one-time token, which opens the same response page without logging in. If a member has not responded after four minutes, the controller sees them highlighted in red and can call them.

The SMS gateway costs about 0.06 euros per message. With 38 members and an estimated 50 call-outs a year, with roughly a third of the members needing a text message, the estimated cost is 38 euros a year in messages plus the gateway's monthly fee of 5 euros.

4.3 The controller's board

The web application shows a board with four columns: Alerted, Responding, On the hill, Returned. Each member appears as a card that moves automatically as their status changes. Members change their own status from the phone application: tapping "On the hill" shares the last known position of the phone. During the call-out the phone sends its position every two minutes while there is mobile coverage and stores positions when there is no coverage, sending them when coverage returns.

The board also shows a count of members with each qualification needed, for example "Casualty carer: 3 of 5 needed" and "Vehicle driver: 2 of 2 needed", based on the responses.

4.4 Qualifications

Each member record has a list of qualifications with expiry dates. The server checks them every night and sends a message to the training officer 60 days and 14 days before an expiry. On the board, a member whose first aid certificate has expired is shown with a warning label, but can still respond. The controller decides.

4.5 Equipment

The equipment list is a simple table: item, location, status (available, in use, needs repair), and last checked date. A call-out records which items were taken. When the call-out is closed, the controller or quartermaster confirms that each item has returned.

4.6 Incident record

During a call-out the controller keeps a timeline by typing short entries (for example "14:32 casualty located at grid ref NY 3512 2398"). Entries are timestamped automatically. When the call-out closes, the tool produces a document with the timeline, the list of members, equipment used and total person-hours. The team leader completes it with the narrative.

4.7 Overdue and welfare checks

When a member taps "On the hill", the controller sets an expected return time for the group (default: four hours). Fifteen minutes before that time the board marks the group amber, and at the expected time it marks them red and plays a sound on the controller's laptop. The controller can extend the time with one click. The tool does not contact anyone automatically at this stage; the controller tries the radio first, then the phone. A later version might send an automatic message to the group leader, but the author prefers not to build that until the team has used the first version in a real incident.

4.8 Handover between controllers

Controllers rotate weekly, but a long call-out can outlast one person's availability. The controller can hand the board over to another controller by choosing a name from a list. The new controller receives a notification and must accept; until then the previous controller keeps control. All timeline entries show who wrote them. Only one controller can edit the board at a time, and others see it read-only.

5. Architecture

5.1 Offline behaviour and synchronisation

The phone application stores the member's own responses and positions in the browser's local database. Each stored item has a random identifier created on the phone and a timestamp from the phone's clock. When coverage returns, the application sends the stored items to the server in the order they were recorded; the server ignores any item whose identifier it has already seen. If a phone's clock is wrong by more than five minutes, the server marks the item with a warning but still stores it. The web application for the controller does not work offline; it needs a connection to the server.

5.2 Interfaces

The server offers a small set of HTTP endpoints, of which the most important are: creating a call-out, listing the current roster, posting a response, posting a batch of positions, adding a timeline entry, and closing a call-out. The board receives updates by a long-lived connection so that cards move without the page being reloaded. If the connection drops, the page reconnects and asks for the full state.

5.3 Components

- The server is a Node.js application using a PostgreSQL database, hosted on a single virtual server from a European provider at 12 euros a month.
- The web application and phone application share one codebase written in a JavaScript framework. The phone application is a progressive web app with a service worker for offline storage.
- Authentication is by email magic link for the controller and phone app. Each member has a phone number and email.
- Push notifications use the browser's web push standard. SMS goes through a third-party gateway.
- Backups: a nightly database dump copied to a storage bucket at a second provider.

6. Data model (summary)

- members: id, name, phone, email, role, active flag
- qualifications: member id, type, issued date, expiry date
- callouts: id, created at, requested by, location text, grid reference, status
- responses: callout id, member id, status, timestamp
- positions: callout id, member id, latitude, longitude, recorded at
- equipment: id, name, location, status, last checked
- equipment use: callout id, equipment id, taken at, returned at
- timeline entries: callout id, timestamp, text, author id

7. Security and privacy

Location data is personal data. We store positions only during a call-out and delete detailed positions after 90 days, keeping only the start and end points for each member. Access to the board is limited to the five controllers and the two team leaders. Members can see only their own record and the current call-out roster. The server is accessed over HTTPS only. We have not yet appointed a person responsible for data protection; the committee needs to decide who.

8. Reliability

Our area has poor mobile coverage in the upper parts of the valleys, and this is where the call-outs happen. The design assumes that members are mostly in coverage when they receive the alert (at home or at work) and that coverage on the hill matters only for positions. The server runs on one machine; if the machine is down, controllers will fall back on the phone tree, which will be kept up to date through a weekly export of the member list to a PDF that each controller keeps on their phone.

9. Rollout

The author proposes to build the first version over the winter, run it in parallel with the phone tree from March to June, and decide in July whether to switch. A trial in a training exercise would take place in April.

10. Cost

| Item | Cost |
|---|---|
| Virtual server | 12 euros a month |
| SMS gateway fee and messages | about 8 euros a month on average |
| Backup storage | 2 euros a month |
| Domain name | 15 euros a year |
| Total | about 23 euros a month |

The author's time is volunteered.

11. Open questions

- Who maintains the tool if the author leaves the team?
- Do we need a second controller screen at the base for the team leader?
- Should members be able to see each other's positions, or only the controller?
- How do we handle members who do not have a smartphone? There are four, and all are over 65 and valued members.
- Should the tool talk to the police system that sends us the call-out requests, which arrive by email and by a phone call?

12. Risks identified by the author

- Alert fatigue: if every small request triggers a full alert, members will stop responding.
- A false sense of confidence: the board shows only what members tap, and the controller may assume the board is the truth.
- The author is a single point of failure.
- Push notifications on some phones are delayed when the phone is in power saving mode.

13. Alternatives considered by the author

- Use a commercial group messaging service and a shared spreadsheet. This would be cheaper and faster to set up, but it gives no board, no qualification warnings and no incident record, and would leave member phone numbers with a third party.
- Buy a call-out product used by other rescue teams. The author found one product at 480 euros a month for teams of our size, which is 20 times our budget.
- Do nothing and train the controllers to run the phone tree faster. The training officer prefers this and points out that the tool will not help if the repeater fails.

14. Testing

The author plans automated tests for the server logic (status changes, roster counts, qualification warnings and the synchronisation of stored items), manual tests on four different phones including two old ones, and a training exercise in April in which 20 members receive an alert at an unannounced time. Success is defined as eight confirmed members within ten minutes in at least four of five exercises.

15. Decisions requested from the committee

1. Approval to start the build, with the cost in section 10.
2. A named person to be responsible for data protection.
3. Agreement on the parallel running period, March to June.
4. Agreement that members without smartphones will be called by the controller as at present.

16. Data migration and member onboarding

The current member list is a spreadsheet with 52 rows, of which 38 are active members; the others are former members and associate members who help with fundraising. Only the 38 active members will be imported. The training officer's qualifications spreadsheet has 214 rows and uses free text for the qualification names ("FA", "First Aid at Work", "first aid 3 day"), so the author will map these by hand to six fixed types: first aid, casualty care, avalanche awareness, rope rescue, vehicle driver and radio operator. The import will be run twice, once as a dry run that lists every row it could not understand, which the training officer corrects before the real import.

Each member will receive a message with a link to install the phone application and confirm their phone number. Members who do not confirm within two weeks will be listed for the team leader. The author will hold two drop-in evenings at the base, on 5 and 12 February, where members can bring their phones and be helped to install it, allow notifications and turn off battery saving for the application.

17. Proposed schedule

| Period | Work |
|---|---|
| Late October to November | Data model, member import, alerting and responses |
| December | Controller board, offline phone behaviour, synchronisation |
| January | Qualifications, equipment, incident record, backups |
| February | Onboarding evenings, internal testing with five members |
| March to June | Parallel running with the phone tree |
| April | Unannounced training exercise |
| July | Committee decision on switching over |

The author estimates 8 to 10 hours a week of his own time, with the first working version in late December if nothing else takes priority. He notes that this estimate does not allow for the winter peak in call-outs, when his time is likely to be shorter.

HEAT SUPPLY AGREEMENT FOR RESIDENTIAL CUSTOMERS
Version 4.2, effective 1 September

I have been asked to referee the manuscript below for a music education journal. It is the methods and results part of a study done in a youth orchestra. Please write a detailed peer review: a summary of what the authors claim, an assessment of the design and the statistics, specific numbered concerns (including any numbers that do not agree with each other), what additional analyses or information you would ask for, and a recommendation on whether to publish.

---

PEER MENTORING IN SECTIONAL REHEARSALS AND ITS ASSOCIATION WITH SIGHT-READING PROGRESS AND ATTENDANCE IN A REGIONAL YOUTH ORCHESTRA

Manuscript submitted to the Journal of Ensemble Music Education. Sections 3 and 4 only (Methods; Results). The Introduction, Discussion and References are provided separately.

3. METHODS

3.1 Setting and participants

The study took place in the Alderbank Youth Orchestra, a regional ensemble that rehearses on Saturday mornings during three school terms and admits players aged 11 to 18 by audition. In the autumn term of the study year the orchestra had 74 registered players: 31 violins, 9 violas, 8 cellos, 4 double basses, 8 woodwind, 9 brass and 5 percussion. Players were grouped into a senior orchestra (grades 6 to 8, 41 players) and a junior orchestra (grades 4 to 5, 33 players). Participation in the study was voluntary; written consent was obtained from players and, for those under 16, from a parent. Seventy of the 74 players (94.6 percent) consented. The remaining four, all in the junior orchestra, were excluded from analysis but took part in rehearsals as normal.

The mean age of the 70 participants was 14.2 years (standard deviation 2.1). Forty-one participants identified as girls, 27 as boys and 2 as another gender or preferred not to say. The median number of years of instrumental study was 5 (range 2 to 10).

3.2 Design

We used a non-randomised comparison with a waiting-list element. The junior and senior orchestras had separate conductors and rehearsal rooms. In the first half of the school year (autumn and spring terms; 22 rehearsals), the senior orchestra used a peer mentoring structure in sectional rehearsals and the junior orchestra continued its usual practice. In the summer term (10 rehearsals), the junior orchestra adopted peer mentoring. We therefore have two periods. In Period 1 the senior orchestra is the intervention group and the junior orchestra is the comparison group. In Period 2 both groups use peer mentoring.

The assignment of orchestras to conditions was made by the music director, on the grounds that the senior orchestra's section leaders were more experienced and better suited to mentoring. We acknowledge that this is a limitation.

3.3 Intervention

In the peer mentoring structure, each 90-minute rehearsal included a 30-minute sectional in which each string and wind section was divided into groups of three or four players. Each group contained one mentor (a player from the upper half of the section by audition rank) and two or three mentees. Mentors were trained in two 60-minute workshops by the first author before the start of the term. Mentors were asked to (a) work with the group on the hardest passage of the week's repertoire, (b) model one sight-reading strategy per rehearsal (for example, scanning for key signature changes and rhythmic hazards before playing), and (c) record, on a one-page form, which strategy was used and how many bars the group read through. Groups were reassigned every four rehearsals. Conductors did not attend the sectionals.

The comparison condition consisted of 30 minutes of sectional work led by the conductor or an assistant tutor with the whole section together, at the discretion of the tutor.

3.4 Measures

Sight-reading. At the first rehearsal (T0), at the end of the autumn term (T1, after 11 rehearsals), at the end of the spring term (T2, after 22 rehearsals), and at the end of the summer term (T3, after 32 rehearsals), each player sight-read a short unseen excerpt, which was recorded and scored by two raters who were blind to condition and time point. Excerpts were composed by the second author at the player's grade level and varied in key and metre across time points. Scoring used a 40-point rubric (pitch accuracy 15, rhythm accuracy 15, continuity and tempo 10). Inter-rater agreement was assessed on a random subset of 56 recordings (20 percent of all) and was ICC(2,1) = 0.88 for the total score.

Attendance. Attendance was recorded by section leaders at the start of each rehearsal. Each player's attendance rate was the proportion of rehearsals attended in the period.

Self-efficacy. At T0 and T2 players completed an 8-item questionnaire on confidence in reading new music (five-point scale; Cronbach's alpha = 0.84 at T0 and 0.86 at T2).

Practice time. Players reported weekly practice minutes on the same questionnaires; these are self-reported and we report them as descriptive only.

3.5 Analysis

For sight-reading scores we fitted linear mixed models with random intercepts for players and fixed effects of time (T0 to T2), group (senior or junior) and the group by time interaction, with age and years of study as covariates. The primary outcome was the group by time interaction for T0 to T2. Attendance was compared with a Mann-Whitney U test because the distribution was skewed. Self-efficacy was compared with independent-samples t-tests on change scores. For Period 2 we describe the change in the junior orchestra from T2 to T3 using paired t-tests. We did not adjust for multiple comparisons. The significance level was set at 0.05. Analyses were performed in R.

Missing data. Players who left the orchestra during the year (n = 3 in the senior orchestra, n = 2 in the junior orchestra) were included in the models using the time points they completed. Players who were absent at a test session (n = 6 across all sessions) were not given a make-up test.

3.6 Ethics and data

The study was approved by the ethics committee of the authors' institution (reference 2024-117). The orchestra's management agreed that results would be reported without identifying individual players. Scores were stored under anonymous codes. Rehearsal attendance and audition rank were supplied by the orchestra's administrator and linked by code.

4. RESULTS

4.1 Participant flow and baseline

Of 70 participants, 41 were in the senior orchestra and 29 in the junior orchestra. Table 1 shows baseline values.

Table 1. Baseline characteristics (mean, standard deviation)

| Measure | Senior (n = 41) | Junior (n = 29) |
|---|---|---|
| Age (years) | 15.9 (1.4) | 11.9 (0.9) |
| Years of study | 6.8 (1.9) | 3.4 (1.1) |
| Sight-reading score at T0 (of 40) | 24.6 (5.2) | 15.8 (4.7) |
| Self-efficacy at T0 (of 5) | 3.6 (0.7) | 2.9 (0.8) |
| Weekly practice (minutes, self-report) | 212 (84) | 138 (61) |

Seniors were older, had studied for longer and scored higher at baseline on every measure. All differences were significant at p < 0.001 (details omitted).

4.2 Sight-reading

Table 2 shows the mean scores at each time point.

Table 2. Sight-reading score (mean, standard deviation; maximum 40)

| Time point | Senior | Junior |
|---|---|---|
| T0 | 24.6 (5.2) | 15.8 (4.7) |
| T1 | 27.9 (5.0) | 17.2 (4.9) |
| T2 | 30.3 (4.8) | 18.0 (5.1) |
| T3 | 31.0 (4.9) | 21.4 (5.0) |

Over T0 to T2, the senior orchestra improved by 5.7 points and the junior orchestra by 2.2 points. In the mixed model, the group by time interaction was significant (estimate = 3.5 points, 95 percent CI 1.9 to 5.1, p < 0.001). We interpret this as evidence that peer mentoring accelerated sight-reading progress. From T2 to T3, the junior orchestra improved by 3.4 points (paired t(26) = 4.1, p < 0.001) during the term in which it adopted peer mentoring, whereas the senior orchestra, which continued the structure, improved by 0.7 points (paired t(37) = 1.3, p = 0.20). The improvement in the junior orchestra during Period 2 was larger than the improvement during Period 1 (3.4 points over one term versus 2.2 points over two terms), which supports the conclusion that the intervention is effective.

Subgroup analysis by section: among string players the senior-junior interaction was 3.9 points (p < 0.001) and among wind and brass players it was 2.4 points (p = 0.09, n = 17 in the two groups combined). We interpret the smaller effect in winds and brass as reflecting the lower number of mentors with strong sight-reading skills in those sections.

4.3 Attendance

Mean attendance in Period 1 was 91.3 percent in the senior orchestra (median 95.5, interquartile range 86.4 to 100) and 84.7 percent in the junior orchestra (median 90.9, interquartile range 77.3 to 95.5). The difference was significant (U = 412, p = 0.012). In the junior orchestra, attendance rose from 84.7 percent in Period 1 to 90.2 percent in Period 2 (p = 0.03). The senior orchestra's attendance in Period 2 was 90.6 percent, essentially unchanged.

4.4 Self-efficacy

Self-efficacy in reading new music rose by 0.7 points in the senior orchestra (from 3.6 to 4.3) and by 0.2 points in the junior orchestra (from 2.9 to 3.1) between T0 and T2. The difference in change scores was significant (t(66) = 3.2, p = 0.002).

4.5 Practice time

Self-reported weekly practice was 212 minutes in the senior orchestra at T0 and 245 minutes at T2; in the junior orchestra it was 138 at T0 and 141 at T2. We did not test these differences formally.

4.6 Mentor effects

Among the 12 senior players who acted as mentors in at least eight rehearsals, the improvement in their own sight-reading score from T0 to T2 was 7.1 points, compared with 5.0 points for the 29 senior players who were mentees only. The difference was significant (p = 0.04). The mentors' scores at baseline (26.9) were higher than the non-mentors' (23.7).

4.7 Mentor strategy logs

The mentor forms were completed for 71 percent of sectionals. The most frequently recorded strategy was scanning for key signature and accidentals (38 percent of logged sectionals), followed by clapping rhythms first (27 percent), and counting through rests (14 percent). The mean number of bars read per sectional was 46 (standard deviation 21). There was no association between the number of logged bars and the player's improvement (r = 0.11).

4.8 Adverse observations

Two junior players and one senior player told the conductors that they felt anxious about being corrected by their peers. In the spring term, one section leader in the senior orchestra reported that two mentees had stopped attending sectionals. These observations were not part of a systematic survey.

4.9 Robustness checks

Because the groups differed so much at baseline, we repeated the primary analysis in a subsample of 28 senior and 29 junior players matched on baseline sight-reading score within three points. The group by time interaction in this subsample was 2.6 points (95 percent CI 0.7 to 4.5, p = 0.008). Excluding the five players who left the orchestra gave an interaction of 3.7 points (p < 0.001). Adding the number of rehearsals attended as a covariate reduced the interaction to 2.9 points (p = 0.004). We also repeated the analysis using only the pitch accuracy subscore and only the rhythm subscore; the interactions were 1.4 points (p = 0.006) and 1.2 points (p = 0.03) respectively, and 0.9 points (p = 0.01) for the continuity subscore.

The raters' mean scores differed slightly: rater A scored 0.8 points higher than rater B on average. We analysed the mean of the two raters. When only rater A's scores were used the interaction was 3.6 points, and when only rater B's scores were used it was 3.3 points.

4.10 Summary of effects

Table 3. Summary of between-group differences in change, T0 to T2

| Outcome | Senior change | Junior change | Difference | p |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sight-reading (points of 40) | +5.7 | +2.2 | 3.5 | < 0.001 |
| Self-efficacy (points of 5) | +0.7 | +0.2 | 0.5 | 0.002 |
| Self-reported practice (minutes per week) | +33 | +3 | 30 | not tested |

Attendance is not included in Table 3 because it was measured only as a level in each period and not at T0.

THE COLD CHAIN

Chapter One

At ten past eleven the loading dock at Pellam & Voss Pharmaceutical Wholesale was lit like an operating theatre and about as warm. Ingrid Haldane stood at the edge of it with her hands in the sleeves of her fleece and watched the last lorry of the evening reverse towards the bay, the beeping of it going up and down the long grey wall of the warehouse like a bird that had learned one note.

She had been the night supervisor for nine years. Before that she had been a picker, and before that a girl who had left school at sixteen and stood in the doorway of this same building asking whether they needed anyone, and a man whose name she had forgotten had said, Can you count? and she had said yes, and that had been the interview. The building had changed since then. The old brick end was now offices and a canteen that smelled of soup. The new end, which had gone up in the year her mother died, was the cold store: forty thousand square feet of racking kept at between two and eight degrees, and inside it, a room within the room, the freezer vault where the vaccines slept.

Behind her, in the glass cabin that everyone called the aquarium, Dessa was eating a sandwich over her keyboard with the care of someone defusing something.

"Fourteen pallets on this one," Dessa said, without looking up. "Eight are Mercer's insulin, four are the eye drops for the hospital group, and two are the usual mess."

"Which mess?"

"It says miscellaneous. It says do not stack."

Ingrid went down the three steps to the dock level. The lorry's doors opened with the drawn-out sigh that big doors make, and the driver, a thin man with a beard the colour of wet sand, climbed down the side with a clipboard like it was a hymn book. His name badge said Corwin. He did not look at her. He looked at the thermometer by the door, the one that Pellam & Voss had bolted to the dock wall in her second year as supervisor, and he said, "Is that right? It says eleven."

"It says eleven because it's eleven degrees on the dock," Ingrid said. "That's why we are very quick. How long has your load been on the road?"

"Left the depot at four. Eight hours with the stops. The reefer unit was reading five all the way."

"Reading," said Ingrid. This was the thing she had learned in nine years. The unit on the lorry read five. It did not say what the pallets read.

They unloaded the way they always did, in a rhythm that nobody had designed: Teodoro on the electric pallet truck, Wren and Ash with the scanners, Oyelaran from the night team ticking each line against the manifest and calling it out in a voice that had never once been raised. Ingrid held the temperature probe. She slid it between the cartons of the first pallet and watched the number settle. 4.2. The second: 4.6. The third: 4.4. At the sixth, the number would not settle. It climbed to 7.8, hovered, and went to 8.3.

"Stop," she said.

Teodoro held the truck in the air, forks raised, the pallet hanging like an exhibit. Nobody spoke. Ingrid removed the probe and put it in again, in a different carton, then a third, and found 8.1, 8.4, 8.2.

"That is the insulin," Dessa said from the dock edge. She had come out after all, the sandwich in a paper napkin. "That is Mercer's. That is the hospital order for Thursday."

"I know what it is."

Insulin that had been above eight degrees for some unknown time was not a catastrophe, she knew; there was a table for it, there were stability data, there were the men at Mercer's who would be asked and would say what they were asked to say. But it was a decision, and decisions were made in the morning by the Responsible Person, whose name was Halvard Pryce, who did not come in before seven-thirty. It was twelve minutes to midnight and there was a pallet in the air and a driver with a clipboard looking at her as though she were going to tell him that he was a murderer or a hero.

"Put it in the quarantine bay," she said. "Cage it and tag it red. Don't open it. Scan the rest as normal, and probe every single pallet, not one in three."

"That's another hour," Wren said.

"Then it's another hour."

Corwin lowered his clipboard. "Is this going to say it was my fault?"

"It's going to say what the probe said," Ingrid told him. "That's all anyone can do."

By one o'clock the lorry was empty. By a quarter past one she had probed all fourteen pallets and found that eight were fine, four were fine, and of the two marked miscellaneous, one was fine and one was not on the manifest at all. She stood in front of it with the scanner and the scanner gave her a long, low, offended tone.

"Dessa," she said into the radio. "Fourteen pallets on the manifest."

"Fourteen on the manifest."

"I have fifteen on the floor."

There was a pause, in which she could hear Dessa swallowing something. "Then it's not ours," Dessa said.

Ingrid looked at the extra pallet. It was wrapped in grey film that gave back her own reflection, bent. There was a white label with a number but no name. No barcode. The cartons beneath the film had no printing on them at all, only a stripe of blue tape across each lid, and when she put the probe against the film, the number settled almost at once, as though it had been waiting for her: 2.0.

Two degrees. The coldest thing on the dock.

Chapter Two

She did not tell Halvard Pryce about the extra pallet, though she told herself that she would, and that the delay was only because the right moment had not yet come. The right moment was the problem. At seven-thirty Pryce arrived in a good coat, with a coffee in a paper cup and the walk of a man for whom problems were things that happened to other people's departments, and she found him in the doorway of his office and reported the insulin. He listened with his head slightly inclined, the way a doctor does, and then said, "Brought in at eight degrees. For how long?"

"I don't know. The lorry's log says five. The probe says eight on six of the fourteen."

"Not on all of them?"

"No. On six. The ones at the back, nearest the doors."

He was quiet. "The doors," he said, "are the problem."

"They're always the problem."

"Then it's a transport deviation, and not ours." He wrote on a pad, the way he wrote on everything, in small square capitals. "Quarantine stays. I'll ring Mercer's and request the stability data and we will see what they say. Send the driver's log to me. And Ingrid, well done on the probe. A lot of people would have let it through."

She thought about the fifteenth pallet, behind the red cage, behind a second, smaller cage she had made out of two pallet collars and a sheet of plywood and put in the corner where the camera did not quite reach. She thought about the blue tape. She said, "Thank you," and went home.

Home was a flat above a launderette on Sorrel Street, two rooms and a kitchen, a bed she had not made since Sunday and a radiator that clanked as though someone were trying to get out of it. She slept until two in the afternoon with a towel over her eyes, and when she woke her mother's old clock on the shelf said a quarter past three, and her phone said that Dessa had called four times.

She rang back. Dessa picked up on the first ring and did not say hello.

"It's gone."

"What's gone?"

"Your pallet. The one that wasn't on the manifest. I came in early to do the quarantine log and went to look at it, because you made me curious, and the little cage is empty. The plywood's still there. The collars are there. The pallet is gone."

Ingrid sat on the edge of the bed, still in last night's clothes. "Who was on the day shift?"

"Everyone. Anyone. It's forty thousand square feet, Ingrid. A pallet truck could take it out the side door and no one would see." Dessa lowered her voice. "I looked at the camera. The camera on the dock. You know that one has a blind corner."

"I know about the corner."

"Between six and ten past seven this morning, the dock camera shows nobody. Then it shows somebody at ten past, walking into frame with a hand truck. I can't see the face. The coat is the good coat."

"The good coat."

"I'm not saying anything," said Dessa. "I'm saying I'm describing a coat."

Ingrid looked at the radiator. It clanked twice, as if offering an opinion. She thought of Halvard Pryce in his doorway with his small square capitals, saying well done on the probe, saying a lot of people would have let it through. She thought about being a girl in a doorway, and a man she could not name asking whether she could count.

"Don't tell anyone you rang me," she said. "I'm coming in. I'll be there at nine, an hour early, before the others arrive. I want to see the log of every door sensor from six to eight."

"The door logs are in the system. The system is Pryce's."

"The system is a database, Dessa. Databases are only secret for as long as nobody asks the right clerk."

She did not leave at once. She sat for a while with her hands between her knees, and then she did what she had not done since the funeral, which was to open the bottom drawer of the shelf under the clock. Her mother's things were in it: a tin of buttons, a pair of reading glasses with one arm mended with tape, and an envelope of photographs. The top one was of the cold store on the day it opened, forty men and women in white coats on the new concrete, a ribbon, a man with scissors. Her mother had been the second from the left, squinting. She had worked in the old brick end for twenty-two years and had been given a coat and a place in the picture because someone in management had wanted it to look like a family.

"They keep a record of everything," her mother used to say, "and they only read the records they like."

Ingrid put the photograph back and shut the drawer. She dressed in the dark, which was how she had dressed for nine years, and went down the stairs.

In the launderette below, the owner, Mr. Abara, who was folding sheets at the counter with a boy's patience and an old man's hands, called to her without turning round. "Miss Haldane. There was a man here asking about you this morning. A man in a good coat."

She stopped at the door. "What did he want?"

"To know if you lived upstairs. I said I could not give out information about my tenants. He said he understood, he was a colleague, he only wanted to leave something for you." Mr. Abara turned at last. In his hands he held a sealed white envelope, the kind that come in boxes of five hundred. "I said I would pass it on. I did not like the way he said it. He smiled with only the front of his face."

She took the envelope. It weighed nothing. On the front, in small square capitals, someone had written her name, and she knew the handwriting at once, and put it in the inside pocket of her fleece unopened, against her ribs, where it stayed all the way to the bus stop like a second pulse.

It had begun to rain in the way that it rains in November, without any drama, as if the sky had run out of ideas. The bus came and smelled of wet wool and oranges. She sat at the back and counted the stops, because she could count, because that was what they had asked her, and because it was easier than thinking about what she would do if the log said what she was afraid it would say.

At the warehouse the car park was nearly empty. The rain had made the building look as if it had been lowered into water. She badged through the side door, up the stairs, past the canteen with its smell of soup, and found the data room unlocked and the light on and a stranger sitting at the terminal in her chair. The stranger was a young woman in a navy jacket with a lanyard Ingrid did not recognise, and a laptop connected to the server by a thin blue cable.

"Oh," said the young woman. "Hi. You must be Ingrid. I'm Nyoka, from the audit team at head office. Mr. Pryce said you would be in at ten. He said you might have some questions about the temperature excursion." She smiled in a friendly, practised way. "I've pulled all the sensor data for the last forty-eight hours. I thought I'd save you the trouble."

Ingrid stood very still in the doorway. On the screen behind Nyoka, in a grid of small grey rectangles, she could see the door sensors for the cold store, row on row, every one of them showing a flat green line. Every one of them, for the whole of the last forty-eight hours, perfectly normal.

"That's helpful," she said. "Thank you."

"Not at all." Nyoka turned back to her screen. "Strange, isn't it? A reading of eight degrees on the lorry pallets, and then not a flicker in any of your own sensors. It's almost as though the building doesn't know."

"Almost," said Ingrid.

# Product Specification: Job Intake and Assignment ("Relay 2.3")

Owner: Hanne Vestergaard (Head of Operations), Draft 4, status: approved for build
Reviewers: Tomasz Brandt (Lead Project Manager), Ines Okafor (Vendor Management), Ravi Chaudhary (Engineering)
Company: Meridian Wordworks, a translation and localisation agency with 14 staff and a pool of about 220 freelance linguists

## 1. Purpose

Today, new translation jobs reach us by email, through a web form, or by phone, and project managers (PMs) copy the details into the job board by hand. Assignment to a freelancer is done through a shared spreadsheet and a chain of emails. This causes duplicate jobs, missed deadlines and unclear ownership. Relay 2.3 replaces both steps with one flow: a job is created once, scored against the freelancer pool, offered to the best candidates in order, and tracked until delivery.

The release does not change invoicing, the client portal login, or the terminology database. Those stay as they are in Relay 2.2.

## 2. Users and roles

- **Client contact**: an employee of a customer company. Can submit jobs through the client portal and see the status of their own company's jobs only.
- **PM**: Meridian staff member who owns jobs. Can create, edit, cancel and reassign jobs, and can see every job.
- **Vendor manager**: Meridian staff member who maintains freelancer profiles, rates and availability. Cannot edit jobs.
- **Freelancer**: an external linguist. Can see only the offers sent to them and the jobs they have accepted.
- **Admin**: Meridian staff member with configuration rights (scoring weights, holiday calendar, languages list).

## 3. Job record

A job has the following fields. Fields marked * are required at submission.

| Field | Type | Rules |
|---|---|---|
| Title* | text | 3 to 120 characters |
| Client company* | reference | Must be an active client |
| Source language* | list | One of the configured languages |
| Target languages* | multi-select | 1 to 8 languages, none equal to the source |
| Service type* | list | Translation, Translation plus review, Review only, Transcreation, Subtitling |
| Word count* | integer | 1 to 250,000. For subtitling, replaced by duration in minutes (1 to 600) |
| Subject area* | list | Legal, Medical, Technical, Marketing, Finance, General |
| Deadline* | date and time | Must be at least 4 working hours after submission, in the client's time zone |
| Files | upload | Up to 20 files, 50 MB each, formats DOCX, XLSX, PPTX, PDF, SRT, TXT, IDML |
| Reference material | upload | Same limits, optional |
| Notes to linguist | text | Up to 2,000 characters |
| Priority | list | Normal (default) or Rush. Rush is set automatically when the deadline is less than 24 working hours away |
| Confidentiality | list | Standard or Restricted |

A job gets a reference number in the form MW-YYYY-NNNNN, assigned at creation and never reused. Numbering restarts at 00001 on the first of January.

### 3.1 Working hours and deadlines

Working hours are 08:00 to 18:00, Monday to Friday, in the time zone of the client. Public holidays come from the holiday calendar configured by an admin for each country. A "working hour" in any rule below means an hour that falls inside these rules. The deadline check at submission counts working hours between the submission time and the deadline.

If a client submits a job outside working hours, the clock for the four-hour minimum starts at the next opening time. The job record stores the deadline exactly as entered and also stores the deadline converted to UTC.

## 4. Submission channels

### 4.1 Client portal

The client contact fills in the form. The form validates every field on the page before submit. On success the contact sees the reference number and receives a confirmation email within two minutes. Files are scanned for malware; if a file fails the scan the job is not created and the contact sees which file was rejected.

### 4.2 Email intake

Clients can send a request to the intake address of their account (for example intake-northvale@example.org). The system creates a draft job, not a live job. A PM must open the draft, complete the missing required fields and press Publish. Attachments in allowed formats are added to the draft. The email subject becomes the title, truncated to 120 characters. Drafts older than 7 days are deleted automatically, and the PM who owns the account is notified two days before deletion.

An email from an address that does not match any contact of an active client is placed in a quarantine list visible to PMs and is never turned into a draft automatically.

### 4.3 Manual creation

A PM can create a job directly, on behalf of a client. The job is marked "Created by PM" and the PM's name is stored. A PM can duplicate an earlier job; the duplicate gets a new reference number, copies all fields except deadline, files and status, and requires a new deadline.

## 5. Duplicate detection

When a job is submitted or published, the system compares it with all jobs of the same client created in the last 14 days. A job is flagged as a possible duplicate when the file name list is identical, or when title, source language and word count all match exactly. A flagged job is held in the state "Needs check" and a PM must either confirm it as new or merge it into the earlier job. Merging adds any extra target languages to the earlier job and deletes the new record, keeping a log entry. Confirming removes the flag and the job continues.

## 6. Scoring and offers

### 6.1 Eligibility

A freelancer is eligible for a job and target language when all of these hold:

1. The freelancer has the language pair on their profile and the profile status is Active.
2. The freelancer has the subject area on their profile, except for General, which every freelancer with the pair has.
3. The freelancer has marked themselves available for the whole period between expected start and deadline, with at least the needed hours free. Needed hours are computed as word count divided by 350 words per hour for translation, 900 for review, and 250 for transcreation.
4. If the job is Restricted, the freelancer has a signed confidentiality agreement on file that has not expired.
5. The freelancer is not on the client's exclusion list.

### 6.2 Score

Each eligible freelancer receives a score from 0 to 100 made of four parts with weights set by an admin. The default weights are:

- Quality rating: 40 (average of the last 10 reviewed jobs, scaled from the 1 to 5 scale to 0 to 40)
- On-time rate: 30 (share of the last 20 jobs delivered before the deadline)
- Rate fit: 20 (full marks if the freelancer's per-word rate is at or below the client's budget rate, falling linearly to zero at 50 percent above it)
- Familiarity: 10 (10 if the freelancer has done at least 3 jobs for this client in the last 12 months, 5 for 1 or 2, otherwise 0)

The weights must add up to 100. The settings page rejects a save where they do not. A freelancer with fewer than 5 reviewed jobs gets the pool average for the quality part and a "New" badge shown to the PM.

### 6.3 Offer round

For each target language the system takes the top three scoring freelancers and sends offers to them one at a time. Each offer shows the title, language pair, word count, subject area, deadline, the rate and the confidentiality level, but not the client's name when the job is Restricted. The freelancer has 30 minutes to answer for a Rush job and 4 working hours for a Normal job. The answer can be Accept, Decline with a reason from a list, or no answer. The first Accept ends the round for that language.

If all three freelancers decline or time out, the language is moved to "Needs manual assignment" and the PM is notified by email and in the board. The PM can then offer the job to any eligible freelancer by hand, or to a freelancer who is not eligible, in which case the system asks the PM to confirm and records the override with a reason.

A freelancer who declines three offers in a row has their next score reduced by 10 points for 14 days. A timeout counts as a decline for this rule.

### 6.4 Multiple languages

A job with several target languages creates one assignment per language. The job status is the least advanced status among its assignments. The job is Delivered only when all assignments are Delivered. A PM can cancel one language without cancelling the others.

## 7. Statuses

Job statuses: Draft, Needs check, Open, In progress, In review, Delivered, Cancelled.
Assignment statuses: Offered, Needs manual assignment, Accepted, Working, Submitted, Approved, Returned.

Allowed transitions:

- Draft to Open (Publish) or to Needs check; Needs check to Open or to Cancelled
- Open to In progress when the first assignment is Accepted
- In progress to In review when all assignments are Submitted
- In review to Delivered when all assignments are Approved; In review to In progress when any assignment is Returned
- Any status except Delivered to Cancelled, by a PM only

A Delivered job cannot be edited, cancelled or reopened. A new job must be created instead, using the duplicate function.

## 8. Changes after publication

A PM can change the deadline, the word count and the notes after publication. A change of word count by more than 10 percent, or a deadline moved earlier, triggers a re-check: every freelancer with an Accepted or Working assignment receives a message and has 2 working hours to confirm or withdraw. If a freelancer withdraws, the assignment goes back to the offer round with the next best candidate, skipping the freelancers who already declined this job.

Changing languages, service type or subject area after publication is not allowed. The PM must cancel the job and create a new one.

## 9. Notifications

- Client confirmation on creation (portal and published drafts)
- Offer notification to freelancers by email and by push message
- Reminder to the freelancer at 50 percent of the response window if no answer has come
- Daily digest to each PM at 07:30 local time listing jobs due within 48 working hours and any assignment in Needs manual assignment
- Alert to the PM who owns the job if an assignment is Accepted but no file has been uploaded 24 working hours before the deadline

Every notification is logged with time, recipient and result. Failed emails are retried three times, 5 minutes apart.

## 10. Reporting

PMs can export the job list to CSV with the filters client, status, date range, language and PM. The export contains at most 50,000 rows; above that the user is asked to narrow the filters. Dates in the export are in the time zone of the person who exports. Admins can view a page showing average time from submission to first Accept, per language pair, for any chosen month.

## 11. Non-functional requirements

- Job form submission completes in under 3 seconds for jobs with up to 5 files of 10 MB.
- The offer round starts within 60 seconds of a job becoming Open.
- The system supports 40 simultaneous PM sessions and 150 simultaneous freelancer sessions.
- All times are stored in UTC and shown in the user's own time zone setting.
- Every change to a job is recorded in an audit log with user, time, field, old value and new value. The log cannot be edited.
- Files are stored encrypted. Restricted job files can be downloaded only by the PM who owns the job and the freelancers with an Accepted assignment.
- The interface is available in English and German. Dates follow the locale of the user.

## 12. Open questions from review

1. Ines asks whether the familiarity score should count jobs for a client's parent company. Hanne's answer: not in 2.3, revisit in 2.4.
2. Tomasz wants a way to pause the offer round while a client confirms a question. Not agreed. Ravi says it would add a new status and needs its own spec.
3. Ravi asks how holidays are handled for a client with offices in two countries. Current rule: the country of the client contact who submitted the job.

## 13. Out of scope

Automatic machine translation pre-processing, translation memory matching, payment of freelancers, and the mobile app for freelancers (the push message opens the web page).

## 14. Freelancer availability calendar

Eligibility in section 6.1 depends on the availability that each freelancer enters, so the rules for it are part of this release.

- A freelancer sets availability in blocks of whole days, each with a number of free hours per day from 1 to 10. Days with no block count as unavailable.
- A block can be recurring (for example every Monday to Wednesday, 6 hours) or one-off. A one-off block overrides a recurring one on the same day.
- The needed hours for a job are spread over the working days between the expected start and the deadline. A freelancer is eligible only if the free hours in that period are at least the needed hours. Hours already promised to other Accepted or Working assignments are subtracted first.
- The expected start is the moment the offer is sent for Rush jobs, and the next working morning at 08:00 for Normal jobs.
- A freelancer can switch on "Holiday mode" with a start and end date. During holiday mode the profile is treated as unavailable, no offers are sent, and existing assignments are not affected.
- The vendor manager can edit any freelancer's availability on their behalf; the audit log records who made the change.
- Availability is read at the moment the offer round starts. A change made afterwards does not cancel offers already sent.

## 15. Rollout and acceptance

Relay 2.3 goes live on the first Monday of the next month. The first two weeks run in "shadow mode": offers are computed and shown to PMs as suggestions, but nothing is sent to freelancers automatically, and PMs continue to assign by hand. After the two weeks, Hanne decides together with Tomasz whether to switch on automatic offers, based on these acceptance criteria:

1. In the shadow period, the freelancer who was finally assigned by the PM is in the top three of the system's list for at least 70 percent of assignments.
2. No job is lost: every job submitted by any channel appears on the board with a reference number.
3. No Restricted job was shown to a freelancer without a valid confidentiality agreement.
4. Notifications are delivered for at least 99 percent of events, measured by the notification log.

Old jobs from Relay 2.2 are not migrated. They stay readable in the archive view, and their reference numbers keep the old format MW-NNNNN.

# Formation conseillers clientèle – Module 3 : traiter une réclamation de facturation

Formatrice : Océane Marchetti, responsable qualité et formation
Durée : une journée (7 heures), groupe de douze stagiaires
Prérequis : modules 1 (outils et accès) et 2 (présentation des offres)

## 1. Pourquoi ce module existe

Dans notre centre, environ 31 % des appels entrants concernent la facture. Ce sont aussi les appels les plus longs : la durée moyenne de traitement (DMT) est de 7 minutes 40 secondes pour une réclamation de facturation, contre 4 minutes 50 secondes pour une question sur le réseau. Une réclamation mal traitée revient presque toujours : le taux de rappel sous sept jours atteint 22 % quand le conseiller n'a pas vérifié la facture avec le client, contre 6 % quand il l'a fait.

Objectifs de la journée :
- savoir lire une facture de revendeur et en expliquer chaque ligne ;
- reconnaître les cinq causes d'écart les plus fréquentes ;
- recalculer à la main un prorata, un remboursement et une TVA ;
- appliquer la méthode en six étapes pour conduire l'appel ;
- connaître les limites de ce que le conseiller peut décider seul.

## 2. Comprendre la facture

Notre client reçoit une facture mensuelle qui comporte quatre blocs.

**Bloc 1 : l'abonnement.** Le prix du forfait pour le mois à venir, facturé d'avance. Exemple : forfait « Souffle 40 Go » à 14,99 € TTC par mois.

**Bloc 2 : les options.** Les services ajoutés : assurance du téléphone (4,00 € par mois), option appels internationaux (3,50 € par mois), supplément de données.

**Bloc 3 : la consommation hors forfait.** Appels vers des numéros surtaxés, SMS vers des services payants, utilisation des données à l'étranger hors zone, achats sur facture. Cette partie est facturée à terme échu, donc pour le mois précédent.

**Bloc 4 : les ajustements.** Remises, avoirs, frais ponctuels (frais de mise en service de 9,99 €, frais de remplacement de carte SIM de 10,00 €), et le prorata en cas de changement de forfait en cours de mois.

Les prix affichés au client sont toujours TTC. La TVA est de 20 %. Pour passer d'un prix TTC à un prix hors taxes, on divise par 1,20. Pour retrouver le montant de TVA, on soustrait le hors taxes du TTC.

> Exemple 1. Le forfait Souffle 40 Go coûte 14,99 € TTC. Hors taxes : 14,99 ÷ 1,20 = 12,49 € (arrondi au centime). TVA : 14,99 − 12,49 = 2,50 €.

## 3. Les cinq causes d'écart les plus fréquentes

D'après l'analyse de 1 200 réclamations du dernier trimestre, voici la répartition :

| Cause | Part des réclamations |
|---|---|
| Prorata après changement de forfait | 34 % |
| Option non souhaitée ou oubliée | 21 % |
| Consommation hors forfait (surtaxé, étranger) | 18 % |
| Fin de promotion (le prix remonte) | 15 % |
| Erreur réelle de notre part (double facturation, remise non appliquée) | 8 % |

Les 4 % restants sont des cas divers : prélèvement rejeté, facture adressée à un ancien titulaire, fraude.

Le point important à transmettre aux stagiaires : seules 8 % des réclamations proviennent d'une erreur réelle. La plupart du temps, le client a raison de s'étonner, mais la facture est correcte. Le rôle du conseiller est d'expliquer, pas de se défendre, et de corriger quand c'est justifié.

## 4. Le calcul du prorata

Quand un client change de forfait en cours de mois, l'ancien forfait est facturé jusqu'à la veille du changement et le nouveau à partir du jour du changement. Le calcul se fait au jour : prix mensuel ÷ nombre de jours du mois × nombre de jours concernés.

> Exemple 2. Madame Leroy passe du forfait à 9,99 € au forfait à 19,99 € le 12 avril (avril compte 30 jours).
> - Ancien forfait : du 1er au 11 avril, soit 11 jours. 9,99 ÷ 30 × 11 = 3,66 € (3,663).
> - Nouveau forfait : du 12 au 30 avril, soit 19 jours. 19,99 ÷ 30 × 19 = 12,66 € (12,660).
> - Total du mois pour l'abonnement : 3,66 + 12,66 = 16,32 €.
> Le client s'attendait à payer 19,99 €, ou 9,99 €. Il est surpris par un montant intermédiaire. Il faut lui montrer le détail ligne par ligne.

Attention : si le forfait est facturé d'avance, le prorata du nouveau forfait apparaît sur la facture du mois en cours et le mois suivant apparaît en plein tarif. Beaucoup de clients voient donc deux montants proches sur deux factures et croient à une double facturation.

> Exemple 3 (remboursement). M. Benali a souscrit par erreur l'option « appels internationaux » à 3,50 € par mois le 3 mars (mars compte 31 jours). Il appelle le 20 mars pour la résilier et signale qu'il ne l'a jamais voulue. Le conseiller constate dans l'enregistrement de vente que le client n'a pas confirmé l'option. L'option est donc annulée avec effet rétroactif et remboursée en totalité : 3,50 € de l'abonnement de mars. Si le client avait voulu l'option, puis résilié, il aurait payé le prorata : du 3 au 20 mars inclus, soit 18 jours, 3,50 ÷ 31 × 18 = 2,03 €.

## 5. Les limites de décision du conseiller

Le conseiller peut décider seul, sans demander à un superviseur :
- un geste commercial jusqu'à 15 € TTC une fois par période de douze mois et par client ;
- le remboursement intégral d'une option non confirmée, sur 3 mois maximum en arrière ;
- la correction d'un prorata erroné, quel que soit le montant, si l'erreur est prouvée dans l'outil de facturation.

Le superviseur doit valider :
- tout geste commercial supérieur à 15 € et inférieur ou égal à 50 € ;
- tout remboursement de consommation hors forfait supérieure à 30 € ;
- toute demande de résiliation sans frais en dehors des cas prévus par la loi.

Le service litiges, par transfert de dossier et non par transfert d'appel, traite : tout montant au-dessus de 50 €, les suspicions de fraude, les clients qui annoncent un recours auprès de la médiation ou d'une association de consommateurs, et les factures adressées à un tiers.

Un conseiller ne doit jamais promettre un résultat qui dépend d'un autre service. La phrase à employer : « Je transmets votre dossier au service concerné ; vous recevrez une réponse par courriel sous cinq jours ouvrés. »

## 6. La méthode en six étapes

Le sigle à retenir est **ACCORD**.

1. **Accueillir** : se présenter, donner le prénom, vérifier l'identité du titulaire (nom, date de naissance, code postal, et les quatre derniers chiffres du numéro de ligne). Ne jamais donner d'information avant la vérification.
2. **Cerner** : laisser le client exposer son problème sans l'interrompre pendant trente secondes environ, puis reformuler : « Si je comprends bien, vous avez payé 31,48 € alors que vous attendiez 19,99 €. C'est bien cela ? »
3. **Contrôler** : ouvrir la facture dans l'outil avec le client, ligne par ligne. Comparer avec l'offre souscrite et l'historique des changements des trois derniers mois.
4. **Où est l'écart ?** : identifier la cause parmi les cinq causes du tableau. Poser une question fermée de confirmation : « Avez-vous changé de forfait le 12 avril ? »
5. **Répondre** : expliquer avec des mots simples, chiffres à l'appui, puis proposer la solution : correction, remboursement, geste commercial, ou explication seule si la facture est correcte.
6. **Désamorcer et clore** : vérifier que le client a compris, résumer les actions décidées, indiquer les délais, noter le dossier dans l'outil. Terminer par une phrase positive.

### Exemple de dialogue (cause : fin de promotion)

Client : « Mon forfait était à 8,99 € et là je paie 16,99 €. C'est du vol. »
Conseiller : « Je comprends que cette hausse vous surprenne, monsieur Fabre. Je regarde votre dossier avec vous. Pouvez-vous me confirmer que vous avez souscrit en octobre de l'année dernière ? »
Client : « Oui. »
Conseiller : « Votre offre comprenait un tarif promotionnel de 8,99 € pendant douze mois. Il s'est terminé en octobre, et le prix du forfait est passé à 16,99 €. Ce changement figurait dans le contrat et dans un message envoyé un mois avant. Je peux vous proposer un forfait équivalent à 12,99 € sans engagement, ou vous accorder un geste de 10 € sur la prochaine facture si vous gardez votre forfait. Qu'est-ce qui vous conviendrait le mieux ? »

On remarque que le conseiller n'accuse pas le client de ne pas avoir lu, il ne s'excuse pas pour une faute qui n'existe pas, il donne des chiffres et propose un choix.

## 7. Les mots à éviter et les mots à préférer

| À éviter | À préférer |
|---|---|
| « C'est normal. » | « Je vous explique d'où vient ce montant. » |
| « Vous auriez dû lire le contrat. » | « Ce point figure dans votre contrat, je vous le montre. » |
| « Ce n'est pas ma faute. » | « Voyons ensemble ce qui s'est passé. » |
| « Je ne peux rien faire. » | « Voici ce que je peux faire dans l'immédiat. » |
| « Vous me redites cela ? » | « Pour être sûr de bien comprendre, je reformule. » |

## 8. Indicateurs de suivi des conseillers

Chaque conseiller est suivi sur quatre indicateurs, calculés chaque semaine.

- **DMT** (durée moyenne de traitement) : cible 7 minutes sur les réclamations de facturation. Une DMT trop courte n'est pas un bon signe, elle peut cacher un contrôle bâclé.
- **RPC** (résolution au premier contact) : part des dossiers sans rappel sous sept jours. Cible 85 %.
- **Qualité d'écoute** : note sur 20 donnée par le coach à partir de cinq appels écoutés par semaine. Cible 15 ou plus.
- **Satisfaction client** : note moyenne de l'enquête envoyée par SMS après l'appel, sur 5. Cible 4,2.

> Exemple 4. Sur la semaine 14, un conseiller a traité 46 appels de facturation pour un temps total de conversation de 5 h 22 min. Sa DMT est de 322 min ÷ 46 = 7,0 minutes, soit 7 minutes pile. Sur ces 46 dossiers, 7 ont fait l'objet d'un rappel sous sept jours. Son RPC est (46 − 7) ÷ 46 = 84,8 %, donc juste sous la cible de 85 %.

## 9. Gestion des clients très mécontents

Trois règles :
1. Ne pas répondre au ton par le ton. Baisser légèrement la voix et ralentir le débit.
2. Nommer l'émotion : « Je vois que cette situation vous a mis en colère, et je le comprends. »
3. Passer rapidement aux faits : « Je vous propose de commencer par vérifier la facture ensemble. »

Si le client insulte le conseiller, celui-ci a le droit de prévenir une première fois : « Je souhaite vous aider, mais je ne peux pas continuer si les propos restent injurieux. » À la deuxième insulte, il met fin à l'appel et signale l'incident au superviseur avec l'heure de l'appel. Aucun conseiller n'est sanctionné pour avoir appliqué cette procédure.

## 10. Exercices pratiques de l'après-midi

Les stagiaires travaillent en binômes, l'un joue le client et l'autre le conseiller, puis ils inversent. Trois scénarios sont distribués :

- Scénario A : prorata (Mme Leroy, exemple 2).
- Scénario B : option non confirmée (M. Benali, exemple 3).
- Scénario C : consommation hors forfait à l'étranger. Une cliente est partie en Suisse, où l'itinérance n'est pas incluse dans son forfait, et elle reçoit une facture avec 41,60 € de données. Le conseiller doit expliquer l'écart, vérifier si un message d'alerte a été envoyé (c'est le cas : un SMS à 20 € de consommation et un autre à 40 €), et décider : le remboursement dépasse 30 €, donc il faut passer par le superviseur.

À la fin de l'exercice, chaque binôme présente au groupe ce qui a été le plus difficile.

## 11. Évaluation de vendredi

L'évaluation comporte vingt questions à choix multiples et deux appels simulés écoutés par la formatrice. Pour valider le module, le stagiaire doit obtenir au moins 14 sur 20 au questionnaire et au moins 12 sur 20 à chaque appel simulé. En cas d'échec, une session de rattrapage est organisée la semaine suivante.

```python
import json
import os
import time

import paho.mqtt.client as mqtt
import psycopg2

conn = psycopg2.connect(os.environ["DATABASE_URL"])
cur = conn.cursor()


def on_message(client, userdata, msg):
    data = json.loads(msg.payload)
    print("got", data)
    cur.execute(
        "INSERT INTO readings (scale_id, weight_kg, temp_c, recorded_at) VALUES ('%s', %s, %s, now())"
        % (data["scale"], data["weight"], data["temp"])
    )
    conn.commit()


client = mqtt.Client()
client.username_pw_set(os.environ["MQTT_USER"], os.environ["MQTT_PASSWORD"])
client.on_message = on_message
client.connect(os.environ["MQTT_HOST"], 1883)
client.subscribe("scales/#")

while True:
    try:
        client.loop_forever()
    except Exception as e:
        print(e)
        time.sleep(5)
```

Some context on how things are used. The portal has about 340 accounts and gets most of its traffic in April and May, when swarm season starts and members book apiary visits. Hive scale readings arrive every 15 minutes from about 60 scales. Members' postal addresses and phone numbers are in the database, so I am nervous about losing it or leaking it. The only deployment that ever happens is when I push to the main branch; sometimes I push on a Saturday evening and the site is down for a minute or two while it rebuilds. We have no staging copy. The association pays about 12 euros per month for the VPS and nothing for the storage bucket, which is a free tier of 5 GB. The database file is currently 380 MB and grows by about 40 MB a month because of the scale readings.

## 1. Summary

The quarter was profitable but weaker than planned. Revenue was 612,400 against a budget of 640,000, a shortfall of 4.3 percent. Operating profit was 118,900 against a budget of 192,000. Three things explain most of the gap: the cost of covering two staff departures with temporary accountants, a write-off on the Kessler Foods engagement, and the licence fees for the new filing software, billed for four months in the quarter (one month in advance), which started before the old system could be switched off.

The most important operational event was a set of late filings in the last week of September for the self-employed client group, caused by the transition to the new software. Seven returns were filed after the deadline. The penalties charged by the tax authority total 3,150 and the firm has decided to pay them directly rather than pass them on to clients. This is covered in section 6.

Client numbers are stable at 912 active clients, down from 918 at the end of June. Fee income per client rose by 1.9 percent. The pipeline for the autumn corporate work is good, with five new engagements signed worth an estimated 84,000 in fees, but staffing for these is not yet confirmed.

In the quarter, two experienced accountants left. Marta Soliz left on 14 July to join a client company, and Pavel Dunne left on 21 August for a position in another city. Both had more than eight years with the firm and between them looked after 74 clients. Their clients were reassigned within a week, but the transfer was done by a simple list, without a handover meeting for the 20 most complex files.

Two temporary accountants were hired from an agency from 1 August, at a cost of 4,150 a month each plus the agency margin, and one contractor was engaged for the payroll team during a period of leave. The cost of temporary staff was 42,900 against a budget of 18,000. The partners must decide whether the temporary positions should become permanent. A recruitment process for two accountants was opened on 1 September, and four candidates were interviewed in September. One offer has been made and is waiting for an answer.

Overtime recorded in the timesheets was 1,420 hours in the quarter, 62 percent above the same quarter last year. The highest individual total was 168 hours. Two staff members have reached the internal limit of 150 overtime hours for the half year. Sick leave days were 61, compared with 38 a year ago, with three longer absences of more than ten working days. The partners should consider whether the current workload is sustainable.

Training: eleven staff members attended the continuing education course on the new rules for foreign income, and nine completed the mandatory anti money laundering refresher. Two staff members have not yet completed the refresher and will be removed from client onboarding until they do.

## 4. Client portfolio

Active clients: 912 at 30 September (918 at 30 June).

- New clients in the quarter: 21, of which 12 are self-employed, 6 are small companies, 3 are individuals with foreign income.
- Clients lost: 27. Reasons recorded: moved away or ceased trading (11), changed to another adviser on price (7), retired or died (5), dissatisfied with service (4).
- The four clients lost for dissatisfaction all cite slow responses after the departure of their accountant. Two of them were in the group of the 20 complex files mentioned in section 3.

The ten largest clients account for 21 percent of revenue, a lower concentration than last year (24 percent). Kessler Foods remains on the list but only for routine accounts. The firm has now introduced a written change-of-scope form for all advisory work above 5,000; it has been used on six engagements since 1 September.

Fee levels: the standard hourly rates were increased by 3.5 percent from 1 July. No client has left because of the increase according to the exit notes, but seven asked for a discount and two received one.

## 5. Software migration

The firm decided in March to replace the old filing system, which is no longer supported by its vendor after 31 December, with a cloud product that connects directly to the tax authority's portal. The contract was signed on 12 May for three years at 6,900 a month. The plan was to run both systems in parallel for the month of July and switch over on 1 August.

What actually happened:
- Data migration of the client master data was completed on 24 July, nine days late, because of duplicate client numbers in the old system (about 140 clients had two numbers).
- Staff training took place on 29 and 30 July for all accountants. Attendance was 19 of 21. The two absent staff members were not trained until 11 August.
- The switch was made on 1 August as planned, but the old system was kept running for reference until 30 September. That is why Q3 shows four months of the new licence fee (27,600, because August was billed in advance in July) together with the last three months of the old one (7,000 included in the total of 34,600).
- The direct link to the tax authority portal for self-employed returns was not certified until 9 September, three weeks later than expected. During that time, returns had to be uploaded by hand.
- Eight support tickets are still open with the vendor, of which two are marked as blocking: the import of payroll data for clients with more than one employer, and the reminder emails that are not sent to clients with a non-standard year end.

The partners should note that the old system will not be supported after the end of the year. All working data must be exported and stored before then, and a decision on how long to keep the archive has not been made. The legal retention period for tax records is ten years.

## 6. Late filings and compliance

Between 24 and 30 September, seven returns for self-employed clients were filed after the deadline of 30 September for those who had requested the extension. The returns were filed between one and four days late. The tax authority has charged penalties of 450 per return, which makes 3,150 in total.

Root cause, as established by Elke Varga and Priya Natarajan on 3 October:
1. The reminder emails to accountants about approaching deadlines had been set up in the old system and were not recreated in the new one.
2. The deadline list was not checked manually in the last two weeks because of the pressure of other work.
3. Four of the seven clients had sent their documents only in the last week. The accountants waited for missing information instead of filing a provisional return, which the rules allow.
4. Two of the seven clients had previously been handled by Marta Soliz, and the deadline was not in the handover list.

Actions already taken: a manual deadline list reviewed every Monday by Elke, a calendar for each accountant with deadlines for their clients, and a written rule that a provisional return must be filed three working days before the deadline if documents are missing. The firm's professional indemnity insurer has been informed as a precaution. No claim has been made by a client.

A second compliance point: an internal audit of 40 client files chosen at random found that 6 had no signed engagement letter on file, all of them clients who joined before 2022. The partners decided in July that the missing letters must be obtained by 31 December. By 30 September, 2 of the 6 had been obtained.

## 7. Risks

| Risk | Likelihood | Impact | Current control |
|---|---|---|---|
| More late filings in the December rush | Medium | High | Weekly deadline review, provisional filing rule |
| Further staff departures from overload | Medium | High | Recruitment, overtime limit |
| Open blocking tickets with the software vendor | High | Medium | Escalated to vendor account manager |
| Old system data lost after support ends | Low | High | No owner assigned |
| Debtor days continue to rise | Medium | Medium | Invoicing now back on schedule |
| Missing engagement letters | Medium | Low | Deadline of 31 December |

## 8. Outlook for Q4

October to December is the busiest period for corporate accounts. Based on the workload forecast, 4,300 chargeable hours are needed in Q4 against an estimated 3,900 hours of capacity with current staffing, excluding temporary staff. With the two temporary accountants the capacity is about 4,350 hours, but this leaves no room for sickness or for the five new corporate engagements, which need about 600 hours. Expected revenue is 655,000 if the capacity is found and the new engagements are staffed, and about 600,000 if they are not.

The budget for Q4 assumes no temporary staff. It needs to be revised.

## 9. Decisions requested from the partners

1. Whether to convert the two temporary accountants to permanent positions, or extend the agency contract to 31 January.
2. Whether to approve the offer to the first candidate already made, and to proceed with the second position.
3. Who will own the archive of the old filing system, and how long it is kept.
4. Whether to continue paying penalties for client delays directly, or to introduce a clause in the engagement letter that allows the firm to pass on penalties caused by late documents.
5. Approval of the revised Q4 budget, to be presented in the next meeting.
