These are the notes I took at the kickoff meeting for our new press installation. Nobody has turned them into a plan yet. Could you write the full project plan from them: phases, tasks, owners, dates, dependencies, a risk register with mitigations, and a list of questions that still need answering before we can commit to dates? Where the notes contradict each other or leave something out, point it out instead of guessing silently.

# Kickoff meeting: Press 4 installation and finishing line relocation
Stanhope & Pike Printers, Halbrook works
Date: Tuesday 6 October 2026, 14:00 to 16:10, Meeting room B
Notes by: Wilhelmina Cray (Production Planner)

Present: Bertrand Stanhope (Managing Director), Oksana Lindgren (Operations Director), Dev Malhotra (Head of Pressroom), Greta Voss (Head of Finishing), Anselm Pike (Facilities and Maintenance), Raúl Ferreira (Finance Manager), Yusuf Demir (Customer Service Manager), Wilhelmina Cray (notes). Apologies: Hannelore Brandt (IT and prepress), who will get the notes.

## 1. Why we are doing this

Bertrand opened by repeating the board decision of 21 September: we buy a new eight-unit sheet-fed offset press (called Press 4 from now on) to replace Press 1, a 22-year-old four-colour machine that has had eleven breakdowns in the last year and that the vendor no longer supports with spare parts. Purchase price agreed with the supplier, Kronwald Machines, is 1.84 million, including a coating unit and the automatic plate loading. A separate 112,000 is reserved for the installation work in the hall: floor reinforcement, power, ventilation and compressed air.

Reasons given: Press 1 downtime cost an estimated 138,000 in lost jobs and overtime last year. The two largest customers (the regional theatre group and the publisher Orlen Books) have asked for coated stock and varnish finishes that Press 1 cannot do. The new press is also about 40 percent faster on make-ready, because of plate loading and inline colour control.

Bertrand wants the new press producing by the middle of January, because the theatre group's spring season brochures arrive in the second half of January and the annual contract with Orlen Books starts on 1 February. Oksana says this is "possible but only if everything goes right" and asked that nobody commits to customers before the plan is checked.

## 2. Timeline as the supplier described it

Raúl read out the delivery schedule from the signed order confirmation:
- Press delivered in 14 modules by lorry to Halbrook on Monday 30 November (the supplier says the week of 30 November, plus or minus a few days).
- Installation team from Kronwald: six technicians for four weeks. They need the hall floor prepared and power connected before they arrive.
- Commissioning and test printing: one week after installation.
- Operator training: five days, by Kronwald's trainer, in the week after commissioning.
- Handover and acceptance test: a 12-hour continuous run at agreed speed with a quality check against the contract's specification.

Anselm pointed out that four weeks plus one week plus one week of training, starting on 30 November, would bring us to the second week of January, and with the Christmas closure (the works is closed from 24 December to 1 January) the real finish would be around 18 January. Dev said that is too close. Nobody disagreed. Bertrand said the supplier had promised to try to reduce the installation to three weeks with a larger team, and Raúl will ask in writing.

## 3. The hall

The new press goes into the north bay of the pressroom, where Press 1 and the old folding machine stand today. Anselm showed a floor plan. Key points:
- The press weighs about 38 tonnes, and the current floor slab was rated for 22 tonnes per machine. A structural survey is needed, and probably reinforced foundations under the press units. Anselm has a quote from a structural engineer for a survey: 3,800, two weeks to complete. He asked for permission to order it this week. Agreed by Bertrand.
- Power: the new press needs a 400 A supply. The existing board is at 260 A capacity, and it is shared with the finishing area. The electricity network operator has to be asked for an upgrade, which Anselm says can take up to eight weeks. Application not yet made. He will do it tomorrow if Raúl approves the fee (about 6,500).
- Compressed air and extraction: the existing compressor is old, and the new press needs a quantity of air that it cannot supply. A new compressor and a dryer are in the 112,000 budget. Delivery time is 6 to 8 weeks.
- Press 1 has to be removed first. Anselm has a scrap and resale dealer who offered 9,000 for the machine, collected, but the dealer needs three days and a crane. Oksana asked whether Press 1 can be sold after the new one is working, so that the plant keeps some capacity until then. Anselm said no, because Press 4 sits in Press 1's space. This is an open question.
- The hall will also lose the old folding machine position, which Greta will use for the relocated finishing line (section 4).

## 4. The finishing line

Greta explained that the relocation of the finishing line is a separate project that was added to this one. Today the cutter, the folder, the saddle stitcher and the perfect binder stand in the south bay, on the other side of the building. The new press produces more sheets per hour than the finishing area can handle if left where it is, because the stacks have to be moved by pallet truck across a public walkway, and finishing is already a bottleneck on 30 percent of jobs.

Plan proposed by Greta: move the cutter and the folder to the north bay, next to Press 4, at the position where the old folding machine now stands. The saddle stitcher and the binder stay in the south bay for now. This needs the folder disconnected and reinstalled by an outside rigging firm (quote requested, not yet received; Greta thinks about 14,000), new floor markings, and a revised workflow for the pallets. She says the move can be done in two days over a weekend.

Raúl asked whether this is in the budget. It is not. The 112,000 does not include rigging or relocation of finishing equipment. Greta said she believes a saving can be found by not buying the pallet conveyor (about 21,000), which was in an earlier version of the request. Bertrand: "Put it to me with numbers next week, not now."

Dev asked who will run the folder during the move period, since it will be out of service for at least two days and during that time the customer jobs that need folding must be sent elsewhere. Greta says she has an arrangement with a trade finisher nearby, Marwick Bindery, who charged 60 an hour before. No contract yet.

## 5. Production during the installation

This was the longest discussion. For roughly six weeks from the start of November to the middle of December, the pressroom will have no Press 1 and no Press 4. Press 2 (a two-colour) and Press 3 (a four-colour) continue to run. Dev's figures: Presses 2 and 3 together can take about 55 percent of the work that currently runs on all three machines. The remaining 45 percent must be moved to trade printers, delayed, or declined.

Yusuf listed the customers who would be most affected: the theatre group's autumn programme reprint (due 20 November), the Orlen Books paperback run (three titles, due in the first week of December), and the annual calendars for two local banks, which are normally printed in the second half of November and are the biggest seasonal job of the year (about 180,000 in revenue). He said that he cannot tell customers anything until he knows which dates are firm.

Decisions and suggestions:
- The calendars will be printed first, by the end of October, on Press 1 before it is taken out, even if that means shifting other jobs. Dev says it is possible if the paper arrives by 16 October. Yusuf will confirm the paper order with the supplier.
- Jobs of 8,000 sheets and above that need coating will be sent to a trade printer, Dunmere Press. Oksana will ask them for a rate and capacity for November. A first guess is that outsourcing costs about 22 percent more than printing in-house.
- Overtime on Press 3 on Saturdays during November: Dev will propose a rota, but he does not have enough trained operators. Two apprentices could be used under supervision.
- Press 1 will print its last job on Friday 30 October. Anselm will start the removal the following Monday.

## 6. People and training

Dev has five press operators and two assistants. Only three operators have worked with a plate loading system, and none with the inline colour control. Kronwald's training of five days can take six people. Dev wants all five operators plus one assistant. Raúl asked about the cost of backfill. Dev said that during the training week Press 3 will have to run with the remaining crew, and he does not think this is possible without agency staff.

Hannelore was absent, but Wilhelmina noted her email from last week: the prepress system needs a software update and a new colour profile for the new press, and the connection from the workflow server to Press 4 requires a network cable run and two licences. She estimates 11,000 and says the work must be done before commissioning. This needs an owner at the meeting and nobody took it, so Oksana asked Wilhelmina to make sure Hannelore picks it up.

## 7. Money

Raúl summarised the figures so far:
- Press purchase: 1,840,000 (financing by the bank loan of 1,500,000 and 340,000 own funds).
- Installation work: 112,000 budget.
- Not yet budgeted: structural survey 3,800, power upgrade application 6,500, rigging for the finishing line about 14,000, prepress work 11,000, agency staff during training (no figure), trade printer extra cost (no figure), Marwick Bindery (no figure).
- Income expected from the sale of Press 1: 9,000.

Raúl said the bank wants a monthly progress report during the installation, and the loan's first draw down is conditional on the signed order confirmation (done) and proof of insurance for the equipment during transport and installation. Anselm will ask the insurance broker for a quote this week.

He also warned that the contract with Kronwald has a penalty for late acceptance on our side: if the hall is not ready on 30 November, the supplier can charge 4,200 per week of delay, and re-schedule the technicians, which can mean several weeks of waiting.

## 8. Risks mentioned in the meeting

- The floor needs more reinforcement than expected, which would delay the delivery date.
- The network operator's upgrade takes longer than eight weeks.
- Compressor delivery arrives late.
- Technicians arrive but the hall is not ready, with penalty.
- Loss of customers during the weeks with reduced capacity.
- The calendar job is not finished before Press 1 is removed.
- Operators are not ready for the new press, and quality in January is poor.
- One of the Kronwald modules is damaged in transport.

No owners or ratings were given in the meeting.

## 9. Next steps agreed in the room

1. Anselm orders the structural survey (this week) and applies for the power upgrade (Wednesday, with approval from Raúl).
2. Raúl writes to Kronwald asking for a three-week installation with a larger team.
3. Yusuf confirms the calendar paper with the supplier by Friday 9 October.
4. Oksana asks Dunmere Press for November rates.
5. Greta gets the quote from the rigging firm and a priced proposal to Bertrand next Tuesday, 13 October.
6. Dev drafts the training and overtime rota for November.
7. Wilhelmina circulates these notes and asks Hannelore to take the prepress work.
8. Next meeting: Tuesday 13 October at 14:00.

Bertrand closed the meeting by asking everyone to keep the project out of customer conversations until the plan is written.

## 10. Any other business

**Certification.** Oksana reminded the group that the FSC chain-of-custody audit is booked for the week of 22 February. The auditor will check that the new press is covered in the procedures, including the paper stock records and the labelling of FSC jobs. The procedures document must be updated and Press 4 added to the equipment list before the audit. Wilhelmina is the document owner and will do this in January, after commissioning, unless the audit date is moved.

**Safety.** Anselm said that the installation will bring outside technicians into the hall for four weeks, and each one needs a site induction and a signed permit to work. He will ask the safety adviser, Prakash Oduya, to run the inductions on the first day. Also, the new press uses a different washing solvent than Press 1, and the solvent store has limited capacity (two 200 litre drums); the safety data sheets must be reviewed before the first delivery. Below is the database for the production and warranty reporting at our bicycle factory (PostgreSQL 15, about 14 million rows in stock_movements and 2.3 million in warranty_claims). Reports have become slow and the numbers sometimes disagree between departments. Please review the schema design, say which indexes and constraints are missing, and rewrite each of the queries at the end in a better form with an explanation of what was wrong and how the new version works. Also list any places where the design allows bad data.

## Schema

```sql
CREATE TABLE suppliers (
    id            serial PRIMARY KEY,
    name          varchar(200),
    country       varchar(50),
    contact_email varchar(200),
    rating        varchar(10),
    active        varchar(5) DEFAULT 'yes'
);

CREATE TABLE parts (
    id             serial PRIMARY KEY,
    sku            varchar(40),
    description    text,
    category       varchar(40),
    supplier_id    integer,
    unit_cost      real,
    reorder_level  integer,
    weight_g       integer
);

CREATE TABLE models (
    id            serial PRIMARY KEY,
    code          varchar(20),
    name          varchar(100),
    type          varchar(30),   -- road, gravel, mountain, e-bike, kids
    launch_date   varchar(20),
    retail_price  numeric(10,2),
    discontinued  boolean DEFAULT false
);

CREATE TABLE bom (
    model_id   integer,
    part_id    integer,
    quantity   integer,
    notes      text
);

CREATE TABLE production_orders (
    id            serial PRIMARY KEY,
    model_id      integer REFERENCES models(id),
    planned_qty   integer,
    started_on    varchar(20),
    finished_on   varchar(20),
    status        varchar(20),   -- planned, running, done, cancelled
    line          varchar(10)
);

CREATE TABLE bikes (
    serial_no           varchar(30) PRIMARY KEY,
    model_id            integer REFERENCES models(id),
    production_order_id integer REFERENCES production_orders(id),

    colour              varchar(30),
    built_at            timestamp,
    qa_passed           boolean,
    qa_notes            text
);

CREATE TABLE dealers (
    id          serial PRIMARY KEY,
    name        varchar(200),
    city        varchar(100),
    country     varchar(50),
    region      varchar(50),

);

CREATE TABLE sales (
    id           serial PRIMARY KEY,
    bike_serial  varchar(30),
    dealer_id    integer,
    sold_on      date,
    price        numeric(10,2),
    discount_pct numeric(5,2)
);

CREATE TABLE warranty_claims (
    id             serial PRIMARY KEY,
    bike_serial    varchar(30),
    claim_date     date,
    part_id        integer,
    failure_code   varchar(10),

);

CREATE TABLE stock_movements (
    id          bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
    part_id     integer,
    moved_at    timestamp,
    quantity    integer,        -- positive in, negative out

CREATE TABLE purchase_orders (
```

Notes about the data: `suppliers.active` holds 'yes', 'no', 'Yes', 'Y' and sometimes NULL. `models.launch_date` is written by hand and has formats like '2019-03-01', '01.03.2019' and 'spring 2019'. In `bom` some model and part pairs appear twice because of an import that was run two times. In `stock_movements`, the `reference` for production movements holds the production order id as text, for example '4517', and for deliveries it holds a delivery note number like 'DN-88231'. About 3 percent of `bikes.production_order_id` are NULL for older bikes. `purchase_orders.received_on` is NULL until the goods arrive, and partial deliveries are booked by overwriting `qty_received`. `qa_checks` holds one row per station per bike, normally six rows, plus extra rows for each rework. `warranty_claims.bike_serial` is not always a serial that exists in `bikes`, because dealers type it in by hand.

## Queries currently in use

### Q1: parts that need reordering (run every morning by purchasing)

```sql
SELECT p.sku, p.description, s.name AS supplier,
       (SELECT SUM(quantity) FROM stock_movements sm WHERE sm.part_id = p.id) AS on_hand,
       p.reorder_level
FROM parts p, suppliers s
WHERE p.supplier_id = s.id
  AND (SELECT SUM(quantity) FROM stock_movements sm WHERE sm.part_id = p.id) < p.reorder_level
  AND s.active = 'yes'
ORDER BY on_hand;
```

### Q2: monthly production by model, last 12 months (finance dashboard)

```sql
SELECT m.name,
       to_char(b.built_at, 'YYYY-MM') AS month,
       count(*) AS bikes_built,
       sum(case when b.qa_passed then 1 else 0 end) AS passed,
       round(100.0 * sum(case when b.qa_passed then 1 else 0 end) / count(*), 1) AS pass_rate
FROM bikes b
JOIN models m ON m.id = b.model_id
WHERE to_char(b.built_at, 'YYYY-MM') >= to_char(now() - interval '12 months', 'YYYY-MM')
GROUP BY m.name, to_char(b.built_at, 'YYYY-MM')
ORDER BY month, m.name;
```

### Q3: bill of materials cost per model (engineering)

```sql
SELECT m.code, m.name, sum(p.unit_cost * bom.quantity) AS material_cost
FROM models m, bom, parts p
WHERE bom.model_id = m.id AND bom.part_id = p.id
GROUP BY m.code, m.name
ORDER BY material_cost DESC;
```

### Q4: bikes sold per dealer region and average realised price (sales)

```sql
SELECT d.region,
       count(s.id) AS units,
       avg(s.price - s.price * s.discount_pct / 100) AS avg_price
FROM dealers d
LEFT JOIN sales s ON s.dealer_id = d.id
WHERE s.sold_on >= '2026-01-01'
GROUP BY d.region
ORDER BY units DESC;
```

### Q5: warranty claim rate and cost per model (quality)

```sql
SELECT m.name,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM warranty_claims w
         JOIN bikes b2 ON b2.serial_no = w.bike_serial
         WHERE b2.model_id = m.id) AS claims,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM bikes b3 WHERE b3.model_id = m.id) AS bikes_built,
       (SELECT sum(w.cost) FROM warranty_claims w
         JOIN bikes b2 ON b2.serial_no = w.bike_serial
         WHERE b2.model_id = m.id) AS total_cost
FROM models m
WHERE m.discontinued = false;
```

### Q6: parts that never appear in any bill of materials (cleanup)

```sql
SELECT sku, description
FROM parts
WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT part_id FROM bom);
```

### Q7: average days to close a warranty claim by failure code, 2026

```sql
SELECT failure_code,
       avg(closed_date - claim_date) AS avg_days,
       count(*)
FROM warranty_claims
WHERE extract(year from claim_date) = 2026
GROUP BY failure_code
HAVING count(*) > 20
ORDER BY avg_days DESC;
```

### Q8: scrap by production order (operations)

```sql
SELECT po.id, m.name, po.line, po.planned_qty,
       sum(abs(sm.quantity)) AS scrapped_parts
FROM production_orders po
JOIN models m ON m.id = po.model_id
JOIN stock_movements sm ON sm.reference = po.id::text
WHERE sm.reason = 'scrap'
  AND po.started_on LIKE '2026-%'
GROUP BY po.id, m.name, po.line, po.planned_qty
ORDER BY scrapped_parts DESC
LIMIT 50;
```

### Q9: the ten dealers with the most warranty claims per bike sold (quality and sales, quarterly)

```sql
SELECT d.name, d.city,
       count(distinct w.id) * 1.0 / count(distinct s.id) AS claims_per_bike
FROM dealers d
JOIN sales s ON s.dealer_id = d.id
LEFT JOIN warranty_claims w ON w.bike_serial = s.bike_serial
GROUP BY d.name, d.city
ORDER BY claims_per_bike DESC
LIMIT 10;
```

### Q10: current stock value by warehouse (finance, month end)

```sql
SELECT warehouse, sum(stock * unit_cost) AS value
FROM (
    SELECT sm.warehouse, sm.part_id, sum(sm.quantity) AS stock
    FROM stock_movements sm
    GROUP BY sm.warehouse, sm.part_id
) x
JOIN parts p ON p.id = x.part_id
GROUP BY warehouse;
```

### Q11: supplier delivery performance, last 6 months (purchasing)

```sql
SELECT s.name,
       count(*) AS orders,
       sum(case when po.received_on > po.promised_on then 1 else 0 end) AS late,
       100.0 * sum(case when po.received_on > po.promised_on then 1 else 0 end) / count(*) AS pct_late,
       avg(po.received_on - po.promised_on) AS avg_delay_days
FROM purchase_orders po
JOIN suppliers s ON s.id = po.supplier_id
WHERE po.ordered_on > current_date - 180
GROUP BY s.name
ORDER BY pct_late DESC;
```

### Q12: bikes that failed QA at least twice at the same station (quality)

```sql
SELECT bike_serial, station, count(*)
FROM qa_checks
WHERE result = 'fail'
GROUP BY bike_serial, station
HAVING count(*) >= 2;
```

### Q13: latest claim for each bike that has had claims (customer service)

```sql
SELECT w.*
FROM warranty_claims w
WHERE w.claim_date = (SELECT max(claim_date) FROM warranty_claims w2 WHERE w2.bike_serial = w.bike_serial);
```

### Q14: slow-moving parts, no movement out for 12 months, with value tied up (finance)

```sql
SELECT p.sku, p.description,
       (SELECT sum(quantity) FROM stock_movements WHERE part_id = p.id) * p.unit_cost AS value_tied_up
FROM parts p
WHERE p.id NOT IN (
    SELECT part_id FROM stock_movements
    WHERE quantity < 0 AND moved_at > now() - interval '12 months'
)
ORDER BY value_tied_up DESC;
```

## Additional context

The factory builds roughly 38,000 bikes a year across five models families. Stock movements are written by the warehouse scanners all day and by the production line software at each station. The reorder report in Q1 takes about 40 seconds and runs while the warehouse is busy, and the finance dashboard in Q2 takes almost two minutes. Purchasing says that Q1 sometimes shows parts that are in fact in stock; production says that Q8 scrap figures never match the figures in the quality reports. Nobody has ever added an index apart from the primary keys. We plan to move to a read replica for reporting next year.

# Design: Donor Appointment and Collection Platform (DACP)

Author: Henrike Sauvageot, platform lead, Marrowbridge Regional Blood Service
Status: Draft 3, for architecture review
Last edited: 14 October

## 1. Background

Marrowbridge Regional Blood Service collects whole blood and plasma across eleven fixed donor centres and about forty mobile sessions a month, held in church halls, factory canteens and school gyms. We supply nine hospitals in the Marrow valley. In a normal year we collect roughly 74,000 units of whole blood and 21,000 plasma donations.

Today the whole process runs on three systems that do not talk to each other well. Appointments are booked in a hosted calendar tool that our call centre staff and a public web form both write to. Donor eligibility is checked on paper questionnaires at the session and then typed into a ten-year-old desktop application called Haemo-Desk. Collected units are labelled with pre-printed barcode sheets and tracked in a separate inventory database that the laboratory owns. Reconciling these three takes two people most of every Monday.

The problems we want to fix are these:

- Donors double-book or fail to show up. Our no-show rate at mobile sessions is 19 percent, and each empty slot costs a nurse's hour plus single-use supplies that are opened but not used.
- Eligibility data is typed twice, once by the nurse and once by an administrator, and the two copies disagree in about 2 percent of records.
- When a hospital reports a transfusion reaction, tracing a unit back to its donor and forward to the other components made from the same donation takes up to a working day.
- We cannot tell a donor in real time that their blood type is urgently needed.

## 2. Goals and non-goals

Goals:

1. One system of record for donors, appointments, screening answers, and collected units.
2. Online self-booking with reminders by text message and email, and waiting list handling when a session fills.
3. Digital screening at the session on a tablet, with deferral rules applied automatically and signed off by a nurse.
4. Unit labelling and traceability from vein to hospital, with a full audit trail.
5. Targeted calls to donors by blood group when stocks fall below thresholds.

Non-goals for this phase: replacing the laboratory's testing instruments or their middleware, handling donations of organs or tissue, and building a donor-facing mobile app. A responsive website is enough.

## 3. Constraints

- Regulation requires that every collected unit can be traced for thirty years. Records may never be hard-deleted inside that period, even if the donor asks for deletion; we must explain this to donors and restrict processing instead.
- The service has no on-call developers at night. Collections happen from 07:00 to 21:00 and the system must be usable throughout, but a four-hour maintenance window after midnight is acceptable.
- Mobile sessions often have poor connectivity. The screening and collection screens must work offline for up to a full session day and sync afterwards.
- The team is five engineers, one tester, and a part-time security officer. We run on a single cloud region chosen by the regional health authority.
- Budget for the build is 410,000 for the year, of which 90,000 is held back for training and the cutover.

## 4. Architecture overview

DACP is a modular monolith written in Kotlin with a PostgreSQL 16 database. We chose a monolith because the team is small and the domain is tightly coupled: a screening answer can defer a donor, which cancels future appointments, which changes forecasts. Splitting it into services would give us distributed transactions in exactly the places where we need simple ones.

The modules are:

- Donor registry: identity, contact details, consent, blood group (once confirmed by the laboratory), deferrals.
- Scheduling: sites, sessions, slots, bookings, waiting lists, reminders.
- Screening: the questionnaire, the rules engine, nurse sign-off.
- Collection: donation events, unit identifiers, bag labels, adverse events during donation.
- Inventory bridge: an adapter to the laboratory's inventory database.
- Outreach: stock thresholds, donor targeting, message sending.
- Audit: an append-only event log written by every other module.

Each module owns its tables, exposes a Kotlin interface to the others, and may not read another module's tables directly. A build-time check enforces this.

Clients are a public web application for donors, a staff web application for call centre and site managers, and an offline-capable tablet application for nurses. The tablet application is a progressive web app that stores work in a local database in the browser and syncs when a connection returns.

## 5. Data model

The central records are:

- `donor`: a surrogate id, name, date of birth, contact details, preferred language, confirmed blood group, consent flags.
- `session`: a site, a date, a start and end time, a capacity per hour, and a state of open, full, closed, or cancelled.
- `booking`: a donor, a slot, a donation type of whole blood or plasma, a state, and a reminder history.
- `screening`: a donor, a session, the answers given, the outcome (eligible, temporarily deferred, permanently deferred), and the nurse who signed it off.
- `donation`: a screening, a unit identifier, start and end time, volume, any adverse event, and the bag lot numbers.
- `deferral`: a donor, a reason code, a start date, and an end date or the word permanent.

Unit identifiers follow the national format of a three-letter site prefix, a six-digit sequence, and a check character. Sequences are allocated in blocks to each tablet before a session starts so that offline tablets never collide.

Personally identifying data lives in the donor registry schema. All other modules refer to donors by surrogate id only. Reports for hospitals and for the regulator are generated from a separate reporting schema that holds the unit identifier but no names.

## 6. Offline operation

A nurse tablet downloads, before a session, the list of booked donors with their last-known deferrals, the questionnaire version, the rules version, and a block of unit identifiers. During the session every action is written to a local queue. When the tablet sees the network, it posts the queue in order. The server applies each item idempotently, keyed by a client-generated id, and answers with any conflict.

The conflicts we expect are few: a donor was deferred centrally after the tablet downloaded its data, or a booking was cancelled. In both cases the tablet shows the nurse a warning at the next sync, and the donation record is kept, flagged for review by a medical officer. We do not want software to refuse a collection that already happened.

## 7. Eligibility rules

Rules are stored as versioned data, not code. A rule has a question reference, a condition, an outcome, and a deferral length. Examples: a tattoo in the last four months gives a four-month deferral; a body weight below 50 kilograms gives a temporary deferral until the donor reports a higher weight; certain medicines give a permanent deferral.

A medical officer edits rules in a staff screen; changes require a second medical officer to approve before they go live. The engine always shows the nurse which rule fired and its wording, because the nurse, not the software, makes the final decision. The nurse can override a temporary deferral only with a written reason, and permanent deferrals cannot be overridden at the session at all.

## 8. Outreach and forecasting

Every night at 02:00 a job computes projected stock by blood group for each of the next fourteen days from the laboratory's inventory feed, expected expiries (red cells last forty-two days, platelets five), and scheduled collections. When projected stock falls below a configured threshold, the outreach module selects eligible donors of that group who have not donated within the minimum interval and have consented to messages, ranks them by distance to the nearest open session, and sends invitations in waves of two hundred. It stops sending when the open slots are filled. A donor cannot receive more than one stock appeal in any ten-day period.

## 9. Security and privacy

Health data about donors is special category data. We apply the following:

- Sign-in for staff uses the authority's identity provider with two-factor authentication. Donors sign in with an email link, with no password.
- Roles are call centre, site manager, nurse, medical officer, laboratory liaison, and administrator. Nurses can see screening answers only for donors booked at their own session.
- All access to a screening record is written to the audit log with user, time, and reason.
- Data at rest is encrypted by the database host; the screening answers column is additionally encrypted with an application key held in the cloud key service.
- Backups are taken every hour and kept for thirty days. A restore is rehearsed every quarter.

## 10. Migration

Haemo-Desk holds 310,000 donor records. We will migrate in three passes: a dry run into a test environment with a data quality report, a rehearsal cutover over one weekend, and the real cutover on a weekend in March. Records with conflicting blood groups, missing birth dates, or duplicates by name and date of birth go to a manual queue for the call centre, which we estimate at around 6,000 records. The old calendar tool is switched to read-only on the Friday and retired a month after cutover.

## 11. Rollout

We start with the two busiest fixed centres, then the mobile team, then the remaining centres. Each stage has an exit check: no unreconciled units for two weeks, no screening forms on paper, and a nurse satisfaction survey of at least seven out of ten.

## 12. Interfaces

Donors and staff use a JSON API over HTTPS, versioned in the path. The tablet application uses the same API plus one bulk endpoint, `POST /sync`, which accepts an ordered batch of up to 500 queued actions and returns a per-item result. The main resources are `/sessions`, `/slots`, `/bookings`, `/donors`, `/screenings` and `/donations`. List endpoints use cursor pagination; none of them accept free-text search on donor names, because name search is only offered through the staff application and is logged.

Outbound messages go through a single messaging port with two adapters, one for text and one for email. The port takes a template id, a language and a set of merge fields, never a free-form body, so that every message a donor can receive has been reviewed by the communications team. Delivery receipts come back through a webhook and are attached to the booking's reminder history.

The inventory bridge is the only module that speaks the laboratory's protocol. It writes one record per completed donation and reads stock levels every fifteen minutes. If the laboratory database is unreachable, the bridge queues writes in our database and raises an alert when the oldest queued item is more than thirty minutes old. Nothing else in DACP waits on the bridge.

## 13. Capacity and performance

Peak load is predictable. Booking traffic spikes for about twenty minutes after a stock appeal goes out; we expect no more than 300 booking requests a minute at those moments, even for the largest appeal. Session day load is dominated by tablet syncs: a busy mobile session of 120 donors produces roughly 1,500 queued actions, posted in batches over a few minutes.

A single database instance with 8 vCPUs and 32 GB of memory handles this several times over. We will run two application instances behind a load balancer for availability, not for throughput. The database has one synchronous standby in a second availability zone, and a failover is expected to take under two minutes.

The one query we worry about is the nightly forecast, which joins collections, expiries and inventory over a fourteen-day horizon. We will run it against a read replica and cap it at ten minutes; if it exceeds that, the previous night's forecast stays in force and an alert is raised.

## 14. Failure modes

| Failure | Effect | Response |
|---|---|---|
| Tablet loses power mid-session | Local queue may be lost if not yet persisted | Every action is written to local storage before the screen advances; nurse sees a recovery prompt on restart |
| Two tablets use the same identifier block | Duplicate unit identifiers | Blocks are allocated centrally with a unique constraint; a tablet that cannot get a block cannot start a session |
| Messaging provider outage | Reminders not delivered | Retry for six hours, then show affected bookings to the call centre |
| Rules version changes during a session | Nurse sees different outcomes than a colleague | A tablet keeps the rules version it downloaded for the whole session and reports it with every screening |
| Laboratory feed stale | Forecast based on old stock | Forecast screen shows the age of the feed and outreach is paused if it is older than six hours |
| Wrong blood group recorded by a donor | Targeted appeals reach the wrong people | Blood group is taken only from the laboratory's confirmed result, never from the donor |

## 15. Testing and quality

The tester will maintain a regression suite that covers the booking flow end to end, the rules engine with a table of two hundred screening scenarios supplied by the medical officers, and offline sync with deliberately interrupted connections. Rules changes cannot be approved until the scenario table has been run against the new version and the differences have been read by the approving officer.

We will run a load test of the booking flow before each stock-appeal season, a restore rehearsal each quarter, and an external penetration test before the first centre goes live and again before the mobile team does. Defects that touch unit identifiers, screening outcomes or the audit log are treated as the highest severity and block a release.

Training is separate from the test plan but linked to it. Each nurse completes a one-hour practice session on a training tenant with fictional donors, and every site gets a printed one-page guide for the offline mode, because that is where staff will be least confident.

## 16. Cost and staffing

| Item | Estimate |
|---|---|
| Engineering (five people, ten months) | 250,000 |
| Cloud hosting for the year | 38,000 |
| Messaging fees at expected volumes | 14,000 |
| External security testing | 18,000 |
| Tablets and mounts for 11 centres and the mobile team | 0 (reuse existing) |
| Training and cutover (held back) | 90,000 |

The total is 410,000. The estimate for engineering assumes no hire is needed, which depends on the part-time security officer staying at two days a week. If the officer leaves, we need to hire or contract before the penetration test.

## 17. Open questions

- Who owns the rules for plasma donations, where the interval and protein tests differ from whole blood?
- Do we send text messages through our own gateway or through the authority's contract?
- The laboratory says its inventory database cannot take more than about ten writes per second. Mobile sync at the end of a busy day could exceed that. We have not measured it.
- Is thirty-year retention satisfied by the database backups alone, or do we need a separate archive?
