My company has just been sent this trade effluent agreement by the wastewater treatment plant that serves our factory, and I have to sign it by the end of the month. I'm not a lawyer and I run operations, not legal. Please explain it to me clause by clause in plain language, tell me what each clause means in practice for our day-to-day work, and then list the biggest risks and the things you would try to negotiate before signing.

TRADE EFFLUENT ACCEPTANCE AGREEMENT

Between Oakhollow Water Reclamation Authority ("the Authority"), operator of the Sedgefield Lane Wastewater Treatment Works ("the Works"), and Brindlemoor Preserves Ltd ("the Discharger"), a producer of jams, sauces and pickles at Unit 4, Tannery Close, Oakhollow.

Agreement reference: TEA-2026-0187. Commencement date: 1 January 2027. Initial term: three years.

1. Definitions

1.1 "Effluent" means liquid waste discharged from the Discharger's premises to the Authority's sewer at the connection point identified as Manhole M-14.
1.2 "Daily Volume" means the volume of Effluent measured over a period of twenty-four hours beginning at 06:00.
1.3 "Strength" means the Chemical Oxygen Demand of the Effluent, expressed in milligrams of oxygen per litre, measured on a composite sample in accordance with the method in Schedule 2.
1.4 "Prohibited Substances" means the substances listed in Schedule 3.
1.5 "Working Day" means any day other than a Saturday, Sunday or public holiday in the region.

2. Permission to discharge

2.1 The Authority permits the Discharger to discharge Effluent at Manhole M-14 on the terms of this Agreement and for no other purpose.
2.2 The permission is personal to the Discharger. It may not be transferred to a successor, a tenant or a sub-contractor without the Authority's written consent, which may not be unreasonably withheld where the successor takes on the premises and the same process.
2.3 The Discharger shall not connect any additional drain, pipe or tanker discharge point to the sewer without prior written approval.

3. Limits on volume and flow

3.1 The Daily Volume shall not exceed 220 cubic metres.
3.2 The instantaneous flow rate shall not exceed 12 litres per second.
3.3 If the Discharger expects to exceed either limit for more than three consecutive days because of seasonal production, it shall notify the Authority at least ten Working Days in advance, stating the expected volumes and dates. The Authority may agree a temporary increase, with a surcharge under clause 8.4.
3.4 Where the Authority reasonably considers that the Works is at risk of overload, it may require the Discharger to hold Effluent in balancing storage and release it between 22:00 and 05:00. The Discharger shall comply within two hours of notice.

4. Limits on quality

4.1 The Effluent shall at all times comply with the limits in Schedule 1. In summary these are: pH between 6.0 and 10.0; temperature not above 40 degrees Celsius; Strength not above 3,000 milligrams per litre as a daily composite; suspended solids not above 800 milligrams per litre; fats, oils and grease not above 100 milligrams per litre; and total sulphite not above 10 milligrams per litre.
4.2 The Discharger shall not discharge any Prohibited Substance, whether or not the limits in clause 4.1 are met.
4.3 The Discharger shall not dilute the Effluent with water for the purpose of meeting any limit.
4.4 The Discharger shall install and maintain a screen with openings not larger than 6 millimetres and a fat trap sized in accordance with Schedule 4 before the connection point.

5. Monitoring and sampling

5.1 The Discharger shall install, at its own cost, a flow meter and a sampling chamber at or near Manhole M-14 by 1 April 2027. Until then, the Authority will estimate the Daily Volume from the Discharger's metered water supply, less an allowance of 8 percent for water leaving the premises as product.
5.2 The Authority may take samples at any time without notice. A sample taken by the Authority is conclusive evidence of the quality of the Effluent unless the Discharger gives written notice of challenge within five Working Days and pays for an independent analysis of a retained split sample.
5.3 The Discharger shall carry out its own composite sampling at least once every two weeks and shall send the results to the Authority within seven days of receiving them from the laboratory.
5.4 The Discharger shall keep records of production, cleaning chemicals used, and flow readings for six years and make them available on request.

6. Notification of incidents

6.1 The Discharger shall tell the Authority by telephone without delay, and in any event within one hour of becoming aware, of any spill, leak or accident that has caused or is likely to cause a breach of this Agreement or the discharge of a Prohibited Substance.
6.2 A written report shall follow within three Working Days, setting out the cause, the quantity and nature of the substance, the actions taken, and measures to prevent a recurrence.
6.3 Failure to report an incident under this clause is a material breach, even if no harm results.

7. Change of process

7.1 The Discharger shall not change its process, raw materials or cleaning chemicals in a way that is likely to alter the volume or quality of the Effluent materially without giving the Authority thirty days' written notice.
7.2 The Authority may, within twenty Working Days of notice under clause 7.1, require a revised assessment, the cost of which shall be borne by the Discharger, and may vary the limits in Schedule 1 to reflect the change.

8. Charges

8.1 The Discharger shall pay the Authority a charge for each quarter calculated by the formula in Schedule 5, which reflects the volume received and the Strength of the Effluent as measured under clause 5.
8.2 The standard unit rates at the Commencement Date are: 1.12 pounds per cubic metre for volume; 0.38 pounds per cubic metre for sewer conveyance; and 0.0161 pounds per cubic metre for each 100 milligrams per litre of Strength above 400 milligrams per litre.
8.3 Rates may be revised each 1 April by the Authority, up to a cap equal to the increase in the national consumer price index over the previous year plus 3 percentage points. Increases above the cap require the Discharger's consent.
8.4 A surcharge of 25 percent applies to the volume charge for any day on which the Daily Volume exceeds the limit in clause 3.1 with the Authority's agreement, and a surcharge of 100 percent applies to any day on which it exceeds that limit without agreement.
8.5 Invoices are payable within thirty days. Interest on late payments accrues at 4 percent a year above the reference rate published by the Authority.
8.6 The Discharger shall pay the Authority's reasonable costs of sampling and analysis, including the costs of any analysis showing a breach, and a fixed administration fee of 450 pounds for each sample showing a breach of Schedule 1.

9. Breach and enforcement

9.1 If the Effluent breaches Schedule 1 or the Discharger breaches clause 4.2, 4.3 or 6, the Authority may by written notice require remedy within a time that is reasonable in the circumstances, and where there is an immediate risk to the Works, the sewer or public health, the Authority may suspend the discharge without notice.
9.2 The Authority may recover from the Discharger the costs it reasonably incurs in dealing with any damage to the sewer or the Works, or in treating Effluent that exceeds limits, including any fine imposed on the Authority by a regulator as a result of the Discharger's breach.
9.3 Three breaches of Schedule 1 in any twelve-month period entitle the Authority to terminate this Agreement on fourteen days' notice.
9.4 Nothing in this clause limits the Authority's statutory powers.

10. Liability and insurance

10.1 The Discharger is liable for loss or damage caused to the Authority, its staff or its property by Effluent not complying with this Agreement, without limit.
10.2 The Authority's liability to the Discharger for any failure to receive Effluent, including by reason of a blockage, flood or breakdown of the Works, is limited to a refund of the volume charge for the days affected. The Authority is not liable for lost production or lost profit.
10.3 The Discharger shall maintain pollution liability insurance of not less than 2 million pounds for each claim and shall produce the certificate on request.

11. Term, renewal and termination

11.1 This Agreement runs for three years from the Commencement Date and then renews for successive one-year periods unless either party gives six months' written notice before the end of the term.
11.2 Either party may terminate this Agreement on ninety days' written notice if a material change in law or in the licence under which the Works is operated makes it impracticable to continue.
11.3 On termination the Discharger shall cap or seal the connection at its own cost within thirty days, unless the Authority agrees otherwise.

12. Confidentiality and data

12.1 Each party shall keep confidential the information the other supplies under this Agreement, except where disclosure is required by law, by a regulator, or in proceedings under this Agreement.
12.2 The Authority may publish aggregated data on trade effluent in its area, provided the Discharger is not named.

13. General

13.1 This Agreement is the entire agreement between the parties about its subject matter.
13.2 Notices must be in writing and sent to the addresses in the Particulars, and are treated as received two Working Days after posting or on the next Working Day after an email sent before 17:00.
13.3 This Agreement is governed by the law of England and Wales. Disputes about the quality of Effluent shall be referred to an independent expert who is a Fellow of the relevant professional body, whose determination is final on matters of fact. Other disputes are for the courts.

14. Access and inspection

14.1 Authorised officers of the Authority may enter the Discharger's premises at any reasonable time, and at any time in an emergency, to inspect pipework, take samples, read meters and check the screen and fat trap, on production of identification.
14.2 The Discharger shall provide a safe means of access to Manhole M-14 and the sampling chamber and shall keep both clear of obstruction. If the Authority cannot sample because access is blocked, the Authority may treat the next result obtained as representative of the intervening period.
14.3 The Authority shall give the Discharger a copy of any inspection report within ten Working Days.

15. Events beyond a party's control

15.1 Neither party is in breach of this Agreement to the extent that it is prevented from performing by flood, fire, strike (other than by its own staff), failure of public utilities or an order of a public authority, provided that it tells the other party promptly and does what it reasonably can to limit the effect.
15.2 This clause does not excuse a failure to pay money, and does not excuse the discharge of a Prohibited Substance.

16. Assignment of the Authority's rights

16.1 The Authority may transfer this Agreement to any successor body that takes over operation of the Works, on notice to the Discharger. The Discharger's rights under this Agreement are unaffected.

Schedule 1 (limits, full table)

Parameter | Limit | Type of limit
pH | 6.0 to 10.0 | any single sample
Temperature | 40 degrees Celsius | any single sample
Chemical Oxygen Demand | 3,000 mg/l | daily composite
Suspended solids | 800 mg/l | daily composite
Fats, oils and grease | 100 mg/l | daily composite
Total sulphite | 10 mg/l | any single sample
Ammoniacal nitrogen | 200 mg/l | daily composite
Total phosphorus | 40 mg/l | daily composite

Schedule 2 (sampling method, summary)

A composite sample is made from at least twelve equal portions taken at regular intervals over the twenty-four hours beginning at 06:00, or from a flow-proportional sampler where one is installed. Samples are stored at not more than 4 degrees Celsius and delivered to an accredited laboratory within twenty-four hours. Each sample is divided into two parts; one is analysed and one is retained, sealed, for fourteen days. Analysis for Chemical Oxygen Demand uses the unsettled sample, shaken before analysis.

Schedule 3 (extract): Prohibited Substances include petrol and other flammable solvents; pesticides and herbicides; whole fruit stones and shell in quantities likely to block pipes; wipes and plastic packaging; hot water above 40 degrees Celsius; strong acid or alkali outside the pH range; and chlorine bleach above 50 milligrams per litre in the Effluent.

Schedule 4 (screen and fat trap)

The screen must be cleared at least daily and its contents disposed of as solid waste, not rinsed into the drain. The fat trap shall have a retention volume of not less than 6 cubic metres and shall be emptied by a licensed carrier at least every four weeks; waste transfer notes shall be kept for six years. The Authority may require a larger trap if the fats, oils and grease results exceed 80 milligrams per litre on two occasions in a quarter.

Schedule 5 (charging formula, summary)

The quarterly charge is the sum of: the volume charge (the metered or estimated volume received, in cubic metres, multiplied by the volume rate); the conveyance charge (the same volume multiplied by the conveyance rate); and the strength charge. The strength charge is the volume multiplied by the strength rate multiplied by the amount by which the average Strength for the quarter, taken from the results of samples under clause 5, exceeds 400 milligrams per litre, divided by 100. Where fewer than three valid results exist for the quarter, the Authority may use the highest result in the preceding twelve months.

Particulars: Authority contact, Trade Effluent Officer, Gwyneth Darrowby, telephone 01632 960 114, email effluent@example.org. Discharger contact, Operations Director, Callum Ashgrove. Out-of-hours emergency line for the Authority: 01632 960 999.

A colleague and I wrote up the methods and results of a trial we ran at our newspaper, and we are about to submit it to a journal on media economics. Please act as a demanding peer reviewer. I'd like a detailed review that covers the design, the statistics, whether the conclusions follow from the numbers, threats to validity, and what you would require in a revision. Rank your concerns by importance and be specific about what analysis or additional data would resolve each one.

Title: Does a curated email digest improve digital subscriber retention at a regional daily? A randomised trial at the Harrowgate Courier

Authors: Odile Thackeray and Benedikt Rowanfield, Audience Research Desk, Harrowgate Courier

Abstract (short form). We randomised 18,000 digital subscribers of a regional newspaper to receive no additional email, a weekly digest of local court, council and schools reporting, or a daily personalised email of up to five articles. Retention at 90 days was 81.2 percent in the control arm, 83.9 percent in the weekly arm and 82.6 percent in the daily arm. The weekly digest raised retention by 2.7 percentage points (95 percent CI 1.3 to 4.1); the daily email by 1.4 points (0.0 to 2.8). Effects were concentrated among subscribers who joined on a promotional price and among those who had read fewer than four articles in their first month.

1. Background

Regional newspapers in our market have lost most of their print readers over twenty years and now depend on digital subscriptions. At the Courier, about 31,000 people pay for digital access at an average of 9.40 pounds a month, and about 2.3 percent of them cancel each month. Newsroom managers believe that subscribers cancel because they do not form a habit of visiting the site, and that reminders to read local stories will reduce cancellations. The editorial team was, however, concerned that a daily email would feel like marketing and train readers to wait for the email instead of coming to the site.

We tested two designs. The weekly digest is edited by a human, appears on Saturday morning, and carries six stories chosen by the news editor, with a short note by the reporter. The daily email is produced by a ranking program that selects up to five unread stories for each subscriber from the last 24 hours, based on the subscriber's reading history and the town or district they chose at sign-up.

2. Methods

2.1 Population. All digital-only subscribers who had been active (paid in the last billing cycle) on 3 March were eligible, except staff, free-trial users, and subscribers who had opted out of all marketing email. This gave 19,126 eligible subscribers. Of these, 1,126 were excluded because the email address bounced in the two weeks before randomisation, leaving 18,000.

2.2 Randomisation. Subscribers were assigned at random to one of three arms in equal numbers (6,000 each) using a seeded pseudo-random number generator, stratified by tenure (under six months, six to twenty-four months, over twenty-four months) and by plan type (full price or promotional price). Assignment was made by a person not involved in the later analysis. Subscribers were not told they were part of a trial; this was approved by the company's data protection officer on the grounds that the emails fell within existing marketing consent.

2.3 Interventions. Control subscribers received the standard account emails (receipts, renewals, password resets) and a monthly company newsletter, as before. Weekly-arm subscribers also received the digest every Saturday for twelve weeks. Daily-arm subscribers also received a personalised email every day at 06:45 for twelve weeks. Subscribers who unsubscribed from the digest or daily email stopped receiving it but stayed in their assigned arm for analysis.

2.4 Outcomes. The primary outcome was retention at 90 days after the start date of 10 March, defined as the subscription still being active (not cancelled and not lapsed for non-payment) on 8 June. Secondary outcomes were the number of days with at least one site visit in weeks 5 to 12, the number of articles read per active week, and the email unsubscribe rate. All outcomes were taken from the billing system and the site's analytics logs.

2.5 Analysis. We compared each treatment arm with control by intention to treat, using a difference in proportions with a normal-approximation confidence interval for the primary outcome and a logistic regression adjusted for the stratification variables as a sensitivity check. We tested whether effects differed by tenure and plan type by adding interaction terms. Visit counts were compared by the Mann-Whitney test. We did not adjust for multiple comparisons in the primary analysis because we pre-specified two treatment-versus-control tests; the subgroup analyses should be read as exploratory.

2.6 Sample size. We assumed 81 percent baseline retention at 90 days and aimed to detect a difference of 2.5 percentage points with 80 percent power at a two-sided 5 percent significance level. This required about 5,300 per arm; we used 6,000 to allow for bounces and unexpected losses.

3. Results

3.1 Balance and flow. The arms were balanced on tenure, plan type, district and prior reading activity (Table 1). Between randomisation and the start date, 62 subscribers cancelled before receiving any email (22 control, 19 weekly, 21 daily); we kept them in the analysis as not retained. Over the twelve weeks, 11.8 percent of the weekly arm and 19.4 percent of the daily arm unsubscribed from the additional email.

Table 1. Baseline characteristics by arm

| Characteristic | Control (n=6,000) | Weekly (n=6,000) | Daily (n=6,000) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Joined under 6 months before | 24.1% | 23.8% | 24.4% |
| Promotional price | 38.5% | 38.9% | 38.2% |
| Mean articles read in prior 30 days | 11.3 | 11.1 | 11.4 |
| Chose a city-centre district | 46.0% | 45.7% | 46.4% |

3.2 Primary outcome. Retention at 90 days was 81.2 percent (4,872 of 6,000) in the control arm, 83.9 percent (5,034) in the weekly arm and 82.6 percent (4,956) in the daily arm. The weekly digest increased retention by 2.7 percentage points (95 percent CI 1.3 to 4.1; p < 0.001). The daily email increased it by 1.4 points (95 percent CI 0.0 to 2.8; p = 0.046). The adjusted odds ratios from the logistic model were 1.19 (1.08 to 1.31) for the weekly arm and 1.09 (1.00 to 1.19) for the daily arm.

3.3 Secondary outcomes. In weeks 5 to 12, active weeks in the control arm included a mean of 2.4 days with a site visit. The weekly arm averaged 2.6 days and the daily arm 3.1 days (both p < 0.001 against control). Articles read per active week were 5.2 in control, 5.5 in the weekly arm and 6.4 in the daily arm. In other words, the daily email produced more reading than the digest but less retention.

3.4 Subgroups. The effect of the weekly digest on retention was 4.6 points among promotional-price subscribers (n=2,334 in that arm) and 1.5 points among full-price subscribers. The interaction was significant at the 5 percent level (p = 0.03). Among subscribers who joined under six months before, the weekly effect was 3.9 points and the daily effect 2.8 points; among those with over twenty-four months' tenure, the effects were 1.1 and 0.4 points, with confidence intervals including zero.

Table 2. Retention at 90 days by arm and plan type

| Plan type | Control | Weekly | Daily |
|---|---|---|---|
| Full price | 85.0% | 86.5% | 85.9% |
| Promotional | 74.9% | 79.5% | 77.1% |

3.5 Light readers. We split subscribers by whether they had read fewer than four articles in their first month. Among 3,402 light readers (all arms), retention in the control arm was 69.8 percent and the weekly digest raised it by 6.1 points. Among heavier readers the weekly effect was 1.4 points. This split was not pre-specified.

3.6 Unsubscribes and complaints. Unsubscribing from the daily email was more common among subscribers in the city-centre districts (22.1 percent) than in the outlying villages (15.6 percent). The customer service desk logged 41 complaints that mentioned the emails, of which 33 were in the daily arm.

3.7 Email delivery and engagement. Open rates, as recorded by the email platform, averaged 46 percent for the weekly digest and 31 percent for the daily email across the twelve weeks. Click-through rates were 9.8 percent and 6.2 percent. Open rates for the daily email fell from 42 percent in week one to 26 percent in week twelve, while the weekly digest fell from 51 percent to 43 percent. Open tracking is unreliable for subscribers who block images, and we treat these figures as indicative only.

3.8 Robustness. A logistic regression that added prior reading activity, district and sign-up channel as covariates changed the odds ratios by less than 0.02 in either arm. Dropping the 62 subscribers who cancelled before the start date raised the weekly effect to 2.8 points and the daily effect to 1.5 points. A complete-case analysis of the 90-day outcome is identical to the main analysis because no subscriber had a missing outcome.

Table 3. Secondary outcomes in weeks 5 to 12

| Outcome | Control | Weekly | Daily |
|---|---|---|---|
| Days with a visit per active week | 2.4 | 2.6 | 3.1 |
| Articles read per active week | 5.2 | 5.5 | 6.4 |
| Unsubscribed from the extra email | not applicable | 11.8% | 19.4% |
| Customer complaints mentioning email | 2 | 6 | 33 |

4. Discussion

The weekly human-edited digest produced a retention gain of about 2.7 points. At the Courier's average revenue per subscriber of 9.40 pounds a month, a gain of 2.7 points in 90-day retention among 31,000 subscribers is worth, on a simple calculation, about 7,800 pounds a month in preserved revenue in the first quarter after rollout, though this is a first-order estimate and assumes the effect lasts. The digest costs roughly one half-day of the news editor's time each week and a small platform fee.

The daily email increased reading more than the digest but did not increase retention by more. One possible reading is that the daily email improves habit but also annoys a share of subscribers, as the higher unsubscribe and complaint rates suggest. A second reading is that what matters for retention is the sense of editorial selection, not volume. We did not test either explanation directly.

The concentration of effects among promotional-price and light-reading subscribers suggests that the digest helps people who are least anchored to the product. This is consistent with the view that cancellations are partly a habit problem. It also suggests that the benefit of the digest may fall if the subscriber base shifts toward heavier readers.

4.1 Practical implications. The newsroom has asked whether to adopt the weekly digest permanently. On our evidence the answer is probably yes, provided the news editor can continue to select the stories. The daily email is harder to justify. It produced a modest and borderline retention gain at the cost of a fifth of recipients opting out and most of the complaints. If the company wants a daily product, we suggest testing a version with a lower frequency, such as three days a week, and an easier way to choose topics before sending it to everyone.

We also note that the digest is an editorial product as well as a retention tool. Reporters told us in interviews after the trial that it gave their court and council coverage a wider audience than it had on the site alone, and the news editor reported that the selection task helped her see which local stories were being missed. These are anecdotes and we have not measured them.

5. Limitations

Several limitations apply. First, 90 days is short; we do not know whether retained subscribers stay beyond six months. We plan to extend follow-up to twelve months. Second, on 24 April, in week seven, the Courier launched a redesigned website and a new app. This applied to all arms but could interact with the email effect, for example by making links in the digest land on a more attractive page. Third, the outcome is subscription status and not reading satisfaction; we have no survey data. Fourth, 1,126 subscribers with bounced addresses were excluded, and these are likely to be less engaged than average, so our results apply to reachable subscribers. Fifth, the study took place in one market, with one newsroom, and a particularly strong court reporting team whose work formed the core of the digest.

6. Ethics and data

The trial was reviewed by the company's data protection officer and the editor in chief. No subscriber was denied any service they had paid for. Individual-level data were held in the company's analytics warehouse and analysed there; the shared dataset used for the tables in this paper has no names or email addresses and has been rounded so that no cell in any subgroup contains fewer than ten subscribers. The pre-registration, written before the start date, is held internally and is available to reviewers on request. The ranking program used for the daily email is proprietary, and we describe its inputs but not its code.

Here are the first four chapters of a short story I'm working on. Please continue it for as long as you can, at least the next two chapters and ideally the ending, in the same close third person, past tense, dry and slightly rueful voice. Keep the characters and the facts I've established, let the Halloran Arms matter to the plot, and don't resolve everything neatly.

THE LAST ROOM IN SKELLIGAN BAY

1.

The first thing Marit Osei learned about hotels was that they were all lying about the pillows.

She learned it in the second month of Nestwell's existence, in a rented room above a bicycle shop in the east end of the city, where three people and a whiteboard did what the investor deck called "building the future of independent stays" and what Leif, the other founder, called "being polite to spreadsheets." The company's idea was simple enough to fit on a beer mat. There were thousands of small hotels, guesthouses and inns that took their bookings by telephone, by email, or on a website last updated by a nephew. There were millions of travellers who did not want to book through the big platforms, which took eighteen percent and offered nothing in return but a ranking. Nestwell would take six percent and give the small hotels a booking page that worked, a calendar that did not double-book, and a way to say, truthfully, what the rooms were like.

The truth was the difficult part. Marit had assumed it would be the software.

"Listen to this one," Leif said, reading from his laptop with the flat voice he used for quoting other people's prose. "'Our rooms are furnished with hypoallergenic goose-down pillows of the highest quality.' It's a guesthouse in Dunmore Cross. They're forty pounds a night."

"And?"

"And I phoned them, pretending to be a customer, and the woman said the pillows come from the cash and carry. She said they were nice and bouncy. She said the word goose might have been her husband's idea."

Marit looked at the whiteboard, where the problem had been written three days earlier in her own handwriting: WHAT DO GUESTS WANT TO KNOW? Under it, in a different pen, someone had added: THE TRUTH. And under that, in Leif's tidy capitals: WHICH TRUTH?

The third member of the team, a quiet developer named Anselm who communicated mostly in pull requests, had built the first version of the booking page in nine days. It was clean and fast and it showed a hotel's rooms the way a good friend would describe them. There was a field for the number of steps to the front door. There was a field for whether the shower was over the bath. There was a field, which Marit had insisted on and which Leif had called "a lawsuit with a text box", for the worst thing about the room. A guesthouse in Dunmore Cross would say, in its own words, that the window looked onto the bins but that the bins were collected on Tuesdays and it was a Friday.

That field was the reason the first fourteen hotels signed up, and the reason forty others did not.

2.

By March they had sixty-one hotels, an office with a door, and a number called the repeat rate, which Leif had learned to say in a hushed tone. It meant the share of guests who booked a second time through Nestwell. It was thirty-four percent. The large platforms, Leif said, were probably at eleven.

The investor was a woman named Philippa Strand who ran a small fund out of an office with a view of a car park, and who had said yes to Nestwell in forty minutes. She came to the office once a month, brought biscuits that nobody ate, and asked questions that sounded gentle and were not.

"What happens," she said in March, sitting in the only good chair, "when you have a bad hotel?"

"We don't have bad hotels," said Leif.

"You have sixty-one hotels. One of them is bad. Or will be. A hotel is a building full of people who are tired, and sooner or later one of them has a morning when the boiler goes and the cook leaves and a guest posts something awful. What does Nestwell do?"

Marit had thought about this at three in the morning many times and had never reached a satisfying answer. She said, "We tell the truth about it."

"To whom?"

"To the next guest."

Philippa looked at her for a moment, in the particular way of someone deciding whether an answer is brave or stupid. "That's the product," she said. "It is also the risk. If you tell the truth about one of your own hotels and it ruins them, you will have ruined a customer. If you don't, you're one more platform. I'd like to be in the first company. I'm just telling you that it costs money."

She left the biscuits. That night, Anselm ate all of them without comment, and Leif, who had been thinking about the repeat rate, said, "She's wrong, you know. The truth is a feature. It's the only feature we have."

Marit did not tell him that she had been thinking about the Halloran Arms.

Instead she opened the dashboard and looked at the thing she looked at every evening, the list of guest comments that the system flagged for human reading. There were four that week. A hotel in a market town had a guest who disliked the carpet. A guesthouse by a railway line had been described as "exactly as noisy as promised, which I respect." A third was a complaint about parking, written in capitals. The fourth was from a man who said only that he had been very happy and that his wife had cried at breakfast, which Anselm had flagged as probable sarcasm and Marit, reading it again, thought was not.

She marked all four as read. It was a small ritual and it did not help. Every comment was a hotel, and every hotel was a person with a mortgage, and the thing she had built was a lens that made all of them a little larger than they wished to be.


The Halloran Arms was in Skelligan Bay, a village on the north coast with one street, one chip shop and a ferry that ran when the weather allowed. It had eleven rooms, a bar with a fire, and a landlord named Declan Abara who had signed up to Nestwell in the first week and whose reviews, on the whole, were the best the company had. Guests wrote that the beds were soft, the breakfast was enormous, and Mr Abara remembered their names. In the "worst thing" field, Declan had written: "The road is long and the signal is bad. If you want to be left alone, this is the place."

There was only one other thing in the file, a note Marit had added herself after a phone call in January. It said: "Dec. mentioned the roof. Said it was nothing. Ask again in spring."

It was spring. She had not asked.

3.

The ferry did not run on the day Marit went to Skelligan Bay, so she drove, which took five hours instead of two and a half, and arrived in the village at a quarter past four with the light already going yellow on the water.

The Halloran Arms looked better than its photographs. This surprised her, because Nestwell's photographs were taken by Anselm, who had no gift for flattery. The building was long and low and painted the colour of old cream, with a slate roof, and a hand-lettered sign swinging by the door. In the bar, a fire was lit though it was April and warm. Behind the counter stood a man in his sixties with a grey beard and the forearms of someone who had carried a lot of barrels, polishing a glass that was already clean.

"You're the girl from the internet," he said.

"Marit. We spoke in January."

"I know who you are. You wrote me a very nice email about pillows." Declan Abara put the glass down. "Will you eat? There's a fish pie. It's the only thing in the kitchen, but it's a good one."

She ate the fish pie, which was a good one, and a young woman named Saoirse, who turned out to be Declan's niece and who worked every job in the building, brought her tea without being asked. The bar filled slowly with the tired, cheerful people of a village evening: two men from the harbour, a retired teacher, a couple on a walking holiday who had booked through Nestwell and recognised the logo on Marit's jacket.

"You're the people with the honest page," the woman said. "We chose you because of the bit about the bins. We thought, anyone who says that must be telling the truth about the rest."

"And was it?"

"The bins were exactly as described," the woman said happily. "There was a seagull on one."

Marit laughed, and felt something loosen in her chest, and was surprised by how tightly it had been held. It was the repeat rate. It was Philippa's question. It was the sixty-one hotels, any one of which might at any moment turn out to be a lie. And here was a woman with a muddy coat saying that a seagull on a bin was proof of integrity, and Marit could have wept.

She waited until the bar had thinned out and then went to find Declan in the kitchen, where he was scraping a pan.

"The roof," she said.

He did not turn around. "Ah."

"In January you said it was nothing."

"I said it was nothing to worry about, which is a different sentence." He set the pan down. He had the manner, she noticed, of a man who had practised this conversation in the mirror. "There's a leak above room nine. I've had a man look. He says it's the whole north slope. He says it's the timbers and not the slates, which means new timbers, which means scaffolding, which means the best part of sixty thousand. I have eleven thousand. I have a bank manager who is very fond of me and very unable."

"When?"

"The man says one more bad winter. Maybe two. I say the Lord is generous with winters." He smiled, and it was not a joke. "I haven't told the others. Saoirse knows. I'm not asking you to put it on the page."

Marit stood in the warm, fishy air of the kitchen, and in her mind she saw the worst-thing field, the little box that Leif called a lawsuit, and what she saw in it was not the Halloran Arms' roof but the line from Philippa's mouth: it costs money. If she wrote that the Halloran Arms had a failing roof, the booking page would be honest, and for the next three months every other guest would see it and think twice. If she did not write it, she would have a company whose entire product was a promise that she was now ready to break for a man who made good fish pie.

"I'm not going to ask you to say anything," she said. "Not yet."

"That's kind."

"It isn't kind. It's me not having worked out what I think." She pushed her hair out of her eyes. "Can I see room nine?"

It was at the end of the upstairs corridor, a clean, white, cold room with a blue quilt and a view of the bay. A bucket stood in the corner under a brown stain the shape of Ireland, and the sound of the sea came through the glass. Marit stood in it for some time. She thought, absurdly, of the woman in Dunmore Cross and her bouncy pillows, and of how little it had taken to make a lie, and how little to make a truth.

When she came back down, Saoirse was waiting at the foot of the stairs with her arms folded.

"Uncle Declan says you're not going to put it on the website."

"He says I haven't decided."

"There's a difference?" Saoirse said. "Because from where I'm standing it looks like a company that tells everyone to be honest, and then gets very quiet when the honest thing is expensive." She said it without heat, in the voice of someone who had been told for years to be pleasant to visitors and had finally lost patience with the habit. "My uncle's going to lose this place. You know that. The only question is whether the next hundred guests know it before they book, or after."

Outside, the ferry horn sounded across the water, late, long and low, as if the sea itself had decided to weigh in.

4.

She was given room four, which had no stain and no bucket and the kind of bed that makes a person suspicious of her own exhaustion. At eleven she sat on the quilt with her shoes still on and phoned Leif, who answered on the first ring, as he always did, as if he slept beside the phone.

"How is it?" he said. "Is it good? Tell me it's good. Tell me they have a great story. Philippa will want a case study."

"It's good," Marit said. "It's the best one we have. The roof's going."

There was a silence in which she could hear him sit up. "Going how?"

She told him: the timbers, the sixty thousand, the eleven, the bank manager who was fond and unable. She told him about the bucket and Saoirse and the seagull on the bin. She did not tell him that she had stood in room nine for a long time, or that she had thought about the woman with the muddy coat, because these things sounded, said aloud, like a person looking for a reason.

"Right," said Leif, in the voice he used for problems that had numbers in them. "So we put it on the page. We say, honestly, there is a roof issue, the owner is repairing it, and, I don't know, we add a donation button. People love a donation button. We could do a fund. We take nothing. Six percent of nothing. We'd be the platform that saved a pub."

"And if they don't give?"

"Then the page says the roof's failing and the bookings drop and Declan goes under in the winter instead of in two years." He stopped. "I'm not saying that's what we do. I'm saying that's the shape of it."

"You said the truth was a feature," Marit said.

"It is." He sounded, for the first time that week, tired. "It's also, apparently, a very expensive thing to be right about."

When she put the phone down the room was dark and the sea was still arguing with the glass. Somewhere below her, the fire in the bar had been banked, and she could hear Declan's slow tread crossing the floor, checking the doors one by one, a man making sure that a house he might lose was safe for the night.

We are about to start testing the system described below and I need a complete test plan for it. Please give me the test strategy, then detailed test cases grouped by requirement (with ID, preconditions, steps, expected result and priority), the negative and boundary cases, the data and environments we will need, and a short list of the cases that must pass before we can go live on the paper machine. Flag any requirement that is ambiguous or untestable as written.

PRODUCT SPECIFICATION
Reel Tracking and Quality Release System (RTQ), version 1.2
Ashgrove Fine Paper Mill, Paper Machine 3 (PM3)
Owner: Quality Systems. Specification author: Wilhelmina Ostrander. Status: approved for build.

1. Purpose

PM3 produces coated and uncoated fine paper in jumbo reels up to 8.4 metres wide, which are rewound into customer reels and sheeted. At present the quality laboratory records its measurements on forms, the operators write the reel number on the reel by hand, and the warehouse learns about quality holds by telephone. Twice last year a reel that should have been held was shipped. RTQ replaces the forms and phone calls with a system that identifies each reel, receives its measurements, decides whether it can be released, and prevents the warehouse from loading a reel that is not released.

2. Definitions

- Jumbo reel: the full-width reel that comes off the machine's reel-up, identified by a jumbo number.
- Child reel: a reel cut from a jumbo at the winder, identified by the jumbo number plus a two-digit position.
- Grade: a product specification, such as G-90C (90 gram per square metre coated). Each grade has limits for basis weight, moisture, caliper, brightness and smoothness.
- Test: a measurement of one property, taken from a sample strip cut from the end of the jumbo reel by the laboratory.
- Hold: a state that prevents loading and shipping of a reel.
- Release: a state that allows a reel to be loaded and shipped.

3. Users and roles

| Role | Can do |
|---|---|
| Machine operator | Start and finish jumbo reels; view test results; request a hold |
| Laboratory technician | Enter and amend test results; cannot release |
| Quality supervisor | Release or reject reels; override a hold with a reason; change grade limits |
| Winder operator | Create child reels from a jumbo; print child labels |
| Warehouse clerk | View status; scan reels for loading; cannot change status |
| Administrator | Manage users and roles |

4. Functional requirements

4.1 Reel identification

REQ-101. When an operator starts a new jumbo reel at the reel-up, the system shall create a record with a unique jumbo number, the grade, the start time and the machine speed at start. Jumbo numbers are the date in the form YYMMDD followed by a three-digit daily sequence that restarts at 001 each day at 06:00.
REQ-102. The system shall not allow two jumbo reels with the same number, and shall not allow a jumbo to be started while another jumbo on PM3 is open, unless the earlier one has been finished.
REQ-103. When a jumbo is finished, the operator shall enter the finishing weight in kilograms and the system shall record the end time. The weight must be between 8,000 and 32,000 kilograms; values outside this range shall be rejected with a message.
REQ-104. The system shall print a label for each jumbo reel containing the number, the grade, the weight, and a Code 128 barcode of the number.

4.2 Test results

REQ-201. The laboratory technician shall enter results for the following properties for each jumbo: basis weight (g/m2), moisture (percent), caliper (micrometres), brightness (percent) and smoothness (ml/min). Each result is stored with the technician, the time of entry, and the instrument identifier.
REQ-202. Test results shall be validated against physical bounds: basis weight 30 to 300, moisture 0 to 15, caliper 20 to 400, brightness 50 to 120, smoothness 5 to 5,000. A value outside bounds shall be rejected.
REQ-203. The system shall compare each result with the limits of the jumbo's grade and mark it as in limits, in warning (within 10 percent of the width of the permitted band from either limit), or out of limits.
REQ-204. A result may be amended by a laboratory technician only within 60 minutes of entry. After that, only a quality supervisor may amend it, and the original value shall be kept in the history with the reason for the change.
REQ-205. For each property a jumbo may have up to three results (the first test and up to two retests). The latest result is used for the decision in 4.3, but all are displayed.

4.3 Automatic decision and release

REQ-301. When all five properties have at least one result, the system shall compute a recommended status for the jumbo: "recommend release" if every latest result is in limits or in warning; "recommend hold" if any latest result is out of limits; "incomplete" if any property has no result.
REQ-302. A jumbo shall be in state Held automatically from the moment it is finished until a quality supervisor releases it. No jumbo is released automatically, even if the recommendation is "recommend release".
REQ-303. A quality supervisor may release a jumbo only if the status is "recommend release", or after an override with a reason of at least 20 characters when the status is "recommend hold".
REQ-304. A quality supervisor may reject a jumbo. A rejected jumbo cannot be released later; it may only be reclassified by creating a new record with a new grade, subject to REQ-303.
REQ-305. An operator may place a released jumbo back on hold at any time by giving a reason. Only a quality supervisor can release it again.
REQ-306. Every status change shall be logged with the user, the time, the old and new state and the reason (where required).

4.4 Child reels

REQ-401. The winder operator shall create child reels from a jumbo by entering for each child the width in millimetres, the diameter in millimetres, and the weight in kilograms. Position numbers are assigned automatically from 01.
REQ-402. A child reel inherits the status of its jumbo. If the jumbo is placed on hold, all of its children are placed on hold, including those already created.
REQ-403. The sum of child weights shall not exceed the jumbo's finishing weight. The system shall warn if the sum is less than 90 percent of the finishing weight and require confirmation to proceed.
REQ-404. The system shall print a label for each child reel with a barcode of the child number, the grade, width, diameter and weight, and the customer order number if one is entered.
REQ-405. A child reel can be assigned to a customer order only if its jumbo is Released.

4.5 Warehouse scan

REQ-501. When a warehouse clerk scans a child reel for loading, the system shall respond within 2 seconds with Released, Held, Rejected or Unknown.
REQ-502. Only reels in the Released state may be added to a shipment. A scan of any other state shall show a red screen and sound a tone, and shall be logged.
REQ-503. A reel may appear on only one shipment. A second scan of an already loaded reel shall show the shipment it is on.
REQ-504. The warehouse shall be able to print a shipment list of reels with their numbers, weights and customer order numbers.

4.6 Notifications

REQ-701. When a jumbo is finished, the system shall display it on the laboratory's work list within 10 seconds, sorted by finish time, oldest first. A jumbo not fully tested 90 minutes after finishing shall be shown in amber, and after 180 minutes in red.
REQ-702. When a jumbo is placed on hold or rejected, the system shall send an email to the quality supervisor on duty, the shift manager and the warehouse supervisor within one minute. The message shall include the jumbo number, the grade, the reason and the number of child reels affected.
REQ-703. When a released jumbo is placed back on hold and any of its children are already on a closed shipment, the system shall flag the shipment as "affected" and display it on the quality supervisor's home screen until acknowledged.
REQ-704. The shift list of the quality supervisors on duty is maintained by the administrator. If no supervisor is on duty, notifications go to the shift manager only and a note is written to the audit log.

4.7 Retained samples

REQ-801. For every jumbo, the laboratory shall record the storage location of the retained sample strip (a rack letter and a slot number, such as C-14). The record is mandatory before the jumbo's first release.
REQ-802. Retained samples are kept for 24 months. The system shall list each month the samples that have passed their retention date, and the laboratory technician shall mark them as discarded.

5. Reports

REQ-601. A daily quality report shall list each jumbo finished in the previous 24 hours, with its test results, status, and the name of the person who released it.
REQ-602. A traceability report, given a child reel number, shall show the jumbo, its tests, its status history and the shipment, within 5 seconds.
REQ-603. A monthly report shall show the percentage of jumbos released first time, the percentage held, the percentage rejected, and the mean time from finish to release.

6. Non-functional requirements

NFR-1. The system shall be available 24 hours a day, every day, with unplanned downtime not exceeding 8 hours a year. Planned maintenance is announced 48 hours in advance.
NFR-2. All screens shall work on the mill's rugged tablets (10-inch, a standard browser) and on desktop computers.
NFR-3. If the network between the laboratory and the server is lost, the laboratory screens shall keep data entered for up to 4 hours and send it when the network returns. Releases and holds are not allowed while offline.
NFR-4. Passwords expire every 90 days. Accounts lock after five failed attempts for 15 minutes.
NFR-5. The audit log is read-only for all users including administrators and is kept for 10 years.
NFR-6. The system shall support 15 simultaneous users with all screens responding in under 2 seconds at the 95th percentile.
NFR-7. Data shall be backed up every night and restored to an alternative server within 4 hours.

7. Interfaces

7.1 Machine control system. At the start and end of each jumbo, the machine control system sends a message with the machine speed and the grade code. If the grade code in the message does not match any known grade, the start is rejected and the operator is told.
7.2 Laboratory instruments. The moisture and brightness instruments export a result file every minute to a shared folder. RTQ reads these files and offers the values to the technician for confirmation; the technician must confirm each value before it is stored. Files that cannot be parsed are moved to an error folder and an alert is displayed.
7.3 Enterprise resource planning (ERP). RTQ receives open customer orders from ERP each night at 01:00 and sends shipment confirmations to ERP when a shipment is closed.

8. Grade limits, initial data

| Grade | Basis weight | Moisture | Caliper | Brightness | Smoothness |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| G-80U (80 g/m2 uncoated) | 78 to 82 | 4.5 to 5.5 | 100 to 108 | 92 to 96 | 150 to 250 |
| G-90C (90 g/m2 coated) | 88 to 92 | 4.8 to 5.8 | 82 to 90 | 94 to 98 | 800 to 1,200 |
| G-115C (115 g/m2 coated) | 112 to 118 | 4.8 to 5.8 | 105 to 115 | 94 to 98 | 800 to 1,200 |

9. Out of scope

Coating recipes, machine process control, maintenance management, and the invoicing of customers are not in this release.

10. Acceptance criteria for go-live

AC-1. All requirements of priority "must" in sections 4 and 6 pass in the test environment with the data in section 8.
AC-2. A complete pilot of five working days on PM3 runs in parallel with the paper forms, with no discrepancy between the system's status and the status on the forms that cannot be explained.
AC-3. Every operator, technician, winder operator, warehouse clerk and quality supervisor has been trained by a trainer from Quality Systems, and has completed a practice session on the training copy.
AC-4. A restore from backup has been demonstrated within the 4 hours in NFR-7.
AC-5. The cutover plan has been agreed with the shift managers of all four shifts. The cutover takes place on a Sunday at 06:00, at the start of the production day, so that no jumbo is open during the change.

11. Priorities

Requirements REQ-101 to REQ-103, REQ-201 to REQ-205, REQ-301 to REQ-306, REQ-402, REQ-405, REQ-501 to REQ-503, NFR-3 and NFR-5 are priority "must". REQ-104, REQ-401, REQ-403, REQ-404, REQ-504, REQ-601, REQ-602, REQ-701 to REQ-704 and NFR-1, NFR-2, NFR-4, NFR-6 and NFR-7 are priority "should". All others are priority "could".

12. Known assumptions

- The machine control system can send the start and end messages in section 7.1; the supplier has confirmed this but the message format has not yet been tested at the mill.
- The two laboratory instruments in section 7.2 continue to export one file per measurement, as they do now.
- A jumbo reel is never split between two grades.
- Time on the server, the tablets and the machine control system is synchronised from the same source.

I teach the Hollowmere Field School and I have to write the season summary for the university and our landowner. Below is the finds table from this year's test-pit programme, with a short description of how it was collected. Please write me a full written analysis: what the data shows by area and by depth, what looks like real archaeological pattern and what could be an artefact of how we collected it, a few clear findings I can state with confidence, and a list of next steps for next season's trenches, including how to fix our data collection.

THE DATA

Hollowmere Field School, summer season 2026 (15 June to 10 July, four weeks). Twenty-two students worked in four teams, each led by one instructor, on a ploughed field and the edge of a former orchard above the river at Hollowmere. The aim was to find out where a suspected farmstead of the later medieval period lay and which part of the field to open next year.

We excavated 14 test pits, each 1 m by 1 m, in four areas laid out on a grid 30 m apart. Pits were dug by hand in arbitrary 10 cm spits (levels) from the surface down to sterile subsoil or clay, or until we ran out of time or the water table came up. All soil was dry-sieved. Each team worked one area, so the team and the area are the same thing in this data.

Columns in the table below:

- unit_id: pit number followed by the top and bottom depth of the spit in cm below the surface.
- area: the area, A to D.
- top_cm: depth of the top of the spit in cm (each spit is 10 cm thick).
- team: T1 (Area A, instructor Okonkwo), T2 (Area B, Vasquez), T3 (Area C, Lindqvist), T4 (Area D, Brandt).
- mesh_mm: the size of the sieve mesh used. Teams T1, T2 and T4 used 3 mm mesh. Team T3 used 6 mm mesh all season because their 3 mm screens broke on the first day and were not replaced.
- soil: a simple description of the soil.
- sherds: number of pottery sherds counted (all periods, including a few modern sherds).
- flakes: number of struck stone flakes (flint and chert).
- bone_g: weight of animal bone in grams, to the nearest tenth of a gram.
- charcoal: Y if any charcoal was seen in the spit, N if not. Not quantified.
- note: a field note where the student or instructor recorded something unusual. Blank means nothing recorded.

PIT SUMMARY (from the site diary)

| Area | Pits | Landscape position | Surface |
|---|---|---|---|

FIELD NOTES FROM THE INSTRUCTORS

Okonkwo (Area A): Pit A3 gave the best group of pottery, a cluster in the 40 to 50 cm spit that included one rim from a cooking pot. The other three pits in A were thin and the cluster seems local. Soil was clean silty clay below 40 cm.

Vasquez (Area B): Pits B1 to B4 gave by far the richest material. A burnt patch at the edge of B2 in the 20 to 30 cm spit grew into an ash-rich fill in the next spit, which I read as the edge of a hearth. A worked bone point came from B4 in the 30 to 40 cm spit. The surface tile fragments in this area were not collected as finds.

Lindqvist (Area C): With the 6 mm mesh we obviously lost small items, and the students were demoralised by the low flake counts. The soil is sandy and drains fast, but the water came up in C1 at the end. The deepest layers had some pottery in all three pits.

Brandt (Area D): The area is mostly stony and shallow, with the topsoil sitting on gravel at about 30 cm in two of the pits. A fragment of modern bottle glass in D1 at 40 to 50 cm suggests disturbance from a later pit or a drain.

Das sind meine Vorlesungsmitschriften zur Fahrtenvermittlung in einer Taxizentrale, und nächste Woche habe ich die Klausur im Modul Verkehrsbetrieb. Bitte erstelle mir daraus einen ausführlichen Lernleitfaden mit den wichtigsten Begriffen, mit durchgerechneten Beispielen zu den Formeln und mit einem Quiz samt Lösungen (etwa fünfzehn Fragen, gemischt aus Verständnis- und Rechenaufgaben). Wenn in meinen Notizen etwas unklar oder wahrscheinlich falsch ist, weise mich bitte darauf hin.

Vorlesung 6: Disposition in der Taxizentrale (Prof. Dr. Reinhild Käferstein, Wintersemester)

1. Aufgaben der Zentrale

Eine Taxizentrale nimmt Fahrtwünsche entgegen (Telefon, App, Internet, Stammkunden), ordnet jedem Wunsch ein Fahrzeug zu und überwacht die Fahrt bis zur Abrechnung. Sie hat vier Hauptaufgaben:

- Auftragsannahme: Erfassen von Abholort, Ziel, Zeit, Personenzahl und Sonderwünschen (Rollstuhl, Kindersitz, großes Gepäck).
- Disposition: Auswahl des Fahrzeugs und Übermittlung des Auftrags.
- Überwachung: Verfolgen der Position, Reagieren auf Verspätungen und Ausfälle.
- Auswertung: Berechnen von Kennzahlen und Planen der Besetzung für die nächsten Wochen.

Wichtig für die Klausur: Die Zentrale arbeitet in einem Spannungsfeld zwischen Kundenwartezeit (kurz) und Auslastung der Fahrzeuge (hoch). Beides gleichzeitig zu maximieren ist nicht möglich.

2. Zustände von Fahrzeugen und Aufträgen

Ein Fahrzeug hat im System einen von fünf Zuständen: frei (am Halteplatz oder fahrend ohne Fahrgast), zugeteilt (auf dem Weg zum Abholort), besetzt (Fahrgast an Bord), Pause und außer Dienst. Ein Auftrag durchläuft die Zustände offen, zugeteilt, gestartet, abgeschlossen. Ein Auftrag kann außerdem storniert werden (durch den Kunden) oder verloren gehen (kein Fahrzeug gefunden oder Kunde nicht angetroffen).

Merke: Die Zeit zwischen Zuteilung und Abholung heißt Anfahrtszeit. Die Zeit zwischen Auftragseingang und Abholung heißt Wartezeit des Kunden. Die Wartezeit ist also immer größer als die Anfahrtszeit, weil sie die Annahme und die Suche nach einem Fahrzeug enthält.

3. Zuteilungsverfahren

3.1 Nächstes freies Fahrzeug. Der Auftrag geht an das freie Fahrzeug mit der kürzesten Fahrzeit zum Abholort. Das Verfahren ist einfach und liefert kurze Anfahrten für den einzelnen Auftrag. Nachteil: Es kann Fahrzeuge aus einem Stadtteil abziehen und dort Lücken reißen, weshalb die nächsten Kunden dort länger warten.

3.2 Zonenwarteschlange. Die Stadt wird in Zonen eingeteilt. In jeder Zone stehen freie Fahrzeuge in einer Warteschlange; wer am längsten wartet, bekommt den nächsten Auftrag der Zone. Das Verfahren ist gerecht gegenüber den Fahrern, aber nicht optimal für die Anfahrt, denn das Fahrzeug an erster Stelle ist nicht unbedingt das nächste. Es wird in Städten mit festen Halteplätzen verwendet.

3.3 Angebotsverfahren (Bietverfahren). Der Auftrag wird an mehrere Fahrzeuge in der Nähe gesendet, und diese bestätigen innerhalb von 15 Sekunden. Das Fahrzeug mit der besten Bewertung (Entfernung, Wartezeit, Qualität) erhält den Zuschlag. Vorteil: Der Fahrer entscheidet mit. Nachteil: Es gibt Ablehnungen, und jede Ablehnung kostet Zeit.

3.4 Bündelung (Batching). Die Zentrale sammelt Aufträge über ein kurzes Zeitfenster, zum Beispiel 20 Sekunden, und löst dann ein Zuordnungsproblem für alle Aufträge und alle freien Fahrzeuge gleichzeitig, mit dem Ziel, die Summe der Anfahrtszeiten zu minimieren. Das Ergebnis ist im Mittel besser als bei sofortiger Zuteilung, aber jeder Kunde wartet im Schnitt 10 Sekunden länger auf die Bestätigung.

Zusammengefasst:

| Verfahren | Anfahrtszeit | Fairness unter Fahrern | Aufwand | Typische Anwendung |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Nächstes Fahrzeug | niedrig | niedrig | niedrig | kleine Flotte, App |
| Zonenwarteschlange | mittel | hoch | niedrig | Halteplätze, Bahnhof |
| Angebotsverfahren | mittel | mittel | mittel | gemischte Flotte |
| Bündelung | sehr niedrig | mittel | hoch | große Flotte, Spitzenzeiten |

4. Kennzahlen

Die wichtigsten Kennzahlen einer Taxizentrale sind:

- Mittlere Wartezeit der Kunden (in Minuten) und der Anteil der Kunden, die länger als 10 Minuten warten.
- Verlustquote = verlorene Aufträge geteilt durch alle Aufträge.
- Leerfahrtanteil = Leerkilometer geteilt durch Gesamtkilometer (Leerkilometer sind alle Kilometer ohne Fahrgast, also auch die Anfahrt).
- Auslastung = Zeit mit Fahrgast (besetzt) geteilt durch Schichtzeit.
- Umsatz je Stunde = Fahrpreise geteilt durch Schichtstunden.

Beispiel 1 (Verlustquote). In einer Woche gingen bei der Zentrale 1.840 Aufträge ein. 1.702 wurden abgeschlossen, 138 gingen verloren. Verlustquote = 138 / 1.840 = 0,075 = 7,5 Prozent. Davon waren 92 Fälle ohne verfügbares Fahrzeug und 46 Fälle, in denen der Kunde nicht am Abholort war.

Beispiel 2 (Leerfahrtanteil). Eine Flotte von 40 Fahrzeugen fuhr an einem Tag zusammen 6.400 km. Davon waren 2.016 km Leerkilometer. Leerfahrtanteil = 2.016 / 6.400 = 0,315 = 31,5 Prozent. Fährt die Zentrale die Anfahrt durch bessere Zuteilung im Mittel um 0,3 km kürzer bei 1.100 Aufträgen am Tag, so sinken die Leerkilometer um 330 km, also auf 1.686 km, und der Leerfahrtanteil auf 27,8 Prozent. (Gesamtkilometer sinken dann auf 6.070 km.)

Beispiel 3 (Auslastung). Ein Fahrer arbeitet eine Schicht von 10 Stunden. Er hat 4 Stunden 30 Minuten besetzt gefahren. Auslastung = 4,5 / 10 = 45 Prozent.

5. Warteschlangen in der Telefonannahme

Die Telefonannahme lässt sich als Warteschlangensystem beschreiben. Anrufe kommen mit der Rate λ (Anrufe je Stunde), und jede Disponentin bearbeitet im Mittel μ Anrufe je Stunde (μ = 1 geteilt durch die mittlere Bearbeitungszeit). Die Verkehrsbelastung ist a = λ / μ. Bei c Disponentinnen ist die Auslastung ρ = a / c, und das System ist nur stabil, wenn ρ kleiner als 1 ist.

5.1 Ein Schalter (M/M/1). Mit einer Disponentin gilt für die mittlere Zahl wartender Anrufe Lq = ρ² / (1 − ρ) und für die mittlere Wartezeit Wq = Lq / λ.

Beispiel 4. λ = 24 Anrufe je Stunde, mittlere Bearbeitungszeit 2 Minuten, also μ = 30 je Stunde. ρ = 24 / 30 = 0,8. Lq = 0,64 / 0,2 = 3,2 Anrufe. Wq = 3,2 / 24 = 0,1333 Stunden = 8 Minuten. Die Anrufer warten im Mittel 8 Minuten, bevor jemand antwortet. Das ist für eine Taxizentrale viel zu lang.

5.2 Mehrere Schalter (M/M/c, Erlang C). Mit c Disponentinnen gibt die Erlang-C-Formel die Wahrscheinlichkeit, dass ein Anrufer warten muss:

C(c, a) = [ aᶜ / c! · 1 / (1 − ρ) ] / [ Σ (von k = 0 bis c − 1) aᵏ / k! + aᶜ / c! · 1 / (1 − ρ) ].

Die mittlere Wartezeit aller Anrufer ist Wq = C(c, a) / (c · μ − λ).

Beispiel 5. In der Spitzenstunde kommen λ = 48 Anrufe je Stunde, μ = 30 je Stunde, es arbeiten c = 2 Disponentinnen. a = 48 / 30 = 1,6 und ρ = 0,8. Der Zähler: a² / 2! = 1,28, geteilt durch (1 − 0,8) ergibt 6,4. Die Summe im Nenner: 1 + 1,6 = 2,6. Also C = 6,4 / (2,6 + 6,4) = 6,4 / 9,0 = 0,711. Mit 71 Prozent Wahrscheinlichkeit muss ein Anrufer warten. Wq = 0,711 / (60 − 48) = 0,0593 Stunden = 3,6 Minuten. Mit zwei Plätzen warten die Anrufer in der Spitze also im Mittel gut dreieinhalb Minuten, was für eine Taxizentrale immer noch zu lang ist.

Beispiel 5b. Setzt man in derselben Stunde eine dritte Disponentin ein (c = 3), sinkt die Auslastung auf ρ = 1,6 / 3 = 0,533. Zähler: a³ / 3! = 4,096 / 6 = 0,683; geteilt durch (1 − 0,533) ergibt 1,463. Summe im Nenner: 1 + 1,6 + 1,28 = 3,88. Also C = 1,463 / (3,88 + 1,463) = 0,274. Wq = 0,274 / (90 − 48) = 0,0065 Stunden, das sind etwa 23 Sekunden. Eine einzige zusätzliche Person senkt die Wartezeit also von 3,6 Minuten auf weniger als eine halbe Minute. Das zeigt, warum sich die Besetzung der Annahme in der Spitze fast immer lohnt.

Merke: Die Wartezeit steigt stark, wenn ρ gegen 1 geht. Deshalb plant man die Besetzung mit einer Auslastung der Annahme von etwa 70 bis 80 Prozent und nicht mit 95 Prozent.

6. Nachfrageprognose und Schichtplanung

Die Nachfrage schwankt nach Uhrzeit, Wochentag, Wetter und Veranstaltungen. Die Zentrale prognostiziert sie aus den Aufträgen derselben Stunde in den letzten Wochen. Ein einfaches Verfahren ist der gleitende Mittelwert über vier gleiche Wochentage, mit einem Zuschlag bei Regen (in unserer Zentrale 18 Prozent) und bei Großveranstaltungen (individuell geschätzt).

Beispiel 6. An den letzten vier Freitagen zwischen 22 und 23 Uhr gab es 96, 104, 88 und 112 Aufträge. Der Mittelwert ist (96 + 104 + 88 + 112) / 4 = 100 Aufträge. Für den kommenden Freitag ist Regen angesagt. Prognose = 100 · 1,18 = 118 Aufträge. Wenn ein Fahrzeug in dieser Stunde im Mittel 1,6 Aufträge schafft (Anfahrt, Fahrt, Rückkehr), werden 118 / 1,6 = 73,75, also mindestens 74 Fahrzeuge im Dienst benötigt. Hat die Flotte nur 65 Fahrzeuge in der Spätschicht, werden voraussichtlich Aufträge verloren gehen oder lange warten.

7. Preisregeln und Vorbestellung

Der Fahrpreis in Städten mit Tarifpflicht besteht aus einem Grundpreis, einem Kilometerpreis und einem Wartezeitpreis. In unserem Beispiel gelten 4,50 Euro Grundpreis, 2,40 Euro je Kilometer und 0,60 Euro je angefangene Minute Wartezeit während der Fahrt. Für Vorbestellungen berechnet die Zentrale zusätzlich 2,00 Euro. Bei Fahrten mit mehr als vier Fahrgästen darf ein Großraumtaxi angefordert werden, für das ein Zuschlag von 5,00 Euro gilt.

Beispiel 7. Eine vorbestellte Fahrt über 7,5 Kilometer mit 4 Minuten Wartezeit kostet 4,50 + 7,5 · 2,40 + 4 · 0,60 + 2,00 = 4,50 + 18,00 + 2,40 + 2,00 = 26,90 Euro.

8. Störungen und Rückfallebenen

Fällt die Zentrale aus, müssen die Fahrer weiter Aufträge bekommen. Es gibt drei Rückfallebenen: Erstens der Funkbetrieb auf einem festen Kanal. Zweitens die Aufträge per Telefon direkt an Stammfahrer. Drittens das Fahren nach Halteplatz ohne Zentrale. Wichtig ist, jede Stufe vorher zu üben, und nach der Störung alle in der Zwischenzeit gefahrenen Aufträge nachzuerfassen, damit die Abrechnung stimmt.

9. Qualität, Barrierefreiheit und Datenschutz

Zur Qualitätssicherung wertet die Zentrale jede Woche Beschwerden, Lob und Rückfragen aus. Typische Beschwerden sind lange Wartezeiten, abgelehnte Aufträge und Umwege. Eine Beschwerde wird innerhalb von zwei Arbeitstagen beantwortet; bei Streit über den Fahrweg liefert die Zentrale den aufgezeichneten Streckenverlauf.

Rollstuhlgerechte Fahrzeuge sind knapp. In unserem Beispiel hat die Flotte 40 Fahrzeuge, davon 5 rollstuhlgerecht. Die Zentrale reserviert diese Fahrzeuge nicht, aber sie vergibt Aufträge mit Rollstuhl bevorzugt an sie. Frage zum Nachdenken: Welche Kennzahl würde man zusätzlich führen, um zu prüfen, ob Kunden mit Rollstuhl schlechter bedient werden? (Antwort der Vorlesung: die mittlere Wartezeit getrennt nach Auftragsart.)

Beim Datenschutz gilt: Positionsdaten der Fahrzeuge dürfen nur für die Disposition und die Abrechnung genutzt werden, Gesprächsaufzeichnungen werden nach 30 Tagen gelöscht, und Kundendaten wie Adressen von Stammkunden werden nur für die Dauer des Vertragsverhältnisses gespeichert. Fahrer müssen über die Ortung informiert werden.

Beispiel 8 (Umsatz je Stunde). Ein Fahrer hat in einer Schicht von 10 Stunden 22 Fahrten mit einem mittleren Fahrpreis von 17,80 Euro. Umsatz = 22 · 17,80 = 391,60 Euro. Umsatz je Stunde = 391,60 / 10 = 39,16 Euro. Zieht man davon die Anfahrten ab, die nicht bezahlt werden, sieht man, warum eine kurze Anfahrt direkt das Einkommen der Fahrer erhöht.

Prüfungshinweise von Frau Käferstein: Erlang C wird nicht auswendig verlangt, die Formel steht im Formelblatt. Man muss aber die Auslastung ρ, die Verkehrsbelastung a und die Wartezeit sicher berechnen können. Die Zuteilungsverfahren werden als Vergleichstabelle abgefragt, und die Kennzahlen als Rechenaufgabe.
