Below is our third-quarter operations report for the Redcliffe cement plant, which I put together for the board pack. I need a section-by-section summary a director could read in ten minutes, followed by your recommendations: what the board should decide, what management should do in the next ninety days, and which numbers worry you most. Please also point out anywhere the report contradicts itself or leaves something unexplained.

REDCLIFFE CEMENT WORKS
Quarterly Operations Report, Q3 (July to September)
Prepared by: Operations Office, for the Plant Manager, Gideon Hartwell

1. Executive summary

Q3 was a quarter of two halves. July and August were the best two consecutive months of the year for clinker output. In September, Kiln 2 was stopped for eleven days after a failure of the refractory lining in the burning zone, and this took the quarter below budget. Clinker production for the quarter was 336,600 tonnes against a budget of 345,000 tonnes (minus 2.4 percent). Cement shipments were 402,000 tonnes against 410,000 (minus 2.0 percent). Heat consumption per tonne of clinker was above target, the alternative fuel rate was below target, and the plant recorded two lost-time injuries, both in September. Emissions were within permit limits on every monthly average, with one short exceedance of the dust limit in August. The EBITDA for the quarter was 7.9 million against a budget of 8.8 million.

2. Production

Clinker production by month and kiln, in tonnes:

| Month | Kiln 1 | Kiln 2 | Total | Budget |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| July | 68,500 | 49,900 | 118,400 | 115,000 |
| August | 70,200 | 51,700 | 121,900 | 115,000 |
| September | 69,700 | 26,600 | 96,300 | 115,000 |
| Quarter | 208,400 | 128,200 | 336,600 | 345,000 |

Kiln 1 ran for 91 of 92 days with one short stop of 14 hours in August for a cooler grate repair. Kiln 2 ran for 81 of 92 days. During the Kiln 2 outage from 4 to 15 September, Kiln 1 was run at its maximum feed rate and averaged about 2,400 tonnes a day, roughly 190 tonnes a day above its July average but well short of the 2,550 tonnes a day it has reached in trials, because the raw mill was limited by a hot-gas fan issue that is discussed in section 6. Kiln 2 averaged only 1,400 tonnes a day on the 19 days it ran in September, against 1,610 in July, because of the slow restart and a reduced feed rate for the first week while the new lining was conditioned.

Clinker stocks at the end of June were 41,000 tonnes. By the end of September they were 29,500 tonnes, which is nine days of cement production. The clinker stock was drawn down to cover shipments in September and has not been rebuilt since. Cement production (clinker plus gypsum, limestone and slag) was 409,000 tonnes against 415,000 budgeted, and the cement mills ran at 91 percent availability.

3. Energy and fuels

Thermal energy consumption averaged 3,520 megajoules per tonne of clinker for the quarter against a target of 3,450. The difference is partly due to the restart of Kiln 2 after the lining repair, which consumed extra fuel in the heating-up period, and partly due to lower preheater efficiency on Kiln 1 caused by build-up in the cyclones in July.

The alternative fuel rate (the share of kiln heat from non-fossil and waste-derived fuels) was 31 percent against a target of 35 percent. Alternative fuel was limited in three ways: a supplier of shredded packaging waste delivered 22 percent below contract in August; the new feeding line for biomass pellets on Kiln 2 was not available during the outage; and a batch of 480 tonnes of derived fuel failed the chlorine specification on delivery and was returned.

Fuel mix for the quarter, as a share of kiln heat:

| Fuel | Share |
|---|---|
| Coal and petcoke | 69% |
| Shredded packaging waste | 14% |
| Biomass pellets | 9% |
| Dried sewage sludge | 5% |
| Waste oil and solvents | 3% |

Electrical consumption was 98 kilowatt-hours per tonne of cement against a target of 96. The cement mill with the older roller press accounted for most of the excess. Peak-tariff electricity represented 11 percent of consumption and cost 1.3 million, which is higher than last year because kiln restarts were scheduled during peak hours.

4. Environment and compliance

Monthly average emissions from the main stacks (milligrams per normal cubic metre, with the permit limit in brackets):

| Parameter | July | August | September | Limit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Dust | 11 | 14 | 12 | 20 |
| Nitrogen oxides | 610 | 640 | 655 | 800 |
| Sulphur dioxide | 180 | 195 | 210 | 400 |
| Hydrogen chloride | 4 | 5 | 4 | 10 |

On 19 August a bag-filter compartment on Kiln 1 failed and for 38 minutes the half-hour average for dust exceeded the daily limit, reaching 31 milligrams. The compartment was isolated and replaced the next day. The event was reported to the regulator within the permitted time. No notice or fine has been issued. Continuous monitoring availability was 99.1 percent.

The annual compliance inspection took place on 22 September. Two minor observations were made: the labelling of two waste oil tanks, and the calibration record for one dust monitor. Both have been closed. The carbon dioxide inventory for the quarter is 262,000 tonnes, which is 0.78 tonnes per tonne of clinker, in line with the year-to-date figure.

5. Health and safety

There were two lost-time injuries in the quarter, both in September, compared with none in Q2. The first was a contractor who suffered a fractured wrist when a hot kiln inspection door slipped during the Kiln 2 outage; the second was an employee who sprained an ankle on a wet stairway at the packing plant. The lost-time injury frequency rate for the rolling twelve months is now 1.8 per million hours, against a target of 1.0. The number of near misses reported rose from 41 in Q2 to 63, which management considers a positive sign of better reporting.

During the Kiln 2 outage, 140 contractors worked on site under a permit-to-work system. Two permits were found to have been signed before isolation had been verified. Both were stopped, and the supervisors involved have been retrained. The investigation of the first injury concluded that the door latch had not been inspected since the previous shutdown and that the inspection task was missing from the shutdown checklist.

Training hours were 2,310 in the quarter, equivalent to 11.7 hours for every person on the payroll.

6. Maintenance and capital projects

The failure of the Kiln 2 refractory lining on 3 September was found when a hot spot appeared on the kiln shell at 02:40. The kiln was stopped, cooled for 36 hours, and 14 metres of bricks in the burning zone were replaced. The bricks had been installed in April, a month earlier than planned, in a previous short stop, and were from a batch with a higher alumina content than specified. The supplier has accepted that the batch did not meet specification and has offered a credit of 118,000. The direct cost of the repair was 640,000 including contractors. The lost production was about 22,000 tonnes of clinker.

Capital projects in the quarter:

| Project | Budget | Spent to date | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| Biomass feeding line, Kiln 2 | 1.9m | 1.7m | Commissioned September; not yet proven |
| Raw mill hot-gas fan replacement | 0.8m | 0.3m | Delivery delayed to November |
| Cement mill 3 roller press overhaul | 2.4m | 0.4m | Planned for the Q1 shutdown |
| Packing plant dust extraction | 0.6m | 0.6m | Complete |
| New weighbridge and truck queuing system | 0.5m | 0.2m | In progress |

The raw mill fan is the main reason Kiln 1 could not exceed its rate during the outage. The fan was ordered in June, and the manufacturer has moved delivery from September to November.

7. Quality

The 28-day compressive strength of the main product averaged 54.2 megapascals against a specification minimum of 52.5, and the standard deviation was 1.6. Three of 92 daily samples were below the minimum, all in the second week of September when Kiln 1 was running at a high feed rate and the burnability of the raw mix changed. Customer complaints about quality fell from 9 to 6. Two were about colour variation in the white-grey product used for architectural panels and have been traced to petcoke ash variability.

8. Sales and logistics

Cement shipments of 402,000 tonnes were split between bulk by road (58 percent), bags on pallets (27 percent), bulk by rail (12 percent) and export by barge (3 percent). The average net price was 87.50 per tonne, 1.2 percent below budget, because the product mix shifted towards the bagged product with higher discounts and because two large infrastructure contracts began at lower prices than quoted.

Delivery performance (orders delivered on the day promised) was 93 percent against a target of 95. The loading queue at the weighbridge exceeded 45 minutes on eleven days; the new queuing system is expected to cut this. The rail wagon supplier cancelled 18 wagons in August, which moved 4,100 tonnes onto trucks at a higher cost.

9. Finance

Revenue was 35.2 million against a budget of 36.1 million. Variable costs were close to budget in total, but with an adverse mix: fuel was 0.9 million above budget in total because of the lower alternative fuel rate and heat consumption, and power was 0.3 million above. Fixed costs were 0.2 million below budget. EBITDA was 7.9 million against 8.8 million budgeted; the largest items in the shortfall were the Kiln 2 outage (about 1.1 million after the supplier credit, counting lost margin and repair costs), the fuel overrun, and the price shortfall. The year-to-date EBITDA is now 3.1 percent below budget.

10. People

Headcount at the end of the quarter was 198 against a budget of 205. Seven positions are vacant, five of them in maintenance, including two electricians. Overtime hours in maintenance were 31 percent above plan. Voluntary turnover over the last twelve months is 7.4 percent. A new apprenticeship intake of eight starts in October.

11. Main risks

- A second refractory failure before the planned shutdown in February. Kiln 2 has the shortened lining life from the faulty batch.
- Continued shortage of alternative fuel, which affects both cost and carbon performance.
- Delay in the raw mill fan, which limits Kiln 1 and the clinker stock rebuild before winter, when demand for cement falls but kiln maintenance concentrates.
- Safety: two serious permit-to-work lapses during the outage and a trend of contractor-related injuries.

12. Outlook for Q4

Clinker production in Q4 is budgeted at 340,000 tonnes. With the clinker stock at 29,500 tonnes, the plant needs to make up the gap on shipments from stock. Management plans to bring forward the cement mill 3 overhaul only if the fan arrives on time. Price increases of 2.5 percent for bagged cement come into effect on 1 November.

13. Appendix A: timeline of the Kiln 2 lining failure

| Date and time | Event |
|---|---|
| 3 Sept, 02:40 | Shell scanner alarm: hot spot of 410 degrees Celsius at 22 metres from the kiln outlet |
| 3 Sept, 03:15 | Shift manager reduces feed by 30 percent and calls the maintenance superintendent |
| 3 Sept, 05:50 | Hot spot reaches 470 degrees; decision to stop the kiln |
| 3 Sept, 06:30 | Kiln stopped; feed and fuel off; barring (slow turning) started |
| 4 Sept to 5 Sept | Cooling for 36 hours; permit-to-work scope agreed; contractors mobilised |
| 6 Sept to 12 Sept | Removal of damaged bricks and installation of 14 metres of new lining |
| 13 Sept to 14 Sept | Drying and heating-up on gas, following the supplier's schedule |
| 15 Sept, 11:20 | Kiln fed and clinker production restarted |
| 15 Sept to 22 Sept | Reduced feed rate while the lining is conditioned |

The count of eleven days in this report runs from the date of stop for repair, 4 September, to the restart on 15 September. The hours between the first alarm on 3 September and the stop are counted as production at a reduced rate.

14. Appendix B: key performance scorecard

| Indicator | Q2 actual | Q3 actual | Q3 target |
|---|---|---|---|
| Clinker production (tonnes) | 331,900 | 336,600 | 345,000 |
| Cement shipments (tonnes) | 397,500 | 402,000 | 410,000 |
| Heat consumption (MJ per tonne clinker) | 3,490 | 3,520 | 3,450 |
| Alternative fuel rate | 33% | 31% | 35% |
| Electricity (kWh per tonne cement) | 97 | 98 | 96 |
| Lost-time injuries (count) | 0 | 2 | 0 |
| Delivery on the day promised | 94% | 93% | 95% |
| Quality complaints | 9 | 6 | 5 |
| Headcount | 200 | 198 | 205 |
| EBITDA (million) | 8.3 | 7.9 | 8.8 |

These are my notes from yesterday's planning meeting at our hearing-aid clinic. We decided a lot but nobody wrote down who does what. Please turn them into a full project plan for the new fitting-room and recall programme, with a named owner for every task, dates, a risk list with ways to reduce each risk, and anything you think we forgot.

MEETING NOTES
Clinic: Brindlewood Hearing Care, main site at Castle Row
Meeting: Autumn planning, Tuesday 6 October 2026, 14:00 to 16:10
Present: Dr Annelise Voss (clinical lead, audiologist), Rutger Penhallow (practice manager), Sunita Karekar (senior hearing-aid dispenser), Corwin Tulloch (dispenser), Beatrix Almqvist (reception and bookings), Hugh Dembinski (finance, part time), Odile Marchetti (supplier liaison, joined by phone for items 3 and 4)
Apologies: Fenella Rask (second audiologist, on leave until 19 October)
Chair: Rutger. Notes: Beatrix, tidied by Sunita.

1. Matters arising from the September meeting

Rutger reported that the broken sound booth at the Castle Row site was repaired on 22 September and re-calibrated on 24 September. The calibration certificate is in the shared folder. The booth was out of use for 11 working days, and Dr Voss estimated that about 46 hearing tests were moved to the Thornby satellite room or to later dates. Beatrix said 9 patients still have not been rebooked and she will call them this week. Sunita asked that the rebooking list be checked against the recall list, because two of the nine are also due for a hearing-aid review.

The new appointment reminder text messages went live on 1 September. Beatrix said missed appointments fell from 14 percent in August to 8 percent in September. Hugh asked whether that saves enough to cover the 0.06 charge per message. Beatrix said yes: 6 percent of roughly 620 appointments is 37 appointments, and each missed 45-minute slot is worth far more than the 640 or so messages cost. Agreed to keep the reminders.

2. Fitting room extension

The plan is to turn the old storage room next to reception into a second fitting room, so that fittings and tests no longer compete for the same two rooms. Rutger has two quotes. The first, from a local builder, is 18,400 including sound insulation, new flooring and a second door, with work taking three weeks. The second quote, 14,900, does not include the acoustic panels, which would be about 3,100 extra from a specialist, giving 18,000 in total and a longer schedule of five weeks because of two separate contractors.

Dr Voss said the sound insulation matters more than the price, because fittings require background noise below 35 decibels to run real-ear measurements properly. She asked that whoever builds the room supplies a measurement report. Hugh said the clinic can pay up to 20,000 from savings without borrowing, but wants to keep 5,000 as a buffer, so the available amount is 15,000 from cash plus about 4,000 from the autumn income, which is tight. Corwin suggested a staged approach: do the room in November, buy the new real-ear measurement equipment in January.

Decision: go with the first quote (18,400) provided the builder agrees in writing to a measurement report and to finish before 4 December. Rutger to negotiate a 10 percent deposit schedule rather than 30 percent. If the builder will not agree, the group meets again on 20 October.

During the build, the reception area will be noisy. Beatrix asked that no hearing tests be booked in the room next to the work. Sunita proposed that the two loudest days, flooring and the second door, be scheduled on the Monday and Tuesday when the clinic already runs reduced hours. Rutger will ask the builder.

3. Supplier change for hearing aids

Odile reported on the supplier review. The clinic currently buys most of its aids from Halvard Acoustics. Their price rose 7 percent in September and their delivery time went from 3 days to 8 days. A second supplier, Nordlicht Audio, offers a comparable range at about 4 percent below the old price, with 4 day delivery, but a minimum order of 12 units a month, and a 60 day trial return period instead of 90. A third, Kestrel Ear Systems, is cheaper by 9 percent but only has two models in the small behind-the-ear size that about a quarter of the patients need.

Sunita said patients care a great deal about the 90 day trial, as many first-time users need it. Odile said Halvard would likely keep the 90 days. Dr Voss said clinical quality is the first test: she wants to try three Nordlicht devices on staff and volunteer patients before agreeing anything. Hugh said the 12-unit minimum is fine since the clinic sells about 30 a month.

Decision: no supplier switch yet. Odile to ask Halvard for a written price freeze for six months and a delivery promise of 4 days. In parallel, Nordlicht sends three sample devices. Sunita and Corwin test them over 3 weeks, and Dr Voss writes a short comparison. Decision on 17 November.

4. Recall programme

This was the longest discussion. About 410 patients have hearing aids that are over four years old and have not been seen for a review in 18 months or longer. Dr Voss is worried about two groups: patients with a steady loss in hearing, who stop using their aids without telling anyone, and patients with a device that no longer matches their hearing. She would like a recall letter and phone call, followed by a free 30-minute check, for everyone on the list.

Hugh asked about the cost. At 30 minutes each, 410 checks is about 205 hours. Dr Voss said she does not expect more than 60 percent to come, so around 125 hours, which is about 16 working days of one audiologist. Rutger said that is not possible with the current rota, particularly while Fenella is away. Corwin proposed that dispensers do the basic check (device cleaning, battery or charger test, a comfort and use questionnaire) and the audiologist is only needed for patients whose answers show a problem. Dr Voss agreed that is safe, if the dispensers follow a written checklist and she signs off the checklist.

Beatrix will need a script for the phone calls, a way to mark who was contacted, and a limit on how many calls to make, since she is also covering reception. Sunita said a letter first and a call only after two weeks of no reply would cut the number of calls by roughly half.

The group agreed on a pilot with the 100 patients who have waited longest. Start letters on 26 October, run checks from 9 November, review at the end of December. Success means at least 50 of the 100 attend and that at least 10 percent of those who attend are found to need a new device or a re-fitting.

Hugh also raised data protection. The recall letters use patient addresses and health information, so the mailing list must stay inside the booking system and not be copied to spreadsheets. Rutger will check that the existing patient consent covers recall contact; if not, a short consent line goes into the next appointment letter.

5. Staffing and rota

Fenella returns on 19 October. Dr Voss proposed that she takes the Thornby satellite room on Wednesdays and Fridays and the recall escalations on Thursday mornings. Corwin asked for one full day a week without patients to do the sample device trials and the checklist work. Rutger said that could be Thursday afternoon, with reception taking only urgent bookings. Beatrix pointed out that the pilot letters will bring a rise in calls in the week of 2 November, so she asked for the part-time receptionist, Ines, to be moved from two days to three days for six weeks. Hugh said that costs about 1,150 for the period and approved it, subject to the budget in item 6.

6. Budget summary

Hugh's current view for the quarter: fitting room 18,400; receptionist hours 1,150; reminder messages about 40 per month; recall letters (printing and postage for 100 letters) about 110; sample devices free of charge but return postage about 60. Expected income from the extra capacity of the second room is about 2,200 a month from January onward, based on 14 more fittings per month, which Hugh called cautious. Total spending this quarter is about 19,800, within the cash limit he set, but he warned that an unexpected equipment failure would hit the buffer.

7. Patient complaints and feedback

Beatrix summarised the complaints log for September. There were six written complaints and eleven verbal ones, compared with four and nine in August. Of the six written, three were about waiting times during the week the sound booth was out of use, one was about a dispenser who did not explain the charger clearly, one was about the car park, and one was about an invoice that showed the wrong aid model. The invoice error was traced to a mistake when the aid was swapped for a different size on the fitting day; Hugh has corrected the invoice and refunded the 35 difference. Sunita said the swap should have triggered a second check of the invoice and proposed adding a line to the dispenser checklist: "re-read the invoice against the final device before the patient leaves."

Dr Voss asked about the positive feedback. Beatrix said 23 patients left comments on the paper cards in the waiting room, and 19 were warm, with several mentioning Corwin by name for his patience with a patient who had trouble with small buttons. Rutger asked that these be shared at the next staff lunch. The group agreed that the car park complaint cannot be fixed by the clinic, because the car park belongs to the council, but Beatrix will put a note on the website with the location of the two nearest accessible spaces and the bus stop.

Decision: add the invoice check to the checklist from 12 October. Rutger will review the complaints log monthly and report any pattern in the first meeting of the following month.

8. Training and equipment

Dr Voss said the new real-ear measurement equipment, which would arrive after the fitting room is built, needs two days of training for each dispenser. The supplier offers an on-site course for up to four people at 1,600 for two days, which is cheaper than sending people away, but it needs a closed clinic or a quiet part of the building. Hugh said the course fee is not in the quarter's budget summary and would come out of the January budget. Corwin and Sunita said they would rather have the course after the room is finished, so the real equipment can be used in the room it will live in.

Separately, Sunita reported that two of the four handheld otoscopes in use are over eight years old and one has a failing light. Replacement units cost about 210 each. Hugh approved buying two now, 420 in total, out of the equipment line. Sunita will order them and keep the receipts.

Odile asked whether the clinic wants to join the supplier's loan scheme for demonstration aids, where the supplier lends up to six current models for a month without charge. The group agreed this would help the comparison in item 3, but Dr Voss said the loan devices must not be fitted to patients who have not given written consent for a trial device. Odile will find out whether the scheme has such a consent form, and if not, Dr Voss will write a one-page version.

9. Satellite room at Thornby

Rutger raised the question of the Thornby room, rented from the community hall for two days a week. The rent will rise from 180 to 215 a month in January. Fenella's proposed Wednesday and Friday cover would make it a three-day service. Rutger asked whether it is worth keeping. The room is used for about 38 appointments a month, and many of those patients are older people who cannot travel to Castle Row easily. Dr Voss said the clinic has a duty to those patients and the extra rent is small. Hugh agreed on cost grounds, as the room earns about 1,900 a month in fees. The group asked that the sound level in the room be measured once, because the hall hosts a toddler group on Thursdays and the noise may carry. Corwin will bring the borrowed meter on his next Wednesday visit.

Decision: keep Thornby, accept the new rent, and ask for a six-month agreement with no further rise.

10. Communication with patients about the building work

Beatrix asked how patients should be told about the building work, since many of them are elderly and some rely on lip reading at the front desk, which becomes harder when there is drilling in the background. Dr Voss said noise during the work is a real accessibility problem, not just an irritation, and suggested three measures: a printed notice posted at the entrance and in the November appointment letters, a reminder in the text message the day before each visit, and a short script for reception so everyone gives the same information. Sunita added that patients with cochlear implants or very sensitive devices may be bothered by the sudden loud sounds and should be offered the Thornby room during the noisy days.

Rutger said the builder has promised to keep the loudest work to between 08:00 and 12:00, and that the clinic can then move the busiest fitting appointments to the afternoon. Beatrix raised a concern that this would make the afternoons very full and leave no slack for urgent repairs. Corwin offered to take the early morning repair walk-ins on the build days so the audiologist can concentrate on fittings. Hugh asked that the reduced hours on Mondays and Tuesdays be announced at least three weeks ahead so that income is not lost through confusion.

Decision: Beatrix drafts the notice and the reception script by 16 October. Sunita reviews the list of patients with implants and sensitive devices and flags them in the booking system. Rutger confirms the builder's noise hours in writing.

11. Any other business

- The clinic's website still lists the old opening hours. Beatrix to correct it this week.
- Sunita raised the shortage of rechargeable-battery chargers for the loan stock; she counted only 4 working. Odile to order 6 more from the current supplier.
- Dr Voss reminded everyone that the regulator's annual infection-control audit takes place in the first half of December, and that the new fitting room must be included in the cleaning log from the first day of use.
- Corwin asked whether the clinic should take part in the hearing-awareness week in November. Rutger said yes in principle, but only if it does not clash with the build. Nobody volunteered to organise it. Left open.

Next meeting: Tuesday 20 October, 14:00, or earlier if the builder refuses the conditions.

Here is the database for our shipyard's job tracking, plus the queries the office runs every week. The reports are getting slow and last month someone found duplicate entries in the timesheets. Can you review the design, point out what is wrong or risky, suggest the indexes we need, and rewrite each query with an explanation of what you changed and why?

```sql
-- Harbourgate Shipyard: job tracking (PostgreSQL)

CREATE TABLE vessels (
    vessel_id      SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    name           VARCHAR(80) NOT NULL,
    imo_number     VARCHAR(12),
    owner_name     VARCHAR(120),
    owner_email    VARCHAR(120),
    vessel_type    VARCHAR(30),
    length_m       NUMERIC(6,2),
    year_built     INTEGER
);

CREATE TABLE berths (
    berth_id       SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    berth_code     VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL,
    max_length_m   NUMERIC(6,2),
    has_crane      BOOLEAN DEFAULT FALSE
);

CREATE TABLE jobs (
    job_id         SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    vessel_id      INTEGER REFERENCES vessels(vessel_id),
    berth_id       INTEGER REFERENCES berths(berth_id),
    job_type       VARCHAR(30),
    status         VARCHAR(20),
    opened_on      DATE,
    due_on         DATE,
    closed_on      DATE,
    quoted_eur     NUMERIC(12,2),
    description    TEXT
);

CREATE TABLE workers (
    worker_id      SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    full_name      VARCHAR(100),
    trade          VARCHAR(30),
    hourly_rate    NUMERIC(6,2),
    hired_on       DATE,
    active         BOOLEAN DEFAULT TRUE
);

CREATE TABLE timesheets (
    entry_id       SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    job_id         INTEGER REFERENCES jobs(job_id),
    worker_id      INTEGER REFERENCES workers(worker_id),
    work_date      DATE,
    hours          NUMERIC(4,2),
    note           TEXT
);

CREATE TABLE materials (
    material_id    SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    sku            VARCHAR(30),
    description    VARCHAR(200),
    unit           VARCHAR(10),
    unit_cost_eur  NUMERIC(10,2),
    stock_qty      NUMERIC(10,2)
);

CREATE TABLE job_materials (
    job_id         INTEGER REFERENCES jobs(job_id),
    material_id    INTEGER REFERENCES materials(material_id),
    quantity       NUMERIC(10,2),
    issued_on      DATE
);

CREATE TABLE invoices (
    invoice_id     SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    job_id         INTEGER REFERENCES jobs(job_id),
    issued_on      DATE,
    amount_eur     NUMERIC(12,2),
    paid_on        DATE,
    status         VARCHAR(15)
);

CREATE TABLE inspections (
    inspection_id  SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    job_id         INTEGER REFERENCES jobs(job_id),
    inspector      VARCHAR(100),
    inspected_on   DATE,
    result         VARCHAR(10),
    comments       TEXT
);

CREATE TABLE subcontractors (
    sub_id         SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    company_name   VARCHAR(120),
    speciality     VARCHAR(40),
    day_rate_eur   NUMERIC(8,2),
    insurance_until DATE
);

CREATE TABLE sub_assignments (
    assignment_id  SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    job_id         INTEGER REFERENCES jobs(job_id),
    sub_id         INTEGER REFERENCES subcontractors(sub_id),
    start_date     DATE,
    end_date       DATE,
    days_billed    INTEGER
);

CREATE TABLE certificates (
    cert_id        SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    worker_id      INTEGER REFERENCES workers(worker_id),
    cert_name      VARCHAR(60),
    issued_on      DATE,
    expires_on     DATE
);

-- Sample data used by the office when testing
INSERT INTO vessels (name, imo_number, owner_name, owner_email, vessel_type, length_m, year_built)
VALUES ('Marta Lindqvist', '9301182', 'Lindqvist Fisheries', 'office@lindqvist.example.org', 'trawler', 38.50, 1998),
       ('Sea Heron', '9455210', 'Northquay Ferries', 'ops@northquay.example.org', 'ferry', 61.20, 2007),
       ('Anselm', NULL, 'J. Brandvold', 'brandvold@example.org', 'yacht', 17.80, 2015);

INSERT INTO berths (berth_code, max_length_m, has_crane)
VALUES ('A1', 25.00, FALSE), ('B2', 45.00, TRUE), ('C3', 70.00, TRUE);

-- Query 1: open jobs with the vessel and berth, ordered by due date
SELECT j.job_id, v.name, b.berth_code, j.job_type, j.due_on
FROM jobs j, vessels v, berths b
WHERE j.vessel_id = v.vessel_id
  AND j.berth_id = b.berth_id
  AND j.status <> 'closed'
  AND j.status <> 'cancelled'
ORDER BY j.due_on;

-- Query 2: labour cost per job
SELECT j.job_id,
       (SELECT SUM(t.hours * w.hourly_rate)
        FROM timesheets t, workers w
        WHERE t.job_id = j.job_id AND t.worker_id = w.worker_id) AS labour_eur
FROM jobs j
WHERE j.opened_on >= '2026-01-01';

-- Query 3: material cost per job, with jobs that have no materials left out
SELECT jm.job_id, SUM(jm.quantity * m.unit_cost_eur) AS material_eur
FROM job_materials jm
JOIN materials m ON m.material_id = jm.material_id
GROUP BY jm.job_id;

-- Query 4: margin report. Quote minus labour minus materials
SELECT j.job_id, v.name, j.quoted_eur,
       COALESCE(l.labour_eur, 0) AS labour_eur,
       COALESCE(mm.material_eur, 0) AS material_eur,
       j.quoted_eur - COALESCE(l.labour_eur, 0) - COALESCE(mm.material_eur, 0) AS margin_eur
FROM jobs j
JOIN vessels v ON v.vessel_id = j.vessel_id
LEFT JOIN (
    SELECT t.job_id, SUM(t.hours * w.hourly_rate) AS labour_eur
    FROM timesheets t JOIN workers w ON w.worker_id = t.worker_id
    GROUP BY t.job_id
) l ON l.job_id = j.job_id
LEFT JOIN (
    SELECT jm.job_id, SUM(jm.quantity * m.unit_cost_eur) AS material_eur
    FROM job_materials jm JOIN materials m ON m.material_id = jm.material_id
    GROUP BY jm.job_id
) mm ON mm.job_id = j.job_id
WHERE j.status = 'closed'
ORDER BY margin_eur;

-- Query 5: overdue jobs and how many days late they are
SELECT j.job_id, v.name, v.owner_email, CURRENT_DATE - j.due_on AS days_late
FROM jobs j
JOIN vessels v ON v.vessel_id = j.vessel_id
WHERE j.due_on < CURRENT_DATE
  AND j.closed_on IS NULL
  AND j.status NOT IN ('cancelled');

-- Query 6: workers who logged more than 10 hours on one day
SELECT w.full_name, t.work_date, SUM(t.hours) AS total_hours
FROM timesheets t
JOIN workers w ON w.worker_id = t.worker_id
GROUP BY w.full_name, t.work_date
HAVING SUM(t.hours) > 10
ORDER BY t.work_date DESC;

-- Query 7: unpaid invoices older than 30 days with the owner's contact
SELECT i.invoice_id, v.owner_name, v.owner_email, i.amount_eur, i.issued_on
FROM invoices i
JOIN jobs j ON j.job_id = i.job_id
JOIN vessels v ON v.vessel_id = j.vessel_id
WHERE i.paid_on IS NULL
  AND i.issued_on < CURRENT_DATE - 30
  AND i.status != 'void';

-- Query 8: vessels that have had more than one failed inspection
SELECT v.name, COUNT(*) AS failures
FROM vessels v
JOIN jobs j ON j.vessel_id = v.vessel_id
JOIN inspections ins ON ins.job_id = j.job_id
WHERE ins.result = 'fail'
GROUP BY v.name
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

-- Query 9: berth usage in the last 90 days (days occupied per berth)
SELECT b.berth_code,
       SUM(LEAST(COALESCE(j.closed_on, CURRENT_DATE), CURRENT_DATE) - GREATEST(j.opened_on, CURRENT_DATE - 90)) AS days_used
FROM berths b
LEFT JOIN jobs j ON j.berth_id = b.berth_id
WHERE j.opened_on IS NULL OR j.opened_on <= CURRENT_DATE
GROUP BY b.berth_code
ORDER BY days_used DESC;

-- Query 10: materials below reorder level, based on the last 60 days of use
SELECT m.sku, m.description, m.stock_qty,
       (SELECT COALESCE(SUM(jm.quantity), 0)
        FROM job_materials jm
        WHERE jm.material_id = m.material_id
          AND jm.issued_on > CURRENT_DATE - 60) / 60.0 * 14 AS two_week_need
FROM materials m
WHERE m.stock_qty < (SELECT COALESCE(SUM(jm.quantity), 0)
                     FROM job_materials jm
                     WHERE jm.material_id = m.material_id
                       AND jm.issued_on > CURRENT_DATE - 60) / 60.0 * 14;

-- Query 11: search for jobs by words in the description
SELECT job_id, description
FROM jobs
WHERE LOWER(description) LIKE '%' || LOWER('rudder') || '%';

-- Query 12: monthly invoiced and collected totals this year
SELECT TO_CHAR(issued_on, 'YYYY-MM') AS month,
       SUM(amount_eur) AS invoiced,
       SUM(CASE WHEN paid_on IS NOT NULL THEN amount_eur ELSE 0 END) AS collected
FROM invoices
WHERE EXTRACT(YEAR FROM issued_on) = 2026
GROUP BY TO_CHAR(issued_on, 'YYYY-MM')
ORDER BY month;

-- Query 13: subcontractor cost per job, only assignments that have finished
SELECT a.job_id, s.company_name, a.days_billed * s.day_rate_eur AS sub_cost_eur
FROM sub_assignments a
JOIN subcontractors s ON s.sub_id = a.sub_id
WHERE a.end_date < CURRENT_DATE;

-- Query 14: workers whose welding or crane certificate expires within 60 days
SELECT w.full_name, c.cert_name, c.expires_on
FROM workers w
JOIN certificates c ON c.worker_id = w.worker_id
WHERE w.active = TRUE
  AND c.cert_name IN ('welding', 'crane operator')
  AND c.expires_on BETWEEN CURRENT_DATE AND CURRENT_DATE + 60
ORDER BY c.expires_on;

-- Query 15: the five most expensive jobs per vessel type this year
SELECT vessel_type, job_id, total_cost
FROM (
    SELECT v.vessel_type, j.job_id,
           COALESCE((SELECT SUM(t.hours * w.hourly_rate) FROM timesheets t
                     JOIN workers w ON w.worker_id = t.worker_id
                     WHERE t.job_id = j.job_id), 0)
         + COALESCE((SELECT SUM(jm.quantity * m.unit_cost_eur) FROM job_materials jm
                     JOIN materials m ON m.material_id = jm.material_id
                     WHERE jm.job_id = j.job_id), 0) AS total_cost,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY v.vessel_type ORDER BY j.quoted_eur DESC) AS rn
    FROM jobs j
    JOIN vessels v ON v.vessel_id = j.vessel_id
    WHERE j.opened_on >= '2026-01-01'
) ranked
WHERE rn <= 5;
```

Our team wrote the design document below for a fault-reporting and dispatch system for the street lights we maintain under contract. I will present it to the technical board on Friday. Please critique it honestly, tell me what is weak or missing, suggest realistic alternatives for the major decisions, and then give me an implementation plan with phases, the order of work and the main risks.

# Design: Lamp Fault Reporting and Crew Dispatch (LFRD)

Author: Gerhard Lindqvist-Amadi, Systems Lead, Brightway Lighting Services
Reviewers: Naledi Whitcombe (Operations), Osric Fennimore (Field Crews), Yasmin Teague (Finance)
Status: Draft 3, for board review
Date: 7 October 2026

## 1. Background

Brightway maintains about 38,400 street lights for three municipal councils: Ashford Vale (14,200 lamps), Corrin Bay (17,100) and the Tarn Valley district (7,100). The contracts require us to repair a reported lamp outage within 5 working days for ordinary lamps and within 24 hours for lamps at pedestrian crossings and junctions. Penalties apply at 40 per lamp per day of delay for the critical class.

Today, faults arrive in four ways: a council call centre emails a spreadsheet every morning, residents phone our office, crews note faults they see during night patrols, and a few councils forward messages from a resident app. All of these end up typed by hand into a shared spreadsheet by two dispatchers. The spreadsheet has no history of who changed what. In the last quarter, we found 212 duplicate reports of the same lamp, 61 faults that were never assigned to a crew, and 9 critical faults that passed the 24 hour limit, costing us roughly 4,300 in penalties.

## 2. Goals

1. Every fault report, from any source, becomes one record with a unique number, a lamp, a location and a clock that starts when the report arrives.
2. Duplicate reports of the same lamp within 10 days attach to the open fault instead of creating a new one.
3. Dispatchers see a map and a ranked list, with critical faults and those closest to breaching their deadline shown first.
4. Crews receive their daily job list on a phone, record what they found and what they did, and can work with no mobile signal.
5. Councils get a monthly report generated automatically, showing response times against the contract.

## 3. Non-goals

- Replacing the asset register of lamps, which stays in the existing database owned by Finance.
- Remote monitoring of the lamps themselves. That is a separate project in 2027.
- Routing optimisation across crews. For version 1, dispatchers will assign jobs by hand with the map.

## 4. Proposed architecture

The system has five parts.

**Intake service.** A small web service that accepts reports: an email parser for the councils' daily spreadsheets, a web form for our office, an API endpoint for the resident app, and an entry screen in the crew app. Each report is matched to a lamp using the lamp number printed on the column, or, if the number is not known, using the nearest lamp to the coordinates given within 25 metres.

**Fault database.** A single PostgreSQL database, hosted by our existing cloud provider, with tables for faults, lamps (a read-only copy synchronised nightly from the Finance asset register), crews, assignments and events. Every change to a fault writes an event row, so the full history is kept.

**Dispatch console.** A browser application for the two dispatchers, showing a map with coloured markers (red for critical, orange for ordinary faults within 24 hours of their deadline, grey for the rest) and a list on the right. The dispatcher drags a fault onto a crew to assign it.

**Crew app.** A mobile application for the 22 field staff, written once and run on both Android and iOS. It stores the day's jobs locally, lets the crew photograph the lamp, choose a cause from a short list (lamp failure, driver failure, cable damage, vandalism, knocked down by vehicle, other), record parts used and close the job. When there is no signal, it keeps the changes on the phone and sends them when the signal returns.

**Reporting job.** A scheduled task that runs on the first day of each month and produces a PDF and a spreadsheet for each council: faults received, faults fixed on time, average repair time by class, repeat faults on the same lamp, and penalties incurred.

## 5. Key decisions

### 5.1 One database, no message queue

We considered an event-driven design with a message queue between the intake service and the database. We decided against it because the load is small. Our peak is about 150 reports on the Monday morning after a storm, which one database handles easily. A queue would add another part to run and watch for a team of three developers.

### 5.2 Synchronisation of crew phones

The crew app keeps a local copy of the day's jobs. When it reconnects, it sends its changes and receives updates. If a dispatcher and a crew member change the same fault while the phone is offline, the later change by time stamp wins. We believe conflicts will be rare because only the crew changes a job once it is assigned to them.

### 5.3 Duplicate detection

A new report is treated as a duplicate if the same lamp has an open fault, or a fault closed in the last 10 days. In the second case the fault is reopened and marked as a repeat. We chose 10 days because the field crews say a lamp that fails again within 10 days has usually had the wrong part fitted.

### 5.4 Deadline clock

The clock starts when the first report arrives at any of our channels, not when a dispatcher reads it. The council spreadsheet is emailed at 07:00, but some of the reports in it are from the previous afternoon. We will use the time the council recorded the report, as given in the spreadsheet, when it is available, and the time of receipt otherwise.

### 5.5 Authentication

Dispatchers and crews sign in with accounts managed in our existing company directory. The resident app endpoint uses a shared key per council. Photos are stored in an object store and linked from the fault, and they are kept for 24 months.

### 5.6 Hosting and backup

The database runs on a managed instance with daily backups kept for 14 days. The recovery target is four hours. We have not yet decided whether to use a second region.

## 6. Data model (summary)

- lamps: lamp_id, council, column_number, latitude, longitude, class (ordinary or critical), lamp_type, installed_on
- faults: fault_id, lamp_id, reported_at, source, class, status, deadline_at, closed_at, cause, repeat_of
- assignments: assignment_id, fault_id, crew_id, assigned_at, planned_for, completed_at
- events: event_id, fault_id, at, actor, kind, details
- crews: crew_id, name, vehicle, lead_name
- parts_used: fault_id, part_code, quantity

## 7. Security and privacy

Reports from residents may include names and phone numbers. We store these only on the fault record, show them to dispatchers, and do not send them to the crew app unless the dispatcher marks the fault as needing a call-back. Personal details are deleted 90 days after the fault closes. The crew app does not store passwords on the phone, and a lost phone can be blocked from the directory.

## 8. Testing approach

We will test the intake matching using the last six months of real reports, about 11,000 records, and check that duplicates are found as the dispatchers would find them. The crew app will be tried by four volunteer crews for two weeks before a general release. We will not run a load test, since the traffic is low.

## 9. Escalation and alerts

Each fault has a deadline, and the system warns people as it approaches. For critical faults, the dispatcher sees an amber marker 8 hours before the deadline and a red marker at 4 hours. At 2 hours, a text message goes to the Operations manager (Naledi Whitcombe) and, outside office hours, to the on-call crew lead. For ordinary faults, the warning is shown at 24 hours before the deadline in the list only, without messages. A fault that is assigned but not marked as started within 3 hours of its planned time is shown with a clock symbol so that the dispatcher can call the crew.

Storm days are handled by a manual switch. When the dispatcher turns on storm mode, the console groups faults by street and by district instead of by individual lamp, and the 10 day duplicate rule is shortened to 48 hours, because after a storm many neighbouring lamps legitimately fail on the same day. Storm mode does not change the contract deadlines. The councils have agreed that deadlines for ordinary faults are extended to 10 working days during a declared storm, but this is a manual decision by the council, and the system only records the date on which the council declared it.

## 10. Monitoring and operations

The intake service writes a heartbeat to the database every minute. If no heartbeat is seen for 5 minutes, the on-call developer receives a text message. Separate checks watch for three kinds of silent failure: no reports arrived from the council spreadsheet by 09:00 on a working day, the nightly lamp synchronisation finished with fewer than 99 percent of the previous lamp count, and the crew app has not sent data from a crew that has jobs assigned for more than 4 hours. We will log every parsed report with the raw source text so that mismatches can be investigated later.

The database size is expected to reach about 6 gigabytes in three years, mostly in the events table. Photos are not stored in the database. The object store for photos is expected to hold about 400 gigabytes by then, assuming two photos per fault at 1.5 megabytes each and 28,000 faults a year. Old photos are moved to cheaper storage after 6 months.

Releases are done on Tuesday mornings, after the dispatchers' peak, and only after the automated tests pass. The crew app is released in two steps: first to the crew leads, and after three days to everybody. The app checks the server on start and refuses to sync if it is too old, showing a message asking the crew to update. The server accepts the previous two versions of the app for two weeks.

## 11. Alternatives considered

We looked at buying an off-the-shelf work-order product used by several utilities. Its licence would cost about 28,000 a year for 25 users, and it does not handle our council spreadsheet format or the 10 day repeat rule without paid customisation, which the supplier quoted at 45,000. We decided to build, but the board may want to compare again if the schedule slips.

We also considered extending the existing spreadsheet with scripts. This would be cheap, but it cannot work offline on phones, and a shared spreadsheet cannot give the history of changes that the councils have asked us for in the next contract round.

Finally, we considered letting the councils log directly into our dispatch console to see their own faults. We left this out of version 1 to limit the number of users and the need for access controls, but the data model supports it, because every fault records its council.

## 12. Reporting details

The monthly report counts a fault as on time if its status changed to fixed before the deadline, regardless of when the dispatcher closed it. Faults that need a part we do not stock, for example a special lantern head, are marked as waiting for parts, and the clock stops only if the contract allows it, which today applies only in the Tarn Valley contract. The report lists such faults separately. Average repair time is the mean of working hours between the start of the clock and the fix, excluding weekends and public holidays, and excluding periods marked as waiting for council access, such as roadworks that block the column. The report also shows the ten lamps with the most repeat faults in the last 12 months, so that the councils can decide whether to replace them.

## 13. Training and change management

The two dispatchers have used the spreadsheet for nine years, and the project depends on them trusting the new console. Osric Fennimore proposed that both dispatchers join a design review every second week from week 3, and that they run the old spreadsheet and the new console side by side for the final two weeks before the switch. Each morning they will compare the two lists and note any fault that appears in only one. The crews will receive a one-page guide and a 45 minute session at the depot, held twice so that the night patrol can attend, and each crew lead gets a short video on closing a job without signal. Yasmin Teague asked that the first month of monthly reports be checked by hand against the old figures before they are sent to the councils.

## 14. Rollout

Phase 1 (weeks 1 to 8): database, intake service, the dispatch console. Dispatchers move off the spreadsheet in week 8. Phase 2 (weeks 9 to 16): crew app and offline mode. Phase 3 (weeks 17 to 20): monthly reports and the resident app link. Go-live for all three councils in week 21, which is the third week of March, before the spring storms.

## 15. Cost

Development effort is estimated at 3 developers for 20 weeks, about 120,000 including a tester for four weeks. Running costs are about 900 a month for hosting and the map provider. Finance expects a saving of roughly 31,000 a year from fewer penalties and one dispatcher hour less per day, which gives a payback of about 4 years if the penalty savings are as expected.

## 16. Open questions

- Who maintains the nightly lamp synchronisation if Finance changes the asset register layout?
- What happens to faults reported for lamps that are not in our asset register, such as lamps owned by private estates?
- Can the councils change the spreadsheet format without telling us? Today they have done this twice in two years.
- Should the crew be able to close a critical fault without a photo?
