I have just joined the committee of our rowing club and I have to vote on this new membership and boat-use policy next week. I am not a lawyer and some of it is hard to follow. Please explain it to me clause by clause in plain language, and then tell me what the risks are for ordinary members, for the club, and for me as a committee member.

MEMBERSHIP, BOAT USE AND SAFETY POLICY
Tidewater Rowing Club (the "Club")
Version 4.0, to take effect on 1 January 2027, subject to approval at the committee meeting of 14 October 2026

1. Purpose and status

1.1 This policy sets out the rules for membership, the use of boats and equipment, safety on the water and the handling of accidents and complaints. It replaces the Membership and Boat Use Policy, version 3.2.
1.2 By joining or renewing membership, each member agrees to follow this policy. The committee may change the policy by majority vote, and must give members at least 28 days' written notice of any change that affects fees, insurance or safety rules.
1.3 Where this policy conflicts with the Club's constitution, the constitution prevails.

2. Membership classes and fees

2.1 The Club has the following classes of membership: Full (age 18 or over, rowing access at all permitted times), Junior (under 18, rowing only under supervision), Student (full-time students with a valid card, same access as Full), Social (no rowing access, use of the clubhouse only) and Honorary (granted by the committee, no fee).
2.2 Annual fees are set by the committee and published on the Club's notice board and website by 1 November each year. The fees for 2027 are: Full 310, Student 170, Junior 140, Social 60.
2.3 Fees are due on 1 January. A member who has not paid by 31 January loses rowing access until payment is received. A member who has not paid by 31 March is treated as having resigned, and any boat storage rights end.
2.4 Fees are not refunded if a member leaves during the year, except where the member is unable to row for more than six months on the written advice of a doctor, in which case the committee may refund up to half the fee for the remaining months.
2.5 A new member must complete a swim test and an induction on the water before taking a boat out alone. The induction costs 25 and is not refunded.

3. Swimming and fitness declaration

3.1 Every member rowing at the Club must be able to swim 50 metres in light clothing and tread water for two minutes. The member confirms this in writing at joining and again every three years.
3.2 Each member must declare any medical condition that could affect safety on the water, including epilepsy, heart conditions and diabetes. The declaration is kept by the Club secretary and shared only with the safety officer and the coach on duty.
3.3 A member who knowingly gives false information on a declaration may have membership ended under clause 11.

4. Use of boats and equipment

4.1 Club boats may be used only by members with rowing access, and only after signing the boat book with name, boat, time out and expected time back.
4.2 Single sculls may be used only by members who have passed the single scull assessment. Quads and eights may be used by any Full or Student member under the direction of a qualified cox or captain.
4.3 A member who damages a boat or equipment through carelessness must report it to the boat officer within 24 hours. The Club may require the member to pay for repairs up to 250 for each incident. Damage caused by a deliberate act or by rowing in conditions that the safety officer had declared unsafe may be charged in full.
4.4 Private boats stored at the Club remain the property of the owner. The owner pays an annual storage fee of 120 and is responsible for insurance of the boat. The Club is not liable for loss or damage to private boats while on its premises, except where caused by the Club's negligence.
4.5 Boats must be washed and put back in the correct rack after use. Members who repeatedly fail to do so may be asked to complete extra duty shifts.

5. Safety on the water

5.1 The safety officer is the person named by the committee for that role. The safety officer may suspend rowing at any time because of weather, river level, debris or any other hazard, and members must follow that decision.
5.2 The river flag system is: green for normal conditions, amber for novices to stay off the water and all others to row only in pairs or larger boats, and red for no rowing. Flags are shown at the clubhouse landing.
5.3 Every boat on the water after sunset or before sunrise must carry a white light at the front and back. Rowing in fog is not permitted.
5.4 Junior members may row only when a qualified coach is present, and the coach must have a current first aid certificate and background check.
5.5 A coaching launch with a working radio or mobile phone and a first aid kit must accompany any outing of novices and any outing under amber flag.
5.6 Lifejackets are required for all coxswains and for all members rowing under amber flag. They are available in the boat store and must be checked monthly by the safety officer.

6. Accidents and near misses

6.1 Any injury, capsize, collision or near miss must be reported to the safety officer on the same day, using the form in the boat store or the online form.
6.2 The safety officer keeps a log and reports it to the committee at each meeting, without naming the member unless the member agrees or the committee needs the name to decide on a safety matter.
6.3 After any serious injury, the committee must review the incident within 14 days and decide whether to change procedures. Serious means any injury needing hospital treatment.
6.4 The Club will inform its insurer of all incidents that may lead to a claim. A member must not admit liability on the Club's behalf or agree to pay compensation without the committee's written agreement.

7. Insurance and liability

7.1 The Club holds public liability insurance of 5 million. This covers claims by third parties for injury or damage caused by the Club's activities. It does not cover injury to a member caused only by the member's own actions.
7.2 Each member takes part in rowing at their own risk, to the extent allowed by law. Nothing in this policy limits liability for death or personal injury caused by the Club's negligence, or for fraud.
7.3 Members are encouraged to hold personal accident insurance. The affiliated national body offers a policy to members for about 18 a year.
7.4 Guests may row once as a taster under the supervision of a qualified member, after signing a waiver. A guest may take part in no more than two tasters in a year.

8. Clubhouse, keys and duties

8.1 Each Full, Student and Social member must complete six hours of club duty each year, such as bar shifts, cleaning, boat maintenance or helping at regattas. Juniors are excused. Members who do not complete their hours by 30 November pay a levy of 15 for each missing hour.
8.2 Members holding keys to the clubhouse must not copy them or lend them. A lost key must be reported within 48 hours, and the replacement lock may be charged to the member up to 80.
8.3 Alcohol may be served in the clubhouse only by the bar volunteers, and must not be consumed while using boats or while on the landing stage.

9. Data protection

9.1 The Club keeps members' names, contact details, emergency contacts, medical declarations and payment records. These are used only to run the Club, to contact members and in an emergency.
9.2 Medical declarations are held by the secretary in a locked cabinet or encrypted file and are deleted two years after a member leaves.
9.3 Photographs may be taken at events and used in Club publications. A member who does not wish to appear must tell the secretary in writing, and the Club will make reasonable efforts to respect this.

10. Complaints

10.1 A member with a complaint should first speak to the person involved or the relevant officer. If this does not resolve it, the member may write to the secretary, who will pass it to the committee. The committee will reply in writing within 28 days.
10.2 A member who is not satisfied may ask for the complaint to be heard by a panel of three members who are not on the committee. The panel's decision is final.

11. Suspension and removal

11.1 The committee may suspend or end a membership if a member seriously breaches this policy, endangers others, damages the Club's reputation or fails to pay money owed.
11.2 Before taking such a step, the committee must tell the member in writing what is alleged and give at least 14 days to reply. The member may bring one other member for support to any meeting about the matter.
11.3 A member whose membership is ended loses all fees paid for the rest of the year, except where the committee decides otherwise.
11.4 In an emergency, the safety officer or the chair may suspend a member immediately for up to 7 days while the matter is considered under clause 11.2.

12. Racing, regattas and selection

12.1 The captain of the Club selects crews for regattas and head races after consulting the coach. Selection is based on recent performance in trials, attendance at training and availability on the race day. The captain must tell members who were not selected the reasons if they ask.
12.2 A member selected for a crew who withdraws less than 72 hours before the race, other than for illness or injury, may be asked to pay any entry fee already paid on their behalf, up to 40.
12.3 Entry fees for regattas are paid by the Club for Junior members and by the member in all other cases, unless the committee decides to support a particular event.
12.4 Members racing under the Club's colours must wear the Club's racing kit, which costs 55 and is bought once. The Club may lend kit to a member in financial difficulty, and any such request is kept confidential.
12.5 Trailers and vehicles used to carry Club boats to events must be driven by a member who holds the correct licence for the combined weight. The Club pays fuel and trailer costs, and members are asked to share lifts where possible.

13. Conduct, social media and welfare

13.1 Members must treat each other, coaches, visitors and other river users with respect. Bullying, harassment, discrimination and abusive language are not accepted, whether in person, on the water or online.
13.2 The committee appoints a welfare officer who is trained in safeguarding. Any concern about the welfare of a Junior member must be reported to the welfare officer at once. The welfare officer decides whether the matter must be reported to outside authorities, and the committee must not delay a report to take a vote.
13.3 Adults must not be alone with a Junior member in a changing room, a boat or a private vehicle, except where a parent or guardian has agreed in writing. Coaches should communicate with Junior members only through group messages that include a parent or guardian.
13.4 Members who post about the Club on social media must not share images of Junior members without the written agreement of a parent or guardian, and must not post material that could identify a member's home address or routine.
13.5 Complaints about conduct follow clause 10, except that complaints about the safeguarding of a Junior member go directly to the welfare officer and the chair.

14. Environment and river users

14.1 Members must give way to other river users in accordance with the national river rules, and must keep the bank clear of rubbish. Fuel, paint and cleaning products must be stored in the locked cupboard in the boat store.
14.2 Members must not row through the nesting area marked by the buoys between 1 March and 31 July, and must slow down when passing moored boats and anglers.
14.3 The Club takes part in an annual river clean-up day. Taking part counts for two hours of duty under clause 8.1.

15. Transitional provisions

15.1 A member who passed the single scull assessment under version 3.2 is treated as having passed it under this policy.
15.2 The fees in clause 2.2 apply from 1 January 2027. Members who paid their 2027 fee early at the 2026 rate will not be asked to pay the difference.
15.3 The six hour duty requirement in clause 8.1 applies in full from 1 January 2027. For 2026, the old requirement of four hours remains.

16. Changes and review

16.1 This policy is reviewed every two years. Any member may propose a change by giving the secretary a written proposal, signed by at least five members, at least 21 days before an annual general meeting.
16.2 The secretary will keep a copy of each version and make the current version available on request and on the website.

17. Definitions

17.1 "Committee" means the elected officers of the Club: the chair, the secretary, the treasurer, the captain, the safety officer, the boat officer, the welfare officer and two ordinary members.
17.2 "Qualified coach" means a coach who holds a current coaching award from the national body, a first aid certificate not older than three years and a satisfactory background check renewed every three years.
17.3 "Qualified cox" means a member who has passed the Club's steering assessment and has been signed off by the coach for the boat class concerned.
17.4 "Duty" means unpaid work for the Club agreed by the committee, recorded by the secretary on the duty sheet in the clubhouse.
17.5 "In writing" includes email to the address the member has given to the secretary, but does not include text messages or social media.
17.6 "Day" means a calendar day unless the clause says working day, and notice sent by post is treated as received two days after posting.

Our maintenance firm wrote up an internal study on whether vibration monitoring can predict elevator door failures, and I am going to submit it to a trade journal. Please write a detailed peer review of the methods and results sections below, as a demanding referee would: strengths, major concerns, minor concerns, questions for the authors, and a clear recommendation on whether it should be published.

Predicting Door-Operator Failures in Passenger Elevators from Vibration Signatures: A Fourteen-Month Field Study

Authors: Ingrid Halvorsen-Mbeki, Casimir Delaney, Thuy Anh Brightwell
Affiliation: Reliability Group, Corbel & Lyle Lift Services

Methods

2.1 Study population

We studied 184 passenger elevators serviced by Corbel & Lyle in the northern service region between 1 March 2025 and 30 April 2026. The elevators were located in 61 buildings: 33 residential blocks, 17 offices, 7 hospitals or care homes, and 4 retail centres. Elevators were included if they had a sliding door operator of one of the two types most common in the fleet (type A, a belt-driven operator, n = 121; type B, a linear-motor operator, n = 63) and if they had been in service for at least two years at the start of the study. We excluded elevators scheduled for modernisation within the study period (n = 9) and elevators with an operator replaced in the previous 12 months (n = 14). The buildings were not chosen at random: we selected those with a technician who agreed to fit and check the sensors, which may favour well-run buildings.

2.2 Sensors and data collection

A small three-axis accelerometer with a sampling rate of 1,600 Hz was fixed to the header of the car door of each elevator. The device recorded a 6 second window around each door opening and closing, and stored a summary of each window on a local memory card. The summary included the root-mean-square acceleration in three frequency bands (below 40 Hz, 40 to 200 Hz and 200 to 800 Hz), the peak acceleration, the duration of the door movement in milliseconds, and the number of reversals (times the door stopped and moved back). Summaries were uploaded once a day through the building's network connection. For 17 elevators, the connection was unreliable, and data were collected by technicians on monthly visits. In total we gathered 41.2 million door cycles. Door cycles with a duration below 1.5 seconds or above 12 seconds were considered sensor errors and removed (0.6 percent of all cycles).

2.3 Outcome definition

The outcome was a door-operator failure, defined as a callout in which the technician's report recorded a fault in the door operator, its drive, belt, rollers, sill or lock, and the elevator was out of service for any time. Callouts caused by a user blocking the door, a power cut, or a fault in the controller were not counted. The classification was made by one of the authors (C.D.) from the free-text technician report, and a second author (T.A.B.) independently checked a random 15 percent sample of 52 reports, agreeing on 49 of them (94 percent). In total there were 143 failures in 112 elevators.

2.4 Features and model

For each elevator and each day, we computed the mean of each summary measure over the preceding 7 days and over the preceding 28 days, and the difference between the two. We also included elevator age, door type, building type, average cycles per day, and the number of failures in the previous year. Because the failures are rare events, we defined a positive example as any elevator-day within 14 days before a failure, and a negative example as any elevator-day with no failure in the following 30 days. Days between 15 and 30 days before a failure were left out to avoid ambiguous labels.

We trained a gradient-boosted tree model. The data were divided into training, validation and test sets by time: March to December 2025 for training (with the last two months used for validation to choose the settings), January to April 2026 for testing. The model produced a daily risk score. An alert was raised for an elevator when the score exceeded a threshold, chosen on the validation set to give 80 percent recall. After an alert, no new alert was raised for the same elevator for 14 days.

2.5 Comparison methods

We compared the model with two baselines. The first was the existing calendar-based schedule, in which every elevator is visited every 8 weeks. The second was a simple rule: alert when the weekly mean of the 40 to 200 Hz band exceeds the elevator's own median by more than 50 percent. We did not compare with other published methods because our data and sensors are different.

2.6 Statistical analysis

We report precision, recall, and the area under the precision-recall curve for the test period, with 95 percent confidence intervals from 1,000 bootstrap resamples of elevators. To estimate the practical value, we calculated the number of alerts per elevator-year, the median warning time before a failure, and the estimated cost, using an average callout cost of 410 and an average planned visit cost of 95. We did not adjust for multiple comparisons, since only three outcomes are reported.

Results

3.1 Description of the data

Over the 14 months, 143 door-operator failures occurred in 112 elevators: 96 in type A and 47 in type B. Fifty-seven failures (40 percent) were belt or roller wear, 31 (22 percent) were sill or guide obstruction or wear, 27 (19 percent) were lock or contact faults, and 28 (19 percent) were drive or motor faults. The failure rate was 0.67 per elevator-year for type A and 0.52 for type B. Residential blocks had a higher rate (0.78) than offices (0.49) and hospitals (0.51). The training set contained 94 failures, the validation set 22, and the test set 27 failures in 24 elevators.

Table 1. Performance in the test period (January to April 2026)

| Method | Alerts | Precision | Recall | Median warning (days) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Calendar visits (8 weeks) | 1,096 visits | 2.1% | 71% | not applicable |
| Simple band rule | 312 | 6.4% | 52% | 5 |
| Gradient-boosted model | 138 | 13.8% | 70% | 9 |

The gradient-boosted model detected 19 of the 27 test failures (70 percent recall) with 138 alerts, giving a precision of 13.8 percent. This is below the 80 percent recall chosen on the validation set, where the model reached 81 percent recall with 15.2 percent precision. The area under the precision-recall curve was 0.21 (95 percent interval 0.14 to 0.31), compared with 0.09 (0.05 to 0.15) for the simple rule. Of the 8 failures the model missed, 5 were lock or contact faults, which produce little change in vibration.

3.2 Warning time

For the 19 detected failures, the median time from the first alert to the failure was 9 days (interquartile range 4 to 12). In 6 of the 19 cases, the warning time was 3 days or less, which would be hard to use in practice, since a technician visit takes on average 4 days to schedule. In the four cases where the alert was raised more than 10 days before failure and a visit followed, a technician found a worn belt or a damaged roller. We did not record whether those components would have failed without the visit.

3.3 Importance of features

The most important features were the change in the 200 to 800 Hz band between the 7 day and 28 day averages, the number of reversals per 1,000 cycles, and the duration of the closing movement. Elevator age and prior failures were less important than we had expected. The model for type B doors had lower recall (58 percent) than the model for type A doors (75 percent), although the difference is based on 8 and 19 test failures, and the interval is wide.

3.4 Alerts per elevator and false alarms

The model produced 138 alerts in the test period, equal to 2.2 alerts per elevator-year. Of these, 119 did not precede a failure within 14 days. We inspected 40 of the false alerts in the field. In 11 of them, the technician found a problem that had not yet caused a failure (a loosened belt, a bent guide), in 9 the cause was a temporary obstruction such as a building delivery, and in 20 nothing was found. If the 11 are counted as useful, the practical precision rises to 21.7 percent, but we did not test this on the other 79 false alerts.

3.5 Cost estimate

Under the 8 week schedule, the 184 elevators received 1,096 visits in the test period, which cost 104,120 at 95 each. A strategy that used only model alerts for these elevators would have involved 138 visits (13,110) plus the 8 missed failures at 410 each (3,280) and the 19 detected failures, assuming each was prevented by a visit at 95 (1,805), a total of 18,195. We therefore estimate a saving of roughly 85,900 in the four months. This calculation assumes that a visit prevents every failure it is triggered for, and that the planned visits under the calendar schedule are only used for door operator maintenance. In practice, the calendar visit also covers safety checks required by regulation, which cannot be removed.

3.6 Sensitivity analyses

When we moved the cut-off between training and test data by two months, recall at the validation threshold fell to 63 percent and precision to 11.9 percent. When we removed the 17 elevators with manual data collection, precision rose to 15.4 percent. When we used a 21 day positive window instead of 14 days, recall rose to 74 percent but median warning time fell to 7 days.

3.7 Performance by failure cause

Table 2. Test-period failures detected by the gradient-boosted model, by cause

| Cause | Failures in test period | Detected | Recall |
|---|---|---|---|
| Belt or roller wear | 9 | 8 | 89% |
| Sill or guide wear or obstruction | 5 | 4 | 80% |
| Lock or contact fault | 7 | 2 | 29% |
| Drive or motor fault | 6 | 5 | 83% |
| All causes | 27 | 19 | 70% |

Detection was good for mechanical wear and weak for lock and contact faults, which are typically electrical and sudden. The confidence interval for lock and contact recall is wide (4 to 71 percent) because only seven failures were available. We did not train a separate model for these faults.

3.8 Performance by building type

Hospital and care home elevators (7 buildings, 22 elevators) generated 11 alerts in the test period, of which 4 preceded a failure (precision 36 percent). Residential elevators (33 buildings, 102 elevators) generated 94 alerts, 11 of them correct (12 percent). Office and retail elevators together generated 33 alerts, with 4 correct (12 percent). The higher precision in hospitals may reflect their greater daily cycle counts, which gives the model more data per day, but it may also reflect the more careful cleaning of sills and tracks. We did not test either explanation.

3.9 Missing data and sensor faults

Over the study, 23 of the 184 sensors had at least one gap of more than 5 days without data, and 6 sensors failed completely and were replaced. During the test period, 4.8 percent of elevator-days had no usable data. Missing days were not imputed, and the model gave no score for the next day when the 7 day window contained fewer than 4 days of data. Of the 27 test failures, 3 occurred in elevators whose sensor was down in the preceding week, and none of these was detected.

3.10 Technician feedback

After the test period, 9 of the 12 technicians who answered a short questionnaire said that most alerts were not useful when they arrived without a reason. They asked for the system to show which measure had moved. When a short explanation was added to 30 later alerts (not part of the test set), technicians reported finding a cause in 14 cases (47 percent), but this was informal and was not compared with a control group. Technicians also pointed out that three of the buildings had changed their door cleaning routine during the study, which could change the vibration signature without any change in the mechanical condition.

3.11 Calibration and stability of the score

We checked whether the risk score is a reliable estimate of probability by grouping test-period elevator-days into five bands by score. In the lowest three bands, together containing 91 percent of elevator-days, the observed rate of a failure within 14 days was 0.04 percent, well below the model's mean predicted value of 0.1 percent, so the model overestimates risk at the low end. In the top band, the observed rate was 1.9 percent against a mean predicted value of 3.6 percent. We did not recalibrate the score. The score for an individual elevator was also unstable from one day to the next: for the 19 detected failures, the score stayed above the threshold on every day between the first alert and the failure in only 7 cases, and in the others it dropped below the threshold for one or more days before rising again. Because alerts are suppressed for 14 days after the first, this instability did not create more alerts, but it would affect any plan to use the score as a continuous measure of condition.

Here are the first four chapters of a short story I am writing, set at a small observatory on a hill. I am stuck on what comes next. Please continue the story at length, in the same voice and tense, for at least two more chapters, keeping the characters and details consistent and moving toward an ending that feels earned.

THE LAST CLEAR NIGHT AT HOLLOWAY HILL

1.

The road to the observatory had not been mended in eleven years, and Marit Oyelaran had learned to drive it the way one learns to walk with a stone in a shoe: without thinking, and with a certain private resentment. She took the third bend slowly, where the ditch had taken a bite out of the verge, and the little grey hatchback shuddered and carried on. At the top, the trees gave way. The dome stood against a sky the colour of dishwater, round and white and slightly dingy, like an egg someone had forgotten in a drawer.

She parked beside the other car, an old estate with a cracked wing mirror held on by tape, and sat for a minute with the engine ticking. It was the first of October. The letter from the university was in her bag, folded in four, and she had read it so many times that the creases had begun to turn soft. She did not take it out. She knew what it said. The Holloway Hill Observatory, after one hundred and four years, would be closed at the end of the year, and its telescope, a fourteen-inch reflector that had been the pride of a long-dead Victorian brewer, would be offered to a museum. The staff, which was to say Marit and one other person, would be thanked.

She had been the observatory's assistant director for six years. Before that she had been a graduate student with an unfinished thesis on variable stars and a strong feeling that real life would begin when she stopped being asked questions she could not answer. She had come to Holloway Hill for what was supposed to be a summer.

The door to the main building was unlocked. It was always unlocked. Inside, the corridor smelled as it always did, of cold radiators, floor polish and old paper, with something faintly sweet under it, like pipe smoke from a decade ago that had never entirely left. A radio was playing somewhere, very quietly. Marit followed it to the kitchen and found Osmund Pettigrew standing at the stove with his back to her, stirring a pan of something that could not decide whether it was porridge or soup.

"You are early," he said, without turning round.

"It is ten past four in the afternoon."

"For you, that is early." He turned. He was seventy-three, tall and stooped, with a long nose and pale eyes that were always a little wet from the cold, and he wore the same green cardigan he had worn on her first day. He had been the director since before she was born. "Tonight will be clear," he said. "I have been watching the high cloud since noon, and it is thinning from the west. I think we will have the first clear night in nineteen days."

Marit put her bag on the table. She thought of the letter. She thought, with the tired cunning of someone who has decided not to say a thing, that it could wait until after the clear night.

"What shall we do with it?" she asked.

Osmund smiled, and his whole face changed. "I thought," he said, "we might look at something we have not looked at for a very long time."

2.

The dome was cold in the way that only large, empty, round rooms are cold: a patient and formal cold, the kind that does not rush at you but waits. They went up the iron stairs at half past six, with flasks and blankets, and Osmund unlocked the shutter with a key the size of a spoon. The slit opened with a groan, and the last of the daylight slid across the floor and went out. The sky above them was already deepening, a hard blue turning toward black, and the first stars came out in no particular order.

The telescope stood in the centre of the floor like a sleeping animal. It was a long black tube on a cast-iron mount, its brass fittings worn pale where generations of hands had held them. The brewer, Ambrose Tilling, had paid for it in 1922 and had been buried, according to local rumour, with a star chart folded in his coat. Marit had never found the grave. She had looked.

"Do you remember," Osmund said, as he checked the clock drive, "the first thing you ever showed me through this tube?"

"Albireo," she said. "You said it was the most honest double star in the sky, because one is gold and one is blue and neither pretends to be something else."

"I said no such thing. I would never say anything so sentimental."

"You said it twice."

He grunted, which was his way of conceding. He was bent over the eyepiece rack now, choosing, and she watched his hands. They were large hands, spotted, with a slight tremor that had not been there when she arrived. He had told her that it was the cold, and she had decided to believe him.

By eight, the sky was entirely dark, and clearer than she could remember. The Milky Way came up over the eastern trees like smoke from a distant fire. Marit slewed the telescope to the Andromeda galaxy, a smear of pale light, and then to the Double Cluster, and then, because it was there and because it was the sort of thing they did, to the Ring Nebula in Lyra, a tiny smoke ring hanging in black space. She found herself speaking quietly, as one does in a church, though no one was listening but the old man. When she looked up from the eyepiece, he was sitting on the observing stool with his hands between his knees and his face turned toward the slit.

"What is it?" she asked.

"Nothing," he said. "I was thinking about the year I came here. Nineteen seventy-nine. We had a comet that spring. I stood out here for six nights and I never once felt cold." He laughed at himself. "Forgive me. It is the kind of night that makes old men talkative."

She wanted to tell him then. The words were ready in her mouth, but he had begun to talk about the comet, and the way the tail had looked like a long, pale finger pointing out of the world, and she could not interrupt. At half past ten, they went down for tea. At eleven, the cloud began to come back from the south-west, thin and silver at first, and then not thin.

"Well," Osmund said, as the last stars went. "That is that. Nineteen days of cloud for three and a half hours of sky. I have been well paid."

3.

The letter came to light the following morning, and not in the way Marit had planned.

She had come down to the kitchen to find Osmund at the table, in the green cardigan, with a cup of tea going cold in front of him and an envelope beside it. It was not her envelope. It was long and cream-coloured, with the university's crest in the corner, and it had been opened with a knife, neatly, along the top. For a moment she thought it was another copy of her own. Then she saw that it was addressed to him alone, and that there was a second page, folded separately, that she had not been sent.

"You knew," Osmund said. He did not look up.

"I was going to tell you last night."

"I think you were going to tell me for about a month." There was no anger in his voice. That was the worst of it. "It is all right. They wrote to me in August. I have known since then."

Marit sat down across from him. The kitchen clock, which ran six minutes fast, ticked on the wall. Outside, the weather had turned: a low grey rain was falling, steady and unpromising, over the lawn where the old transit instrument stood under its tarpaulin.

"August," she said. "You said nothing."

"I wanted one more clear night." He turned the cup in its saucer. "That was all I wanted. I thought, if the autumn gives me one, I will tell her afterwards, and we will be sorry together. And the autumn gave me one. Last night. So that is done." He smiled, a little crookedly. "I did not quite plan how to be sorry."

She noticed the second page then, and reached for it, and he let her. It was a short, formal note from the dean's office. It did not concern the closure. It said that the Tilling bequest, the small endowment that had paid for the dome's upkeep since 1931, was to be wound up, and that a sum of forty-one thousand pounds would be released to the observatory "for such final purposes as the director may reasonably determine, provided these are completed before the thirty-first of December."

"Final purposes," Marit said.

"Yes."

"What does that mean? What can you do with forty-one thousand pounds?"

"I have been asking myself since August." He leaned back. The chair creaked. "I could repair the roof, which leaks. I could send the plate archive to the library, where it will sit in a basement. I could buy a very handsome plaque." He paused. "Or I could do something I have wanted to do for thirty years, which is to finish the survey."

She knew about the survey, though not well. It lived in a cabinet in the east room: sixty-three notebooks in Osmund's small, upright handwriting, begun in 1996 and abandoned, as far as she could tell, around 2011. It was a visual record of a patch of sky in the constellation Cygnus, two hundred and twelve variable stars, each one checked by eye on every clear night, week after week, year after year. It was the sort of project that nobody asked for and nobody would ever read. When she had once asked him why he stopped, he had changed the subject.

"The notebooks are not finished," she said carefully.

"No. There are gaps. Some years the weather was unkind and some years I was." He did not explain the last part. "Fourteen of the stars were never closed out. Their periods are long, you see. Some would take another winter or two, if they are to be understood at all. And I do not have another winter or two, Marit, the observatory does not, but the stars do not know that."

The rain strengthened against the window. She listened to it, and to the clock, and to the faint steady ticking of a house that had been loved for a century and would be empty by Christmas. She was aware of a decision approaching her from a long way off, as one watches a figure come up a road.

"There are eleven weeks," she said slowly.

"Eleven weeks and two days."

"At this time of year, in this country, we will get perhaps ten clear nights. Maybe fewer."

"I know."

"And you would need every one of them."

He looked at her then, directly, and for the first time since she had known him, he looked old: not frail, but unguarded, like a house with the shutters taken down. "I would not ask it of you," he said. "It is not your survey. You have a career to think about, and an offer from the institute in the spring, which I know about, because Pauline at the village post office cannot keep a secret." The ghost of a smile. "I am only telling you what I am going to do, so that you will not be surprised when you find me on the lawn at three in the morning in a blanket."

Marit picked up the cold cup of tea and drank it, all of it, to give herself something to do. Then she stood, went to the cabinet in the east room, and took down the first of the sixty-three notebooks.

4.

The notebooks smelled of pencil and damp. She carried the first six to the kitchen table and opened them one by one under the lamp, while Osmund made a second pot of tea and pretended not to watch her. The early pages were beautiful. Each night had its own heading: the date, the time, the transparency of the sky graded from one to five, and then the long columns of magnitudes, estimated by eye against a ladder of comparison stars. Beside each number was a small mark, a tick or a dash, in a code she did not yet understand.

"The dash means I could not see it," Osmund said, setting down the cups. "The tick means I could, and the circle means I wasn't sure. Do not trust the circles. Most of the circles are me being kind to myself."

By noon the rain had settled in as if it meant to stay. They worked through the kitchen's slow afternoon, the lamp on in the middle of the day, and Marit began to see the shape of the thing. The survey was not a catalogue. It was a long conversation with two hundred and twelve stars, most of which had answered faithfully, rising and falling in their small private rhythms, and fourteen of which had gone quiet, or strange, or too slow to follow. Next to the entry for a star in Cygnus labelled only by a number, in a margin note dated March 2009, she found a line that was not about magnitudes at all.

She read it twice. Osmund was at the sink with his back to her.

"It says," she said, "'M. asked tonight whether the star would still be here when we are not. Told her yes. Did not say how many of them are not.'"

The tap ran. After a moment he turned it off, and dried his hands on a tea towel, thoroughly, one finger at a time.

"My wife," he said. "Margarethe. She used to come up in the winters and hold the torch. She was a terrible observer. She talked through everything, and she could never remember which way was north." He folded the towel and hung it on the rail. "She died in the spring of 2011. After that I did not feel like writing down numbers for a while, and then a while was a long time."

Marit did not say she was sorry. She had learned, in six years at Holloway Hill, that Osmund Pettigrew could be thanked or argued with but not consoled, and that the kindest thing was to turn the page. She turned the page.

"Then these are the fourteen," she said, and began to list them on the back of an envelope: their numbers, their last recorded magnitudes, the dates they had gone silent. By four o'clock she had a table. By five, she had worked out that nine of the fourteen could be closed out in a single winter if the weather gave them eight clear nights, and that the other five would need a second season, which they did not have, or a different method, which they might.

"A different method?" Osmund said.

"The camera," she said. "The one in the cupboard. The one you said you did not trust."

"I do not trust it."

"I know. But it would count photons on the five faint ones while you did the other nine by eye, in the old way, and if we are very careful we could tie the two scales together on the nights they overlap." She heard her own voice quicken and felt the old thesis come back into her hands, the pleasure of a problem that had edges. "It would not be the survey you started. It would be a survey with a seam in it."

Osmund considered this for a long time. Outside, the rain was easing, and a thin, cold light was coming back into the garden, and the tarpaulin over the transit instrument was shining like the back of a seal.

"A seam," he said at last, "is better than a hole. I have always said so." He had never said so. She let it go. "Very well. We shall begin tonight, if there is any sky at all, and if there is none, we shall begin tomorrow."

She looked at the sheet of figures on the table. There were eleven weeks and two days. The offer from the institute would wait until spring, or it would not. For the first time since she had come up the road on the first of October, with a letter in her bag she could not bring herself to mention, Marit Oyelaran felt neither dread nor resentment. She felt something quieter and more difficult to name: the feeling of being, however briefly, exactly where she meant to be.

Somos el equipo de calidad de una cadena de ópticas y nos han pasado la especificación de la nueva aplicación de citas y pedidos de gafas. Necesito un plan de pruebas completo: casos de prueba concretos con pasos, datos de entrada y resultado esperado, agrupados por función, e incluye también las pruebas de límites, errores y seguridad que la especificación no menciona pero que deberíamos hacer.

ESPECIFICACIÓN DE PRODUCTO
Aplicación "VistaClara": citas, graduaciones y pedidos de gafas
Óptica Mirador, cadena de 23 tiendas
Versión 1.2 del documento, 5 de octubre de 2026
Responsable del producto: Fermín Salazar-Ochoa

1. Objetivo

VistaClara permite a los clientes de Óptica Mirador reservar cita para una revisión visual, consultar su graduación, encargar gafas y lentillas y seguir el estado del pedido. También permite al personal de las tiendas registrar la graduación después de una revisión, preparar el pedido y avisar al cliente. La aplicación existirá como página web adaptada a móviles y como aplicación para iOS y Android. Esta versión no incluye pagos de lentillas por suscripción, que se tratarán en la versión 2.

2. Usuarios y roles

2.1 Cliente: persona registrada con correo electrónico y contraseña. Puede ver sus citas, su graduación vigente y su historial de pedidos.
2.2 Óptico-optometrista: personal con titulación que realiza revisiones y registra graduaciones. Solo puede ver las citas de su tienda.
2.3 Dependiente: personal de tienda que prepara pedidos, gestiona la caja y atiende al cliente. No puede modificar graduaciones, pero sí verlas.
2.4 Responsable de tienda: puede ver los informes de su tienda y modificar horarios y bajas del personal.
2.5 Administrador central: gestiona catálogo, precios, promociones y las 23 tiendas.

3. Registro e inicio de sesión

3.1 El cliente se registra con nombre, apellidos, fecha de nacimiento, correo electrónico, teléfono móvil y contraseña. La contraseña debe tener al menos 10 caracteres, con una mayúscula, una minúscula y un número.
3.2 Tras el registro se envía un correo con un enlace de confirmación que caduca a las 48 horas. Sin confirmar el correo, el cliente no puede reservar citas.
3.3 Un menor de 14 años no puede registrarse. Entre 14 y 17 años, la cuenta exige el correo de un padre, madre o tutor, que debe aceptar un enlace antes de que se active.
3.4 Después de 5 intentos fallidos de inicio de sesión en 15 minutos, la cuenta se bloquea durante 30 minutos y se envía un aviso al correo del cliente.
3.5 La sesión caduca tras 20 minutos de inactividad en la web y tras 14 días en la aplicación móvil, salvo que el cliente cierre la sesión antes.
3.6 El personal inicia sesión con el usuario corporativo y un segundo factor mediante código de un solo uso. El código es válido durante 60 segundos.

4. Reserva de citas

4.1 El cliente elige tienda, tipo de cita y fecha. Los tipos de cita son: revisión visual completa (30 minutos), revisión para lentillas (45 minutos), ajuste de gafas (15 minutos) y revisión infantil (40 minutos, solo para menores de 14 años acompañados).
4.2 El sistema muestra únicamente los huecos libres. Un hueco está libre si hay al menos un óptico-optometrista disponible durante toda la duración de la cita y la sala de revisión está libre.
4.3 No se pueden reservar citas con menos de 2 horas de antelación ni con más de 60 días de antelación.
4.4 Un cliente puede tener como máximo 3 citas futuras al mismo tiempo, y solo una de cada tipo.
4.5 Al confirmar la cita se envía un correo y un mensaje de texto. Un recordatorio se envía 24 horas antes y otro 2 horas antes.
4.6 El cliente puede cambiar o cancelar su cita hasta 4 horas antes sin coste. Con menos de 4 horas, el cambio no está permitido en la aplicación y debe llamar a la tienda. Si un cliente no acude a dos citas seguidas sin avisar, la aplicación le pide que confirme por teléfono la siguiente.
4.7 Si el óptico-optometrista cae enfermo, la tienda puede reasignar las citas a otro profesional. Si no es posible, el sistema avisa a los clientes afectados y les propone los tres primeros huecos libres en esa tienda o en otra a menos de 10 kilómetros.
4.8 Para dos citas simultáneas en la misma tienda a la misma hora, la segunda reserva debe ser rechazada con el mensaje "El hueco acaba de ser ocupado, elija otro".

5. Graduación y ficha del cliente

5.1 Tras la revisión, el óptico-optometrista registra para cada ojo: esfera (de -20,00 a +20,00 dioptrías, pasos de 0,25), cilindro (de -8,00 a +8,00, pasos de 0,25), eje (de 0 a 180 grados, números enteros), adición (de 0,75 a 3,50, pasos de 0,25) y distancia pupilar (de 50 a 75 mm, en pasos de 0,5). La distancia pupilar se registra una sola vez para ambos ojos, y puede además registrarse por separado para cada ojo.
5.2 Si el cilindro es distinto de cero, el eje es obligatorio. Si el cilindro es cero, el eje debe estar vacío.
5.3 La graduación es válida durante 24 meses para adultos y 12 meses para menores de 18 años. Después de ese plazo, la aplicación la muestra como "caducada" y no permite encargar gafas graduadas ni lentillas con ella.
5.4 Una graduación firmada no puede modificarse. Si hay un error, el óptico-optometrista crea una nueva graduación que sustituye a la anterior, y la antigua queda en el historial marcada como "anulada" con el motivo.
5.5 El cliente puede ver su graduación y descargarla en PDF. El PDF incluye nombre, fecha, tienda, profesional y todos los valores, y un número de colegiado del profesional.
5.6 Los datos de salud son datos de categoría especial. Se almacenan cifrados, solo el personal de la tienda donde se hizo la revisión y el cliente pueden verlos, y cada consulta se registra con usuario, fecha y hora.

6. Pedidos de gafas

6.1 El cliente o el dependiente elige montura del catálogo, tipo de lente (monofocal, bifocal, progresiva), material (orgánico 1,50, orgánico 1,60, orgánico 1,67), tratamientos (antirreflejante, filtro de luz azul, endurecido, fotocromático) y color.
6.2 El sistema comprueba que el tipo de lente sea compatible con la graduación: una adición mayor que cero exige bifocal o progresiva, y una esfera con valor absoluto superior a 6,00 recomienda índice 1,60 o superior. Si el cliente elige un índice inferior, se muestra una advertencia y debe confirmar que lo ha entendido.
6.3 El precio se calcula sumando montura, lentes y tratamientos, menos la promoción vigente. Dos promociones no se pueden combinar, salvo la de socio (10 por ciento), que se aplica al final.
6.4 El pedido exige un anticipo del 30 por ciento en tienda o por pago con tarjeta en la aplicación. El pago con tarjeta lo gestiona un proveedor externo, y la aplicación no almacena números de tarjeta.
6.5 El plazo de entrega prometido es de 5 días laborables para lentes orgánicas 1,50 sin tratamientos especiales, de 8 días para el resto y de 12 días para progresivas con fotocromático.
6.6 Estados del pedido: recibido, en laboratorio, en montaje, listo para recoger, entregado y cancelado. Cada cambio de estado envía un mensaje al cliente. El estado "listo para recoger" envía además un recordatorio a los 7 días, y a los 30 días el sistema avisa a la tienda para decidir si se devuelve el stock.
6.7 El cliente puede cancelar un pedido hasta que pase a "en laboratorio" con devolución íntegra del anticipo. Después, el anticipo no se devuelve, pero se puede ceder a un nuevo pedido en los 60 días siguientes.
6.8 Si la montura elegida no tiene existencias en la tienda, el sistema la pide al almacén central, lo que añade 2 días laborables, e informa al cliente al confirmar el pedido.

7. Lentillas

7.1 El cliente puede encargar lentillas solo con una revisión para lentillas vigente (menos de 12 meses) y una graduación no caducada.
7.2 Las lentillas se piden por cajas. Una caja contiene 30 lentillas diarias, 6 mensuales o 2 quincenales, según el producto. El máximo por pedido es de 12 cajas.
7.3 Si el cliente intenta cambiar de marca o de curva base respecto a la ficha, el sistema bloquea el pedido y pide revisión con el profesional.
7.4 Las lentillas se envían a domicilio en 2 o 3 días laborables, o se recogen en tienda. El envío es gratuito a partir de 40 euros.

8. Informes

8.1 El responsable de tienda puede ver, por semana y por mes: citas reservadas, citas atendidas, ausencias, pedidos recibidos y entregados, y tiempo medio entre pedido y entrega.
8.2 El administrador central ve los mismos informes por tienda y para toda la cadena, y puede exportarlos a una hoja de cálculo.

9. Requisitos no funcionales

9.1 Las páginas principales deben cargarse en menos de 2 segundos con conexión 4G.
9.2 El sistema debe soportar 1.500 usuarios simultáneos, con picos los lunes por la mañana y los días de promoción.
9.3 La aplicación debe cumplir con la normativa de protección de datos, y permitir al cliente descargar o borrar sus datos. La baja se ejecuta en 30 días, salvo los datos que la ley obliga a conservar.
9.4 La web debe cumplir el nivel AA de accesibilidad, algo fundamental para un público con problemas de visión: tamaños de letra ajustables, buen contraste y compatibilidad con lectores de pantalla.
9.5 Disponibilidad objetivo del 99,5 por ciento mensual, con mantenimiento solo entre las 02:00 y las 05:00.

10. Notificaciones

10.1 Los mensajes se envían por correo y por mensaje de texto. El cliente puede desactivar los mensajes de promoción en su perfil, pero no los mensajes de citas, pedidos y seguridad.
10.2 Si el envío de un mensaje de texto falla (número no válido o sin cobertura), el sistema lo reintenta una vez a los 10 minutos y, si vuelve a fallar, lo envía por correo.
10.3 Los mensajes no pueden enviarse entre las 21:30 y las 08:00, salvo los códigos de verificación y los avisos de bloqueo de cuenta. Los mensajes retenidos se envían a las 08:00.
10.4 Cada mensaje incluye el nombre de la tienda, la fecha y hora de la cita o el número de pedido, y un enlace para gestionarlo. Los enlaces caducan a los 7 días y contienen un identificador que no revela datos personales.

11. Catálogo y precios

11.1 El administrador central da de alta cada montura con referencia, marca, material, medidas (ancho de lente, puente, varilla), color, precio y fotografías. Una montura sin al menos una fotografía no se muestra al cliente.
11.2 Los precios se guardan con dos decimales e incluyen el impuesto. Un cambio de precio entra en vigor a la hora indicada y no afecta a pedidos ya confirmados.
11.3 Las promociones tienen fecha de inicio y fin, tiendas a las que se aplican y un tope de unidades. Una promoción no puede crearse con la fecha de fin anterior a la de inicio, ni con un descuento superior al 50 por ciento sin la aprobación de un segundo administrador.
11.4 Las monturas que se retiran del catálogo desaparecen de las búsquedas, pero siguen visibles en los pedidos anteriores.
11.5 El stock de cada tienda se actualiza al recibir mercancía, al confirmar un pedido y al entregarlo. Si dos dependientes reservan la última unidad a la vez, solo una reserva se acepta.

12. Caja y entrega

12.1 Al entregar un pedido, el dependiente comprueba la identidad del cliente con el código que aparece en la aplicación o con el número de pedido y un documento de identidad.
12.2 La entrega exige cobrar el 70 por ciento restante. Se admite efectivo, tarjeta y vale de regalo. Si el cliente paga con vale, el importe del vale se descuenta y el resto se cobra por otro medio.
12.3 El sistema emite una factura numerada, sin saltos en la numeración, y la envía por correo. Una factura emitida no puede modificarse, solo rectificarse con una factura de abono.
12.4 El cliente dispone de 30 días desde la entrega para solicitar un ajuste gratuito de las gafas y de 60 días para reclamar si no se adapta a las lentes progresivas. En ese caso, el dependiente abre una incidencia, que la tienda debe resolver en 10 días.
12.5 Las gafas con una incidencia abierta no pueden marcarse como "entregado" hasta que la incidencia se cierre.

13. Integraciones

13.1 El laboratorio recibe los pedidos mediante un fichero que se genera cada hora, y devuelve los cambios de estado en otro fichero. Si un pedido aparece en el fichero del laboratorio con un número desconocido, se ignora y se registra el error.
13.2 El proveedor de pagos informa del resultado de cada cobro. Si el pago queda pendiente más de 15 minutos, el pedido se mantiene en "recibido" y se avisa al cliente de que no se ha completado el pago.
13.3 La aplicación se conecta con el sistema de contabilidad de la cadena una vez al día, a las 23:00, y envía un resumen de facturas y cobros por tienda. Si la conexión falla, el envío se repite durante tres noches seguidas y después se avisa al administrador.
